topics.title: Incremental Displacement table
topics.text: Incremental Displacement table An Incremental Displacement history table reports the stage-by-stage deformation of a structure. It tabulates the relative displacements between each construction stage, which can then be used in setting-out of structures built using sequential construction methods. In the Incremental Displacement table example shown below, the stage identified for each row is the ‘to’ loadcasse, with the previous row defining the ‘from’ loadcase for the increment. In the case of the first stage row, the displacement increment is ‘from’ the undeformed mesh. This is true even if particular loadcases are not specified for inclusion, as shown where Row 6 reports the displacement from Stage 2 to Stage 4. Associated nodes are considered active (and therefore valid for inclusion) if they are active in either of the ‘from’ or ‘to’ loadcase stages. Notes applicable to all tables The first two rows of each table always show the ID of the selected point and the ID of the implied node that the column refers to. The first column of each table contains the Loadcase ID of the loadcase used to form the stage, followed by the name of the loadcase. If an analysis has a time component (as it does for the example tables shown) an additional Time column will be prepended to the start of the displacement column data. This will be left blank if an analysis has selected loadcases without a time component. Where the table is not limited to displacements in the vertical axis direction an additional header row will be included where axes labels related to the global direction of displacement for that column. Table values are reported in model units, with the exception of any time-based values. Fixed column and row headings (duplicating the information inside the first column and row) are provided for assistance when viewing and scrolling large amounts of data in LUSAS, or when copied to a spreadsheet for third-party graphing purposes. See also: Construction tables Construction tables

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview The Crack Width calculation facility is accessed using the Bridge / Civil> Crack Widths to EN 1992-1-1 menu item. This is provided in selected Bridge and Civil & Structural software products only. It enables plotting of contours of design crack widths in accordance with the EN 1992-1-1 design code. The calculations carried out are for reinforced concrete structures that are modelled using the Smoothed Multi Crack Concrete Model, that have steel reinforcement modelled with reinforcement attributes, using a linear steel material model. See Crack Width Calculation Methods Available Crack Width Calculation Methods Available for other crack width calculation options.

topics.title: Crack width parameters : Coefficients to be stated

headings: Crack width parameters : Coefficients to be stated
topics.text: Crack width parameters : Coefficients to be stated Coefficient for load duration (kt) a factor dependent on the load duration, (EN 1991-1-1:2004 equation 7.9) Coefficient for bond properties (k1) takes account of the bond properties of the bonded reinforcement, (EN 1991-1-1:2004 equation 7.11) Coefficient for strain distribution (k2) takes account of the distribution of strain, (EN 1991-1-1:2004 equation 7.11) Coefficient for cover influence (k3) Coefficient controlling the influence of cover on crack spacing. (EN 1991-1-1:2004 equation 7.11). In clause 7.3.4(3), k 3 is an NDP. It requires special treatment for some nations and is taken to be of the form: where generally k 3B ≥0 and k 3C ≤0. For most nations, k 3A =3.4, k 3B =0 and k 3C =0, but defaults are set as appropriate to the National Annex. This equation accommodates the requirements of the two national annexes that account for cover and bar diameter. Coefficient for bar diameter (k4) controls the influence of bar diameter on crack spacing, (EN 1991-1-1:2004 equation 7.11) Note that the distribution of strain is considered to be accounted for in the nonlinear concrete model and therefore it is recommended that k2=1.0

topics.title: Additional options
topics.text: Additional options Include effective concrete area checks The effective depth of concrete is limited by EN 1991-1-1 to less than or equal to half the beam depth or to one third of the depth minus the neutral axis. Due to the nature of the analysis the location of the neutral axis is unknown and therefore this check cannot be carried out. The option to limit the effective concrete height to half the section height is provided and for this the section height must be entered manually. The default approach to neglect the check is considered conservative. Display summary on screen The option to display a summary of crack width information is provided. Ignore thermal bar strains In coupled (Structural and Thermal) analyses steel strains include both temperature and mechanical strains. In calculating the crack widths it is generally only the mechanical strains that are of interest. The option to ignore thermal strains should therefore be used in coupled analyses when crack widths are to be calculated based on the mechanical steel strains only. Calculate crack widths for strains less than the concrete limit It is assumed that cracking only occurs when the tensile strain limit of the concrete is exceeded. This assumption can be overridden and theoretical crack widths calculated for concrete strains less that the theoretical cracking strain by selecting this option
topics.search_text: Additional options Crack Width Calculation to EN 1992-1-1 Application Manual (Bridge, Civil and Structural) Crack Width Calculation to EN 1992-1-1 Overview Using the Crack Width Calculator Additional options Bridge Crack Widths idh crack widths.htm Additional options Include effective concrete area checks The effective depth of concrete is limited by EN 1991-1-1 to less than or equal to half the beam depth or to one third of the depth minus the neutral axis. Due to the nature of the analysis the location of the neutral axis is unknown and therefore this check cannot be carried out. The option to limit the effective concrete height to half the section height is provided and for this the section height must be entered manually. The default approach to neglect the check is considered conservative. Display summary on screen The option to display a summary of crack width information is provided. Ignore thermal bar strains In coupled (Structural and Thermal) analyses steel strains include both temperature and mechanical strains. In calculating the crack widths it is generally only the mechanical strains that are of interest. The option to ignore thermal strains should therefore be used in coupled analyses when crack widths are to be calculated based on the mechanical steel strains only. Calculate crack widths for strains less than the concrete limit It is assumed that cracking only occurs when the tensile strain limit of the concrete is exceeded. This assumption can be overridden and theoretical crack widths calculated for concrete strains less that the theoretical cracking strain by selecting this option

topics.title: Results displayed
topics.text: Results displayed Crack width contours are plotted along the bar elements (actually on the surface of the fleshed bar section) corresponding to the steel strains used in the calculation, and not on any concrete face or surface in the model. They are plotted for an active loadcase (or combination) and are re-computed if a different loadcase is set active. This visualisation method is used because the approach to calculating crack widths in EN 1991-1-1:2009 is generally unclear as to where the crack width calculation applies. Crack width information can be plotted for the Contour and Values layers as components of Maximum Crack Width under the Crack Widths EN1991-1 entity. These settings are automatically made when the Crack Width calculation facility is used. A Crack Widths Control dialog provides an easy means of returning to and changing the crack width calculation parameters used. A typical crack width contour plot for a 2D plane strain model is shown below. Notes All calculations are based upon EN1992-1-1 clause 7.3.4. Crack width calculation to EN1991-1-1 can only be carried out using this utility when a nonlinear concrete material, that has a concrete tensile strength, such as Smoothed Multi Crack Concrete Model, is used, bar reinforcement is modelled with reinforcement attributes reinforcement attributes , and a linear steel material model is used to represent the steel reinforcement. This is because of the steel strains used in the calculations. Crack width calculation relies on attributes being assigned to geometry and available during calculation so the menu item is disabled and not available when only a results file is loaded. If reinforcement attribute values are changed the model must be re-solved prior to running the Crack Width calculation facility. See also: Reinforcement Attributes Reinforcement Attributes Crack Width Calculation Methods Available Crack Width Calculation Methods Available

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview The grillage wizard is available for use with Bridge and Civil software products only. It is accessed from the Bridge > Grillage wizard menu item and comprises a series of dialogs that enable orthogonal, skewed and curved grillages to be generated from user-defined data. When creating a grillage model some basic guidelines should be considered:- Grillage wizard models are created with one line mesh division for each grillage element. Additional line mesh attributes can be created and assigned to the model should this ever prove to be required. Longitudinal grillage members should be placed along lines of design strength. For a slab model this could be where there was a concentration of reinforcement in the slab itself. For a composite bridge this could be at the location of a steel girder / prestress beam. The aspect ratio between the length of the transverse and longitudinal members should be set so that a good static distribution of loading is achieved. An aspect ratio of 1 to 1 is normally used but an aspect ratio of up to 1 to 3 is acceptable. Whenever possible it is recommended that a grillage model should have supports located at the intersection of longitudinal and transverse members. The grillage wizard automatically places rigid supports onto the model at bearing locations. These supports can be overwritten with new attributes of, say, an elastomeric bearing using a spring support. The supports should be chosen to as closely represent the actual structure as possible. If the results from a coarse grillage are in doubt for any reason a more refined grillage should be used to check the results.

topics.title: Grillage Wizard : Step 1 - Grillage Type
topics.text: Grillage Wizard : Step 1 - Grillage Type Select the type of grillage model that you require. Both slab deck and spaced beam with slab deck constructions are supported and cracked section may be included. Spaced beam and slab deck models will automatically have elements defined for the allocation of cracked properties. By default 15% of the span (over internal supports) will be assumed to be cracked but this value can be modified if required. The wizard accounts for multiple spans and applies support conditions. Groups of members are created in the Groups Treeview to enable geometric and material properties to be easily assigned.

topics.text: Grillage Wizard : Step 2 - Straight or Curved Deck Select whether a straight grillage or curved grillage is required. For a straight grillage a skew angle can be set. For a curved grillage a radius of curvature needs to be entered. For a straight grillage if any angle other than zero is entered, when the Next button is selected a dialog allowing a skewed or orthogonal transverse beam arrangement will be shown.

topics.text: Grillage Wizard : Step 2a - Skewed or Orthogonal Beams If an angle has been entered for a straight grillage the geometry can be formed from skewed grillage elements or orthogonal grillage elements. If the skew angle is above 20 degrees then an orthogonal arrangement is recommended.

topics.text: Grillage Wizard : Step 3 - Longitudinal Beam Detail The width of the grillage and the number of longitudinal beams can be set on this dialog. The longitudinal beams can be evenly spaced or a user defined spacing can be specified.

topics.title: Software Products Covered
topics.text: Software Products Covered This manual covers application-specific modelling, analysis, results and design checking facilities for LUSAS Bridge and LUSAS Civil & Structural software products. Menu entries for these application products are inserted onto the main menu based upon the software key you have installed on your system or, if you are using LUSAS Academic software, by the selection of a software product during the set-up procedure. Some facilities for LUSAS Bridge and LUSAS Civil & Structural software products may also appear on the general LUSAS Modeller menu. This manual describes the options available for the following menu items: Bridge Civil Design More detailed on-line help information on each of the application specific features described can be accessed from the Help button on the relevant dialog. Separate manuals describe the capabilities of the LNG Tank Analysis and Design System LNG Tank Analysis and Design System .

It provides access to the following bridge engineering specific facilities, according to the software product in use: Grillage Wizard Grillage Wizard - Enables orthogonal, skewed and curved grillages to be generated from user-defined data. Masonry Bridge Wizard Masonry Bridge Wizard - Generates 2D and 3D models of single and multi-span masonry arch bridges, including piers and abutments, with or without a skew. Bridge Loading Bridge Loading - Gravity, Surface loading, and Static vehicle loads Moving Load Moving Load - Used to track the path of a static vehicle load (or a set of vehicles) across a structure Temperature profiles Temperature profiles - Temperature profile loading to the requirements of a specified design code Shrinkage strains Shrinkage strains - Shrinkage profile loading to the requirements of a specified design code Pedestrian loading wizard Pedestrian loading wizard - Used to generate the vertical pedestrian loading to supported design codes. Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation - Identifies the most onerous train loading arrangement for pre-defined track layouts for a supported design code. The Export to Composite Deck Design option and the menu item will appear greyed-out if not available.

topics.text: Making manual modifications to the model created by the wizard Bridge models created by the masonry bridge wizard can be manually modified within LUSAS Modeller. Examples of modifications that may be required include: Defining abutment and pier foundations and subsequent re-positioning / re-defining any relevant spring supports. Defining reference paths reference paths to carry out a moving load analysis moving load analysis . Defining tracks and train loading to design codes using the rail load optimisation rail load optimisation facility. Defining carriageways and vehicle loading to design codes using the vehicle load optimisation vehicle load optimisation facility. Note that if a nonlinear model has been created by the Masonry Bridge Wizard, copying the base analysis and converting it to use linear materials will allow influence attributes to be added and Traffic Load Optimisation or Rail Load Optimisation to be modelled. See also: Solve the model Solve the model

topics.title: Analysis type
topics.text: Analysis type Select either 2D Analysis or 3D Analysis If '2D Analysis' is selected, the width to be considered for a 2D model can be defined to be automatically calculated, or a user-defined parameter stated. If the 'Auto (Railway)' radio button is selected, a transverse distribution of the train loads is considered at 40 degrees under the sleepers until the lateral extent of the arches is reached, the width is then calculated according to the relationship: 2D model width = s + 2*tan (adiff ) * Hr where s = Track gauge = 1.435m adiff = 40° (diffusion angle). Hr = min(hfi+tcri/2) for i=1….number of spans.

topics.title: Constant details
topics.text: Constant details The values entered in the upper grid are constant along the length of the bridge. The values required are: Bridge width, wbr - The real width of the bridge used for 3D analysis or the width used in 2D model if the 'User defined' radio button is selected. External Spandrel wall thickness, tsw - Self-explanatory. The parapet thickness is assumed to be the same value Parapet height, hp - Self-explanatory. Skew angle (anti-clockwise) (For 3D models only) - A positive skew angle gives an anti-clockwise skew in plan with respect to the Y axis. Skewing the bridge model in the plan view retains all Y coordinates and only modifies the corresponding values in X, such that the distance between arch springing points measured along the face of the arch is retained. Plan view showing skew operation performed on an illustrative model

topics.title: Abutment details
topics.text: Abutment details Geometric data for the left and right abutments can be specified separately in the lower grid. This data is used in the definition of 2D and 3D linear and nonlinear models. Note that data entered for one abutment can be copied and pasted for another by using the Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V keys. The values required are: Height, ha - Height of abutment to arch springing. Wall thickness at base, tab - Self-explanatory.. Wall thickness at springing, tas - Must be less than or equal to the wall thickness at base. Side face batter q at - Angle in degrees. Depth below ground level, hag - Amount of face of abutment beneath ground level. When changing data present in this and other dialogs the Apply button should be pressed to save the changes prior to creating a model.

topics.title: Notes
topics.text: Notes The abutment can be modelled with a variable section along its height from the base to the springing of the arch. Transversely, the abutment has a width at the springing assumed to be the same as the width of the bridge 'wbr' and a width at the base which is equal to wbr + 2*ha*tan( q at) In a 2D analysis even if a non-zero side batter is defined, the width of the abutment remains constant and equal to the "2D model width" defined above, for simplicity. Supports are modelled by distributed springs (defined on the Modelling Modelling tab) that are applied along the lines (2D models) or surfaces (3D models) of the soil-structure interface. The horizontal springs are placed at full height behind the abutment, whilst towards the bridge they are placed up to a height of 'hag' representing the average height of the underground part. The corresponding attribute is assigned to the single line/surface defining the whole height of the abutment (ha) and a Function Limit of Ymax truncates the springs by utilising a value of zero above 'hag'. The abutment and pier foundations are not explicitly modelled by the wizard. The vertical support they provide is modelled by spring supports. If required, foundations can be added to the model after it has been generated, and spring supports moved accordingly. See also: Model data : Model data : Span data Span data

topics.title: Model data: Loading
topics.text: Model data: Loading The Loading tab is used to define values related to self-weight and/or traffic loads.
topics.search_text: Model data: Loading Model data: Loading Application Manual (Bridge, Civil and Structural) Masonry Bridge Wizard Defining a masonry bridge model Model data: Loading Bridge Masony Bridge Wizard model data loading.htm Model data: Loading The Loading tab is used to define values related to self-weight and/or traffic loads.

topics.title: Self weight and traffic loading
topics.text: Self weight and traffic loading The Self-weight and Traffic loads check boxes activate or deactivate the relevant parts of the dialog to allow permanent or traffic actions to be defined. If neither the 'Self weight' or 'Traffic Loads' check boxes are selected, models will be generated without any self-weight or traffic loading being assigned. In this case, only two empty loadcases will be created in the Analyses Treeview, namely 'Loadcase 1' in the 'Linear_Analysis' entry and 'Loadcase 2' in the 'Nonlinear_Analysis' entry. If only the 'Self weight' check box is selected a model will be generated without any traffic loads. In this case, two loadcases will be created in the Analyses Treeview, namely: 'Self Weight' in the 'Linear_Analysis' entry and 'Self Weight nonlinear' in the 'Nonlinear_Analysis' entry. In the left-hand grid, the following parameters are required: Number of tracks/lanes - The number of tracks/lanes on the bridge is limited to a maximum of 2. They are centred transversely with respect to the bridge with the spacing for two tracks or lanes specified by the user. Track/lane spacing - The distance between the nominal centrelines of two tracks/lanes. When created, track/lane 1 will have a higher Y coordinate than track/lane 2. Partial factor on permanent loads/traffic loads - Used only for nonlinear analysis (2D and 3D). For linear analysis, the wizard generates the model with nominal (unfactored) loading which, must then be combined according to requirements. Dynamic coefficient - This is applied to traffic loads for linear and nonlinear analysis.

topics.title: Track/lane information
topics.text: Track/lane information In the right-hand grid, the data needed to identify and position traffic loads may be entered on the tabs named Track/Lane 1 and Track/Lane 2 (if the number of tracks/lanes stated was 2). Each row of the grid will generate one or more load cases and requires the following parameters: Vehicle - Discrete loads previously defined with LUSAS Modeller will be available for selection from the droplist in this cell. New loading types can be specified within the wizard by selecting the ' New... ' droplist option. Moving - This check box, when ticked, provides access to the moving load settings Move load along path in equal divisions or Move load by incremental distance along path where selection of either will generate as many load conditions as the number of defined positions. Location – The specific X distance in the global coordinate system, that has the origin to the outer edge of the left abutment. This field is disabled if the 'Moving' check box is ticked.. Nonlinear analysis – When checked, this check box includes loadcases in the nonlinear analysis as well as the linear analysis. Unchecked, loadcases are only included in linear analysis. Add , Delete and Import from Library buttons provide the means to manually edit or otherwise populate the grid. Any previously defined discrete point, patch or compound loads defined for the model are available for selection from the dropdown list of the Vehicle column. If no discrete loads have been defined before running the wizard, it is possible to define one by choosing the 'New (Loading…)' item from the droplist. If chosen, the general Structural Loading dialog will be displayed to allow definition of a discrete point, patch or compound load. The Masonry Bridge Wizard can be saved at any time, with incomplete data, by pressing the OK button, and a discrete load generated using the Bridge > Loading menu, if required.

topics.title: Loading example
topics.text: Loading example The Analyses Treeview that follows shows an example of the load conditions generated by the wizard for the supplied illustrative example bridge and for a 3D analysis where the terms in brackets represent multiplication factors of the load or "load factoring." The self weight loadcases are multiplied by a factor of 1.35 in the 'Nonlinear_Analysis' entry and a factor of 1.0 in the 'Linear_Analysis' entry. The traffic load, which is present only in the 'Nonlinear_Analysis' entry is multiplied by a factor of (1.15 x 1.45) = 1.6675 (where the factor of 1.15 is the dynamic coefficient and 1.45 is the combination factor for ULS, as defined during the input phase).

topics.title: Nonlinear analysis control settings explained
topics.text: Nonlinear analysis control settings explained The Nonlinear and Transient settings dialog shows that self weight is applied using Automatic incrementation, controlled by the following parameters: Starting load factor : 0.05 Max change in load factor : 0.2 Max total load factor : 1.00 The use of a 'Max change in load factor' of 0.2 is a compromise between accuracy and speed of solution. No arc length incrementation procedure is in use. Fine integration for stiffness and masses is in use. The solution strategy is characterised by the following values: Max number of iterations : 12 Residual force norm : 0.1 Incremental displacement norm : 0 Displacement norm : 0.1 The same loading is then frozen with a 'Manual' increment in the next loadcase, named 'Freeze'. The subsequent loadcase or loadcases that are created for traffic loads have 'Automatic' incrementation, with following parameters: Starting load factor : 0.1 Max change in load factor : 0.2 Max total load factor : 5.00 The same solution strategy is used as for the dead load in loadcase 1. If the analysis reaches the 'Max total load factor' of 5.00, this factor must be increased in order to obtain the ultimate load factor.

topics.title: Materials
topics.text: Materials For the structural components listed below, the material to be used for linear and nonlinear analysis must be specified using the droplists provided. Arch barrel Piers and Abutments Backing Arch fill Spandrel wall Pier core Any materials defined for the model prior to running the wizard will be available for selection in the droplists. Only linear materials are available in the 'Materials Linear Analysis' cells. It is possible to define a new material from this dialog by choosing the 'New' option from the droplist. This provides the following options: New (Elastic)... - Selecting this displays the LUSAS isotropic material dialog. New (Concrete)... - Selecting this displays the LUSAS nonlinear concrete material dialog. Although the dialog defaults to a Eurocode creep and shrinkage material (model 86), the example bridge uses the cracking and crushing concrete material (model 109) without creep or shrinkage, which has been found to provide acceptable results as an approximation to masonry when used with suitable values.

topics.title: Notes
topics.text: Notes For a 2D analysis, the spandrel walls and pier fill materials are not modelled, giving conservative results. The wizard is set up to offer the LUSAS smoothed multi-crack concrete material (Model 109) to represent masonry. This model is a plastic-damage-contact model in which damage planes form according to a principal stress criterion and then develop as embedded rough contact planes. The use of the concrete cracking and crushing material to represent masonry in a "macro modelling" approach requires the acceptance of some approximations. It should be noted that masonry typically exhibits some degree of orthotropy, which is overlooked when using the concrete model. The compressive strength of masonry, as a composite material, depends upon factors including the elastic properties of the units and the mortar and the tensile strength of the units, as is widely documented. It should also be noted that the compressive strength used in the concrete cracking and crushing material relates to a cylinder strength, which is not directly comparable to masonry strengths which might be used for mechanism methods or in codified equations for masonry. Typically compressive strength in a cylinder sample is lower than that in a wallette or "prism" (as in a cube test), due to containing stresses arising from friction on the plates of the testing apparatus. Ideally values would be derived from tests pertinent to the structure in question. Masonry mechanical parameters E, F cm and Mass density are very dependent upon the type of bricks, the type of mortar, the thickness of mortar, and the transverse connection of bricks. References can be found, for example, in "UIC Code 778-3, Recommendations for the inspection, assessment and maintenance of masonry arch bridges" and in other National Codes of Practice with values dependent on local materials. Typical values for materials used in masonry arches tend to be of the order: E is in the range from 1 to 5 E6 kN/m 2 F cm is in the range from 1000 to 10000 kN/ m 2 Mass density is in the range 1.4 to 2.3 t/m3 (including values for fill) The tensile strength of masonry is difficult to assess, being dependent upon the surface texture, water absorption and moisture content of the units; composition, additives, sand grading, air content and water retention of the mortar and environmental factors at the time of construction e.g. dust, temperature, humidity, workmanship and curing conditions. Use of a tensile strength of zero will lead to numerical difficulties. Ideally values would be derived from tests pertinent to the structure in question. In the absence of such test results, recourse to literature e.g. tests by Pluijm (1992) may be helpful in determining values for both tensile strength and fracture energy per unit area. Experience correlating analyses with bridge data in the past suggests that the following values may be a suitable starting point, and so are presented as default values in the 'Example Bridge' and 'Example Material' data: F td = F cd /30 G = 0.1 kJ/m 2 Setting a value of F t = F cd /30 has been found to assist convergence of the nonlinear analysis, while having relatively little effect upon the ultimate strength of the bridge determined from the analysis. The relatively higher value of G = 0.1 kJ/m 2 (a value more consistent with concrete rather than with masonry) has been found, likewise, to assist convergence while having little effect upon any bridge capacity determined. A graphical representation of the stress-strain curve (taken from the LUSAS Theory Manual) is shown below. Reference material characteristics

It should be noted that masonry typically exhibits some degree of orthotropy, which is overlooked when using the concrete model. The compressive strength of masonry, as a composite material, depends upon factors including the elastic properties of the units and the mortar and the tensile strength of the units, as is widely documented. It should also be noted that the compressive strength used in the concrete cracking and crushing material relates to a cylinder strength, which is not directly comparable to masonry strengths which might be used for mechanism methods or in codified equations for masonry. Typically compressive strength in a cylinder sample is lower than that in a wallette or "prism" (as in a cube test), due to containing stresses arising from friction on the plates of the testing apparatus. Ideally values would be derived from tests pertinent to the structure in question. Masonry mechanical parameters E, F cm and Mass density are very dependent upon the type of bricks, the type of mortar, the thickness of mortar, and the transverse connection of bricks. References can be found, for example, in "UIC Code 778-3, Recommendations for the inspection, assessment and maintenance of masonry arch bridges" and in other National Codes of Practice with values dependent on local materials. Typical values for materials used in masonry arches tend to be of the order: E is in the range from 1 to 5 E6 kN/m 2 F cm is in the range from 1000 to 10000 kN/ m 2 Mass density is in the range 1.4 to 2.3 t/m3 (including values for fill) The tensile strength of masonry is difficult to assess, being dependent upon the surface texture, water absorption and moisture content of the units; composition, additives, sand grading, air content and water retention of the mortar and environmental factors at the time of construction e.g. dust, temperature, humidity, workmanship and curing conditions. Use of a tensile strength of zero will lead to numerical difficulties. Ideally values would be derived from tests pertinent to the structure in question. In the absence of such test results, recourse to literature e.g. tests by Pluijm (1992) may be helpful in determining values for both tensile strength and fracture energy per unit area. Experience correlating analyses with bridge data in the past suggests that the following values may be a suitable starting point, and so are presented as default values in the 'Example Bridge' and 'Example Material' data: F td = F cd /30 G = 0.1 kJ/m 2 Setting a value of F t = F cd /30 has been found to assist convergence of the nonlinear analysis, while having relatively little effect upon the ultimate strength of the bridge determined from the analysis. The relatively higher value of G = 0.1 kJ/m 2 (a value more consistent with concrete rather than with masonry) has been found, likewise, to assist convergence while having little effect upon any bridge capacity determined. topics.text: Supports The required parameters to be entered for the abutments and piers are the following: Fixed base vertical support - Defines if vertical supports are fixed. That is, rigid rather than sprung. Vertical Winkler coefficient - Defines the stiffness of the vertical springs on the horizontal underside of abutments and piers. Horizontal Winkler coefficient - Defines the stiffness of the horizontal springs on the vertical faces of abutment and piers

topics.title: Notes
topics.text: Notes Spring supports are modelled by distributed springs applied along the lines (2D models) or surfaces (3D models) of the soil-structure interface. In the abutments the horizontal springs are placed at full height behind the abutment. Between piers and abutments they are placed up to a height of 'hag' as defined on the Bridge data tab. The corresponding attribute is assigned to the single line/surface defining the whole height of the abutment and a Function Limit of Ymax limits the effective presence of values different from zero in the definition of the stiffness variation. In the piers the horizontal springs are placed up to a height 'hpg' (defined on the Span data Span data tab) representing the average height of the underground part. The relevant attribute is assigned to the single line/surface defining the whole height of the pier (hp) and a Function Limit of Ymax truncates the springs by utilising a value of zero above 'hpg'. The foundations are not explicitly modelled by the wizard. If required, foundations can be added to the model after it has been generated, and the supports applied by the wizard de-assigned and re-assigned accordingly. Typically, with hollow piers, adding foundations to the model in this way is recommended. Some engineers prefer to neglect the stiffness of soil backfill and the consequent load-spreading effect, and its contribution to stability by way of lateral earth pressures. This can be achieved by entering very low elastic modulus values, and this is the approach adopted in the model that is created when using the 'Example bridge' button. While this can be useful, it is noted that the use of very small stiffnesses can lead to large deformations in the fill which may be misleading. They may also give rise to unexpected differences between a 2D and 3D representation of the same bridge, with the soft soil being "snagged" on the spandrel walls in the 3D model. They can also lead to convergence difficulties if other parts of the model are nonlinear. See also: Model data: Model data: Loading Loading

Spandrels are typically added as pairs of walls, spaced to match a relevant track gauge in use. The parameters to be entered are self-explanatory and should be defined with reference to the associated image on the dialog. Internal spandrels - This check box permits modelling of internal spandrel walls. Number of pairs of internal spandrels A value of 1 or 2 is permitted. Wall thickness, tisw Thickness of each spandrel wall. Gauge distance for each pair, dp - Measured from centreline to centreline of each pair of spandrel walls. Centre to centre distance between pairs, dpc - Measured between the nominal centreline of each pair of spandrel walls Depth from top level, dtl – The depth from top surface of the fill to top of spandrels.

topics.title: Span dimensions
topics.text: Span dimensions Span length, ls The distance between arch springing points measured along the face of the arch (whether it is skewed or not). Arch rise, hr The vertical distance to the soffit of the arch measured from the arch springing point. Crown thickness, tcr The thickness of the arch barrel at this location. Thickness at springing, tsp The thickness of the arch barrel at this location. Backing depth, hh This is measured from the springing at the intrados, to the top of the backing, which is taken to be the same value on both sides of each arch. Overall depth, hr + tcr +hf The distance between the running surface of the fill and the arch springing point. This parameter is required for the first span only, and defines the level of the running surface of the fill, which is taken to be constant for the length of the bridge. As shown, it is possible to input a different arch thickness at the crown section (tcr) to the thickness at the springing section (tsp).

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview Whilst masonry arch bridges may be modelled manually within LUSAS, masonry bridges with semi-circular or segmental arches may be modelled more easily and quickly using the Masonry Bridge Wizard. The Masonry Bridge Wizard generates 2D and 3D continuum models of single and multi-span masonry arch bridges, including piers and abutments, with or without a skew, using linear or nonlinear materials. Models are defined using a series of tabbed pages on which geometric values, material properties, any skew and optional train loading are defined. Any consistent set of units can be used, with the dialog cells showing the expected units. Model data is saved as a utility entry within the Utilities Treeview. When a model is generated, common features are grouped together and added to the Groups Treeview to allow for easy manipulation of the model, or selective viewing of results after it has been solved. Models created may be further edited using general facilities within Modeller. The continuum models produced by the Masonry Bridge Wizard are for "macro modelling" of masonry, where the masonry is considered as a continuous composite material - as opposed to "micro modelling" where each block and each mortar joint is modelled explicitly. Micro modelling is rarely very pragmatic for civil structures like bridges, in consideration of the large amount of input required, processing time and the volume of output created. The concrete cracking and crushing material may be used to approximate the cracking and crushing behaviour of masonry.

topics.title: Data for an illustrative example
topics.text: Data for an illustrative example Pressing the Example bridge button on the bottom of the dialog populates the wizard dialog with values for an illustrative 3-span masonry arch bridge, and additionally imports material attributes and a train load (2D or 3D), depending on the Analysis type chosen in the 'Bridge data' tab. Pressing the Example material button on the bottom of the dialog populates the Attributes Treeview only with a selection of masonry and fill materials.

topics.text: Generating a masonry bridge wizard model Once all required data has been defined, a model can be generated by using the Bridge > Masonry Bridge Wizard > Generate bridge menu item, or by selecting the Generate defined bridge option from the context menu of the MBW data entry in the Utilities Treeview. The wizard will always create two analyses in the Analyses Treeview; one linear and one nonlinear - named 'Linear_Analysis' and 'Nonlinear_Analysis' respectively.

topics.text: Notes Once a model has been created from the masonry bridge wizard model data, that model data may no longer be edited within the wizard. If generation of a model fails, or is not as expected, the File > Import / Export Model data facility may be used to save the entered data to a library for re-use and editing when defining a new model. The masonry bridge model data utility may be renamed prior to saving to a library, to prevent overwriting of any existing library utility of the same name.

headings: Exporting and importing masonry bridge wizard data
topics.text: Exporting and importing masonry bridge wizard data To create a new masonry bridge based upon the masonry bridge wizard data already entered for a saved model, use the File > Import / Export Model Data menu item and the 'Export from model to library' option to export from that model the utility MBW Data, the material attributes and the Traffic load, into the library. Masonry bridge model data that was saved to a library may be imported by using the File > Import / Export Model Data menu item and the 'Import from library to model' option. This creates a Masonry Bridge Wizard utility within the Utilities Treeview. To make any changes to this data, use the context menu for this entry and select the 'Edit...' option.

topics.title: Viewing results
topics.text: Viewing results Results can be viewed as contours of principal stress, vector plots and, when nonlinear analysis is carried out, as cracking and crushing patterns, capacity curves, and graphs of a nodal displacement versus Total Load Factor (TLF). By showing results only on selected groups, the effect on particular aspects of the model can be easily visualised. topics.title: Notes
topics.text: Notes The results available after solution include all those increments which converged (whether the target load factor was reached or not). This allows the examination of the deformations, strains and cracks as they develop with the incrementation of the load. In many cases, including the example bridge included in the wizard, convergence failure corresponds to the formation of a mechanism, and so can be correlated to a possible physical collapse. However other criterion should be considered by the engineer when assessing a failure load, or indeed a safe load level, such as the strain in the masonry (usually a maximum in the arch barrel), which might be best limited to 0.35%, for example. Such considerations must be made on a project-by-project basis and may refer to bridge-specific test data See also: Masonry Bridge Wizard Masonry Bridge Wizard

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview The moving load generator is accessed from the Bridge> Moving Load... menu item. It is used to track the path of a vehicle (or a set of vehicles) across a structure by automatically setting up a number of static loadcases at prescribed locations along a selected line. These loadcases produced can then be enveloped to provide the maximum effect of the vehicle passing over the structure. Prior to using the moving load generator a slab or grillage model that will allow the application of discrete loads must have been created. Ensure that the discrete load group representing the vehicle to be moved across the structure has been defined in the Treeview and that a line representing the vehicle path across the structure has been defined and selected. The line representing the vehicle path should not be one of the lines forming the model. If a combined line is selected then the generator will use the points joining the lines within the combined line as the locations for the application of the vehicle loads. For straight lines or arcs the generator will split the selected line representing the vehicle path into a number of segments and create a loadcase for the vehicle in each load position. Only the first line within the selection will be processed. Moving vehicle load Select the pre-defined vehicle load to be moved along the line Search area Search area can used to restrict the area of application of point and patch loads to pre-defined part of the model. Generally, for grillage models, a search area is not required. Project over area needs to selected if the vehicle load is to be applied to a grillage or slab model (3D) Project onto line needs to be selected if the load is to be applied to a line beam model (2D) Starting loadcase number can be set to whatever loadcase number is required but by default will be set to be the next free loadcase number. Vehicle path options define whether the vehicle is to be moved across the structure by a equal number of divisions or by an incremental distance of the line representing the vehicle path. Vehicle direction allows for forward (defined by the geometric line direction) and reverse passing of the loading.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview A LUSAS model that is used to determine natural frequencies for the simple criterion in EN1990 clause A2.4.3.2(2) can be easily updated to include dynamic actions. Nonlinear behaviour (such as tensioning-stiffening associated with the use of cables) can also be incorporated. The LUSAS pedestrian load wizard creates the necessary moving and varying-magnitude load, based on input such as the recommended Bridge class (NA to EN1991-2, Table NA.7). Its use: Simplifies and automates pedestrian load generation Generates all loadcases to model the passage of pedestrian groups Provides results that can be printed, exported to spreadsheets, or graphed Pedestrian types (walking or joging/running) control the reference load and speed of the moving pulsating load representing the pedestrian or pedestrian group. Both forward and reverse moving loading is possible. Graphs of loading can be automatically created, and results can be printed and exported to spreadsheets or graphed using standard graphing facilities to assess, for example, the acceleration or displacement at a selected node against time.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview Modelling of prestress loading is available for selected LUSAS Bridge and LUSAS Civil & Structural software products only. To model prestress loading requires the following: Definition of tendon profiles Definition of tendon profiles either manually, copied and pasted from a spreadsheet, or generated by selecting lines, arcs or splines that are defined or imported into LUSAS Modeller. Definition of tendon properties Definition of tendon properties in accordance with a chosen design code. Definition of tendon loading Definition of tendon loading which associates a prestress force and associated jacking and slip (anchorage set) details with a particular tendon profile and tendon property. Assignment of tendon loading attributes Assignment of tendon loading attributes to selected features and loadcases in a model. Tendons are typically installed sequentially as part of a construction stage analysis, in which case the tendon loading should be assigned to the range of loadcases in which they persist, which is normally from the installation stage to the final stage of the analysis, and not to each loadcase individually in this situation. Solving the model Solving the model for the prestress loading applied.

topics.title: Modelling time dependent effects
topics.text: Modelling time dependent effects If time dependent effects at every stage of construction are to be evaluated, certain tasks need to be carried out prior to solving a model to calculate prestress loading. These are: The concrete material used must include the parameters required to determine creep and shrinkage for the calculation of losses for any of the Codes of Practice for which LUSAS supports time dependent loss calculations - by one of the following means: Material library (Advanced define) Material library (Advanced define) Such a material is linear elastic and so does not display actual creep and shrinkage deformations, it merely enables the calculation of suitable tendon losses. This can be misleading but may be an acceptable approximation for some purposes. Concrete (Nonlinear) Concrete (Nonlinear) material may be used. Such a material will display creep and shrinkage deformations, and the tendon losses which correspond may also be calculated. Age Age attributes need to be defined and assigned to all concrete members for which tendon loss calculations are required. These enable the creep and shrinkage calculations to take account of the maturity of the concrete at the time of installation, and the curing time (the time before drying shrinkage starts). Time must be introduced into the analysis, in order to calculate the losses associated with each stage of construction. This is most easily done using the Time Management Time Management option, which allows a length of time in days to be associated with each stage of construction in the model. When using Material library (Advanced define) Material library (Advanced define) for linear elastic material, stages of construction require a Nonlinear control (usually a 'Manual incrementation' and the application of total loads in each stage is appropriate). A suitable Nonlinear control is added automatically if using the Time Management module. When using a Concrete (Nonlinear) Concrete (Nonlinear) material, a Nonlinear and Transient control is required (namely a 'Manual incrementation' and 'Viscous' control). A suitable Nonlinear and Transient control is added automatically if using the Time Management module.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview Rail Load Optimisation is provided for use with selected Bridge software products only, and only for licences that support this facility. Rail load optimisation (RLO) makes use of influence lines and direct method influence analysis for rail use direct method influence analysis for rail use to identify the most onerous train loading arrangement for pre-defined track layouts track layouts , for a supported design code, and applies these train loading patterns to LUSAS models. It reduces the amount of time spent generating loadcases to replicate design code-based train loading on models and leads to more efficient and economic design, assessment or load rating of rail bridge structures. It is for use where decks of structures are modelled with beam, plate or shell elements; models with spans represented by single line beams are not currently supported. Direct Method Influence Direct Method Influence analysis for rail use is carried out to evaluate worst-case effects arising from a unit load applied to a rail location for chosen track loading configurations.

Stage 4: Run a Rail Load Optimisation Analysis
topics.text: Stage 4: Run a Rail Load Optimisation Analysis Running the Rail Load Optimisation wizard requires the selection of a design code, and specifying the influences to be used, the track layout to be considered, and whether loading patterns should be created. Once run, the critical loading pattern can be optionally displayed prior to calculating the effects of the loading on the model. A successful analysis will add a Rail Direct Method Influence Analysis entry as well as a RLO Analysis entry (and RLO runs) to the Analyses Treeview. These entries permit viewing of influence shapes and rail loading patterns prior to solving the model for those loading patterns. Any number of RLO Analysis entries can be created in the Analyses Treeview. Each RLO Analysis entry can contain any number of RLO runs (shown by this symbol ), with each run containing loadcases generated by the rail load optimisation software according to the chosen design code and associated settings chosen. Each loadcase comprises train and track loadings appropriate to the design code selected that, when solved, will generate the most adverse positive or negative loading effect for each of the influence points of interest, as defined on the model. topics.title: Superposition
toc_path: Performing a rail load optimisation analysis
headings: Performing a rail load optimisation analysis
topics.text: Superposition The Rail Load Optimisation facility inherently uses the principal of linear superposition. In a linear static analysis this assumption holds true for all results components that are calculated by a LUSAS Solver, but note that it does not hold true for some results components that are post-processed by LUSAS Modeller. For example, Wood Armer calculations are not linear calculations, therefore superposition is not safe for these. Similarly, the definition of any user-defined results components (that can be used in the definition of a Direct Method influence) may include equations with terms or constants that are not scalable.

topics.text: Rail Load Optimisation Wizard Rail Load Optimisation is provided for use with selected Bridge software products only, and only for licences that support this facility. The rail load optimisation wizard can be accessed from the Bridge > Rail Load Optimisation > RLO Run menu item. It provides the means to define parameters, for a particular design code, in order to generate the most critical train loading arrangement for each influence shape under consideration for a selected track layout. Prior to accessing the Rail Load Optimisation (RLO) wizard to run an RLO analysis influence attributes influence attributes must have been assigned to selected nodes or points of interest on a model. A track layout (requiring track definitions) also needs to be defined and selected. See Rail Load Optimisation Overview Rail Load Optimisation Overview for a general description of how to carry out a rail load optimisation analysis. topics.title: Optional Loading Parameters
toc_path: Design codes supported by Rail Load Optimisation (LUSAS RLO)
headings: Design codes supported by Rail Load Optimisation (LUSAS RLO)
topics.text: Optional Loading Parameters The following parameters are available for selection: Longitudinal increment specifies the increment used when moving the train loading along the track. The smaller the increment, the more accurately the effect of the train loading across the structure is calculated, giving more accurate results. A larger increment gives quicker RLO runs, but with less accuracy. A generally suitable default value is provided, but users can specify an alternative value based upon experience. Transverse increment Not applicable for Rail Load Optimisation since loading is always assigned to rails that are a specified distance apart. Vehicle Direction specifies the direction which is used to calculate the effects of each train on each track. Train axles are defined positively from the last axle to the leading axle. Forward The train loading is moved along a track in a forward direction from the starting point of the track. The start of a track is as defined on the track definition dialog. Reverse The train loading is moved along a track from the starting point of the track, but with the normally trailing axle leading. Both applies both forward and reverse cases. This is the suggested and default choice. For an asymmetric train loading, either forward or reverse could produce the greatest effect, dependent upon the shape of the influence surface and the increments used.

topics.text: Setting-up Influence Surfaces The List of available influences shows all assigned influence attributes influence attributes for the model. These can be included in a rail load optimisation analysis by individual selection or by selecting all. The following additional settings can be made: Include all influence surfaces - selects all the influence surfaces in the model for use in the rail load optimisation. Dynamic Factor (for NR-GN-CIV-025 loading only) is provided if the option “Specify for each influence selected" is chosen from the Optional Code Settings dialog. A different dynamic factor is needed for each influence because it depends on the span length, and on whether the influence is Positive moment, Negative moment, Shear, Bearing reaction, L (m) (for UIC 776-1 only) This is an option to introduce the length (in model units) of the influence used. For use in calculation of the dynamic factor. Positive and/or Negative Train loading can be placed on either Positive or Negative areas by checking the Positive or Negative (or both) checkboxes for each of the included influences. Note that clicking in the header cell of a column will select the whole column so that checking (ticking) one entry in the column will check (tick) all entries in that column. Selection of multiple columns is also possible.

topics.text: Other settings View onerous effects table Shows tabbed and sorted results for all chosen influences at nodes that are visible, with the most onerous result shown in the first row of the table. Displayed results can be filtered by subsequently selecting features or mesh objects of interest. For more information see Onerous Effects Table Onerous Effects Table below. Create loading patterns To run a Rail Load Optimisation analysis with optimised loading select this check box, selecting either the All chosen influences option, which generates loads and loadcases for all chosen influences; or the Most onerous option, where for each influence attribute the loads and loadcases are only generated for the influence assignment that gives the most onerous effect. For both options, loading entries are created in the Attributes treeview and an entry is created in the Analyses Treeview under the corresponding RLO Run. To visualise the loading patterns a loadcase must be set active and appropriate loading visualisation settings loading visualisation settings made. Note that discrete point traffic loads are visualised in a different colour to discrete patch traffic loads. The Analysis name provided creates an appropriate entry in the Analyses Treeview. Note that an analysis can contain up to 1000 RLO Runs. Separate user-defined analysis entries can be created to hold different RLO Runs using the 'New' analysis option on the drop-down menu for the Analysis entry, but for speed of solving, note that it is more beneficial to have all RLO Runs contained within one analysis. The Rail Load Optimisation Name is used to identify each RLO Run. Short names are recommended since RLO Run names are used to create filenames that also include the influence name and coordinate and element details, and if collectively this is too long, the Windows path limit of 260 characters may be exceeded. See File and folder naming in LUSAS File and folder naming in LUSAS for details. When the OK button is pressed LUSAS will carry out the influence surfaces analysis and carry out a Rail Load Optimisation analysis based on the country design code selected. The results from the analysis will be loaded into the LUSAS model in readiness for the model to be solved using the Solve Now Solve Now button on the main toolbar. When the model is solved for the selected track layout, the results from the analysis will be seen in the Rail Load Optimisation entry in the Analyses Treeview. Notes For models with numerous influence assignments of the same type, potentially un-necessary load generation can be avoided, and solution time can be saved, by ensuring that the‘Create loading patterns’ option is not selected on the main RLO dialog, to allow for only the most onerous loading patterns to be created from the subsequent RLO onerous results table listings. The time taken to evaluate critical rail loading effects for a structure depends upon the design code in use; the type of train loading being applied; the number of tracks present in a track layout; the number of spans; the mesh size; the values used for longitudinal load increments; whether one-way or two-way direction is specified; and the number of influence points to be evaluated. An approximate assessment of the time that will be required to evaluate a particular loading scheme for a large number of influence points can be achieved by initially timing how long it takes for just one influence point to be evaluated and factoring by the number of influences required, but note that for the first time RLO is run, displacement and influence files are generated that will be used by subsequent runs - so subsequent runs will be faster.

headings: Design codes supported by Rail Load Optimisation (LUSAS RLO)
topics.text: Onerous Effects Table When a RLO analysis is run, a RLO onerous effects table can be optionally displayed which shows sorted results for all chosen influences at nodes that are visible, with the most onerous result shown in the first row of the table. For Direct Method Influences these values are due to train loading for the specified load effect of interest at specified locations on the model. That is, a single value direct from the LUSAS Rail Load Optimisation facility, without the need for a further static solution. In the onerous effects table a results tab is present for each <Influence attribute – Sign – Design Case> group listed. This group is referred to as an 'Influence Design Loadcase'. Load patterns can be created on a case-by-case basis if not already created by means of the 'Create loading patterns' setting on the main RLO dialog. On each results page, the following column headings are present: Influence Assignment The location (coordinate and feature/object type) of the assigned DMI attribute. Node The node at which the assignment was made. Note that the Find context menu option for the cells in this column will, when clicked, highlight the corresponding node in the model View window by animating concentric shrinking squares. This easily identifies the assignment location. ' Chosen results effect ' For Direct Method Influence, this column is named after the result entity component selected in the DMI attribute (e.g. Mx, Fz, etc); the values in this column show the effect of the train loads at locations of interest. Caused by states the name of the loading type which produced the most onerous effect. Create loading Creates loading entries in the Attributes Treeview and a loadcase in the Analyses Treeview that cause the onerous effect listed. If the option to ‘Create loading patterns’ was chosen on the main RLO dialog, Loading folders will additionally appear for each influence loadcase added to the Analyses Treeview, and the RLO results table will show ‘Loading created’ alongside all influence assignment entries. If ‘Create loading patterns’ was not selected on the main RLO dialog the most onerous loading effects can be created individually by using the ‘Create Loading’ button that appears instead of the ‘Loading Created’ one. For the influences where no loading is produced by LUSAS RLO (because for the specified location there aren’t any loads that can be placed to produce an adverse effect), the 'Chosen results effect' and 'Caused by' cells will be empty.
topics.search_text: Onerous Effects Table Rail Load Optimisation Wizard Application Manual (Bridge, Civil and Structural) Bridge Loading Rail Load Optimisation Design codes supported by Rail Load Optimisation (LUSAS RLO) Onerous Effects Table Bridge Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation Wizard.htm Onerous Effects Table When a RLO analysis is run, a RLO onerous effects table can be optionally displayed which shows sorted results for all chosen influences at nodes that are visible, with the most onerous result shown in the first row of the table. For Direct Method Influences these values are due to train loading for the specified load effect of interest at specified locations on the model. That is, a single value direct from the LUSAS Rail Load Optimisation facility, without the need for a further static solution. In the onerous effects table a results tab is present for each <Influence attribute – Sign – Design Case> group listed. This group is referred to as an 'Influence Design Loadcase'. Load patterns can be created on a case-by-case basis if not already created by means of the 'Create loading patterns' setting on the main RLO dialog. On each results page, the following column headings are present: Influence Assignment The location (coordinate and feature/object type) of the assigned DMI attribute. Node The node at which the assignment was made. Note that the Find context menu option for the cells in this column will, when clicked, highlight the corresponding node in the model View window by animating concentric shrinking squares. This easily identifies the assignment location. ' Chosen results effect ' For Direct Method Influence, this column is named after the result entity component selected in the DMI attribute (e.g. Mx, Fz, etc); the values in this column show the effect of the train loads at locations of interest. Caused by states the name of the loading type which produced the most onerous effect. Create loading Creates loading entries in the Attributes Treeview and a loadcase in the Analyses Treeview that cause the onerous effect listed. If the option to ‘Create loading patterns’ was chosen on the main RLO dialog, Loading folders will additionally appear for each influence loadcase added to the Analyses Treeview, and the RLO results table will show ‘Loading created’ alongside all influence assignment entries. If ‘Create loading patterns’ was not selected on the main RLO dialog the most onerous loading effects can be created individually by using the ‘Create Loading’ button that appears instead of the ‘Loading Created’ one. For the influences where no loading is produced by LUSAS RLO (because for the specified location there aren’t any loads that can be placed to produce an adverse effect), the 'Chosen results effect' and 'Caused by' cells will be empty.

Viewing, filtering and saving onerous effects tables
topics.text: Viewing, filtering and saving onerous effects tables RLO onerous effects results tables can be re-displayed for all influences at any time by selecting the View table results... context menu for a RLO Run entry in the Analyses Treeview. A table for a single particular influence can be created by double-clicking on the relevant onerous results table entry in the Analyses Treeview. Results displayed in the tables can be filtered by selecting features or mesh objects of interest in the view window. So, for instance, with table results displayed in one view window, it is possible to select a line representing a span in a bridge in the model view window and have the results table only display the results for the nodes in the elements within that line. Similarly it is possible to select a surface representing a span of a slab and view only the results for the nodes in the elements within that surface. Use the Window > Layout > Multiple documents menu item and the Window > Tile facility to see the onerous results table data and model view window side-by-side. Column data can be sorted by clicking on column headers. Table results for an active table can be saved to a spreadsheet using the File > Save as Microsoft Excel menu item.

topics.text: Usage Once the onerous effects for each 'Influence Design Loadcase' have been obtained, and if the option to ‘Create loading patterns’ was not chosen on the main RLO dialog, the corresponding loading will need to be created on a case-by-case basis, if not already done. Whilst generated loading patterns can be visualised, results are available only after the RLO analysis has been solved. Once solved, the resulting loadcases should be combined with self weight and factored accordingly to create design combinations.

topics.title: Track Layouts
topics.text: Track Layouts The rail track layout dialog is accessed by using the Bridge> Rail Track Optimisation > Railway Track Layout menu item. A track layout defines which track definitions track definitions can be loaded in a single run of a Rail DMI analysis Rail DMI analysis . Multiple track layouts can be defined by including and excluding track definitions and changing the track layout name before pressing the Apply button on the dialog each time. Examples of track layouts are shown below. Rail track layouts created using this dialog are added as entries within a Rail Track Layout folder in the Utilities Treeview. Like other utilities track layouts are not directly assignable to geometry and can only be edited using this dialog.

topics.title: Track Definition
topics.text: Track Definition The track definition dialog is accessed by using the Bridge> Rail Track Optimisation > Track Definition menu item. Track definitions are used by rail track layouts track layouts to specify particular track loading scenarios for use with the Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation facility. The dialog allows the centrelines of lengths of track to be defined: By coordinates By copying and pasting data from a spreadsheet By selecting lines and arcs that are added to the LUSAS model to represent track centrelines. This is perhaps the most commonly used method. For any method, the transverse distance between rail loads on the track must also be stated. Once defined a track is shown on the model by the drawing of non-selectable lines that represent the rails and sleepers. The rail track definition is stored and viewed in the Utilities Treeview. Like other utilities, track definitions are not directly assignable to geometry and can only be edited using this dialog.

topics.title: Notes
topics.text: Notes Lines used to define a centreline of a track should lie in a common plane. If desired, the lines defining the centreline of a track can be defined to lie above a model rather than be defined in the same plane as the surfaces on which the rail loading will be applied. Bridge decks with a variable longitudinal vertical profile (such as a vertically curved deck) must be modelled 'flat' in a primary (X,Y), (Y,Z) or (Z,X) plane. For bridge decks with a constant longitudinal vertical profile (such as a horizontal or inclined bridge deck) the lines representing a track centreline may lie in a primary plane or in the same plane as the bridge deck.

headings: Defining the centreline of a track by coordinate input
topics.text: Defining the centreline of a track by coordinate input The centreline of a track can be defined by adding rows to a table and specifying the coordinates of each defining point along the path. Values are entered in global coordinates. As the coordinates are entered the centreline of the track that they define is visualised in the adjacent graphs. Type Clicking on the drop-list button in this cell of the table allows the type of line to be specified. Options are Straight, Arc Bulge, Arc Centre, and Parabola Bulge. Insert , Delete and Reverse buttons provide the means to create a new row above a selected row, to delete selected rows, and to reverse the order of all of the rows in the table. Use the tab key to create a new row at the bottom of the table. The definition grid shows track geometry and allows specification of line segment type when a reference path has been generated using lines or arcs in Modeller. Splines are not supported.

topics.text: Defining the centreline of a track by spreadsheet import The geometry and line segment information that defines the centreline of a track can be imported from a spreadsheet using standard copy and paste facilities. Both four column (type and coordinate data) and three column (coordinate data only) widths are supported. With four column import the data in the first column is expected to be text. Three column data is expected to be numeric and will paste into the coordinate cells wherever it is pasted. Selecting the top left row / column box allows copying and pasting of data from a spreadsheet using Ctrl + C and Ctrl + V keyboard shortcuts.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview The LUSAS Rail Track Analysis software option permits track/bridge interaction analysis to the International Union of Railways Code UIC774-3. Use the Bridge > Rail Track Analysis UIC774-3 menu item to access dialogs that enable model building, definition of loading and post-processing of results. Track and bridge interaction models are built automatically in LUSAS from geometric, material property, and loading data defined in a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Both thermal loading to the track and deck along with train loading due to acceleration and braking forces can be defined. In accordance with the UIC774-3 code of practice, a user-specified element length is used to define the longitudinal embankment and bridge features. Rail clips, ballast movement, bearings and pier stiffness are all included in the analysis model. The model building dialogs allow for either one train crossing one or more structures, or for multiple trains crossing the same structure. When running an analysis, temperature loading can be considered in isolation for subsequent analysis of multiple rail configurations, or a full analysis can be carried out considering the combined temperature and rail loading. Since the response of the ballast and/or clips is nonlinear a nonlinear analysis always needs to be carried out. Results can be produced in either Microsoft Excel spreadsheet or standard LUSAS results file format. User-defined load combinations can be specified. Spreadsheet results include deformations, forces/moments and axial stresses in the rails of the tracks and deformations and forces / moments in the deck structure with associated charting. Automatic post-processing includes enveloping and results tables to identify peak relative railbed displacements, relative deck movements, longitudinal reactions and axial rail stresses along with which train configuration / position they are occurring for and where in the structure the peak result has occurred. The use of individual dialogs is explained in the online help. For more detailed information refer to the Rail Track Analysis Manual.

topics.title: UIC774-3 Chart Options
topics.text: UIC774-3 Chart Options The charts that will be included in the track and deck results within the Microsoft Excel results spreadsheet can be customised. When a model is first post-processed all standard charts will be included in the post-processing for both the tracks and the decks. The charts to include in the post-processing can be changed by setting the options in the dialog.

topics.title: Track charting options
topics.text: Track charting options Railbed / track / deck chart - Check box is selected by default. Axial rail stress chart (single track) - Check box is selected by default. Axial rail stress chart (multiple tracks) If this check box is selected, two additional inputs that control the appearance of the chart become active. Limits are required because the displaying of multiple axial stress curves for tracks on top of each other on the same chart can lead to the chart becoming illegible and unreadable very easily. The inputs are: Limit for all curves to have peaks labelled – Controls the maximum number of curves (tracks) that are allowed to be plotted where all of the peak axial tensile/compressive stress values will be plotted on each of the curves (default = 3) Limit on total number of curves in chart – Controls the maximum number of curves (tracks) that are allowed to be plotted. If more than this number of curves are attempted the chart will be omitted from the post-processing (default = 5) Note that creation of a multiple track axial stress chart for larger models with more than two tracks can cause issues in some versions of Microsoft Excel.

topics.title: UIC774-3 Model Builder
topics.text: UIC774-3 Model Builder Prior to using the UIC774-3 Model Builder a spreadsheet describing the model geometry, properties and loading should have been defined. To do this use the template located in the <Lusas Installation Folder>\Programs\Scripts\User directory and enter the required information into the appropriate locations. All units for the analysis are metric and are listed for the sections within this spreadsheet. Note that each ‘rail’ in the Geometric Properties definition represents a single track on the structure and therefore should have geometric properties equal to double that of a single rail. Up to two tracks can be present on the structure. Use the Bridge > Rail Track Analysis UIC774-3 > Build Model... menu item to name and locate the data to be used to build a model for use with the Rail Track Analysis software option Rail Track Analysis software option . Model filename If a single analysis is being carried out then a model filename should be specified with or without the *.mdl extension. A directory should not be specified with this model filename as the current working directory is used for saving the model. Microsoft spreadsheet The Microsoft Excel filename should be entered or located using the Browse… button.

topics.title: Batch Processing Multiple Structures
topics.text: Batch Processing Multiple Structures If multiple models are to be built and analysed the batch processing facilities can be used. For this a batch text file (with a *.txt extension) should be created that contains the name of one valid Excel spreadsheet per line that defines the models. If the spreadsheet exists and contains valid data then the model will be built and solved in the same directory as the Excel spreadsheet. The number of Excel spreadsheets is unlimited. The batch text filename should be entered into the dialog or located using the Browse… button and choosing 'Batch text file (*.txt)' as the file type. No model filename should be entered as this will be defined by the basename of the Excel spreadsheet in the batch text file.

topics.text: Common Input for Single or Multiple Structures Element size The element size to use in the finite element mesh should be specified in this box. According to the UIC774-3 Code of Practice, the maximum element size that is permitted in an analysis is 2.0m (Clause 1.7.3). The dialog therefore generally allows element sizes of 0 < Element Size ≤ 2.0m for the building of the models. Larger element sizes can be used (up to the length of the smallest bridge deck span) but a warning will be issued about non-compliance with the UIC774-3 Code of Practice. Note that for large bridges and/or embankments the use of small element sizes can generate excessively large models which take significant time to manipulate / solve. Use of element sizes below 1.0m should be used with caution. Apply temperature and rail loads in same analysis By default, only the temperature loading is applied to the decks of the structure which allows multiple train load configurations to be applied to the same structure. If, however, the combined deck temperature and rail loading is to be solved in a single analysis then the Apply temperature and rail loads in same analysis option should be selected. Wait for solution If the option to wait for the solution is selected then all of the analyses will be run from Modeller and nothing can be carried out in the current Modeller window until the solution has finished. For relatively small structures or analyses with a limited set of parametric trainset loading locations this is may be fine. If a large number of parametric trainset loading locations are included in an analysis and/or a large number of models are being built using the batch processing then waiting for the solution can take a considerable amount of time. On clicking the OK button the model(s) will be built and solved automatically by the software. A log file called 'UIC774-3_BuildModel.log' will be created in the current working directory if batch processing is used to report any errors encountered during the batch process. See also: UIC774-3 Rail Loads UIC774-3 Rail Loads
