topics.title: UIC774-3 Modify Included Output
topics.text: UIC774-3 Modify Included Output The extent of the model to be included in the post-processing can be customised. When a model is first post-processed all tracks, Train Loading Groups and rail track length will be included in the post-processing but the limits of the post-processing may need to be modified to focus on a particular track, trainset configuration in one of the Train Loading Groups or on a particular length of rail track. The extent of the post-processing can be controlled by setting the limits in the dialog.

topics.title: Tracks to include
topics.text: Tracks to include By default all tracks in the model will be included in the post-processing. Deselecting the All tracks option will allow individual tracks to be selected. At least one track must be included in the post-processing.

Deselecting the All tracks option will allow individual tracks to be selected. At least one track must be included in the post-processing.

topics.title: Train Loading Groups to include
topics.text: Train Loading Groups to include By default all Train Loading Groups will be included in the post-processing with all trainset(s) positions considered for each. Deselecting the All Train Loading Groups option will allow individual Train Loading Groups to be included in the post-processing (the positions within the Train Loading Groups cannot be included/excluded, all positions of a Train Loading Group will either be included or excluded). At least one Train Loading Group must be included in the post-processing.

At least one Train Loading Group must be included in the post-processing.

topics.title: Extent of railtrack to include
topics.text: Extent of railtrack to include By default the whole rail track length (both embankment lengths and the rail track over the structure) will be included in the post-processing. Deselecting the 'Whole railtrack' option will allow a different length of rail track to be specified. As long as the model has not been modified significantly the dialog will report the coordinates of the left and right embankments along with the structure to assist in the entering of the start and end coordinates. The rail track length must include a part of the structure to allow track-structure-interaction calculations to be carried out. Clicking the Defaults button will return the output extents to the default settings of all tracks, all Train Loading Groups and all rail track extent. See also: UIC774-3 Post-Processing UIC774-3 Post-Processing

topics.title: UIC774-3 Post-Processing
topics.text: UIC774-3 Post-Processing Use the Bridge > Rail Track Analysis UIC774-3 > Extract results to Excel... menu item to post-process results from a rail track analysis. Models created by the Rail Track Analysis software can be post-processed in Microsoft Excel by using the dedicated post-processing dialog. This allows the extraction of the results along with automatic generation of charts and enveloping in Microsoft Excel. In addition, if enveloping is performed in Microsoft Excel then additional summary tables are generated for key quantities that need to be checked for compliance with UIC774-3 and other similar Codes of Practice. On startup of the dialog: If valid UIC774-3 model groups are found, namely "Track 1", "Track 2" (or any other tracks) and "Decks", then the results can be extracted using these groups or for individual selected rail nodes. If model groups are not found then the current selection will be used if this selection contains lines with thick 3D engineering beams assigned. If no valid groups or selection are found then the post-processor will report an error. To use the post-processor, enter the filename for the Microsoft Excel file that will be created. The directory in which to place the Microsoft Excel file can be selected but is, by default, the current working directory.

topics.title: Post-Processing Using Model Groups
topics.text: Post-Processing Using Model Groups When a track-structure-interaction model is first post-processed the extent of the output will be the whole analysis with All tracks, Train Loading Groups and rail track length included in the post-processing extracted to the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. The post-processing can be adjusted by clicking the Modify... button which allows the selection of individual tracks, Train Loading Groups and the length of rail track to be includedModify in the post-processing. If the track-structure-interaction model is saved the modified post-processing will be saved with the model so it is available the next time the model and results are loaded and post-processed. See Modify Included Output Modify Included Output for more details. Generate envelopes and peak results tables in Microsoft Excel By default the post-processor will generate envelopes for the behaviours of the track(s) and deck(s) along with peak results tables of key quantities such as the longitudinal relative railbed displacement, longitudinal reaction and axial rail stress with information about where these peaks are occurring. If the structure has more than a single deck then additional tables of the relative displacements between the ends of the decks will also be output. This output can be disabled, if required, by deselecting the Generate envelopes and peak result tables in Microsoft Excel when processing groups option. Generate charts in Microsoft Excel The post-processor will, by default, generate charts for the post-processing in Microsoft Excel to assist with the interpretation of the behaviour of the track-structure-interaction. When a track-structure-interaction model is first post-processed all of the default charts will be included in the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. All of the charting for the track-structure-interaction output can be disabled, if required, by deselecting the 'Generate charts in Microsoft Excel' option. The charts to be included can be modified by clicking the Options... button which allows the selection of the individual charts. If the track-structure-interaction model is saved the modified chart selection will be saved with the model so it is available the next time the model and results are loaded and post-processed. See Chart Options Chart Options for more details. Clicking the Defaults button will turn the enveloping and charting back on if they have been disabled, it will not change the extents of the post-processing or the selection of individual charts. To change either of these you must make the required modifications in the relevant dialog. On clicking the OK button the post-processor will extract the results from all of the results loadcases of the track-structure-interaction analysis. If multiple results files are loaded, for example if multiple rail load configurations have been analysed and the results loaded into Modeller (either through the use of Train Loading Groups or manually), then the results for all of these results files will be extracted into the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. On opening the spreadsheet, if the model originally contained the UIC774-3 groups ("Track 1", "Track 2" and "Decks") then the results for each item will be placed into a separate worksheet within the spreadsheet. Additional worksheets will also be generated if enveloping is carried out in Microsoft Excel.

topics.title: Post-Processing Using Rail Nodes or Selected Lines

headings: Post-Processing Using Rail Nodes or Selected Lines
topics.text: Post-Processing Using Rail Nodes or Selected Lines If individual rail nodes were selected and post-processed, the spreadsheet will contain a separate worksheet for each node that lists the rail stresses seen at the location of the node for all of the results analysed. The stresses in these individual rail node worksheets will be nodal averaged stress results and may differ very slightly from the element unaveraged nodal stress results reported in the "Track 1" and other track worksheets. If a selection of lines was used for post-processing a single worksheet will be placed into the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet that contains the results extracted for the beams assigned to the selected lines. The post-processing of selected lines obeys the Train Loading Groups post-processing extent and it can therefore be modified in the same way it was for the post-processing of the groups by clicking the Modify... button in the output control section. The post-processing of selected lines will also generate envelopes when this option is selected but peak tables (of quantities such as longitudinal relative railbed displacements) are not created since these are only valid for the post-processing of the track-structure-interaction groups. See also: UIC774-3 Modify Included Output UIC774-3 Modify Included Output UIC774-3 Chart Options UIC774-3 Chart Options

topics.title: UIC774-3 Rail Loads
topics.text: UIC774-3 Rail Loads Use the Bridge > Rail Track Analysis UIC774-3 > Apply Rail Loads... menu item to apply rail loading to a model created by the UIC774-3 Model Builder. If only the temperature effects have been applied to the model using the UIC774-3 Model Builder dialog then single or multiple rail configurations can be applied using this dialog. Note: Attempting to use this dialog on a model that has not been created using the model builder dialog or that has loading other than temperature loads will generate an error message.

toc_path: Analysing a Single Structure with One Rail Load Configuration
headings: Analysing a Single Structure with One Rail Load Configuration
topics.text: Analysing a Single Structure with One Rail Load Configuration If a single rail load configuration is to be analysed for a single structure either enter the filename of the existing LUSAS temperature model created using the model builder or select it using the Browse… button. Enter the filename for the new model (omitting any path description as the model will be saved in the current working directory). This filename can be the same as the original model but it is recommended that an alternative filename is used so the original model remains unchanged. Finally enter the filename for the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet that contains the rail load configuration description or select it using the Browse… button.

topics.text: Analysing a Single Structure or Multiple Structures with Multiple Rail Load Configurations If multiple models and / or multiple rail load configurations are to be analysed then only the batch text file should be entered or selected using the Browse… button and choosing "Batch text file (*.txt)" as the file type. The batch text file should be TAB delimited and contain the filename of the original model file, the filename of the new model to be created and the filename of the Microsoft Excel spreadsheet containing the rail loading, e.g. Viaduct 1.mdl Viaduct 1_RailConfig1.mdl Viaduct 1_RailConfig1.xlsx Viaduct 1.mdl Viaduct 1_RailConfig2.mdl Viaduct 1_RailConfig2.xlsx Viaduct 1.mdl Viaduct 1_RailConfig3.mdl Viaduct 1_RailConfig3.xlsx Viaduct 2.mdl Viaduct 2_RailConfig1.mdl Viaduct 2_RailConfig1.xlsx Viaduct 2.mdl Viaduct 2_RailConfig2.mdl Viaduct 2_RailConfig2.xlsx In the above example, two different viaduct temperature models have been selected and three rail load configurations chosen for the first and two for the second models. The number of entries in the batch text file is unlimited.

topics.title: Box Section Property Calculator
topics.text: Box Section Property Calculator The Box Section Property Calculator is provided in Bridge and Civil & Structural software products only. It is recommended it is accessed from the Attributes > Geometric > Section Calculators menu item, or from the Attributes > Geometric > Section Library Item . For both of these, a section utility is created in the Utilities Treeview and the ability to create a corresponding geometric line attribute in the Attributes treeview is provided. This can be assigned directly to selected lines in a model. It can also be accessed from the Bridge > Box Section... menu item, but note that this option only creates a utility in the Utilities Treeview that will need to be selected as part of defining a geometric line attribute for subsequent assignment to selected lines in a model.

topics.title: What does it do?
topics.text: What does it do? The box section property calculator calculates general section properties from user-defined dimensional data. The section shape can be defined either as a simple box section simple box section or as a complex box section complex box section created from as many points as are required to form a suitable representation of the true cross-sectional shape. A void can be included or excluded from a section. The sections generated are of a type typically used in precast and segmentally constructed bridges. General section properties (area, moments of inertia and torsion constant etc.) of the section are computed automatically once a valid set of dimensions have been defined, using model units. Extreme fibre positions for use when plotting stresses on beams are also calculated. The resulting section can additionally be visualised to check for correct values being entered and to see the automatically defined fibre locations.

A void can be included or excluded from a section. The sections generated are of a type typically used in precast and segmentally constructed bridges. General section properties (area, moments of inertia and torsion constant etc.) of the section are computed automatically once a valid set of dimensions have been defined, using model units. Extreme fibre positions for use when plotting stresses on beams are also calculated. The resulting section can additionally be visualised to check for correct values being entered and to see the automatically defined fibre locations.

topics.title: Defining a complex box section
topics.text: Defining a complex box section The main box cell, section and cantilever setting out dimensions for a complex box section are shown dimensioned with a height (H), width (W), slab thickness (T) and in the case of three or more celled sections, a breadth, (B). Slab thickness specifies the thickness of the slab at the location shown on the section dialog. Note that on multi-celled box sections, dependent upon the thickness specified, this may represent the distance from the top of the slab to the bottom of an internal fillet (Tt) or the distance from the bottom of the slab to the top of an internal fillet (Tb). In addition to these primary dimensions extra points can be defined to model a particular box section shape. Some extra points are mandatory as in the case of points P1 and P2. Others such as t1, b1, e1, i1, c1 etc. are optional.

topics.title: Notes on defining a complex box section
toc_path: Notes on defining a complex box section
headings: Notes on defining a complex box section
topics.text: Notes on defining a complex box section Points P1 and P2 define the extent of the interior face of the external web. These points must be defined in the Extra Points grid in all cases, even when no fillets are required. Points P1 and P2 will lie at the corners of a void if no fillets are specified. Additional points can be defined to either model a particular cantilever shape, a side wall shape or to model simple fillets at top or bottom slab locations. Selecting the location and number of the points required in the No. of extra points cell will add fields to the Extra Points grid to allow offsets (O) and heights (H) for these points to be defined. As an example, to define fillets at the junction of the upper slab and the side and internal walls of a two cell box section, two internal points in the Top slab drop-down list would need to be specified (t1 and t2) in addition to specifying a thickness (Tt) from the top of the slab to the bottom of the fillet. Defining fillets for the lower slab/wall connections would be similar. See the Complex Box Section Examples for details. To model a curving external box section profile as many points on the web exterior face and cantilever slab can be defined as necessary to approximate the actual profile. A camber in the top slab can be optionally created by entering a value for the height of the midpoint of the slab (Hm).

topics.text: What does it do? It allows you to define the section geometry for a range of infilled or encased section types either with reference to sections held in the main section library, or from user-defined values. Note that at the time of definition, only illustrative section properties can be calculated for the section based upon a user-defined modular ratio for the two different materials that can be defined. The actual section properties can only be determined when chosen materials have been assigned to the section as part of completing its definition when adding a section to the Attributes Treeview.

topics.title: Notes
toc_path: Concrete shrinkage loading to AASHTO LRFD 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Concrete shrinkage loading to AASHTO LRFD 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Notes In a grillage-type model, the shrinkage (strain profile loading) attribute should be assigned to the line features which represent the longitudinal members (main girders and tributary width of deck slab) and optionally the transverse members also, in a loadcase representing permanent effects. Depending upon the modelling method used this may include Bridge Deck (Grillage) Bridge Deck (Grillage) geometric attributes, which define the section types. In such a case, the primary self-equilibrating stresses in the girder will be determined and a Strain profile (TMPE) loading is used, applying an equivalent overall moment/axial load to the grillage or beam members. Any secondary effects (due to continuity at intermediate supports) will arise as a natural consequence of analysis and equilibrium conditions. In a shell-type model, the shrinkage strain (stress and strain loading) attribute should be assigned to the surface features which represent the deck slab in a loadcase representing permanent effects. In such a case, the self-equilibrating stresses in the girder - both primary (direct) effects and secondary effects (due to continuity at intermediate supports) - will arise as a natural consequence of analysis and equilibrium conditions. When used in conjunction with Composite Bridge Deck Design Composite Bridge Deck Design a single shrinkage load attribute must be assigned in the loadcase that is referenced on the 'In Service Loadcases' tab for Phase 2b of the Design Results Utility Design Results Utility . The load attribute is used to calculate the strain in the slab and corresponding self-equilibrating stresses. These stresses are then added to the secondary effects computed in the analysis. The effects of creep and shrinkage in concrete are time-dependent and a better representation of these effects is obtained by using an analysis in which the time domain is represented - a so-called "Viscous" analysis, using Concrete (Nonlinear) Concrete (Nonlinear) material attributes. Such an approach may be more suitable in certain circumstances. See also: Bridge deck shrinkage profile loading to design codes Bridge deck shrinkage profile loading to design codes Composite Bridge Deck Design Composite Bridge Deck Design

topics.title: Vehicle loadings in general
topics.text: Vehicle loadings in general Vehicle loadings have a loading origin at their centre and, when relevant, have a direction of travel shown or stated on the dialog. Once defined, discrete point and/or patch load attributes are added to the Attributes Treeview for subsequent assignment to a point on a model. For some country loading types a compound discrete loading attribute may also be created and, if done, this loading (which comprises a set of discrete point or patch loads to define a loading type) should be assigned to the model instead. During assignment a patch transformation can be used to mirror, rotate or otherwise transform the discrete patch load that represents the vehicle, so that the desired orientation of loading is obtained.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview The Steel Composite Bridge Wizard generates the model geometry and corresponding mesh, geometric, material, support and local coordinate attributes for models of slab-on-beam composite I-girder bridges where the slab and web are modelled with shell elements and the top and bottom flanges, web stiffeners and bracing are modelled using beam elements. Models can be defined that accommodate: Straight or curved decks of constant radius. An arbitrary skew, where a skew can additionally be set per support and interpolated across the spans. Any number of spans and supports. Square and skew bracing. Transverse stiffeners. Design attributes for design checking against supported design codes (for licences that support this facility). Note that loading of models is not carried out by the wizard. Example bridge data Example bridge data is provided for a two-span bridge, as is a fully worked example. Example of a curved multi-span steel composite bridge deck with bracing as created by the wizard

Models can be defined that accommodate: Straight or curved decks of constant radius. An arbitrary skew, where a skew can additionally be set per support and interpolated across the spans. Any number of spans and supports. Square and skew bracing. Transverse stiffeners. Design attributes for design checking against supported design codes (for licences that support this facility). Note that loading of models is not carried out by the wizard. Example bridge data Example bridge data is provided for a two-span bridge, as is a fully worked example. Example of a curved multi-span steel composite bridge deck with bracing as created by the wizard

topics.title: Defining bridge geometry
topics.text: Defining bridge geometry Bridge geometry is defined from the Bridge > Steel Composite Bridge Wizard menu item. Using the menu items shown, a series of re-usable components can be defined for composite sections, girders, spans, supports and bridges. The menu items for these components are arranged in the order in which they would normally be defined. Since a bridge is made of spans and supports, and a span is made of girders and bracing runs, and a girder is made of sections and stiffeners, the smallest components (sections) are best defined first, because they can then be referenced directly by the next component up in the hierachy (girders), and so on, until the final bridge 'definition' is specified. To define basic bridge geometry requires the following steps to be carried out: Define Composite I-Girder Section(s) Define Composite I-Girder Section(s) - one for each different section type to be used on the structure. Define Girder(s) Define Girder(s) with optional stiffeners Define Span(s) Define Span(s) with optional bracing runs between spans Define Supports Define Supports with optional bracing assemblies between supports Define Bridge type Define Bridge type with a choice of straight or curved decks Once data has been defined for these five steps, an initial bridge model can be generated. See generating a steel composite bridge model generating a steel composite bridge model . Defining the basic bridge geometry (without stiffeners or bracing) allows a model to be created for visualisation and checking purposes prior to then adding more detail, by re-visiting the wizard.

topics.title: Generating a steel composite bridge model
toc_path: Generating a steel composite bridge model
headings: Generating a steel composite bridge model
topics.text: Generating a steel composite bridge model Once a bridge type bridge type has been defined referencing all required bridge components, a steel composite bridge model can be generated from the Bridge > Steel Composite Bridge Wizard > Generate defined bridge menu item, or by selecting the Generate button on the Steel Composite Bridge Wizard toolbar. Select the bridge to be generated from the drop-list provided, and press the Generate button to create the LUSAS model. Note that generating a bridge model using the bridge wizard (by selecting the Bridge > Steel Composite Bridge Wizard > Generate Defined Bridge menu item or by pressing the Generate toolbar button) will cause any additional changes that have been made to the model since the wizard was last run (such as the addition of extra geometry, or the assignment of loading to additional analyses) to be lost when the bridge is re-generated using the latest data that exists in the Utilities treeview. When a model is generated the various bridge wizard utilities present in the Utilities treeview are used to create corresponding mesh, geometric, material, support and local coordinate attribute entries in the Attributes treeview and to create all bridge geometry. Note that: Wizard-generated attributes assigned to the model are shown with the 'assigned' symbol. Geometric line attributes created by the wizard when bridge design material is specified for I-girder utilities are not assigned directly to the model. The wording "(Bridge Design Section)" is appended to these names, and these attributes are shown with an 'unassigned' symbol. These attributes are solely for use by the composite bridge deck design facility when a design check is carried out.

headings: Generating a steel composite bridge model
topics.text: Model geometry Bridge models are generated with the local x-axes of all lines representing longitudinal members following the control centreline of the bridge. All lines representing transverse members and bracing are created with x-axes being perpendicular to the control centreline of the bridge. Deck slab and girder webs are modelled with thick shell quadratic elements, and the top and bottom flanges of the girders are modelled using thick shell beam elements, with mesh divisions as set by the user. headings: Editing of bridge wizard generated data
topics.text: Editing of bridge wizard generated data Once a model has been created by the Steel Composite Bridge Wizard, assigning, deassigning, deleting or editing attributes that have been created by the Bridge Wizard is initially prevented by default. Selection of the 'Allow modification of LUSAS-generated attributes' option on Attributes tab of the Model properties dialog enables editing of Bridge Wizard-generated attributes. This allows for editing of attribute data such as changing the thickness of web or flange plates, or changing the section sizes of bracing directly in the appropriate treeview without having to re-run the Bridge Wizard. Note: Re-generating a bridge model using the bridge wizard (by selecting the Bridge > Steel Composite Bridge Wizard > Generate Defined Bridge menu item or by pressing the Generate toolbar button) will cause any additional changes that have been made to the model since the wizard was last run (such as the addition of extra geometry, or the assignment of loading to additional analyses) to be lost when the bridge is re-generated using the latest data that exists in the Utilities treeview.

topics.text: Usage Once created, a general temperature profile loading attribute temperature profile loading attribute is added to the Analyses Treeview. This can be edited directly using the 'Edit Attribute' context menu option (and from which the temperature profile can be visualised for a stated visualisation height), or the original data can be edited by using the 'Edit Definition' menu option. Note that editing the definition will edit both heating and cooling versions of the attribute. When using the composite bridge deck design facility and waning to calculate the self-equilibrating stresses for design, a design code-specific temperature profile attribute must be assigned to relevant features in a model for a particular loadcase and Phase. topics.title: Temperature differences (deg F)
topics.text: Temperature differences (deg F) Where possible, the numerical values of the positive and reverse temperature differences are determined from settings made and dynamically displayed in the dialog. For Groups 1 and 2 the values depend on the surfacing type and thickness alone, for Group 3 on the surfacing and the slab depth, and for Group 4 on the surfacing and the section height. For Group 4 no temperature differences are displayed as they depend on the geometric section the attribute is assigned to. For each construction group, a droplist shows the corresponding discrete thicknesses or slab depth values as shown in BD 37/01 Appendix C, Tables 22-24. An extra custom droplist option enables custom values to entered for 'Depth' and 'Thickness'. If an intermediate value is entered in the surfacing thickness or the slab depth, a linear interpolation provides an appropriate value. As implemented, because there was ambiguity in the design code as to what value should be used for 0mm surfacing when interpolating values between 0mm and 20mm for construction groups 1 and 2, and surfacing values between 0mm and 50mm for groups 3 and 4, “waterproofed” values for 0mm surfacing are used. The locations of temperature values within the depth of the superstructure are shown on the following images which replicate BD37/01 Figure 9. Reproduction of Construction Group 1 profiles from BD37/01 Figure 9. Reproduction of Construction Group 4 profiles from BD37/01 Figure 9.

topics.title: Implementation notes
toc_path: Temperature profile loading to CS 454 rev 0
headings: Temperature profile loading to CS 454 rev 0
topics.text: Implementation notes In CS 454, in Table D.27 for Slab depth 0.2m and surface thickness 150mm, the positive T1 temperature difference is stated to be 13.5. In BD37/01, on which the temperature profile loading for CS 454 was based, this value is stated as 10.5. This is considered a typo and 10.5 was adopted in this implementation. The inequality in CS 454 Table D.24 for the h3 dimension in group 4 decks was incorrectly transcribed from BD37/01 Figure 9, on which the temperature profile loading for CS 454 was based. As implemented, the inequality in BD37/01 has been used on the advice of the authors of CS 454.

headings: Temperature profile loading to Canada CSA S6-06, S6-14 and 6:19
topics.text: Temperature profiles Temperature profile loading attribute data can be created for Positive winter and / or Negative winter and / or Positive summer For Construction types A and C, three profiles with linear temperature difference variation across the section’s height are defined: Positive winter , Negative winter and Positive summer . For each of those profiles, the temperature differential between the top and bottom of the cross section are obtained from Figure 3.6 of the code for a given section height. The correct temperature differential is saved into the attribute as an expression of its height so that it is correct for any section to which it is assigned. For Construction type B, a single Positive profile is defined with a temperature difference of 30 degrees Celcius. The temperature difference takes place only through the slab depth, which must be specified. Below the slab depth the temperature is assumed constant according to the code.

headings: Temperature profile loading to Canada CSA S6-06, S6-14 and 6:19
topics.text: Usage Once created, a general temperature profile loading attribute temperature profile loading attribute is added to the Analyses Treeview. This can be edited directly using the 'Edit Attribute' context menu option (and from which the temperature profile can be visualised for a stated visualisation height), or the original data can be edited by using the 'Edit Definition' menu option. Note that editing the definition will edit both heating and cooling versions of the attribute. When using the composite bridge deck design facility and waning to calculate the self-equilibrating stresses for design, a design code-specific temperature profile attribute must be assigned to relevant features in a model for a particular loadcase and Phase. See Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility See also: Bridge deck temperature profile loading to design codes Bridge deck temperature profile loading to design codes Composite Bridge Deck Design Composite Bridge Deck Design

topics.text: Calculated parameters Where possible, the numerical values of the temperature differences are determined from settings made and dynamically displayed in the dialog. From settings made, LUSAS uses EN 1991-1-5:2003 Tables B.1, B.2 and B.3 rather than Figure 6.2 to calculate the temperature profiles as these allow for variation in surface thickness. The locations of temperature values T1, T2, T3 and T4 within the depth of the superstructure are shown on the following image which replicates EN 1991-1-5:2003 Figure 6.2a. topics.title: Implementation notes
topics.text: Implementation notes Note that due to the definition of the reverse profile of the Steel or Composite structure, the structure depth needs to be at least “Slab depth+h2” for the profile to be defined correctly, otherwise the attribute isn't suitable for assignment. If the profile is assigned to a member with a section height less than that required, then for that member one of the profile segments will have negative thickness “H-Slab depth-h2” and upon assignment of the profile, warnings relating to the profile will be produced in the Text Output window.

toc_path: Temperature profile loading to JTG D60 - 2004 and 2015
headings: Temperature profile loading to JTG D60 - 2004 and 2015
topics.text: Temperature differences Where possible, the numerical values of the temperature differences are determined from settings made and dynamically displayed in the dialog. The temperatures T1, T2 are obtained from Table 4.3.10-3 from the settings made. The temperature at the top of the steel beam will also be calculated if the structure type was specified to be 'Steel with concrete deck'. As implemented, for a specified pavement concrete thickness between 0 and 100mm, the temperature difference values are interpolated from those stated in Table 4.3.10-3. For a concrete pavement thickness larger than 100mm, the temperature difference values corresponding to the 100mm thickness from same table are used. The locations of temperature values T1 and T2 within the depth of the superstructure are shown on the following image which replicates JTG D60 2015, Figure 4.3.10 Reproduction of JTG D60 2015, Figure 4.3.10

topics.text: Notes Whilst these codes may suggest suitable or simplified coefficients for studying thermal profiles, in LUSAS the more accurate thermal expansion coefficient of the material that is assigned to each member is used instead. Note that bridge deck grillage sections use both thermal coefficients that are assigned in the bridge deck grillage material. These codes do not explicitly make provisions for a steel-only deck (as used, for example, for a railway bridge). If a structure type of 'Steel with concrete deck” is selected, it is not possible to enter an associated deck thickness of zero for this option since the temperature difference in that case would be uniform through the section. However, if a uniform temperature profile were required for a "steel-only" deck, a very small concrete deck thickness, e.g. 0.001mm could be stated.

topics.title: Implementation notes
toc_path: Temperature profile loading to SP/M/022 Third Edition
headings: Temperature profile loading to SP/M/022 Third Edition
topics.text: Implementation notes Note (i) of Figure 3.3 of the code states: “For structures shallower than 1400mm the two parts of the solid curve are to be superimposed”. As implemented, this has been interpreted as meaning “lay one profile over the other” or overlap, in agreement with other codes of practice, and not in the commonly used engineering translation of superposition (eg. of forces) that translates to adding the two profiles. If the blacktop thickness specified is larger than 100mm, then ty' becomes negative using the design code formula and the positive profile of a deck above enclosed cell reverses. In case that both blacktop thickness> 100mm and the positive profile of a deck above enclosed cell is checked, a warning messageis produced for the improbable large value of the thickness and the temperature gradient is capped at 0.0 to avoid reversal of the profile. If the blacktop thickness is larger than 160mm, then the base temperature T becomes negative for the positive surfaced profiles (the standard positive profile and the one for a deck above enclosed cell). If the blacktop thickness is indeed larger and any of those affected profiles is ticked to be created, an invalid data warning message is produced, preventing saving and use of the data entered.

headings: Bridge deck temperature profile loading to design codes
topics.text: General temperature profile loading For general non-codified use, temperature/strain profile loading can be defined by stating the temperature of the top of the section followed by defining a series of segment thicknesses and corresponding values for the specific height at which the expression is being evaluated. This method also makes it possible to replicate expressions in bridge industry Codes of Practice and define code-specific profiles that are not currently supported elsewhere in LUSAS. See Structural Loading Structural Loading in the Modeller Reference Manual for more details.

headings: Bridge deck temperature profile loading to design codes
topics.text: Implementation notes Whilst individual Codes of Practice may suggest suitable or simplified coefficients for studying thermal profiles, in LUSAS the thermal expansion coefficient of the material that is assigned to each member is used instead. As such it is up to the user to ensure that the correct value is used. Note that bridge deck grillage sections use both thermal coefficients that are assigned in the bridge deck grillage material. Temperature profile loading is limited to vertical temperature variations applied to structural members modelled using line beam elements. It is not possible to assign these load attributes to shell models. Temperature profile loading attributes created according to a specified design code using the 'Bridge > Temperature profiles' menu item cannot be copied. This is an intentional and currently valid restriction. Note however that temperature profile loading attributes created manually using the 'Attributes > Loading > Temperature profiles' menu item can copied. Export/import of temperature profiles is not supported. This is due to the string expressions saved into the attributes which are unit-specific.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview The time management facility provides the means to manage a simple construction schedule and easily adjust the duration of pre-defined construction stages in a staged construction analysis. It can be accessed using the Bridge> Time Management menu item. It can also be accessed from the context menu for each analysis entry in the Analyses Treeview. It can be used to easily and automatically update the total response time values in nonlinear and transient controls that have been previously specified for each loadcase of a staged construction analysis.

topics.title: Stages
topics.text: Stages For time management purposes, a construction stage is considered to be a loadcase in which elements are activated by use of the activate and deactivate activate and deactivate facility. A green 'Plus' symbol in the first column of the grid indicates that a loadcase has been identified as a construction stage (that is, some elements are activated in it). Loadcase This column lists the names of the loadcases that are present in the Analyses Treeview. Age at placement Age at placement This is taken directly from the assigned Age attribute. It is the age at activation time of the members in that construction stage. If for a particular stage of construction multiple concrete segments are added to a structure each with a different age, the word Multiple will appear. Otherwise if each segment had the same age, the single value common to all would be seen instead. Age at shrinkage Age at shrinkage This is taken directly from the assigned Age attribute. The age when shrinkage begins is used to determine the amount of shrinkage taking place in the concrete during construction stages, which excludes the shrinkage before placement. Stage duration The length of time that the loading (as defined in the loadcase) is applied for in this stage. This value can be edited in the time management grid, and if done, will automatically update the total response time value that was previously specified in the nonlinear and transient controls for each loadcase in the Analyses Treeview. Response time A cumulative value measured from the start of the analysis to the end of each loadcase. Notes For loadcases that are considered to be construction stages the age of concrete at placement and curing time will initially be populated from any assigned age attributes. Loadcases in which no elements are activated will also appear in the Stages grid. For these loadcases, which are considered to be an intermediate stage, no values can be provided for the concrete age, since no new elements are born. Only a duration can be provided, and changing this will affect the Response Time of the subsequent loadcases. The units of time displayed in the Time Management dialog are reported in days regardless of the model's timescale units in use. Only whole days are reported because the implementation in this facility of a third-party Gantt chart that only reports in days.

topics.title: Overview
topics.text: Overview Vehicle Load Optimisation is provided for use with selected Bridge software products only, and only for licences that support this facility. Vehicle load optimisation (VLO) makes use of influence surfaces and influence analysis influence analysis to identify the most onerous vehicle loading patterns on bridges for a chosen design code and to apply these loading patterns to LUSAS models. It reduces the amount of time spent generating loadcases to replicate design code-based traffic and lane loading on models and leads to more efficient and economic design, assessment or load rating of bridge structures. It can be applied to grillage, line beam and plate/shell models. Two influence analysis methods are available: the Reciprocal Method and the Direct Method. This general overview of VLO applies to both except where stated.

headings: Performing a vehicle load optimisation analysis
Stage 3: Running a Vehicle Load Optimisation Analysis
topics.text: Stage 3: Running a Vehicle Load Optimisation Analysis Running the Vehicle load optimisation facility requires the selection of a design code, and specifying the influence lines to be used, and the selection of the kerb lines to be used to limit the placement of vehicle loading patterns, and whether loading patterns should be created. It interrogates each influence surface and calculates the critical loading pattern for the chosen effect. Once run, the critical loading pattern can be optionally displayed prior to calculating the effects of the loading on the model. A successful analysis will add a Reciprocal Influence or a Direct Method Influence Analysis entry (depending upon influence attributes used) as well as a VLO Analysis entry (and VLO runs) to the Analyses Treeview. These entries permit viewing of influence shapes and traffic loading patterns prior to solving the model for those loading patterns. Any number of VLO Analysis entries can be created in the Analyses Treeview. Each VLO Analysis entry can contain any number of VLO runs, with each run containing loadcases generated by the vehicle load optimisation software according to the chosen design code and associated settings chosen. Each loadcase comprises vehicle and lane loadings appropriate to the design code selected that, when solved, will generate the most adverse positive or negative loading effect for each of the influence points of interest, as defined on the model. If desired, it is possible to set-up one VLO run to investigate Positive effects and a separate run to investigate Negative effects, or they can be combined into one run, all within the same Analysis. VLO runs can be copied and pasted between different VLO analyses.

topics.title: Superposition
toc_path: Performing a vehicle load optimisation analysis
headings: Performing a vehicle load optimisation analysis
topics.text: Superposition Vehicle Load Optimisation software supported by LUSAS inherently uses the principal of linear superposition. In a linear static analysis this assumption holds true for all results components that are calculated by a LUSAS Solver, but note that it does not hold true for some results components that are post-processed by LUSAS Modeller. For example, Wood Armer calculations are not linear calculations, therefore superposition is not safe for these. Similarly, the definition of any user-defined results components (that can be used in the definition of a Direct Method influence) may include equations with terms or constants that are not scalable.

topics.title: Optional Loading Parameters
toc_path: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
topics.text: Optional Loading Parameters The following parameters are available for selection: Longitudinal increment specifies the increment used when moving the abnormal vehicle along the carriageway. The smaller the increment the more accurately the effects of the vehicle across the structure are calculated, giving more accurate results. A larger increment gives quicker VLO runs, but with less accuracy. A generally suitable default value is provided, but users can specify an alternative value based upon experience. Transverse increment specifies the increment to be used when positioning the vehicle across the carriageway. The smaller the increment the more accurately the effects of the vehicle across the structure are calculated, giving more accurate results. A larger increment gives quicker VLO runs but with less accuracy. Care should be taken to ensure that the transverse increment stated will enable a load to sit up against a kerb for certain lane types. A generally suitable default value is provided, but an alternative value can be specified as necessary. Vehicle Direction specifies the vehicle direction which is used to calculate the effects of each vehicle. Vehicle axles are defined from the leading axle. Forward means the vehicle is run in a forward direction along the carriageway from the starting point of the carriageway. Reverse means the vehicle is run with the normally trailing axle leading along the carriageway from the starting point of the carriageway. Both means both cases are run. For an asymmetric vehicle, either forward or reverse could produce the greatest effect, dependent upon the shape of the influence surface and the increments used. The default is both directions.

topics.title: Defining Carriageways
toc_path: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
topics.text: Defining Carriageways Lines defining the width of the carriageway must be present in the model and selected. Where lines already represent the edges of a structure, or the centreline of a carriageway, lines representing the width of a carriageway can be easily added using the Geometric> Line> By offsetting menu item. Note that these lines do not have to form a structural part of the model. Once done the following parameters are available for selection: Kerb positions - define the width of each carriageway. Note that it is not possible to define kerb positions via tabular input. Kerb from Selection - The kerb positions of carriageways are defined by selecting those lines defining the kerbs on either side of a carriageway in the view window prior to accessing the Vehicle Load Optimisation dialog. Straight lines, arcs or a combination of these two feature types can be used and selected to describe the extent of the carriageway. Multiple sets of carriageways can be defined by selecting multiple sets of those lines defining the extent of each carriageway.

topics.title: Permissible kerb arrangements
toc_path: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
topics.text: Permissible kerb arrangements Pairs of straight lines defining kerb positions must be parallel, and the start and end points of each kerb must be orthogonally opposite each other. Pairs of arcs defining kerb positions must be concentric and have the same subtended angle Consecutive straight lines and arcs can be used to define kerb positions but opposite pairs of lines that define the kerb positions must of the same type, that is, either both straight lines or both arcs, and not a mixture. Consecutive straight lines and arcs must be tangential. Using only consecutive straight lines to define kerb positions is invalid unless the intersection points are filleted. Kerb lines should lie in a common plane. For bridge decks with a variable longitudinal vertical profile (such as a vertically curved deck) a primary (X,Y), (Y,Z) or (Z,X) plane must be used. For bridge decks with a constant longitudinal vertical profile (such as a horizontal or inclined bridge deck) the kerb lines may lie in a primary plane or in the same plane as the bridge deck. Kerb lines must be transversely within the limits of any Direct Method Influence grid, if one is used during influence attribute assignment. Valid kerb arrangements showing the resulting loadable regions in darker shading are shown: Straight kerbs Curved kerbs Straight and curved kerbs - opposing pairs of lines and arcs are of the same type) Definition of multiple sets of carriageways

topics.title: Setting-up Influence Surfaces
toc_path: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
topics.text: Setting-up Influence Surfaces The List of available influences shows all assigned influence attributes influence attributes for the model. These can be included in a vehicle load optimistion analysis en-mass, or by individual selection. Note that any coincident influence assignments are not shown. The following additional settings can be made: Include all influence surfaces - selects all the influence surfaces in the model for use in the vehicle load optimisation. Magnification factor (for AASHTO LRFD 7th Edition Louisiana (June 2016) only) is provided if the option “Apply magnification factor (LADV-11 loading)” is chosen from the Optional Code Settings dialog. A different magnification factor is needed for each influence because it depends on the span length, and on whether the influence is Positive moment, Negative moment, Shear, Bearing reaction, Factored support reaction or Service support reaction, as per LRFD Bridge Design Manual No 2 (June 2016) table in section A.3.6.1.2. L (m) (for Sweden TDOK 2013:0267, some Sweden rail codes, and EN1991-2 Denmark 2015 only) This is an option to introduce the length (in model units) of the influence used. For use in calculation of the dynamic factor. Positive and/or Negative Vehicle loading can be placed on either Positive or Negative areas by checking the Positive or Negative (or both) checkboxes for each of the included influences. Note that clicking in the header cell of a column will select the whole column so that checking (ticking) one entry in the column will check (tick) all entries in that column. Selection of multiple columns is also possible. Alternative load pattern (for AASHTO LFD Standard Specifications clause 3.11.3, AASHTO LRFD clause 3.6.1.3.1, and Korean lane loads on continuous spans only). When the column is checked, the influence surface referred to in that row of the grid will be treated as set out in the clauses mentioned above - an option suitable for negative moments between points of contraflexure or reactions of interior piers. Checking the box will use two concentrated (knife edge) loads per lane (LFD) or two trucks per lane (LRFD) in the load pattern generation (other rules in the referenced clauses relating to spacing and reduction factors are included, as appropriate also). Search Area to be used for reciprocal analysis - The search area choice applies only to the assignments of reciprocal influences. Direct method influence assignments will automatically use the search area (if any) of the direct method influence analysis in which the influence attribute was assigned. Use of a search area will restrict the applied vehicle loading to a specified portion of the model. If a search area is not specified the generated vehicle loading will be projected onto the whole model ("Default"). For models where multiple intersections of the load projection occur it is necessary to restrict the loading to the required face using a search area.

topics.title: Solution Process Options
toc_path: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
topics.text: Solution Process Options View onerous effects table Shows tabbed and sorted results for all chosen influences at nodes that are visible, with the most onerous result shown in the first row of the table. Displayed results can be filtered by subsequently selecting features or mesh objects of interest. For more information see Onerous Effects Table Onerous Effects Table below. Create loading patterns To run a Vehicle Load Optimisation analysis with optimised loading select this check box, selecting either the All chosen influences option, which generates loads and loadcases for all chosen influences; or the Most onerous option, where for each influence attribute the loads and loadcases are only generated for the influence assignment that gives the most onerous effect. For both options, loading entries are created in the Attributes treeview and an entry is created in the Analyses Treeview under the corresponding VLO Run. To visualise the loading patterns a loadcase must be set active and appropriate loading visualisation settings loading visualisation settings made. Create envelopes When 'Create loading patterns' is selected this option becomes available. Envelopes can be created By design case or By influence and design case . The Analysis name provided creates an appropriate entry in the Analyses Treeview. Note that an analysis can contain up to 1000 VLO Runs. Separate user-defined analysis entries can be created to hold different VLO Runs using the 'New' analysis option on the drop-down menu for the Analysis entry, but for speed of solving, note that it is more beneficial to have all VLO Runs contained within one analysis. The Vehicle Load Optimisation Name is used to identify each VLO Run. Short names are recommended since VLO Run names are used to create filenames that also include the influence name and coordinate and element details, and if collectively this is too long, the Windows path limit of 260 characters may be exceeded. See File and folder naming in LUSAS File and folder naming in LUSAS for details. When the OK button is pressed LUSAS will carry out the influence surfaces analysis and run a vehicle load optimisation analysis based on the country design code selected. The results from the analysis will be loaded into the LUSAS model in readiness for the model to be solved using the Solve Now Solve Now button on the main toolbar. When the model is solved for any selected onerous vehicle loading arrangements, the results from the analysis will be seen in the relevant Vehicle Load Optimisation entry in the Analyses Treeview. Notes For models with numerous influence assignments of the same type, potentially un-necessary load generation can be avoided, and solution time can be saved, by ensuring that ‘Create loading patterns’ is not selected on the main VLO dialog, to allow for only the most onerous loading patterns to be created from the subsequent VLO onerous results table listings. The time taken to evaluate critical vehicle loading effects for a structure depends upon the design code in use; the types and numbers of vehicles to be considered; the number of lanes; whether any remaining areas exist after lane loading is positioned according to particular design codes; the number of spans; the mesh size; the values used for longitudinal and transverse load increments; whether one-way or two-way vehicle direction is specified; and the number of influence points to be evaluated. A good assessment of the time that will be required to evaluate a particular loading scheme for a large number of influence points can be achieved by initially timing how long it takes for just one influence point to be evaluated and factoring by the number of influences required.

topics.title: Onerous Effects Table
toc_path: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
topics.text: Onerous Effects Table When a VLO analysis is run, a VLO onerous effects table can be optionally displayed which shows sorted results for all chosen influences at nodes that are visible, with the most onerous result shown in the first row of the table. For Direct Method Influences these values are due to traffic loading for the specified load effect of interest at specified locations on the model. That is, a single value direct from the LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation facility, without the need for a further static solution. If, for Direct Method Influence attributes only, coincident effects for selected components have been requested, these will also be present in the table. In the onerous effects table a results tab is present for each <Influence attribute – Sign – Design Case> group listed. This group is referred to as an 'Influence Design Loadcase'. Load patterns can be created on a case-by-case basis if not already created by means of the 'Create loading patterns' setting on the main VLO dialog. On each results page, the following column headings are present: Influence Assignment The location (coordinate and feature/object type) of the assigned DMI or Reciprocal Influence attribute. Node The node at which the assignment was made. Note that the Find context menu option for the cells in this column will, when clicked, highlight the corresponding node in the model View window by animating concentric shrinking squares. This easily identifies the assignment location. ' Chosen results effect ' For Direct Method Influence, this column is named after the result entity component selected in the DMI attribute (e.g. Mx, Fz, etc); the values in this column show the effect of the traffic loads at locations of interest. For reciprocal influences, the column is named according to the influence type (i.e. Shear/Moment/Reaction/Displacement). Caused by states the name of the loading type which produced the most onerous effect. Create loading Creates loading entries in the Attributes Treeview and a loadcase in the Analyses Treeview that cause the onerous effect listed. If the option to ‘Create loading patterns’ was chosen on the main VLO dialog, Loading folders will additionally appear for each influence loadcase added to the Analyses Treeview, and the VLO results table will show ‘Loading created’ alongside all influence assignment entries. If ‘Create loading patterns’ was not selected on the main VLO dialog the most onerous loading effects can be created individually by using the ‘Create Loading’ button that appears instead of the ‘Loading Created’ one. For the influences where no loading is produced by LUSAS VLO (because for the specified location there aren’t any loads that can be placed to produce an adverse effect), the 'Chosen results effect' and 'Caused by' cells will be empty.
topics.search_text: Onerous Effects Table Vehicle Load Optimisation Wizard Application Manual (Bridge, Civil and Structural) Bridge Loading Vehicle and Traffic Load Optimisation Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation Onerous Effects Table Bridge Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation Wizard.htm Onerous Effects Table When a VLO analysis is run, a VLO onerous effects table can be optionally displayed which shows sorted results for all chosen influences at nodes that are visible, with the most onerous result shown in the first row of the table. For Direct Method Influences these values are due to traffic loading for the specified load effect of interest at specified locations on the model. That is, a single value direct from the LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation facility, without the need for a further static solution. If, for Direct Method Influence attributes only, coincident effects for selected components have been requested, these will also be present in the table. In the onerous effects table a results tab is present for each <Influence attribute – Sign – Design Case> group listed. This group is referred to as an 'Influence Design Loadcase'. Load patterns can be created on a case-by-case basis if not already created by means of the 'Create loading patterns' setting on the main VLO dialog. On each results page, the following column headings are present: Influence Assignment The location (coordinate and feature/object type) of the assigned DMI or Reciprocal Influence attribute. Node The node at which the assignment was made. Note that the Find context menu option for the cells in this column will, when clicked, highlight the corresponding node in the model View window by animating concentric shrinking squares. This easily identifies the assignment location. ' Chosen results effect ' For Direct Method Influence, this column is named after the result entity component selected in the DMI attribute (e.g. Mx, Fz, etc); the values in this column show the effect of the traffic loads at locations of interest. For reciprocal influences, the column is named according to the influence type (i.e. Shear/Moment/Reaction/Displacement). Caused by states the name of the loading type which produced the most onerous effect. Create loading Creates loading entries in the Attributes Treeview and a loadcase in the Analyses Treeview that cause the onerous effect listed. If the option to ‘Create loading patterns’ was chosen on the main VLO dialog, Loading folders will additionally appear for each influence loadcase added to the Analyses Treeview, and the VLO results table will show ‘Loading created’ alongside all influence assignment entries. If ‘Create loading patterns’ was not selected on the main VLO dialog the most onerous loading effects can be created individually by using the ‘Create Loading’ button that appears instead of the ‘Loading Created’ one. For the influences where no loading is produced by LUSAS VLO (because for the specified location there aren’t any loads that can be placed to produce an adverse effect), the 'Chosen results effect' and 'Caused by' cells will be empty.

headings: Design codes supported by LUSAS Vehicle Load Optimisation
Viewing, filtering and saving onerous effects tables
topics.text: Viewing, filtering and saving onerous effects tables VLO onerous effects results tables can be re-displayed for all influences at any time by selecting the View table results... context menu for a VLO Run entry in the Analyses Treeview. A table for a single particular influence can be created by double-clicking on the relevant onerous results table entry in the Analyses Treeview. Results displayed in the tables can be filtered by selecting features or mesh objects of interest in the view window. So, for instance, with table results displayed in one view window, it is possible to select a line representing a span in a bridge in the model view window and have the results table only display the results for the nodes in the elements within that line. Similarly it is possible to select a surface representing a span of a slab and view only the results for the nodes in the elements within that surface. Use the Window > Tile facilities to see the onerous results table data and model view window side-by-side. Column data can be sorted by clicking on column headers. Table results for an active table can be saved to a spreadsheet using the File > Save as Microsoft Excel menu item.

topics.text: Usage Once the onerous effects for each 'Influence Design Loadcase' have been obtained, and if the option to ‘Create loading patterns’ was not chosen on the main VLO dialog, the corresponding loading will need to be created on a case-by-case basis, if not already done. Whilst generated loading patterns can be visualised, results are available only after the VLO analysis has been solved. Once solved, the resulting loadcases should be combined with self weight and factored accordingly to create design combinations.

topics.title: Smart Combination (Utilities menu)
topics.text: Smart Combination (Utilities menu) Defines a smart combination which enables results to be factored and combined for results processing. Once defined, combinations are contained in the Analyses Treeview . Each smart combination is made up of two entries in the Analyses Treeview . The maximum entry contains the most adverse positive effects and the minimum entry the most adverse negative effects. Unlike basic combinations smart combinations require you to define either a benficial and adverse factor, or a permanent and a variable load factor. The beneficial or permanent factor is applied to all results components but the adverse or variable factor is only applied if the effect of the chosen result component is more adverse. Shortcut Right - click menu in the Analyses Treeview

topics.title: Cycle Feature
topics.text: Cycle Feature Changes the selected geometry definition order by a specified number of cycles. In this example, the original Surface defined by Lines L1, L2, L3 and L4 is shown in grey. Cycling by 1 permutation changes Surface definition to L2, L3, L4, L1. Cycle 2 defines Surface as L3, L4, L1, L2 and cycle 3 defines Surface as L4, L1, L2, L3. Surface normal directions remain consistent throughout. Note, it is not the Lines that change, but the Surface definition order, i.e. 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th. The Surface local axes is defined from the first Line in the Surface definition.

topics.title: Selection Tool
topics.text: Selection Tool Selection Tool Used to select parts of the model by clicking on a feature, or by dragging a box around an area. The type of feature selected can be filtered using one of the drop buttons. Note. To select multiple features hold the Shift button down whilst clicking on each feature. To deselect a selected feature hold the Control button down whilst clicking on the feature. Drop Buttons To display the drop buttons right - click on the button. The normal cursor will select anything, i.e. Points, Lines, Surfaces, Volumes, (nodes and elements). The other cursors are all specific to a certain geometry type, i.e. the Line cursor can only select Lines, the Surface cursor only selects Surfaces and the mesh cursor only selects mesh. Note. The Select Feature cursor selects only Points, Lines, Surfaces and Volumes. The Select Mesh cursor selects only Nodes and Elements.

topics.title: Spline by tangent vectors (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Spline by tangent vectors (Geometry Menu) Defines a Spline passing through two or more selected Points. The end directions are defined by entering end tangent vectors. In this example Line 1 is defined by specifying Points 1;2 and inputting start and end tangents by vectors (1, 0, 0) and (0, -1, 0) respectively. Both the direction and length of the end tangents control the spline shape. In this example, a different shape of spline would be defined, passing through the same Points, if the end tangents were changed to (3, 0, 0) and (0, -0.5, 0) respectively. Shortcuts Drop tool (Smart Line)

topics.title: Geometry (Attributes Menu)
topics.text: Geometry (Attributes Menu) Defines a new Geometric Properties dataset. Geometric properties are used to describe geometric attributes which have not been defined by the feature geometry, for example: Plate/Membrane/Shell Elements If a structure is modelled using shell elements, the third dimension out of plane is undefined. This is specified by a geometric property dataset containing the element thickness about a nodal plane. Eccentric behaviour can also be specified for certain element types. See the LUSAS Element Reference Manual for details of the geometric property input for each element type. Bar/Link Grillage Thin/Thick Beam Elements structures modelled using bar or beam elements require section properties to be defined. These are defined in a geometric property dataset and assigned to the underlying Line features. Click here Click here for more information.

topics.text: Line by coordinates (Geometry Menu) Defines a Line by entering the X, Y and Z coordinates (Z is optional). Two coordinates define a straight Line, three or more define a Spline. If a non - Cartesian local coordinate system is in use the coordinates are specified in the coordinate system of that local coordinate set. Coordinates can be entered using global (default) and local coordinate systems. Shortcuts Drop tool (Smart Point)

topics.text: Line by intersecting Surfaces (Geometry Menu) Defines a Line where 2 or more selected Surfaces intersect. Surfaces may be intersected in pairs by adding the first set to memory. Intersections may be full or partial, but only ruled or analytical Surfaces can be intersected. Intersected features can be split and deleted if required. In this example a Spline is defined where two cylinders intersect. Shortcuts Drop tool (Smart Line)

topics.text: Lines by joining sets of Points (Geometry Menu) Defines a number of Lines by joining two sets of Points. The first set defines the start of each Line, the second set defines the end of each Line. Add the first set of Points to memory , select the second set with the cursor. The Points should pair up equally. Lines are joined according to the order in which the Points were selected, (or Point number when boxing a selection), i.e. first point in memory joins to first point selected with cursor ,etc. In this example, add Points 1 to 3 to memory, then select Points 4 to 6. Lines 1 to 3 will then be defined. Shortcuts Drop tool (Smart Line)

topics.title: Discrete loading
topics.text: Discrete loading Discrete loads (typically point and patch loading) are used to distribute a given loading pattern over a number of geometric features. Therefore they are independent of the model geometry (different to Structural Loads which are feature dependent). Also known as General Loads. Click here Click here for more information.

topics.title: Structural Loading
topics.text: Structural Loading Structural loads are assigned to geometric features and are effective over the whole of the feature to which they are assigned. This is different to Discrete loads which are used to distribute a given loading pattern over a number of geometric features and which are independent of the model geometry. topics.title: Local coordinates (Attributes Menu)
topics.text: Local coordinates (Attributes Menu) Defines a new Local coordinate axes. Local Coordinate datasets contain coordinate systems that differ from the default global Cartesian system. Local coordinate datasets have three uses in LUSAS: Feature Definition They may be defined and activated when entering coordinates in place of the global coordinate system. When a local coordinate system is active, all dialog entries relating to global X, Y and Z coordinate input use the transformed axis set as a basis for input. Transforming Nodal Freedoms when assigned to features the effect is to transform the degrees of freedom on the mesh on those features. This has the effect of transforming the directions of applied global load and support conditions. As an example, global freedoms are transformed to radial directions by assigning a cylindrical coordinate set to the Lines around the hole. This method of transforming nodal freedoms is only valid for small deflections, since the freedom directions are not updated during analysis. Note that this affects Concentrated and Global distributed loads (both tabulating CL loads), does not affect 'Body Force' and 'Stress and Strain' loads, and is not applicable for Face loads. Results Transformation when activated during post - processing results output directions can be altered to lie in the local coordinate system axes. Note that this affects Concentrated and Global distributed loads (both tabulating CL loads), does not affect 'Body Force' and 'Stress and Strain' loads, and is not applicable for Face loads

topics.title: Manifold Surface (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Manifold Surface (Geometry Menu) Existing Surfaces may be projected or laid onto an existing Surface. A Surface to be projected onto is placed into Selection Memory and the Surface to be projected is then selected prior to choosing the Geometry> Surface > By Manifolding menu item. The new Surface is created normal to the selected item (in selection memory) and will lie on the map of the underlying Surface.

topics.title: Manifold by points (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Manifold by points (Geometry Menu) Defines a Line on an existing Surface, (added to selection memory), between two specified Points. The Points can be, but do not have to be, on the boundary of the Surface. In the example Points 7 and 8 lie within the Surface boundary, while Points 13 and 14 lie on the boundary. Points 9 to 11, 15 and 16 are created during the manifold process.

topics.title: Fatigue Loadcase (Analyses menu)
topics.text: Fatigue Loadcase (Analyses menu) Defines a Fatigue Loadcase which enables previously defined S - N curves and fatigue spectra to be combined. Only available when a linear analysis results file is open and when S - N curves and fatigue spetra have been defined. Also, fatigue calculations can only be carried out for continuum elements. Once defined, Fatigue Loadcases are contained in the Loadcases section of the Analyses Treeview. Click here Click here for more information.

topics.title: Point by cursor (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Point by cursor (Geometry Menu) Allows you to define a series of Points on the screen using the cursor. The Points can snap to grid at a predefined Z plane, or to existing Lines or Surfaces (Surfaces must be ruled or analytical). This facility is useful for positioning Points on Lines or Surfaces for later splitting the Line or Surface. Tip. When placing the Points use ruler and the Status bar coordinate display for guidance. Right - click to cancel the Point by cursor command.

topics.text: Point by coordinates (Geometry Menu) Defines a Point by entering the X, Y and Z coordinates (Z is optional). If a non - Cartesian local coordinate system is in use the coordinates are specified in the coordinate system of that local coordinate set. Coordinates can be entered using global (default) and local coordinate systems. The dialog box labels will be updated to reflect the required coordinate input. Shortcuts Drop tool (Smart Line)

topics.title: Point by intersecting lines (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Point by intersecting lines (Geometry Menu) Defines a Point at the intersection of two selected Lines. Intersection is limited to straight lines and arcs. Selecting a group of Lines creates Points at all valid intersections. When the Lines selected do not physically intersect, an attempt is made to locate intersections on the projected lines (as shown in the diagram right), but if two lines intersect in more than one place the command is not executed. Arcs are projected in a circular path. Shortcuts Drop tool (Smart Point)

topics.title: Selection Memory (Edit Menu)
topics.text: Selection Memory (Edit Menu) Provides options to put selected objects into memory, and add to, remove from, recall, clear, or report on the state of the memory. Can also be accessed from the view window by right-clicking and selecting from the resulting context menu. Examples of using selection memory are geometry definition where two unique sets of features are required to be selected (prior to joining features by creating new features), or where features are used to define a transformation dataset (moving, copying or sweeping features). See also Selecting model features Selecting model features

topics.title: Section Through 3D (Utilities menu)
topics.text: Section Through 3D (Utilities menu) Allows a section of a 3D model to be cut using the cursor. Sections are taken vertically or horizontally, rotate the model first if required. LUSAS creates a group containing the section. Results can be visualised on the section in the usual way. To view results on the section only right - click the model in the group Treeview and switch off Show results , then switch this on for the section. Click here Click here for more information.

topics.title: Split line by cursor (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Split line by cursor (Geometry Menu) Splits an existing Line into two new Lines of the same type by indicating the splitting position with the cursor. This method is for use when the position of the intermediate Point does not need to be specified exactly. Split Lines defining a Surface may be deleted and replaced by a Combined Line. In the example shown here Line 1 is split at a position indicated by the cursor and Lines 2 and 3 are created.

topics.title: Split line by points (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Split line by points (Geometry Menu) Splits an existing Line into two new Lines at a selected Point on the Line. Arcs can only be split using a Point on the arc. In the example shown here Line 1 is split at Point 3 to create 2 new Lines. If required, the original Line feature can be deleted after splitting has occurred. Split Lines defining a Surface may be deleted and replaced by a Combined Line. A splitting tolerance can be set to increase the distance that a splitting Point can be from a straight Line being split.

Split Lines defining a Surface may be deleted and replaced by a Combined Line. In the example shown Line 1 is split into 4 new Lines of equal length, and the original Line is deleted.

topics.title: Split line by parametric coordinates (Geometry Menu)
toc_path: Split line by parametric coordinates (Geometry Menu)
headings: Split line by parametric coordinates (Geometry Menu)
topics.text: Split line by parametric coordinates (Geometry Menu) Splits an existing Line into a number of divisions based on specification of parametric distance values along the Line. Split Lines defining a Surface may be deleted and replaced by a Combined Line. The direction of the existing line is used to calculate the splitting positions. A new line is created at each division. In this example Line 1 is split at a parametric distance of 0.75. Line 2 is created at 3/4 of the original length and Line 3 at 1/4. Specification of a parametric divisions list as 0.1;0.5;0.75 will split a line at 1/10, 1/2 and 3/4 distance into 4 new lines.

topics.text: Split surface by cursor (Insert menu) (Geometry Menu) Splits a selected Surface at two boundary positions indicated by the cursor. A new Line will be manifolded onto the existing Surface and the Surface will be split at this Line. In the example shown here, Surfaces 2 and 3 are created in the parametric space of the original Surface using cursor locations on the boundary. The new Line is manifolded onto the original Surface.
