topics.text: Table content explained The results table consists of a summary page and separate tabbed pages for each of the design checks requested in the RC Slab/Wall Design RC Slab/Wall Design loadcase/results dialog. Detailed results for any selected row are also available. All results tables contain information describing the location of each check (line, element/inspection location, node/internal point/index, section) and, when relevant, any internal forces used in the check (load, primary component, internal forces (Fx, My, Mz)). Utilisation values of greater than 1 are coloured red to identify over-utilised sections. A colour coded column at the right of the grid also provides an indication of utilisation capacities for each section location, with colours of grey, green, yellow, orange and red used when utilisations are under 0.7, from 0.7 to 0.8, 0.8 to 0.9, 0.9 to 1.0, and over 1.0 respectively. Clicking in a column header will sort the data in that column according to its content. Note that the column names and results listed are dependent upon the settings made in the RC slab/wall design attribute dialog for each code. Tooltips for each column header provide additional information, including references to applicable clauses.

topics.text: Summary results The summary page table shows the location of the check (the section number, surface number, element and node (or inspection location), and the utilisations of the section at the stated location for each design check. topics.text: Enveloped results The enveloped results table contains information describing the location of the checks, the types of check, and provides the following results: Util(As) - Maximum utilisation of reinforcement out of all checks. This excludes the utilisation of the maximum reinforcement requirement, since the action that the user has to take differs if the reinforcement is more than required or less than required. Util(Max(As)) - Maximum utilisation of the maximum reinforcement check (if check exists). Util(TC) - Maximum utilisation of tension control. Not available for Clark-Nielsen. Util(Sc) - Maximum utilisation of concrete stress among all checks. Util(CC) - Maximum crack control utilisation (if SLS crack control check selected). Util(Max) - Maximum overall utilisation for each location.

topics.title: Table content explained
toc_path: RC Slab/Wall Tabulated Results and Calculations
Tabulating RC Slab/Wall Design results for NZS 3101-1:2006 and NZTA Bridge Manual v3.3
headings: Tabulating RC Slab/Wall Design results for NZS 3101-1:2006 and NZTA Bridge Manual v3.3
topics.text: Table content explained The results table consists of a summary page and separate tabbed pages for each of the design checks requested in the RC Slab/Wall Design RC Slab/Wall Design loadcase/results dialog. Detailed results for any selected row are also available. All results tables contain information describing the location of each check (line, element/inspection location, node/internal point/index, section) and, when relevant, any internal forces used in the check (load, primary component, internal forces (Fx, My, Mz)). Utilisation values of greater than 1 are coloured red to identify over-utilised sections. A colour coded column at the right of the grid also provides an indication of utilisation capacities for each section location, with colours of grey, green, yellow, orange and red used when utilisations are under 0.7, from 0.7 to 0.8, 0.8 to 0.9, 0.9 to 1.0, and over 1.0 respectively. Clicking in a column header will sort the data in that column according to its content. Note that the column names and results listed are dependent upon the settings made in the RC slab/wall design attribute dialog for each code. Tooltips for each column header provide additional information, including references to applicable clauses.

headings: Tabulating RC Slab/Wall Design results for SABS 0100-1 (Ed. 2.2)
topics.text: Table content explained The results table consists of a summary page and separate tabbed pages for each of the design checks requested in the RC Slab/Wall Design RC Slab/Wall Design loadcase/results dialog. Detailed results for any selected row are also available. All results tables contain information describing the location of each check (line, element/inspection location, node/internal point/index, section) and, when relevant, any internal forces used in the check (load, primary component, internal forces (Fx, My, Mz)). Utilisation values of greater than 1 are coloured red to identify over-utilised sections. A colour coded column at the right of the grid also provides an indication of utilisation capacities for each section location, with colours of grey, green, yellow, orange and red used when utilisations are under 0.7, from 0.7 to 0.8, 0.8 to 0.9, 0.9 to 1.0, and over 1.0 respectively. Clicking in a column header will sort the data in that column according to its content. Note that the column names and results listed are dependent upon the settings made in the RC slab/wall design attribute dialog for each code. Tooltips for each column header provide additional information, including references to applicable clauses.

topics.text: Summary results The summary page table shows the location of the check (the section number, surface number, element and node (or inspection location), and the utilisations of the section at the stated location for each design check. For each location the maximum utilisation calculated from the loadcases included in the RC Slab/Wall Design loadcase is provided. The following results are provided: Util(ULS) - Maximum utilisation for the 'ULS' check. This only appears if the ULS check on the RC Slab/Wall design results dialog is ticked. Util(Asmin,Asmax) - Maximum utilisation for the 'Min-max reinforcement' check. Util(CC) - Maximum crack control utilisation. Util(Max) - Maximum utilisation from all checks carried out.

Tabulating RC Slab/Wall Design results for SABS 0100-1 (Ed. 2.2)
headings: Tabulating RC Slab/Wall Design results for SABS 0100-1 (Ed. 2.2)
topics.text: Enveloped results The enveloped results table contains information describing the location of the checks, the types of check, and provides the following results: Util(As) - Maximum utilisation of reinforcement out of all checks. This excludes the utilisation of the maximum reinforcement requirement, since the action that the user has to take differs if the reinforcement is more than required or less than required. Util(Max(As)) - Maximum utilisation of the maximum reinforcement check (if check exists). Util(TC) - Maximum utilisation of tension control. Not available for Clark-Nielsen. Util(Sc) - Maximum utilisation of concrete stress among all checks. Util(CC) - Maximum crack control utilisation (if SLS crack control check selected). Util(Max) - Maximum overall utilisation for each location.

topics.title: Overview
toc_path: Reinforced Concrete Slab and Wall Design
headings: Reinforced Concrete Slab and Wall Design
topics.text: Overview Design code checking of reinforced concrete slabs and walls can be carried out for a specified design code. This includes Strength/ULS and SLS checks based on flexural, twisting and in-plane effects, shear, stress limits, minimum and maximum areas of reinforcement and crack widths or spacing considerations as appropriate. Design checks are performed as a results processing operation following the solving of a model and requires the assignment of reinforced concrete material, reinforcement arrangements, design code specific RC slab/wall design attributes, and results transformation attributes to surfaces in the model that represent concrete slabs or walls. The use of reinforced concrete materials and reinforcement arrangements is for design check calculations only. The reinforced concrete material comprises both a "section" material (concrete) and a "reinforcement" material (steel). When this material is assigned to features in a model, it is the "section" material which is used for analysis, along with the section properties as defined by the corresponding Geometric Attribute. Contours and values that indicate utilisations based on flexural, twisting and in-plane effects, shear and concrete stresses at Ultimate Limit State (ULS), and design crack widths, concrete stresses and reinforcement stresses at Serviceability Limit State (SLS) can be plotted or tabulated for design codes that support these calculations. Maximum and minimum quantities of reinforcement can also be obtained. The calculations carried out are for reinforced concrete slabs or walls (without prestressing) that are modelled using plate or shell elements. For ULS, both bending only (using a Wood-Armer approach) and bending and in-plane effects (using a Clark-Nielsen or a Sandwich model approach) can be considered, according to design code. For SLS, both bending-only (using principal moments), and bending and in-plane effects (using principal stresses) can be considered, if supported by a chosen design code. RC slab/wall design is available for use with selected Bridge and Civil software products only, for licences that support this facility.

topics.title: Meshing and analysis considerations
toc_path: Reinforced Concrete Slab and Wall Design
headings: Reinforced Concrete Slab and Wall Design
topics.text: Meshing and analysis considerations Surfaces representing reinforced concrete slabs and walls must be assigned a surface mesh, which has to be plates (2D) or shells (3D), both of which support transverse (local z-direction) loading. Membrane elements (3D), plane stress and plane strain elements (2D) are not supported by the RC Slab/Wall designer. Section capacity checks for selected slabs/walls can be carried out at nodes (for averaged or unaveraged results) or at inspection locations. For averaged nodal results Modeller's averaging rules will apply to ensure that, for example, there is no averaging at a jump in section thickness, at a support, a change in material etc. Whilst any number of elements could be assigned to a surface, using an excessive element assignment will increase the time required to carry out the design checks.

topics.text: Carrying out a reinforced concrete slab/wall design check For a model that is otherwise complete in all respects, that is, a linear static analysis with the appropriate loads and design (factored) load combinations in place, the following steps are required to carry out a design check of reinforced concrete slabs/walls that are modelled with plate or shell elements. Specify the design code Specify the design code to be used for the design attribute and eventual check by selecting the Design> RC Slab/Wall Design menu item. Define reinforced concrete material Define reinforced concrete material and assign to all surfaces representing reinforced concrete slabs or walls Define the slab/wall reinforcement Define the slab/wall reinforcement and assign to each slab/wall for which that reinforcement arrangement is applicable. Define results transformation attributes Define results transformation attributes and assign to each slab / wall to transform the results according to reinforcement directions. Define RC slab/wall design attributes Define RC slab/wall design attributes These provide design code related information and should be assigned to all surfaces representing slabs or walls. Specify the results required Specify the results required and the loadcases/combinations upon which each ULS/SLS check will be carried out by selecting the Design > RC Slab/Wall Design Results menu item. View the design check results View the design check results either on the model by using contours or values layers, or as "Table Results", and as rendered calculations for a selected surface or location using the "Design Calculation Viewer".

topics.title: Notes
toc_path: Reinforced Concrete Slab and Wall Design
Carrying out a reinforced concrete slab/wall design check
headings: Reinforced Concrete Slab and Wall Design
Carrying out a reinforced concrete slab/wall design check
topics.text: Notes The top and bottom faces of a slab (or the faces either side of a wall) are defined by the surface axes, with surface normal (a positive local z-direction) representing 'top', therefore it is helpful if axes for each type all point in the same respective directions. Because slab/wall reinforcement details and RC slab/wall design attributes have no impact on a structural analysis they can be defined and assigned either before or after a model has been initially solved. However, a Concrete (Reinforced) material is necessary for design, and since it could have a different "Section" material from any material previously assigned to surfaces in the model, when it is assigned, the analysis results are considered invalid until re-solved. When carrying out RC slab/wall design checks, the units used to create a model are automatically converted into units required by the design code chosen for the design check. The modelling units of the model itself are not changed. This would allow for a model to be constructed in US imperial units, and a design check on that model to be made to a metric design code, or vice-versa. If RC slab/wall design calculations are based on a moment field (Mx, My, Mxy) only, users should ensure that in-plane effects are not significant, since slab/wall design based upon Wood-Armer components may be unconservative in this case. See Background to RC Slab/Wall Calculations Background to RC Slab/Wall Calculations for additional information.

topics.text: RC slab/wall design attributes Reinforced concrete slab/wall design attributes are used to specify additional information about the design checks (information that is specific to the Code of Practice and to the slab or wall to which they are assigned in the model). Attributes are defined using the Attributes> Design> RC Slab/Wall Design... menu item, which is available in Bridge and Civil software products only, and for licences that support this facility. Prior to defining a design attribute a supported RC slab/wall design code supported RC slab/wall design code must have been chosen. Typical information defined in a RC slab/wall design attribute includes: Calculation methodology Parameters for stress limitation and crack control Minimum reinforcement ratios Creep parameters Once defined, an RC Slab/Wall Design attribute entry is created in the Attributes Treeview ready for assignment to selected surfaces representing concrete slabs or walls in a model.

topics.text: Specify the RC slab/wall design results required Use the Design> RC Slab/Wall Design Results menu item to bring together loadcases / combinations appropriate to specific design checks and identify slabs for which calculations are required, along with other calculation options. One or more RC Slab/Wall Results objects must be created in order to view graphical or tabular results from design check calculations. The settings available on the dialog are described here. On completion an RC Slab/Wall Design loadcase / results container entry is created in the Analyses Treeview. Multiple RC Slab/Wall Design results loadcases can be defined enabling design calculations to be carried out for different extents (surfaces) within a model, at different locations on or within a surface, and for chosen load groups and design checks. For example, by using the groups groups facility, and setting up an RC Slab/Wall results entry for individual spans or for all slabs at one level in a model and a separate entry for any walls would limit the number of design checks to be carried out each time a change is made and a design check is requested.

topics.text: Notes: For a design check selection of 'Averaged Nodal' or 'Unaveraged Nodal', colour-filled line contours can be viewed. These can also be drawn on fleshed sections. For a design check selection of 'Inspection Locations', a colour-filled spot contour plot is produced showing the value of the chosen component at each node. When making changes to geometric attributes a re-solving of the model will normally be necessary since, as an example, when a slab thickness is modified its weight is also modified. However, to test a modification the design object can be set active in order to have the RC Slab/wall results updated for the revised thickness, giving an idea of the utilisation with the new thickness albeit using the existing moments and shears etc. This may be helpful to indicate whether the change in thickness is likely to have the desired effect. A re-solve following a change to a geometric attribute will show the actual result of that change. When making changes to reinforcement quantities there is no need to re-solve the model; the RC Slab/Wall Design calculations will be automatically re-run according to the changes made. RC slab/wall design checks cannot be carried out if geometric properties used in different analyses that are set-up within a single model are in conflict.

topics.text: Notes Slab /wall design results are calculated for x and y' axes, where y' is measured from the x axis according to the skew angle of the reinforcement specified in the RC Slab/Wall Reinforcement RC Slab/Wall Reinforcement attribute. Values and results contours for a chosen results component can be displayed for a previously chosen Code of Practice. Results are based on the active loadcase (or combination), using the results transformation assigned to each surface. Results are re-computed if a different loadcase is set active. Values and results contours are only available for surfaces assigned with all required design check related assignments. If the ULS calculation for bending with in-plane forces is based on Clark-Nielsen, then this can be shown to be inaccurate if in-plane forces are negligible. In addition it provides no guarantee that the section is "tension controlled" and no check for this is carried out since forces at the top and bottom faces are calculated separately. Design results are considered to be "Derived Components" in LUSAS. This means they may be computed for smart combinations only when a valid primary component is selected. Valid primary components are any of the corresponding thick beam stress resultants Fx, Fy, Fz, Mx, My, Mz. For more on derived components see Raw and Derived Components Raw and Derived Components .

topics.text: Creating a Member Report Use the Design > RC Frame Design > Member Report menu items to generate and display reports of all calculations carried out for a previously selected member or members. Three options are available: Table Results... - displays tabulated results for only the selected surface(s). This, in effect, provides the same results as those obtained when tabulating the results for the model as a whole, but only calculates and displays the results for the selection made. Selected Surface... - displays a member report for a single selected surface, which allows viewing of all calculations for the most critical location i.e. the one with the highest utilisation within the surface selected. Specified location... - generates and a displays a report of calculations carried out for particular location, namely a surface number, element number or node number.

topics.title: Lateral torsional buckling in non-prismatic sections
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
Lateral torsional buckling in non-prismatic sections
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
Lateral torsional buckling in non-prismatic sections
topics.text: Lateral torsional buckling in non-prismatic sections AASHTO requires that lateral torsional buckling be assessed for the largest value of flange stress within an unbraced length (6.10.1.6). The composite bridge design checks are carried out at discrete locations where slice resultants are computed. Users should ensure that sufficient design locations are specified to capture this maximum stress. Where a section is not prismatic this maximum stress must be assessed against the minimum capacity within the unbraced length (6.10.8.2.3 & A6.3.3). If the section is deemed to be non-compact, LUSAS will assess the LTB capacity for each section in accordance with 6.10.8.2.3 and use the minimum capacity for each design location using a moment gradient modifier (Cb) of 1.0. Where the section is compact however LUSAS cannot assess the capacity for all sections because some of these sections may be non-compact/slender and therefore the rules of appendix A6 do not apply. In this case LUSAS will resort to using the rules of 6.10.8.2.3 and results will therefore be conservative. It should be noted that for tapered sections the capacity is evaluated at each end of the braced length (as well as the design locations) and the minimum used in both cases. It is noted that this is a very approximate method and therefore a warning is issued to users for further investigation.

topics.title: Overhang bending
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Overhang bending During construction of a composite bridge deck external steel beams can be subject to a torsion resulting from “deck overhang” loads. These loads result in lateral bending of the flanges that need to be considered. In a shell model these values may be included by slicing forces from elements defining the member flanges. In a 2D model however this is not possible. An approximation has been included in which the torsional moment in the beam maybe resolved into equivalent forces at the top and bottom flanges. These forces are assumed to be uniformly distributed between brace points from which a lateral moment is computed as wl 2 / 12 as per equation C6.10.3.4.1-2. Whilst this is optional the approach is somewhat approximate since the resulting lateral forces depend on the arrangement of the deck overhang bracket. This option should therefore be used with caution.

topics.title: Axial forces
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Axial forces The rules for composite bridge deck design in AASHTO in bending are valid with an axial force up to 5% (9th Edition) or 10% (8th edition) of the axial capacity of the section, after which case members should be designed as compression members (see commentary clause C6.10.6.1 in both editions). LUSAS composite bridge deck design checks will include axial force in the stress calculations but no check is performed to ensure they are below the threshold of 5% or 10% of the axial capacity according to the code in use. It is therefore the user’s responsibility to ensure that this is the case.

topics.title: Shear connection strength design
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Shear connection strength design The strength design for shear connectors is carried out for lengths of the member considered to be positive bending and negative bending. AASHTO provides equations for determining the force over a positive bending region and a negative bending region but simplifies the design into two regions in the span, from the end support to maximum positive bending and from maximum positive bending to the interior support. The force over the first “shear span” is that arising from positive bending, the force over the second “shear span” is determined from the positive + negative forces. Rather than determining these lengths from the slice results, a ratio of the end span to the point of maximum bending can be entered. For interior spans it is assumed that the span is divided equally in two with each “shear span” comprising negative and positive forces. See also: Composite Bridge Deck Design Composite Bridge Deck Design

topics.title: Stiffened girders
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
topics.text: Stiffened girders CSA-S6-14 defines rules for a stiffened plate girder additional to a normal beam or girder. Typically this means a fabricated girder which includes a slender web requiring stiffening. In LUSAS the user identifies whether a girder is considered stiffened or not via the fabrication type on the material dialog. This allows for the design a stiffened girder without actually defining stiffeners everywhere.

topics.text: ULS Shear connection ULS shear connection verifies that the number of shear connectors within a given “shear span” is sufficient. A shear span is defined as a length of span between a maxima and zero point of bending. The user defines these ratios on the Shear span dialog. The user also defines a series of “stud runs”, in the member dialog, which are lengths of span consisting of similar shear studs at a given spacing. The shear connection check therefore must resolve how many shear runs are in a shear span to determine exactly how many studs are present in the shear span and the corresponding capacity. The calculation may be a little confusing at first because it refers to proportions of stud runs. For example: We define a single stud run in the member dialog, 3 studs per row at 521mm centres for the entire span. For an end span we have 3 shear lengths with the following span ratios 0.4, 0.4, 0.5. For the first shear span we therefore take 0.4 x the number of studs in the stud run, so too for the second and 0.5 for the third (the third being the hogging region). If the studs were defined in a number of runs you can see it would be possible for a shear length to overlap a number of stud runs and therefore the rendered output reflects this by considering a ratio contribution of each stud run.

topics.text: Stepped sections Stepped sections are locations where two sections of different sizes are joined either by welding or splicing. CSA-S6-14 provides no guidance on computing buckling capacities of members with such transitions so the program simply calculates the capacity at the given design location. It is therefore recommended that design locations be specified at segment ends to ensure that design checks are carried out for each section.

topics.title: Shrinkage effects
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
topics.text: Shrinkage effects The primary effects resulting from shrinkage strain are computed for a slab with an effective modulus of concrete adjusted for creep at the same age as the shrinkage strain is computed. The examples in CISC however apply two additional factors to this approach (c=0.5 and χ=0.73) which reduces the effect considerably. The resulting restraining force computed in LUSAS is 5% different to that of the example but is thought to be more in keeping with the requirements of the bridge code, rather than inferring methodology from elsewhere. The crack widths calculation defines parameter kc as either 0.5 for bending or 1.0 for pure tension. Example calculation use the 0.5 value on the basis that the whole section is in bending but arguably this is wrong since the slab is actually in pure tension. The option has been given to the user to decide. Additionally it is unclear whether short term or long term properties should be used to evaluate stresses at initial cracking. The CISC example ignores this part of the calculation, and hence the option “simplified value of rebar strains” is provided to match this. LUSAS implementations would normally use long term properties in crack widths calculations but there are occasions when the short term properties lead to a worse case as a result of the higher forces required to crack the softer concrete. For this reason the option has been given to the user.

topics.title: Bearing stiffeners

headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
topics.text: Bearing stiffeners Bearing stiffeners are only designed for the vertical reaction. This assumes that the members are sufficiently braced to transfer any lateral forces through a bracing system rather than bending of the stiffeners. They are currently limited to symmetrical stiffeners on both sides of the web although it is noted that is only a preference in the code (10.10.8.2).

headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
topics.text: Loadcases and primary components Where the selected loadcases contain smart combinations and/or envelopes, LUSAS automatically applies the primary components to generate multiple loadcase variations. For section design each loadcase will be considered with primary components for Fz and My in max and min variations. Where the top flanges are to be sliced independently to determine the most onerous lateral bending effects a Mz primary component in used. For intermediate stiffener design, only Fz is considered since the shear value is the only component in the design check. For bearing stiffener design the global FZ reaction component is used.

topics.title: Biaxial bending
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN/CSA S6-14
topics.text: Biaxial bending For straight bridges CSA-S6-14 does not explicitly define any requirements for consideration of biaxial bending however clause 10.10.3.5 provides a simple equation for capacity of a section bent about the minor axis. Where this occurs in LUSAS (discretely braced members) the utilisation of the vertical bending effects have been combined with the utilisation of the lateral bending effects. This is consistent with the approach in the CISC examples and is considered to be conservative. This check is always applied to bottom flanges but may be ignored for top flanges on the basis that restraint may exist to prevent this lateral deflection. This is not the same as preventing buckling however and the LTB check will still be carried out if this option is selected. For curved girders the interaction is handled in the dedicated section on curved girders 10.13. For beam models the value of lateral bending is taken simply as the beam lateral bending, beam torsion is ignored. Hence for a beam model the user must add in a lateral load to represent any expected bottom flange bending during construction. In a 3D shell model this will be handled more precisely by slicing the beam flanges to accurately determine any lateral flange bending.

toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN CSA S6-14 and CAN CSA S6-:19
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN CSA S6-14 and CAN CSA S6-:19
topics.text: Stiffened girders CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19 define rules for a stiffened plate girder additional to a normal beam or girder. Typically this means a fabricated girder which includes a slender web requiring stiffening. In LUSAS the user identifies whether a girder is considered stiffened or not via the fabrication type on the material dialog. This allows for the design of a stiffened girder without actually defining stiffeners everywhere.

topics.text: Loadcases and primary components Where the selected loadcases contain smart combinations and/or envelopes, LUSAS automatically applies the primary components to generate multiple loadcase variations. For section design each loadcase will be considered with primary components for Fz and My in max and min variations. Where the top flanges are to be sliced independently to determine the most onerous lateral bending effects a Mz primary component is used. For intermediate stiffener design, only Fz is considered since the shear value is the only component in the design check. For bearing stiffener design the global FZ reaction component is used.

topics.title: Biaxial bending
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN CSA S6-14 and CAN CSA S6-:19
headings: Implementation Notes for Composite Bridge Deck Design Checks to CAN CSA S6-14 and CAN CSA S6-:19
topics.text: Biaxial bending For straight bridges CSA-S6-19 does not explicitly define any requirements for consideration of biaxial bending however clause 10.10.3.5 provides a simple equation for capacity of a section bent about the minor axis. Where this occurs in LUSAS (discretely braced members) the utilisation of the vertical bending effects have been combined with the utilisation of the lateral bending effects. This is consistent with the approach in the CISC examples and is considered to be conservative. This check is always applied to bottom flanges but may be ignored for top flanges on the basis that restraint may exist to prevent this lateral deflection. This is not the same as preventing buckling however and the LTB check will still be carried out if this option is selected. For curved girders the interaction is handled in the dedicated section on curved girders. See 10.13. For beam models the value of lateral bending is taken simply as the beam lateral bending, beam torsion is ignored. Hence for a beam model the user must add in a lateral load to represent any expected bottom flange bending during construction. In a 3D shell model this will be handled more precisely by slicing the beam flanges to accurately determine any lateral flange bending.

topics.text: Code options User specified modular ratio By default the modular ratio is computed from the selected materials Long term reinforcement reduction factor for cracked section This option allows a cracked section to be reduced for the effects of creep. A reduction factor is applied to the area of reinforcement in long term properties. This is not required by the design code nor is it considered standard practice but it is used in the FHWA examples and therefore has been included as an option. Ignore reinforcement in positive moment plastic capacity Option to consider a more conservative design by neglecting reinforcement in the plastic capacity calculated in accordance with appendix D6.1 Do not calculate Cb, always take as 1.0 The Cb factor accounts for the shape of the bending moment over the unbraced length and increases the buckling capacity when the moment varies substantially. A preliminary or conservative design may ignore this benefit. Supports are skewed less than 20 degrees Appendix A6 can be used to determine the bending capacity of non-slender sections in straight bridges with skews less than 20 degrees. This option must be selected to indicate that this condition is met. LUSAS will then determine the section classification and use Appendix A6 as appropriate. If a conservative design is required this option can be left unchecked (unticked) and the section capacity will be based on elastic stresses. Cross bracing is contiguous and parallel to supports (6.10.6.2.3) Ensure this check box is ticked for this situation. Appendix A6 can be used to determine the bending capacity of non-slender sections in straight bridges with contiguous bracing. This option must be selected to indicate that this condition is met. LUSAS will then determine the section classification and use Appendix A6 as appropriate. If a conservative design is required this option can be left unchecked (unticked) and the section capacity will be based on elastic stresses. Projected 75 year single lane Average Daily Truck Traffic (ADTT) SL Define a value for average daily truck traffic. This value is used in fatigue design checks.

topics.title: Grillage/Beam model options
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Grillage/Beam model options These options are only applicable for beam models. For shell models the flange groups should be defined and lateral effects taken from the model. Use approximation from C6.10.3.4.12 for deck overhang loads in constructibility . This approximates lateral bending effects that occur during construction from a wet concrete deck overhanging an edge girder. The approach is to calculate an equivalent lateral force from the torsion in the girder and use the equation for lateral bending in C6.10.3.4.1-2 to calculate bending over the unbraced length. This approximate approach should only be used with beam models, in shell models the option to use flange lateral bending from the model should be used instead. Use approximation from C.4.6.1.2.4b-1 for lateral bending in curved structures . Curved structures exhibit twisting due to the differential bending of the members. Twisting is resisted by the structure through the bracing system which results in lateral bending of I girder flanges. In grillage/grid models these forces are not represented and therefore clause C4.6.1.2.4b-1 provides an approximation based on the radius and magnitude of vertical bending.

topics.text: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility The Design> Composite Bridge Deck Design Results menu item is used to identify the design members for which calculations are required and brings together the loadcases / combinations appropriate to the various limit state checks, and from which tabulated results can be viewed. On completion, a Composite Bridge Deck Design results utility is created in the Utilities Treeview. Multiple Composite Bridge Deck Design results utilities can be defined allowing member design calculations to be carried out in isolation from other design members within a model. If differential effects such as shrinkage and temperature profiles need to be considered, these need to be added into the composite bridge deck design calculations prior to viewing results. See Including self-equilibrating stresses and temperature loading Including self-equilibrating stresses and temperature loading within this topic for details.

topics.text: Design members Composite design members Composite design members that have been defined for the model are listed in the design members panel. Whilst multiple members may be listed (named as External Girder, Internal Girder, Internal Girder 2 etc.), it is suggested that, since each member will typically have loading specific to that member, only one member is chosen for each results utility created. If done, the time taken to carry out the design checks will be kept to a minimum. If more than one design member is chosen they will share a results utility and the time taken to carry out the design checks will be increased.

Whilst multiple members may be listed (named as External Girder, Internal Girder, Internal Girder 2 etc.), it is suggested that, since each member will typically have loading specific to that member, only one member is chosen for each results utility created. If done, the time taken to carry out the design checks will be kept to a minimum. If more than one design member is chosen they will share a results utility and the time taken to carry out the design checks will be increased.

topics.title: Deck pour sequence
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
topics.text: Deck pour sequence To allow constructability design checks to be carried out, the deck pour sequence must be defined. Each stage represents the casting of a section of the deck slab and is mapped to a pre-defined named group of elements representing these elements. These groups will typically have been created as part of creating the model. This information is used to determine whether a design location is considered composite for a given stage of construction, and if so, appropriate design checks for the loadcases specified are carried out according to settings made on the Construction Loadcases tab. Use the Add button to add a stage to the Deck pour sequence, and select a group that represents that stage. The Delete button will remove a selected row.

topics.title: Construction Loadcases
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
topics.text: Construction Loadcases Construction loadcases defined for the model should be mapped to each stage of construction as specified in the design results utility for each member to be designed. Each loadcase that is mapped should be a fully factored design combination as required by the design code. By default a single stage of 'Steel Only' exists. Additional stages that are defined on the Members tab are available for selection in the Stage drop list. Construction loadcases are only used for constructability design checks and are not carried through to final design. They represent the various temporary stages of construction where stresses may be reversed and where sections are unstable before the concrete deck has cured. Select a Member and a Stage from the drop-lists, and a Construction loadcase, and Use the Add button to create an entry for all three. The Delete button will remove a selected row.

topics.title: In Service Loadcases
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
topics.text: In Service Loadcases In Service loadcases represent loading applied to the fully constructed bridge. Three limit states are considered - service, fatigue and strength, and appropriate loadcases (with the correct factors applied to those loadcases) must be assigned to each limit state. Service Factors for all phases are based upon the requirements of table 3.4.1-1. Fatigue Phase 1 and Phase 2a are based upon the requirements of clause 6.10.5.3 and require unfactored permanent loads. Strength Factors for all phases are based upon the requirements of table 3.4.1-1.

topics.title: Phases
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
topics.text: Phases There are three phases of loading in a composite bridge: Phase 1 is the loading applied to the steel structure before it acts compositely with the deck slab. Typically this is the weight of the steel and the weight of the wet concrete. These forces are carried by the steelwork alone. Phase 2 is the permanent or long term loading that is carried by the composite section. The composite section properties are adjusted for the effects of creep in this phase. The phase is split into two sub phases '2a' and '2b'. Phase 2a represents the permanent loading acting on the composite section Phase 2b represents the permanent effects induced by shrinkage of the concrete. The section properties are computed from an age-adjusted modulus defined by the creep parameter determined in the shrinkage calculation. It is therefore dependent on the time at which shrinkage is being considered. The self-equilibrating stresses arising from such loading are computed and included in the design checks. Phase 3 is the variable or short term loading that is carried by the composite section. The composite section properties are computed using the short term modulus of concrete. Phase 3 is also divided into two sub phases: '3a' and '3b'. Phase 3a represents temperature effects. The self-equilibrating stresses for this loading are computed and included in the design checks. Phase 3b represents transient short term loading, such as traffic and wind.

headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
topics.text: Name On the main Composite Bridge Deck Design dialog specify the name of the Composite Bridge Deck design results utility entry to be created in the Utilities Treeview. Note that appropriate primary components of My and Fz will be automatically considered to optimise for bending and shear. In addition, where slice resultants are requested for flanges, a primary component of Mz will be used to optimise the lateral flange bending effects. This is independent of the main primary component My or Fz.

topics.title: Including shrinkage stresses and temperature loading
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
Including shrinkage stresses and temperature loading
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
Including shrinkage stresses and temperature loading
topics.text: Including shrinkage stresses and temperature loading Differential effects such as shrinkage and temperature profiles cause self-equilibrating stresses in a composite section. In a beam model these stresses are not included in the analysis but in a shell model these effects can be captured. The design forces used in the composite deck design calculations are taken from beam shell slice results, and the section stresses for design are recomputed from the slice resultants. So, for either a beam-only model, or for a beam and shell model the self-equilibrating stresses need to be added into the composite bridge deck design calculations as described below.

topics.title: Shrinkage stresses
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
Including shrinkage stresses and temperature loading
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Defining a Results Utility
Including shrinkage stresses and temperature loading
topics.text: Shrinkage stresses In order for the composite bridge deck design facility to calculate the self-equilibrating effects from shrinkage, a design code-specific shrinkage load attribute must be created and assigned to relevant features in a model. This load can then be assigned to lines in the model that have been assigned Bridge Deck (Grillage) Bridge Deck (Grillage) geometric attributes (which define the section types), or to the surfaces (meshed with shell elements) representing the deck slab in a 3D mixed element model. Note that the assignment of a single shrinkage load attribute should be made to the loadcase that is referenced on the In Service Loadcases In Service Loadcases tab for Phase 2b. The shrinkage load attribute is used to calculate the strain in the slab and corresponding self-equilibrating stresses in the section. These stresses are then added to the secondary effects computed in the analysis. See Shrinkage profile loading to design codes Shrinkage profile loading to design codes for more details.

topics.text: Temperature loading In order for the composite bridge deck design facility to calculate the self-equilibrating stresses for design, a design code-specific temperature profile attribute must be created and assigned to relevant features in a model. A temperature load can then be assigned to lines in the model that have been assigned Bridge Deck (Grillage) Bridge Deck (Grillage) geometric attributes (which define the section types), or to the surfaces (meshed with shell elements) representing the deck slab in a 3D mixed element model. Note, however, in the latter case the temperature profile is only applied to the deck slab, and this will be incorrect where the profile extends into the steel girder. In this case equivalent temperature loads would need to be applied to the elements of the steel girder. Variations Variations , which allow parameters in attributes to be varied over the assigned geometry, may be of use in these instances. If necessary, contact LUSAS technical support for more details. See Temperature profile loading to design codes Temperature profile loading to design codes for more details. headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member Composite Bridge Deck Design members are defined by selecting the Utilities > Bridge Design > Composite Design Member menu item. They are created automatically when a bridge model is generated using the Steel Composite Bridge Wizard Steel Composite Bridge Wizard when bridge design materials are specified for all I-girder utilities. Composite deck design members typically represent a run of longitudinal beams over a number of spans of a bridge deck, and are used to carry out design checks on that member according to a supported design code.

headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Defining span lines A composite deck design member must reference lines from which the individual span lengths will be determined. These span lengths are then used in specifying design locations along the member and hence the corresponding slice locations on the model. Lines representing span lengths can be defined above a model or be created in-plane with other features. Examples are shown below for a three span grillage, and for a three span curved composite deck created using the Steel Composite Bridge Wizard. Span lines (highlighted in black) created above a grillage model defining a single composite design member Span lines (highlighted in black) created at bridge deck level defining four composite design members Note that a group named 'Girder span lines', that contains the lines representing the position of all girders in each span is automatically created by the Steel Composite Bridge Wizard Steel Composite Bridge Wizard when a bridge model is generated, is added to the Groups treeview. By selecting 'Set as only visible' from its context menu, the individual lines comprising each composite deck member (as shown below) can then be selected to isolate and define each composite design member in turn. Individual girders can also be 'Set as only visible' in the treeview in the same manner. Selection of a set of three span lines to define a single composite design member

topics.text: General information When the lines defining a composite design member are selected, as the design member is being defined a schematic image at the top of the dialog will update to show the locations of spans, bracing, web stiffeners, shear connectors and design locations. Each is drawn in a different colour. See the relevant tab details that follow for more information. Add , Insert , Copy and Delete buttons allow for adding and editing of rows on some tabs. With the exception of span lengths that are shown on the General Arrangement tab, length or positional values defined on other tabs can be specified with respect to Parametric distances or Actual distances . The default and recommended setting is 'Actual distances'. Note that this radio button setting applies to the dialog as a whole and should not be changed when specifying data on each tab. topics.title: General arrangement
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: General arrangement The general arrangement tab is used to identify the span lines in the model that define the slice path along which the results will be created, as well as the element groups that constitute the composite member being defined. Span lines The 'Span lines' panel defines the slice path along which results for the design member will be created. Span line IDs and span lengths are populated automatically if lines representing the named composite design member are selected in the model prior to entering this dialog. Alternatively, span lines may be selected whilst the dialog is open by choosing appropriate lines and pressing the Selection button. to update the span line ID details and span lengths. This removes all previous data in the span line table. Add Adds the line ID of a selected line in the model to the bottom of the span line table. Insert Inserts a row in the span line table above the selected row. Delete Deletes the selected row. Element groups The design member must reference a group containing all the elements that constitute the member in the bridge model. The group is used to define the extents of the beam/shell slicing when extracting results for this member. An effective slice width may be additionally specified, the centre of which is defined by the member line. For 3D models constructed in beam and shell elements, additional groups can be specified for the top and bottom girder flanges, and if the model was additionally created by the steel composite bridge wizard these will be created automatically. When specified these groups will be used to extract lateral bending moments from the flanges to accurately calculate warping stresses in the flanges as required in supported design codes. Horizontal radius By default the horizontal radius is determined from the span lines at each design location. This can be overidden if it is required to see the effect on the design of using a different radius. Care must be taken to ensure the member line axes are orientated correctly, that is, the local element z axes are aligned with the global Z axis. The vertical bending moment in the design calculations is taken as the beam shell slice component My and shear is taken as Fz, hence it is important that the correct axis is defined as the vertical axis.

A segment represents a length of span that is defined by a constant or tapered cross-section.

topics.title: Span segments
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Span segments For each span of the named bridge design member, the sections that comprise each segment of each span, their material and length over which each section applies must be specified. Design Sections are either selected from the drop-list (if previously created) or are defined by selecting the New Section.... button, which displays the Bridge Deck (Grillage) geometric attribute Bridge Deck (Grillage) geometric attribute dialog. Sections defined may be of constant or tapered section. Stepped sections can be accommodated but it is recommended that each segment is defined explicitly in the member dialog rather than being specified indirectly as a multi-varying section. This way each section has a unique reference. If the model has been created by the Steel Composite Bridge Wizard Steel Composite Bridge Wizard and bridge design material was requested to be created on its Composite I-Girder Section dialog, unassigned Design Sections will be present in the Attributes treeview and will be listed here for selection. Design Materials are either selected from the drop-list (if previously created) or defined by selecting the New Material.... button, which displays the Bridge Design Girder Material Bridge Design Girder Material dialog. For beam models the design material definition for the design check partly duplicates the material defined for the 'analysis model', however this does allow for design materials to be changed to investigate the effects of making those changes without affecting the analysis results. Note that the Design Material column is removed if 'Member for export to Composite deck design EC4' is selected. Segment Length requires the lengths of each segment to be stated.

topics.title: Bracing
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Bracing The Bracing tab is used to define whether flange bracing is discrete or continuous, and to specify where it occurs. Discrete bracing is represented on the schematic design member by blue filled circles at each bracing location. Continuous bracing is represented on the schematic design member by blue horizontal lines of the length specified. Bracing Type Discrete bracing points represent positions on the design member where the compression flange is braced. Bracing is assumed to be similar to both top and bottom flanges and is applied at member ends by default, so any bracing specified is for intermediate bracing runs only. Where a member is continuously braced this will be reflected in design calculations by neglecting instability calculations at that location. Unbraced lengths elsewhere are determined between points of bracing that are continuous or discrete. Bracing is specified by entering a Start of run and End of run position along the span, additionally stating the number of braces occurring in that length for Discrete bracing.

topics.title: Intermediate stiffeners
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Intermediate stiffeners Intermediate web stiffeners are represented on the schematic design member by vertical magenta lines. Stiffener Sections are either selected from the drop-list or defined by selecting the New Stiffener... button, which displays the Bridge Design Transverse Stiffener Bridge Design Transverse Stiffener dialog. Web stiffener spacing is specified by entering a Start of run and End of run position along the span and the Number of stiffeners at that position. Web stiffener spacings are not only used for design of stiffeners but also for the design of the web and allow the program to calculate the web panel aspect ratio and slenderness parameters.

toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Bearing stiffeners Bearing stiffeners are represented by vertical green lines at each support location. Stiffener Bearing stiffeners are either selected from the drop-list or defined by selecting the New Stiffener... button, which displays the Bridge Design Transverse Stiffener Bridge Design Transverse Stiffener dialog. Bearing stiffeners must be specified with reference to a point in the model from which the reactions will be taken for the bearing stiffener design. If bearing stiffeners are omitted, no bearing stiffener design checks will take place.

topics.title: Shear Connectors
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Shear Connectors Design checks carried out assume that the section is composite throughout regardless of the definition of any shear connectors. Shear connectors are assumed to be studs rather than channel or any other connection type. Start and end distances of stiffener runs are specified with respect to the start of each span. Multiple extents of stiffeners may be defined by adding extra rows to the table and specifying appropriate start and end values. At each design location the relevant shear connector details will be used. If no studs are specified at a given location then the shear connector checks will be omitted but the section is still considered to act compositely for other design checks. Shear connectors are represented on the schematic design member by dotted horizontal purple lines within the slab showing the length over which they apply.

topics.title: Design locations
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Design locations Design locations are the locations along the design member where design checks will be carried out. There are two types: Section design locations - where section design checks are carried out. These can be specified to be at the start and end of each segment, and /or at bracing locations. Stiffener design locations- where stiffener design checks are carried out. These may be added at stiffener locations. Additional section design locations can be added throughout the member measured from the start of each span, or spaced evenly as required. Section design locations are represented on the schematic design member by vertical red dotted lines. Stiffener design locations at intermediate stiffener locations are shown by vertical magenta lines.

topics.title: Section design locations
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Section design locations For each specified section design location additional slices will be automatically taken through the unbraced length of girder to determine moment shapes. See notes for details. Section design locations can be specified: At segment ends On by default. When selected, section design checks are carried out at these locations. At bracing locations Off by default. When selected, section design checks are carried out for the girder only.

topics.title: Additional section design locations
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Additional section design locations Add, Insert and Delete buttons allow additional design locations to be specified, and edited. Specify location An absolute value measured from the start of the stated span. Specify spacing A relative value measured from the start of the stated span. Specify number Includes locations at the start and end of the stated span. Note that for these specified locations, section design checks are only carried out for the girder, and not for any stiffeners that may coincide with a specified location. Ensure that 'Slice locations for stiffener design' is selected if design checks are required for any stiffeners at coincident locations.

topics.text: Stiffener design locations For intermediate stiffener design, locations must have been specified on the Web stiffeners Web stiffeners tab. Slice locations for stiffener design Off by default. When selected, design checks are only carried out for the stiffener. Note if a stiffener location coincides with a section design location, but the 'Slice locations for stiffener design' check box is not ticked, a section design check is only carried out for the main girder at that location.

topics.title: Note
toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
topics.text: Note For each section design location six slice locations are automatically created. These represent the positions of the nearest bracing locations and the quarter points between them as well as the actual design locations itself. These slice locations are used to determine the shape of the bending moment diagram over the unbraced length as well to compute the maximum lateral bending in the flanges. Note that unlike manually defined slice locations, these automatically created locations will not have an associated entry in the Utilities Treeview. The creation of these slices is solely controlled by accessing the Composite Design Member dialog for each defined girder. Name Once named and created, the composite design member is added to the Utilities Treeview, and additionally a Composite Design Member tab is added to the Utilities layer properties dialog, which provides control of visualisation of design members.

toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
Visualisation of beam/shell slice locations on the model
headings: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
Visualisation of beam/shell slice locations on the model
topics.text: Visualisation of beam/shell slice locations on the model Slices are created for each design location specified and interpolated locations. By default, slice local axes, planes and labels are drawn in red, but these and other visualisation settings relating to slice axes, slice planes and slice labels can be specified from the Utilities layer properties dialog, which is accessed from the Utilities entry in the Layers Treeview. On the corresponding LUSAS model the size of the drawn slice plane representing a design location depends upon the elements that are sliced. For 3D models, slices will have a width and height. For 2D grillage-type models, and models that only use 3D beams, no slices will be visible since the design locations specified effectively represent a single 'point' on the model. In these cases only slice local axes and slice labels can be viewed. topics.title: Viewing composite bridge deck design results
toc_path: Viewing composite bridge deck design results
headings: Viewing composite bridge deck design results
topics.text: Viewing composite bridge deck design results To view results for a previously specified design code, in the Utilities Treeview right-click on a composite bridge deck design result utility and select the Show results context menu item. Design checks are carried out immediately with progress being shown in the text output window, if active. On completion, values are displayed in a tabular format, in a series of named tabs. Note that the design checking facilities convert all model units into those required by the design code selected for the design check, and all results are reported in those units. As a result is possible to define a structure in imperial units and carry out a design check to a non-imperial design code, or vice-versa. topics.title: Longitudinal shear
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19
topics.text: Longitudinal shear Area of transverse deck reinforcement (per unit length) The total area of transverse reinforcement per unit length in the deck slab. Note that this assumes a consistent transverse reinforcement arrangement throughout the bridge deck. Selecting the Shear span definitions... button Design of longitudinal shear connection is carried out for a shear span. This is defined as the length of span between zero and “peak” bending (positive and negative). Hence there are 3 shear spans for an end span and 4 shear spans for an internal span, however these are considered symmetrical and therefore only two are effectively considered. where: S1 ratio of span length from zero to maximum sagging moment in the end spans S2 ratio of span length from maximum to zero sagging moment in the end spans H1 ratio of span length from maximum to zero hogging moment in the end spans S3 ratio of span length from support to zero sagging moment in the internal spans S4 ratio of span length from zero to maximum sagging moment in the internal spans H2 ratio of span length from maximum to zero hogging moment in the internal spans

topics.text: Code options User specified modular ratio By default the modular ratio is computed from the selected materials. Override moment factor omega2 for Mu calculation The omega2 factor takes into account the shape of the bending moment over the unbraced length. This may be overridden to produce a more conservative design for lateral torsional buckling. Ignore biaxial bending in the top flange during construction of straight members. Covers the situation where sufficient restraint is provided to the top flange such that lateral bending effects can be ignored. This is not the same as restraint against lateral torsional buckling which will still be checked. In curved girders this is not applicable where biaxial bending is always considered. Effective length factor (K) for bearing stiffeners (10.10.8.3) . This is the “k” factor applied to the bearing stiffener length to determine the axial buckling capacity. It must be greater than 0.75 as per clause 10.10.8.3.

topics.title: Grillage/beam models
toc_path: Composite Bridge Deck Design - CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19
topics.text: Grillage/beam models Use approximation for lateral bending in curved structures (10.13.6.1.2) Curved structures exhibit twisting due to the differential bending of the members. Twisting is resisted by the structure through the bracing system which results in lateral bending of I-girder flanges. In grillage/grid or beam models these forces are not represented and therefore clause 10.13.6.1.2 provides an approximation based on the radius and magnitude of vertical bending. The equation for flanges continuous over one point of restraint is always applied conservatively. This option is only really applicable for beam models. For shell models the flange groups should be defined and lateral effects taken from the analysis model.

topics.title: Export to Eurocode Composite Design
topics.text: Export to Eurocode Composite Design The Design> Export to Eurocode Composite Design menu item is used to identify the design members for which calculations are required and brings together the loadcases / combinations appropriate to the various limit state checks, from which tabulated results of interest can be exported. On completion, an 'Export to Composite Deck Design EC4' results utility is created in the Utilities Treeview. Multiple results utilities can be defined allowing member design calculations to be carried out in isolation from other design members within a model. From the results provided by LUSAS, design checks can be carried out in the Composite Deck Designer (Ponti EC4). Refer to the separate User Manual for this software option for details of the design checks available.

topics.title: In Service Loadcases
topics.text: In Service Loadcases In Service loadcases represent loading applied to the fully constructed bridge. Three limit states are considered - service, fatigue and strength, and appropriate loadcases (with the correct factors applied to those loadcases) must be assigned to each limit state. Service Factors for all phases are based upon the requirements of EN 1990 6.5.3 (2a) for SLS Characteristic and EN 1990 (2b) for SLS Frequent. Fatigue Factors for all loadcases are based upon the requirements of EN 1992-1-1 6.8.3 Strength Factors for all phases are based upon the requirements of Fundamental ULS combination from EN 1990 6.4.3.2 (3)

topics.title: Phases
topics.text: Phases There are three phases of loading in a composite bridge: Phase 1 is the loading applied to the steel structure before it acts compositely with the deck slab. Typically this is the weight of the steel and the weight of the wet concrete. These forces are carried by the steelwork alone. Phase 2 is the permanent or long term loading that is carried by the composite section. The composite section properties are adjusted for the effects of creep in this phase. The phase is split into two sub phases '2a' and '2b'. Phase 2a represents the permanent loading acting on the composite section Phase 2b represents the permanent effects induced by shrinkage of the concrete. Phase 3 is the variable or short term loading that is carried by the composite section. The composite section properties are computed using the short term modulus of concrete. Phase 3 is also divided into two sub phases: '3a' and '3b'. Phase 3a represents temperature effects. Phase 3b represents transient short term loading, such as traffic and wind. Use the Add... button to access the following dialog and select a loadcase from those available for assignment to a chosen phase of construction. Note that for smart combinations and envelopes, only a single entry is listed, but when this is selected both 'Max' and 'Min' versions of the loadset will be considered. The Edit... button will display the same dialog for a selected row. The Delete button will remove a selected row.

toc_path: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member
Composite Bridge Deck Design - Girder Material
headings: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Girder Material
topics.text: Composite Bridge Deck Design - Girder Material Girder material for design checking use can be defined by using the Utilities > Bridges Design > Girder Material... menu item, or by selecting the New... drop-list option from within the Segments tab of the Composite Design member Composite Design member dialog. Specifying and referencing 'girder design material' for a girder in a composite design member provides the additional data required to carry out design checks for that member to the chosen design code. Slab concrete strength, reinforcement grade, and the type of shear connectors must be specified. Girder fabrication can be Rolled or Welded. For design codes CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19 the choice of welded girder fabrication will cause the design to consider the girder as a “Stiffened plate girder” as per the code regardless of the presence of stiffeners. Hybrid sections are supported for design codes AASHTO 8th and 9th Editions, allowing different steel grades to be assigned to the top flange, web or bottom flange of a girder. Once created, a girder material utility is added to the Utilities Treeview. See also: Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member Defining a Composite Bridge Deck Design Member

topics.title: Summary results
toc_path: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Summary results The Summary tab displays the most onerous case of each type of design check. Full results of all checks are displayed on the tabbed pages. Each design check has the following common columns to identify the location of the design check. Span The span number of the design check location. Section ID The section ID is made up of two numbers, the Bridge Deck (Grillage) Geometric attribute ID and the Composite Design Girder Material utility ID. Where a section is tapered the section ID is of the form 1025 / 2 where the Deck (Grillage) Geometric attribute ID of '1' has appended to it '.025' to show the proportion along the segment length (25%). Location This is the location of the design check from the start of the design member and is presented in design code units. Design Combination This is the design category as specified on the loadcase selection dialog. Primary component The primary component used in evaluating smart combination results. It will be accompanied by '(Max)' or '(Min)' to indicate the max/min variation of a loadset or '(Range)' in fatigue where both are used. Flexure represents the direction of the major bending moment, which will be either "positive" or "negative". The AASHTO sign convention is different to LUSAS and here the design code sign convention is used but enclosed in inverted commas to represent a name rather than a value. Utilisation Utilisation factor for the check.

topics.title: Design checks
toc_path: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Design checks Design check results are listed on separate tabs. Some checks are independent of loadcase, such as the Section Proportions tab; others are based on the limit state; and additional tabs are provided for design not associated with a section, such as fatigue details and stiffeners. Each table of design checks presents a series of headline results. Some results may not be available and for these the cells are greyed out. This can occur for a number of reasons such as limits of slenderness being met or not being met, compact or noncompact sections, direction of bending, presence of other forces etc. The Messages tab shows those messages that were generated during the design checking. These should be reviewed to ensure the validity of the design checks.

topics.text: Check explorer The Check Explorer provides outline results of the desig n check carried out and allows the drilling down into the various parts of the design check. In the left-hand panel the design check is displayed hierarchically and follows the code clauses and their references. Design checks are coloured green to indicate a pass, and red to indicate a failure. Black items represent intermediate calculations such as capacity or factors that are used in the design check but are not checks themselves. Each item in the left-hand panel that is clicked shows a relevant calculation summary in the right hand panel.

topics.title: Analysis results
toc_path: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Analysis results The Analysis results page displays the section dimensions and section materials, and forces, properties and stresses used in the various phases of design, to allow checking of such details. The table of 'Section bending stress' displays the stresses contributed by each phase. For phases 2b (Shrinkage) and 3a (Thermal), both primary and secondary stresses are shown denoted by 1 and 2 respectively. The table of 'Bending profile in unbraced length' shows the variation of bending moment over the unbraced length in which the design check location is located. This information is used in design checks for buckling in most codes. Where the lateral bending of flanges is assessed by slicing, the profiles of the top and bottom flanges will be displayed here too.

topics.title: Section Stresses
toc_path: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
headings: Viewing composite bridge deck design results - AASHTO 8th and 9th Edition
topics.text: Section Stresses The section stresses dialog shows the stress profiles of the various load phases. The loadcase providing the analysis results for each phase is given. Thermal effects can lead to a nonlinear through-section stress profile. Section stresses are calculated using the section properties appropriate to each phase. Where the bending moment is hogging ("negative" in AASHTO) the slab is assumed to be cracked and the section properties are based on the steel girder plus reinforcement, where the section is in sagging ("positive" in AASHTO) bending the stresses are based on the composite section. Primary stresses from Thermal and Shrinkage loading are only applied at sections that are uncracked under permanent loads. Such loads should not be assigned by users to sections in hogging ("negative" in AASHTO) bending under permanent effects. The assumption is that cracked slabs cannot transfer shrinkage or thermal effects since any strains are lost once the cracks form. Concrete stresses are determined assuming linear stress-strain behaviour. AASHTO places a limit of 0.6fc’ for Service loading (6.10.4.2.1) which ensures this is assumption is approximately valid. 6.1.1.1.1d requires that concrete stresses are determined using the short term modular ratio for both permanent and short term, loads. For tapered sections horizontal and vertical stresses are computed for the bottom flange, the longitudinal stresses are the design stresses used in the orientation of the flange. Tapered sections are assumed to vary in depth at the bottom flange only.

topics.text: Edit Section The Edit Section dialog allows for editing of section dimensions and having the design check calculations re-evaluated instantly based on the new section data and using the previously solved results from the model. This provides the ability to make what-if changes to try and ensure a valid design before re-visiting and updating the bridge model.

Location This is the location of the design check from the start of the design member and is presented in design code units. Design Combination This is the design category as specified on the loadcase selection dialog. Primary component The primary component used in evaluating smart combination results. It will be accompanied by '(Max)' or '(Min)' to indicate the max/min variation of a loadset or '(Range)' in fatigue where both are used. Flexure represents the direction of the major bending moment, which will be either "positive" or "negative". The CSA S6-14 and CSA S6:19 sign convention is different to LUSAS and here the design code sign convention is used but enclosed in inverted commas to represent a name rather than a value. Utilisation Utilisation factor for the check.
