topics.title: Clarify Assignment(s) to Act On
topics.text: Clarify Assignment(s) to Act On The Clarify Assignment dialog will appear when Modeller is unable to automatically carry out an operation on a set of objects to which an attribute is assigned. This will occur when the chosen attribute appears within more than one analysis entry in the Analyses Treeview. It will also occur when the chosen attribute appears within only one analysis entry, and this analysis is not the one that contains the active loadcase. The analysis containing the active loadcase is stated on the dialog, and up to four options are provided to clarify which assignments are to be considered. The clarification options available depend upon the analyses and the assignments made. Note that the wording of the options differs according to usage. Active loadcase, considering all inherited and overridden assignments - only available for attributes that support the overidding of assignments. Assignments made to the analysis of the active loadcase / made to the active loadcase - ignores inherited and overidden assignments. All assignments - carries out the requested operation for all assignments made of the attribute throughout all analyses and loadcases. Assignments made to specified analyses (or loadcases) / made to specified loadcases / made to specified loadcase ranges - allows selection of individual analyses and, when applicable, their associated loadcases. The Analysis and Loadcase tree panel on the dialog is populated with only those analyses (for materials and geometric attributes) and loadcases (for loadings, supporrts and activate and deactivate attributes) in which the assigned attribute of interest is present. The active loadcase (and hence analysis) is marked with a check box if it contains the assigned attribute of interest. Notes If the 'All assignments' setting is used the chosen operation will be carried out on all objects to which an attribute is assigned in those Analyses listed in the Analysis and Loadcase tree. If the 'Assignments made to specified analyses (or loadcases)' setting is used, a range of loadcases may be selected by checking the appropriate boxes. See also: About Model Attributes About Model Attributes

topics.title: Cyclic Constraint
topics.text: Cyclic Constraint Cyclic Translation Points or Cyclic Translation Coordinates Cyclic translational symmetry may be used to model a section from a continuous strip. The mesh on the two planes of symmetry may be different. Meshes on Master and Slave need not match. Cyclic Rotation Points or Cyclic Rotation Coordinates Cyclic rotational symmetry may be used to model a section from a continuous ring. The mesh on the two planes of symmetry may be different. Meshes on the Master and Slave Lines need not match. See also: Constraint Equations Constraint Equations Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes

topics.title: Geometric Constraint
topics.text: Geometric Constraint Assigning a constraint of this type to Lines on either side of a gap maintains the underlying undeformed node positions relative to each other as if a rigid block were in place between the structures. Rigid Displacement The nodes in the assigned features may be constrained to be rigid, the group of nodes may translate and/or rotate but their positions relative to one another remain constant. Only translational displacements can be constrained using this type of constraint. This type of constraint is only valid for small displacements. Rigid Link A rigid link will create a rigid fixity between two features. It is similar to the Rigid Displacements constraint type, except that rotational freedoms are also constrained to be rigid Planar Surface A surface may be constrained to remain plane, the surface may translate and/or rotate but remains plane. Nodal positions may vary relative to other nodes on the surface. This type of constraint is only valid for small displacements. Straight Line A straight line may be constrained to remain straight, the line may translate and/or rotate but will remain straight. Nodal positions may vary relative to other nodes along the line. This constraint type is only valid for small displacements. See also: Constraint Equations Constraint Equations Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes

Constant Constraint is used where a nodal freedom value is constant but unknown across all the nodes in the assigned features. P ath Constraint The nodes in the assigned features may be constrained to move along a specified vector defined by 2 Points or by 2 sets of X, Y and Z coordinates. topics.title: Tied Constraint
topics.text: Tied Constraint Ties nodes along Master and Slave Lines to restrict relative movement. The underlying nodes maintain their original relative positions under loading. Meshes on Master/Slave need not match. Note that tied nodes have all freedoms constrained. Tied Mesh Normal Defines the search direction to detect the tied nodes as normal to the Master/Slave surfaces. Tied Mesh Specified Constraint Uses a defined point on a Master line and an equivalent point on a Slave line to define a search direction vector to detect tied nodes on the Master/Slave surfaces. Use Rigid Constraints Ensures that the two sets of assigned features will both rotate with respect to their initial defined positions. headings: Viewing and Editing of Multiple Attribute Assignments
topics.text: Viewing and Editing of Multiple Attribute Assignments The Assignments editor is displayed when one or more attributes of the same type are selected for editing in the Attributes Treeview by using the View Assignments context menu item. The editor can also be accessed from any assignments that exist in the loadcases panel of the Analyses Treeview. It allows simultaneous viewing, editing and management of any number of attribute assignments. Editing of data can be by individual selection, or by selection of the parent folder containing a set of attributes. The dialog is expandable.

topics.text: Top-right panel The properties grid in the upper-right of the dialog shows any common properties for selections made in the upper-left panel, and states 'Different properties' if different values are present. When an attribute is selected within the editor's attribute treeview, property and value data for just that selection is shown instead. As an example, for load attributes, typical editing options allow you to: Change the assigned attribute - where the change will also be seen in the top-left treeview, as the assignment will be moved to belong to the correct parent. Change the feature type to which it is assigned - where a text string is used to represent assignment to multiple objects. E,g. "1" (line 1 only) or "1;3;7" (Lines 1, 3 and 7 only), or "1T14" (lines 1 through to and including line 14. If all Assign to fields are left blank the attribute will be de-assigned. Change the assigned scope - where the assignment can be changed to be 'Single loadcase', 'All loadcases', 'Specified loadcases' or 'Range of loadcases'- where a range will need to be specified by further selection in this panel. [Other assignments listed] Other assignments will be listed according the attribute type being viewed/edited.

topics.title: Background Grid
topics.text: Background Grid Background grid meshing is a method of controlling the size of elements generated during automatic meshing. It is generally only used when specification of spacing and stretching parameters at Points is required to grade the mesh pattern locally when irregular surface meshing. A background grid is a collection of triangular or tetrahedral shapes which completely encompasses the features to be meshed. The background grid generated will usually be defined to surround the whole model but localised selections may also be made. If the model is subsequently edited or extended the background grid may need to be automatically regenerated. Background grids can be defined by using any of these options: From Points - by selecting points on the model Enclose Selection - by defining a region of the model to be enclosed using the cursor Enclose Whole Model - by enclosing the whole model Once defined a background grid is added to the Utilities treeview Notes When defining a background grid from points a suitable point mesh attribute should be assigned to each of the points generated by this command. Use the Attributes > Mesh > Point menu item to do this. When enclosing a selected part or the whole of a model the number of elements in the X, Y and Z directions must be specified. For a linear grading of elements, a single background grid element in X, Y and Z will be sufficient. Specifying more elements permits different element spacings to be defined at each background mesh point to grade elements differently around those points. The title given is the name used to identify the background grid in the Utilities treeview. See also: Background Grid Background Grid

topics.text: Activate and Deactivate - Activate Activate attributes are used to activate previously deactivated elements in a chosen loadcases as an analysis proceeds. They must be assigned to model features (or to elements in a mesh-only model). See also: Activate and Deactivate Activate and Deactivate Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes

topics.title: Activate and Deactivate - Deactivate
topics.text: Activate and Deactivate - Deactivate To model the absence or removal of a part of a model, a deactivate attribute is assigned to those features that are to be removed. In a structural analysis, the underlying elements have their stiffness matrix reduced in magnitude, while for field analysis the conductivity matrix (or other analogous quantity) is reduced. This ensures the deactivated elements have a negligible effect on the behaviour of the remaining model. The element stresses and strains, fluxes and gradients and other analogous quantities are all set to zero.

In a structural analysis, the underlying elements have their stiffness matrix reduced in magnitude, while for field analysis the conductivity matrix (or other analogous quantity) is reduced. This ensures the deactivated elements have a negligible effect on the behaviour of the remaining model. The element stresses and strains, fluxes and gradients and other analogous quantities are all set to zero.

topics.title: Stiffness reduction factor
topics.text: Stiffness reduction factor The stiffness reduction factor provides control over the amount that the stiffness matrix is reduced in magnitude when elements are deactivated. It enables different reductions in stiffness to be applied to different deactivated elements such that their relative stiffness is changed, which is useful as a means of controlling the deactivated elements. For example, it may be desirable for the final connecting mesh between two cantilevered-out deck ends to have a lower stiffness reduction factor than the cantilevers whilst deactivated.

topics.title: Percentage to Redistribute
topics.text: Percentage to Redistribute In a deconstruction situation a deactivate attribute controls the way in which internal forces in an loaded structure are processed by specifying how much of the internal forces should be redistributed to the remaining elements. Zero Redistribution 0% of the internal forces in a deactivated element are redistributed in the remaining elements (if this is prescribed in a static analysis, and the load remains constant, the stress, displacements etc. in the other elements will remain unchanged). Full Redistribution 100% of the internal forces in a deactivated element are redistributed in the remaining elements (this has the same effect as re-assigning very weak material properties to the element). Fractional Redistribution A percentage of the internal force to be redistributed is specified. Provides a solution which is part way between the two extremes. Any remaining internal equilibrating force associated with a deactivated element is maintained in the system until the element is subsequently activated. When an element is activated it is assumed that the element has just been introduced to the model (although all elements must be defined at the outset). The current (deformed) geometry for that element is taken as the initial geometry and the element is assumed to be in a stress/strain free state (unless initial stresses or strains are defined). All internal forces that exist in the element are redistributed and the computed strains are incremented from the time at which the element becomes active.

topics.title: Composite Layup Options
topics.text: Composite Layup Options Composite layups can be defined using the following options: Solids and Shells Solids and Shells - allows a manual definition of the composite lay-up where orientations and thicknesses for the plies can be specified. The orientation angles can be applied with respect to the local element x-axis (in the x-y plane) or with respect to the x-axis of a predefined Cartesian set. The z-axis defines the direction of the lay-up with ply 1 located at the bottom of the stack. Draped Solids and Shells Draped Solids and Shells - utilises the native draping functionality in LUSAS. A start point (which should lie inside or on the boundary of the surface to be draped) can be defined for each ply and the start direction is defined by the x-axis of a predefined Cartesian set. The orientations of fibres following the drape are computed by LUSAS and are tabulated with respect to the x-axis of the local element axes. As with the Solids and Shells option, it is essential that the z-axis of the volumes to which the composite is to be assigned are consistently oriented. FiberSIM Solids and Shells FiberSIM Solids and Shells - This option reads in the composite stack details from an external xml file. The dialog prompts for the location of the file and a default fibre volume fraction can be specified. By default it is assumed that all plies are of the same thickness but this can be modified on the composite dialog. It is not necessary to select a draping surface or to define a start point when using this option. Simulayt Solids and Shells Simulayt Solids and Shells - This option reads in the composite stack details from an external layup file. The dialog prompts for the location of the file and a default fibre volume fraction can be specified. By default it is assumed that all plies are of the same thickness but this can be modified on the composite dialog. It is not necessary to select a draping surface or to define a start point when using this option. See also: Composite Composite

topics.title: Beam Cross-Section
topics.text: Beam Cross-Section Beam cross-section information defines fibre locations as used in results processing, the number and location of integration points for Cross Section Beam elements (for advanced use only), and quadrilateral cross-sectional data used to define the beam's actual shape. Fibre locations define positions on the beam cross-section at which stresses can be plotted when visualising results. Sections in the standard section libraries have default fibre locations stored for each section. Sections created by using the Arbitrary Section Property Calculator that are saved in the user or server libraries have fibre locations defined automatically - one for each extreme position in each quadrant with respect to the centroid of the section. If additional fibre definitions are required use Modeller to obtain the properties of any additional points on the saved cross-section model and enter in the fields provided. Number of integration points for the current selection is an advanced facility for use only with Cross Section Beam elements and would not normally be used for general use. When using cross-section beams in plasticity problems the plasticity is monitored at integration points. The number of integration points (also known as gauss points) in the local y and z directions may be defined for each quadrilateral section. Quadrilateral cross-section properties are used to visualise a beam's cross-section and ensure its correct display if fleshing is done. The coordinate of each quadrilateral must be defined in local cross-section coordinate pairs at each node, y1, z1, y2, z2, y3, z3, y4, z4. When defining a cross-section by this method the coordinate pair must be defined anti-clockwise and the centroid of the section must reside at 0,0. Any number of quadrilateral cross-sections may be defined to make up the beam's actual shape. Sections in the standard section library have their cross-sectional geometry pre-defined. See also: Beam Cross Section Geometric Properties Beam Cross Section Geometric Properties Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes

topics.title: Direction
topics.text: Direction The influence direction specifies the direction in which a chosen influence component lies. The influence Direction drop-down list presented depends upon the type of entity selected. Nodal (only available for Entity types Reaction, Reaction Stress and Displacement). Uses the nodal axes of the node/point to which the attribute is assigned Local Uses the local coordinate of the element to which the attribute is assigned Local Coords Uses a consistent direction defined using a local coordinate local coordinate . Path Requires a reference path reference path to have been defined where the path can be selected in the adjoining drop-down list. A default path of longitudinal = global X is provided to cater for a common scenario where element axes lie in this direction, without having to actually define a path. This default path does not appear in the Utilities Treeview and is not editable. Otherwise for most models, the specification of a path will require a reference path to have been previously defined prior to selection. If a reference path has been defined incorporating a skew angle then selecting the Skew check-box will ensure that all elements lying at that skew angle will be considered to be transverse elements. Otherwise, by default, transverse elements are assumed to be those elements orthogonal to longitudinal elements. Specification of a direction using the Path facility is recommended for grillage models and for curved decks modelled with beams, plates or shells where longitudinal and transverse effects are of interest. A path cannot be selected for 2D line beam elements; for these, all components are calculated using the element local x-axis. Feature Uses the local coordinate of the parent line or surface feature to which the attribute is assigned. Global Uses the global axes. The setting of an influence direction is conceptually similar to the setting of a results transformation when viewing results.

topics.title: Flux (Patch) Load
topics.text: Flux (Patch) Load Flux Patch loads provide a loading per unit length or per unit area. The Heat Flux value for each point of a discrete patch flux loading needs to be specified (for example, in Watts/m 2 if SI units are being used). Flux Patch loading types are: 8 node patch - used to define a curved sided quadrilateral 4 node patch - used to define a straight sided quadrilateral Multi node patch - used to define a straight sided patch of any number of points Straight line - requires 2 specified coordinates to define a straight line load Curve - requires 3 specified coordinates to define a curved line load Projection Vector is used to work out which features are actually loaded. The vector is followed (in both directions) and any features intersected by the assigned discrete load vertices projected in the direction of the projection vector are loaded accordingly. Patch load divisions specify the numbers of divisions in the local x and y directions of the patch being assigned. topics.title: Rate of Heat Inflow (Point) Load
topics.text: Rate of Heat Inflow (Point) Load Rate of Heat Inflow (Point) loads provide concentrated loading at specified locations. These Point loads can be defined singly or as a set of discrete point loads in 3D space. Each individual load can have a separate load value. Point loads can be defined via Arbitrary input or by specifying a Grid input. Each discrete point requires a Rate of Heat Inflow load to be specified (for example, in Watts if SI units are being used). Arbitrary permits the definition of any number of Point loads. If the points are defined in an expected grid order (see Grid entry), then the loading components can be optionally projected along the columns and rows of the patch load grid into a search area (if used), otherwise the loading is applied to the nearest load location in the search area. Grid adds the correct number of rows to the point load definition grid for the number of x and y values defined and expects the coordinate points to be defined in a particular order so that any loads that may overhang a search area (if used), can be optionally projected to be included into the search area. For a grid of points of x=3, y=2 the expected order of coordinate input is x1,y1, x2, y1, x3, y1, x1, y2, x2, y2, x3, y2. Projection Vector is used to work out which features are actually loaded. The vector is followed (in both directions) and any features intersected by the assigned discrete load vertices projected in the direction of the projection vector are loaded accordingly. See Discrete Thermal / Hygro-Thermal Loads: Flux Point Load Discrete Thermal / Hygro-Thermal Loads: Flux Point Load for diagrams of loading types. topics.title: Compound load
topics.text: Compound load Compound loads may be created to simplify the definition and assignment of more complex load patterns. A compound load can be formed from a set of previously defined discrete loads and be subsequently assigned to a model as one loading. A compound load may be defined from any combination of existing point, patch and compound discrete loads. For example a discrete patch load representing a vehicle may be included in a compound load twice with the distance between the vehicles specified. x, y, z offsets and a translation can be specified to locate the compound loading from away from an assigned point. When created, compound discrete loads are held in the Loading section of the Attributes Treeview in their own section named Compound. See Discrete Structural Loads Compound Load Compound Load for a diagram of a compound load type. Options are: X , Y , Z , XYZ , Patch x , Patch y , or Surface normal . topics.title: Distributed to Perimeter loading
topics.text: Distributed to Perimeter loading Distributed perimeter loading is a load type that can be applied to unmeshed surfaces that represent a floor, or the unmeshed surfaces representing the loadable vertical facade of a building in a frame model. The loading applied is distributed to the edge beams based upon the spanning direction of the floor or wall framing system and any definition of sub-beams. It is primarily of use in loading concrete floor slabs and facades in buildings, without voids, where the floor or facade panel itself is not modelled in full in order to reduce the complexity of the model. Surfaces representing the extent of each floor slab or facade must be defined but no mesh assignment is required. Lines forming the Surface must, however, be assigned a suitable line mesh. Sub-beams that may support a floor slab or facade (other than those beams that support its perimeter) can be defined without the need to model those beams as line features or elements in the model. Loading on sub-beams as a result of distributed loading and their self weight is represented as equivalent loads at the locations where the sub-beams meet the supporting beams at the perimeter of a surface. The full range of settings and options available are described below:

The loading applied is distributed to the edge beams based upon the spanning direction of the floor or wall framing system and any definition of sub-beams. It is primarily of use in loading concrete floor slabs and facades in buildings, without voids, where the floor or facade panel itself is not modelled in full in order to reduce the complexity of the model. Surfaces representing the extent of each floor slab or facade must be defined but no mesh assignment is required. Lines forming the Surface must, however, be assigned a suitable line mesh. Sub-beams that may support a floor slab or facade (other than those beams that support its perimeter) can be defined without the need to model those beams as line features or elements in the model. Loading on sub-beams as a result of distributed loading and their self weight is represented as equivalent loads at the locations where the sub-beams meet the supporting beams at the perimeter of a surface. The full range of settings and options available are described below:

topics.title: Distribution type
topics.text: Distribution type One-way distribution would be used to represent a slab or facade system that is designed to span in one direction. Each unit load is transferred along the slab to the nearest sub-beam or perimeter beam, and along any sub-beam to the supporting perimeter beam. Where the end of a sub-beam meets the perimeter boundary, a point load is used to model the effective load due to the sub-beam. The perimeter beam also receives a distributed load from that portion of the floor or facade that is resting directly on the beam, and has not been transferred to a sub-beam. Two-way distribution would be used to represent a slab or facade that is designed to span in two directions. Load is simply distributed to the nearest perimeter or sub-beam, and along any sub-beam to the supporting perimeter beam. Where the end of a sub-beam meets the perimeter boundary, a point load is used to model the effective load due to the sub-beam. The perimeter beam also receives a distributed load from that portion of the floor or facade that is resting directly on the beam, and has not been transferred to a sub-beam. Polygon centroid distribution divides the floor or facade into triangles having their apex at the centroid of the floor or facade and their base on the perimeter of the surface, and applies the load due from each triangle to the corresponding perimeter line as distributed load. In this type of distribution, there are no sub-beams. This type of loading is meaningless in a floor or facade where the centroid lies outside the boundary or where the dividing triangles cut the perimeter lines. Polygon length distribution divides the load proportionally to the perimeter line lengths and applies each as distributed load. Automatic when used in conjunction with the specification of a Maximum aspect ratio for two-way spanning causes Modeller to consider any surface with an aspect ratio of greater than the specified value as one-way spanning.

topics.title: Load direction
topics.text: Load direction The loading on the floor slab or facade is defined by a load direction and a fixed intensity per unit area. There are 4 options for defining the load direction: Surface normal Vertical axis loading is applied in the same direction as the vertical axis vertical axis Global coordinates Defined Cartesian local coordinate sets , used in conjunction with the particular axis. The axis is irrelevant when 'Vertical axis' or 'Surface normal” is chosen. Positive values of loading are assumed to follow the chosen axis direction. To reverse the load direction, enter a negative value for load intensity.

topics.title: Reference direction
topics.text: Reference direction For 'One-way' and 'Two-way' loading it is necessary to define a reference direction across the floor or facade from which the Sub-beam angle and (for one-way loading only) the One-way distribution angle may be measured. There are 3 options for defining the reference direction, with all used in conjunction with a chosen particular local or global axis. The z axis is excluded when 'Surface axes' is chosen as this vector direction would not have a projection in the floor or facade. topics.title: Number of sub-beams
topics.text: Number of sub-beams For “one-way” and “two-way” loading the number of sub-beams (if any) may be specified. A value of zero would be used for a floor or facade without sub-beams. The location of the sub-beams is determined by subdividing the floor or facade into equal divisions between the extreme locations measured perpendicular to the sub-beam direction.

topics.title: Sub-beam load per unit length
topics.text: Sub-beam load per unit length The self weight of the sub-beams is defined per unit length and may use a variation variation . The sub-beam loading is integrated along the beam and assigned as point loads to the ends of the sub-beam where they contact the surface perimeter, and is always applied in the vertical direction. No geometry or elements are created by the sub-beams, the division is all done internally within LUSAS leaving the floor or facade surfaces unchanged.

topics.title: Area reduction function
topics.text: Area reduction function An expression defined in terms of “A”, for area. This reduces the load on a line based on the total surface area assigned to that line. The function is constrained to always return a value <= 1.0 so that the function cannot increase the load. The function is defined in building design codes or may be left with the default value of 1.0.

topics.title: Thermal link geometric properties
topics.text: Thermal link geometric properties Thermal link geometric properties are defined using the Attributes > Geometric > Thermal Link menu item. Define thermal link geometric properties for assignment between one of the following: Points - for which an Area must be specified in model units. Lines - for which a Thickness must be specified in model units. When solved, the thickness entered will be multiplied by the length of each portion of the line represented by each link, and tabulated as the area of each link. An average value is taken if the lengths / thicknesses vary between master and slave lines. Surface - for which nothing is required to be specified. When solved, the area of each surface is calculated and tabulated. An average value is taken if the areas vary between master and slave surfaces. See also: Geometric Properties Geometric Properties

topics.title: Hygro-thermal supports
topics.text: Hygro-thermal supports Hygro-thermal support conditions describe the heat flow at the model boundaries. Hygro-thermal support types are: Temperature Capillary pressure Degrees of freedom can be set to Free - heat will not flow through the node (the insulated condition). Fixed - heat will flow through the node to maintain temperature at zero (or at a prescribed temperature). By default all freedoms are Free. Notes A hygro-thermal support refers to a Degree of Freedom that has a prescribed value. Use the Attributes> Loading> Hygro-thermal menu item to define a prescribed load. When a prescribed Degree of Freedom has already been assigned to the model its removal should be done from the Hygro-Thermal supports dialog. It cannot be done from the ‘Prescribed’ dialog even though it offers the option ‘Free’. The degrees of freedom which may be restrained for any analysis depend on the chosen element type. Those applicable for each element are defined in the Element Reference Manual. See also: Support Conditions Support Conditions Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes

topics.title: Inspection Location
topics.text: Inspection Location An inspection location is a defined position of interest on a model for results extraction / viewing purposes. Inspection locations can be defined and assigned to a model either before or after a model has been solved, and are saved when a model is saved. Models can have multiple inspection locations defined, such as defining locations of interest at 1/8th points along a line beam representing a bridge span or at the centre and quarter points within a building floor slab. Appropriate results can then be viewed for all defined inspection locations by selecting the Inspection Locations option from a relevant results dialog.

topics.title: Distance type
topics.text: Distance type For assignment to a line a distance type of Parametric from start , Parametric from end , Actual from start , or Actual from end can be stated. These options create an inspection location at a specified parametric or actual distance along a line in the local coordinate system of any line to which the attribute is assigned. For lines multiple inspection locations can be defined either by entering 0.5, 2@0.25, 3@0.1 (for example) in one cell, or by entering each required location position in separate cells by use of the Tab key. For assignment to a planar surface defined by three or four lines, or a volume, a distance type of Parametric , or Actual can be stated. These options create an inspection location at a specified parametric or actual (in-plane) distance in a surface or within a volume with respect to the local coordinate system of the feature.

topics.text: Joint Line Assignment (Automatic insertion of Joint) When assigning a joint line mesh to a single line feature the following options are available: Joints between surfaces (e.g. hinge) This assumes that the lines selected for assignment are not meshed. Options are: Joints between two surfaces - Inserts a single set of joints between surfaces sharing a common line. Joints between two sets of surfaces (selection memory clarifies) Inserts a set of joints between a set of surfaces that have been added to selection memory selection memory and other surfaces that connect to those surfaces at a common line. Joints to isolate meshed line This assumes that the lines selected for assignment are meshed. Options are: All surfaces and volumes together - Inserts a set of joints between a common line and all connecting features to isolate that line entirely from those features. Each surface independently - Inserts a set of joints between the common line and each surface connecting to that line. From surfaces in selection memory Inserts a set of joints between the common line and each surface that has been added to selection memory selection memory . To be used when many surfaces meet at a line, and not all are required to be connected the common line with a set of joints. Support line via joints Adds joints along the line selected to 'ground' that object by fully fixing the free end of the joint element.

topics.text: Geometric Joint Properties Analysis category Shows the analysis category analysis category in use. Eccentricity (in the local z direction for 3D, and the local y direction for 2D Inplane) is an optional geometric property for certain Joint elements. Use joint length For joint elements with rotational degrees of freedom, if this option is unchecked, then the element nodes should be coincident as the transverse forces and moments in the joint will be uncoupled. If the joint length is to be considered, and the element nodes are not coincident, then a parametric distance (between 0.0 and 1.0) can be specified from node 1 which defines the position where the transverse shear springs are to act. For the local y direction it is measured from node 1 (dy=0) along the local x direction to node 2. For the local z direction it is measured from node 1 (dz=0) along the local x direction. topics.title: Specifying the mesh divisions (not applicable for joint elements)
toc_path: Specifying the mesh divisions (not applicable for joint elements)
headings: Specifying the mesh divisions (not applicable for joint elements)
topics.text: Specifying the mesh divisions (not applicable for joint elements) Define the mesh discretisation using any of the following methods: Use default spacing uses default line mesh divisions as specified on the File > Model Properties menu item Number of divisions Defines how many segments the line will be sub - divided into when meshed. By default uniform spacing is used. Spacing permits a non-uniform mesh spacing along a line to be obtained either by specifying an element length ratio for the first to the last element along a line, or by specify an exact spacing. Element length Line mesh density may be specified in terms of an element length. In this case the number of elements is calculated automatically. If the line is not exactly divisible by the element length then the number of elements is rounded upwards. If the line mesh size is set to zero a background grid may be used to compute the element length. End conditions may be specified for either an end release end release or a rigid zone rigid zone end condition.

topics.title: Line Mesh Assignment (General)
topics.text: Line Mesh Assignment (General) 3D beam elements and joint elements require the element xy-plane to be defined on assignment. This is done using one the following methods: Beta angle This is the rotation angle between the line axes and the element axes. Used to orientate a beam's cross-section when a geometric line attribute is assigned to a line, and to orientate local loading. Ignore local coords assigned to point When joints are defined between non-coincident lines the local x-axis is orientated from Master (Line 1) to Slave (Line 2) and the element local z is then defined in the xZ plane unless the local x axis is aligned to the global Z axis in which case the element local z axis is aligned with the global Y axis. When joints between coincident lines are assigned a Line Mesh the local axes are aligned to the global axes. This method is also used when no Local Coordinate is assigned to the Master line. By point in selection memory A point in selection memory is used in combination with the line assigned to define the xy-plane. Not applicable for line interface mesh assignment. By specified local coordinates The element axes are defined using a previously defined local coordinate, or by creating a new local coordinate using the New... option. Used to orientate cross-sections when geometric line attributes are assigned to lines. Note that local coordinate attributes should not be assigned directly to a line for the purposes of orientating beam element axes. This will actually transform nodal freedoms and will affect the direction of global loads and supports.

headings: Included Joints / End Releases for Beam Elements
topics.text: Start of line Include Joint Selecting this check box disables all freedoms and inserts a joint at the end of a line (or at the transition between the rigid zone element and the non-rigid elements if rigid zones have additionally been defined) to which the line mesh attribute is assigned. These joints, which are automatically inserted by Modeller, are chosen according to the non-rigid elements to which they connect. The inserted joints are given default linear joint material properties (also based upon the material and geometric properties of the line on which they occur). When using rigid zones the material properties given will be sufficient for a suitable rigid connection to be achieved. Note that the attributes for joints created in this way do not appear in the Attributes treeview. If required, different joint material properties can be defined and assigned to relevant ends of lines to overwrite the default joint values. Point-type joint material properties can be assigned to the ends of lines with rigid zones in addition to the material properties assigned to the line for the beam elements. Different joint properties may be assigned to each end of the line or the same properties may be assigned to both ends according to the selection made on the assignment dialog. So, in any given analysis, it is possible for any line to have three material assignments – one for itself, one for the joint at its start, and one for the joint at its end. The latter two must be joint materials, and must be assigned using the 'Assigned to line end(s)' option when the assignment is made. Translation and Rotation freedoms. Check (tick) a freedom to release that freedom. Pinned Specifically releases the rotations about the element y and z axes for a 3D element, and the rotation about z for a 2D elements. Fixed Disables all the freedom check boxes. Releasing freedoms can be used as an alternative to using joint joint elements, for example when defining a Pin between beam elements.

topics.title: Torsional warping about x
toc_path: Included Joints / End Releases for Beam Elements
headings: Included Joints / End Releases for Beam Elements
topics.text: Torsional warping about x For thick beams that support torsional warping, specific options are available: Restrained Freedoms at the ends of the element are restrained about the element local x direction. Free Freedoms at the ends of the element are free to rotate about the element local x direction Continous Default selection. See notes below. Notes: For a structural connection where several beams and columns are connected at a point it is important to assign correctly the warping degree of freedom depending on the angle at which these members meet as well as the details of the arrangement of the connector elements (bolts, welds, etc.). For the example shown below: For the column the warping condition is 'Restrained' If only the web of an I-beam is connected to a column while its flanges are free to move out of their original plane, the warping condition is 'Free'. If the flanges of the beam are welded to the column, as in this case, they cannot move out of plane, so the warping condition is 'Continuous' (fixed) Beam / column connection Beam / column modelling of torsional warping in members Whilst the beam/column arrangement above could be modelled using separate nodes (see adjacent image) this would require the use of constraint equations. The connection can be modelled more easily using a single node (i.e. node =1=2) with line mesh end conditions as shown. Rigid zones Rigid zones can be used to model the length of the beam that extends from the nodal intersection with one beam or column - the 'intersection of interest', to a position on the beam that defines the extent of a rigid zone for modelling and analysis purposes. When solved (and for historical reasons) 'Restrained' restraints are tabulated as 'C' in the Solver data file, 'Free' restraints are tabulated as 'F', and 'Continuous' restraints are tabulated as 'R'. See also: Joint/Interface Element Meshes Joint/Interface Element Meshes Rigid Zone for Beam Elements Rigid Zone for Beam Elements Beam End Conditions Beam End Conditions

topics.title: Rigid Zone for Beam Elements
topics.text: Rigid Zone for Beam Elements When modelling the connection between beams and columns in a steel or concrete building frame, a short rigid length of beam element may be required to model the length of the beam that extends from the nodal intersection with one beam or column, to a position on the beam that defines the extent of a rigid zone for modelling and analysis purposes. The following options are available to define a rigid zone as part of defining a line mesh attribute for assignment to selected lines.
topics.search_text: Rigid Zone for Beam Elements Rigid Zone for Beam Elements Rigid Zone for Beam Elements dlg4attr idd line mesh rigid zones.htm Rigid Zone for Beam Elements When modelling the connection between beams and columns in a steel or concrete building frame, a short rigid length of beam element may be required to model the length of the beam that extends from the nodal intersection with one beam or column, to a position on the beam that defines the extent of a rigid zone for modelling and analysis purposes. The following options are available to define a rigid zone as part of defining a line mesh attribute for assignment to selected lines.

topics.title: Start of line
topics.text: Start of line None No rigid zone is to be defined. Specified Length A user-specified rigid zone length is to be used Beam / column connection A formula based calculation is to be used based on the sum of the percentage of the width and depth of connecting column and beam members allowing for any eccentricity can be entered via a Specify button. For example, a rigid length of a beam could be defined as being 100% of the distance from the nodal line to the face of a column (a) minus 25% the beam's own depth (b), as in Length =(1 x a) - (0.25 x b). One of two options inform Modeller what to do when automatic beam /column detection for the above option fails: Report error and fail to mesh Any error will be written to the text output window, describing the condition(s) that prevent(s) rigid zones being calculated for the features selected. Assume no rigid mesh For ends of columns, such as those at the foot of the structure, no rigid zone will be assumed since no beams frame-in to the column at these locations. Rigid zone factor specifies the degree of rigidity of the rigid end zone element that is inserted at the end of a beam element. The value is constrained between 0 (fully flexible) and 1 (fully rigid). Include mass allows the inclusion or exclusion of mass from the rigid end zone elements. If mass is excluded then the material density is tabulated as zero for the rigid end zone elements.

topics.text: Line Mesh Spacing Line mesh spacing is, by default, uniform alone a line. Uniform transition permits specifying a ratio to govern the size of the first element with respect to last along a line. General spacing permits an exact mesh spacing to be achieved. Use the Tab key to create new entry rows. A Number of 3 with a Ratio of 1, followed by a Number of 2 with a Ratio of 0.5 will create a line mesh of 5 divisions of a spacing that can be seen on the spacing diagram. topics.title: Prescribed Hygro-Thermal Loading
topics.text: Prescribed Hygro-Thermal Loading Thermal loading describes the temperature or heat input into an analysis. Thermal loads are feature based and hence are assigned to the model geometry. When a thermal load value is entered the variation button appears. This allows the value to be varied over the feature using a previously defined variation. While structural analysis cannot be carried out without supports, transient thermal or hygro-thermal analysis can be done without ‘supports’. In hygro-thermal analysis prescribed loading is not used often because it is rarely the case that the temperature or the relative humidity at a point or surface or volume remain constant, with a known value for some period of time covered by the analysis. Note: Prescribed loading is equivalent to ENVT loading with a very high convection coefficient. Even when concrete is in contact with a body with a fixed temperature it might be more accurate to model it as an ENVT load which can account for the thermal and hygro barrier imposed by the rough contact between them. See also: Hygro-Thermal Loads Hygro-Thermal Loads Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes Local coordinate systems Local coordinate systems Variations Variations

topics.title: Prescribed Loading
topics.text: Prescribed Loading Prescribed Loading describes the initial values for displacement, velocity and acceleration at a node. Prescribed loads are feature based and hence are assigned to the model geometry. Prescribed loads can have a Free or Fixed degree of freedom. When stated to be Fixed, a displacement, velocity or acceleration can be specified according to the initial prescribed loading selected. Free For structural analyses the degree of freedom is completely free to move. Fixed For structural analyses the degree of freedom is completely restrained from movement. When a prescribed load value is entered the variation button appears. This allows the value to be varied over the feature using a previously defined variation. Rotations are measured in radians. Large prescribed rotations will require a geometrically nonlinear analysis. A prescribed Displacement defines a nodal movement by either a Total or Incremental prescribed distance in global (or transformed) axis directions. Freedoms which are assigned a non-zero prescribed value will be restrained. Incremental loading adds displacements to a previous increment, whereas Total requires the full displacement to be specified on each increment. See also: Prescribed Loads Prescribed Loads Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes Local coordinate systems Local coordinate systems Variations Variations

Radiation surfaces allow for the calculation of diffuse view factors. Radiation surfaces are defined from the Utility> Heat Transfer menu item.
topics.search_text: Radiation Surface Radiation Surface Radiation Surface dlg4attr idd radiation surface page.htm Radiation Surface Diffuse radiation exchange may be modelled with a radiation surface that is defined by any number of thermal surfaces thermal surfaces . Radiation surfaces allow for the calculation of diffuse view factors. Radiation surfaces are defined from the Utility> Heat Transfer menu item.

topics.title: Defining thermal surfaces
topics.text: Defining thermal surfaces Thermal Surfaces A radiation surface may be defined by any number of existing thermal surfaces. Thermal surfaces defining a radiation surface may form a closed loop or may form any number of discontinuous segments. Radiative heat transfer will only take place between thermal surfaces used in the definition of the same radiation surface. Previously defined Thermal Surface attributes are listed in the left side box. Click on the thermal surface attributes that will define the radiation surface. Shading Thermal Surfaces Defines which of the thermal surfaces are shading surfaces, partially or fully blocking the view between other thermal surfaces in the radiation surface. Correctly identifying the shading surfaces will speed up the view factor calculation. However if in any doubt about shading within a radiation surface then the fully obstructed option should be used (all selected). All thermal surfaces defining the radiation surface are assumed to obstruct the view between segments in the radiation surface. Deselect the Select shading surfaces checkbox to allow individual thermal surfaces to be set.

topics.title: Symmetry mirror plane
topics.text: Symmetry mirror plane If a model uses planes of symmetry, and those planes cross the radiation surface, then they should be defined here. Any number of planes can be defined. The mirror planes of symmetry can be defined in two ways: Mirror transformation dataset Mirror transformation dataset Using a mirror transformation defined using the Utilities> Transformation menu item. The transformations must all be 'mirror' types. Equations The symmetry plane equation coefficients are the coefficients Cx, Cy, Cz and C in the plane equation Cx.X + Cy.Y + Cz.Z = C. Any number of plane equations may be input with the coefficients being specified in groups of 4. Notes The number of transformations, or plane equations, and the order in which they are specified must be such as to enable LUSAS to generate the full radiation surface by reflecting the defining segments in each symmetry plane successively. A plane of symmetry may be used in either a 2D, axisymmetric or 3D analysis. In a 2D analysis the plane of symmetry must be parallel to the global Z axis of the model. In an axisymmetric analysis a plane of symmetry must be perpendicular to the axis about which the model is spun and parallel to the global Z axis of the model. See also: Thermal Surfaces and Heat Transfer Thermal Surfaces and Heat Transfer

topics.text: Defining Reciprocal Influence Attributes Influence attributes that use Reciprocal Influence Method define the result component and methodology that, when assigned to a part of the structure, and in combination with an influence analysis, influence analysis, will be used to create an influence surface.

topics.title: Influence type
topics.text: Influence type This may be specified as a shear force, a moment, a reaction or a displacement: Shear - breaks the mesh and automatically imposes a unit relative displacement at that position Moment - breaks the mesh and automatically defines constraint equations to fix the displacements and rotations of the nodes at the break. Reaction - defines constraint equations to impose a unit displacement or rotation in the specified direction. Displacement - for unit forces or moments applied at nodes. Note that a shear or moment influence type is mesh dependent.

topics.title: Rigid Zone - Formula based calculation
topics.text: Rigid Zone - Formula based calculation This is accessed via the Specify button on the Rigid zone page of the Line Mesh End Conditions dialog. A formula-based calculation is used by some design codes to define a rigid zone length for a beam or column based upon the sum of the percentage of the width of any connecting member allowing for eccentricities, and the depth of the member for which the rigid zone length is being defined.

For 3D slidelines in is not important which surfaces are defined master and slave.

topics.title: Discrete Structural Loading
topics.text: Discrete Structural Loading Discrete structural point and patch loads are defined in relation to their own local coordinate system and are always assigned to points. Discrete loads differ from feature based loads in that they are not limited to application over whole features and may be effective over full or partial areas of the model. Search areas may be used to restrict the area of application of a discrete load. Separate discrete loads may be applied to a model as a load set or load train using the Compound load option. topics.title: Structural supports
topics.text: Structural supports A summary of the structural support types is given here: Free For structural analyses the degree of freedom is completely free to move. For pore water analyses no flow will occur through the node. For thermal supports no heat will flow through the node. Fixed For structural analyses the degree of freedom is completely restrained from movement. For pore water analyses flow will occur through the node. For thermal supports heat will flow through node to maintain temperature at zero (or at a prescribed temperature).

topics.title: Spring Stiffness Distribution
topics.text: Spring Stiffness Distribution Spring stiffness is applied either uniformly, per unit length or per unit area. Spring stiffness values can be applied uniformly to all nodes meshed on the assigned feature, or their values may vary over a feature by applying a variation variation . Stiffness applies the spring stiffness uniformly to all nodes meshed on the assigned feature. Stiffness/unit length and Stiffness/unit area distribute the total spring stiffness between the nodes on the assigned feature. For axisymmetric models stiffness/unit length is a stiffness per unit length, per radian.

topics.title: Simple lift-off supports
topics.text: Simple lift-off supports A simple lift-off support can be specified by pressing the Lift-off button and selecting the appropriate radio button for the degree of freedom that will control the lift-off condition for the support. For this a single value for the lift-off freedom needs to defined, where the lift-off value to be stated is the value that would be required to overcome the reaction or restraint at that support. This means that a positive lift-off value would be entered to overcome a negative reaction. Entering a negative lift-off control value effectively reverses the lift-off behaviour. A Lift-off value is set for either Force , Moment , Hinge rotation , or Flow for a chosen degree of freedom. Lift-off will take place once a stated value has been exceeded. Additional behaviour can be specified for when lift-off has occurred: Release restraint in lift-off direction only releases only the specified restraint (controlling freedom), leaving all other restraints applied. Release all restraints releases all restraints.

topics.title: Advanced lift-off supports and touchdown (contact)
topics.text: Advanced lift-off supports and touchdown (contact) More advanced lift-off behaviour can be modelled and specified using the Contact button. This provides for both lift-off and touch down and requires setting the appropriate contact conditions for the degree of freedom that will control the lift-off/contact behaviour. For lift-off (whether for all directions or the chosen direction), the support fixity part of the dialog describes the behaviour before the lift-off has occurred. For contact/touchdown, the support fixity part of the dialog describes the behaviour after the touchdown has occurred.

topics.title: Contact control settings for Displacements or Pore Pressure
toc_path: Contact control settings for Displacements or Pore Pressure
headings: Contact control settings for Displacements or Pore Pressure
topics.text: Contact control settings for Displacements or Pore Pressure Contact control for a Displacement or a Pore pressure based support condition is set using a Gap condition. For this, a supported node is free to move within an upper value and lower value. Touch down (contact) will occur when a limiting value is exceeded. This option would be used to restrict the movement of a pipe in a pipe support, or the movement of a bridge beam or deck supported by a displacement-restricted bridge bearing for example.

topics.title: Lift-off / Contact examples
topics.text: Lift-off / Contact examples Notes The degrees of freedom which may be restrained for any analysis depend on the chosen element type. Those applicable for each element are defined in the Element Reference Manual. For structural problems Translation in X, Y, Z and Rotation about X, Y, Z refer to freedoms along and about the global axes unless a local coordinate local coordinate is assigned in which cases the axis directions refer to local directions x, y, z. A hinge (loof) rotation is a local freedom which refers to rotation about the side of an element. Pore pressure is a special freedom type used in two phase elements. For thermal (field) problems there is only one freedom type, temperature (or the field variable). A support can only be set to have lift-off or contact properties, not both. If a particular freedom has been chosen as the freedom that controls lift-off / touchdown, it must either be either a restrained of spring freedom, it may not be ‘free’. When loadcases that contain supports with lift-off or contact behaviour are used in load combinations or envelopes, a warning symbol is added to the load combination/envelope symbol to signify that lift-off/contact supports are defined and that the principal of superposition is not true for these results. These combinations can be expanded to enable a nonlinear analysis to be carried out. See Combinations and Envelopes Combinations and Envelopes for details. See also: Support Conditions Support Conditions Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes

topics.title: Support Assignment
topics.text: Support Assignment Specify the feature types, analyses and loadcases to which the support attribute should be assigned. LUSAS will only assign the support to features are valid for it. Notes For linear and modal analysis supports apply to all loadcases. For nonlinear and transient analysis supports may be applied or modified on any analysis step by selecting (or entering) the appropriate loadcase from the drop down list. This means a support applied on loadcase 1 will apply to all subsequent loadcases unless overwritten. A support may thus be fixed at the start of the analysis and then freed or vice versa. Only supports from the first loadcase of a base analysis can be inherited between analyses.Supports in other loadcases are not inherited. topics.title: Geometric Surface Properties
topics.text: Geometric Surface Properties Geometric properties specify any relevant geometrical information that is not inherent in the feature geometry, for example section properties or thickness. Eccentricity (in the local z direction) and thickness are optional geometric properties for certain Surface elements namely Membrane, Plate or Shell. The properties may be varied by specifying a previously defined variation. To do this press the variation button when you enter a value in any field. Notes Geometric properties are not required for plane strain or axisymmetric solid elements. Thickness is required for axisymmetric shell elements but not for axisymmetric solid elements The geometric properties are specified in generic form but only the properties required for the intended element need be specified. For example eccentricity is ignored by semi - loof shell elements. The Surface thickness and eccentricity properties may be fleshed using the fleshing button or from the Attribute treeview. See also: Geometric Properties Geometric Properties Manipulating Attributes Manipulating Attributes Variations Variations

If the surfaces are coincident the element axes will follow the global axes. Ignore assigned local coordinates Ignores any local coordinates assigned to the point or line or surface. By point in selection memory A point previously placed into selection memory selection memory is used to define the element xy plane. By specified local coordinates The element axes can be defined using a previously defined local coordinate, or by creating a new local coordinate using the New... option.

topics.title: Thermal Gap
topics.text: Thermal Gap Thermal gap properties define heat transfer across a gap and heat transfer by contact when a gap is deemed to have closed. They combine Gap and/or Contact Surface property attributes with one or two Thermal Surfaces. Thermal gap attributes are defined from the Utilities> Heat Transfer menu item, which is only available for a Thermal Analysis. Heat flow is dependent upon whether the thermal surface is facing an open environment or across a gap or enclosure. When there is a gap between two thermal surfaces or a single thermal surface such as the inside of a sphere, gap conductance properties are used to describe how heat is transferred across the gap. The heat flow across the gap can be constant or a linear function of the gap length. The conductance of the gap links is given a constant value for when the gap is closed and also a variable value which depends on the length of the gap. The links are formed by projecting a normal from within the segment to where it intercepts with another segment. Heat is then said to flow between these two points along the link.

topics.title: Gap conductance properties
topics.text: Gap conductance properties Specify the gap conductance properties that will be used on the thermal surfaces defining the gap. Gap conductance for a closed gap [ko] Convective coefficient for a closed gap [hco] Variation of gap conductance with gap opening [dk/dL] The value of the gradient. Variation of gap convective coefficient with gap opening [dh/dL] The value of the gradient. Maximum link length [Lmax] limits the range of validity of the link element to which these gap properties will be applied. If the length of the link is calculated to be greater than this value, then heat will flow either to an environmental node, to the general environment or the surface will be considered to be insulated, depending on the Environmental Surface Properties input. Reference temperature The temperature at which all the preceding values are valid Note that gap openings are calculated by evaluating the intersection of the surface normal, originating from a point 1/4 the distance from a segment node to the segment centroid, with an opposing surface.

If the slideline surface pressure is greater than the contact pressure specified here, then the contact pressure value is used.

topics.title: Thermal surfaces defining gap
topics.text: Thermal surfaces defining gap Previously defined thermal surfaces are presented in the drop-down list. Select the appropriate surfaces to define the gap. Only one thermal surface is required to define a thermal gap. Links will then be set up between segments of this surface alone. A second thermal surface may be specified for numerical efficiency. The search for linkage between the two defined segments commences with segments on the second Surface, if no possible link is found, the first surface is then checked.

topics.title: Options
topics.text: Options Update geometry Controls the updating of the geometry in a coupled LUSAS analysis. You may want to deselect this option to prevent the update and subsequent re-calculation of thermal links when geometry is read from a coupled structural analysis. Element shading Checks for shading of elements defining the thermal gap. This options forces a complete search of all possible thermal surface segments. The nearest segment with which it is possible to form a link is then taken as the linkage segment. Gap initially Specifies whether a gap is initially active or inactive. Setting a gap to be inactive suppresses the thermal gap which has the effect of insulating flow across it. A gap may be re-activated at a later stage in the solution be re-defining the thermal gap. topics.title: Discrete Thermal Loading

Discrete loads differ from feature based loads in that they are not limited to application over whole features and may be effective over full or partial areas of the model. Search areas may be used to restrict the area of application of a discrete load. topics.title: Specifying the mesh type
topics.text: Specifying the mesh type Define the mesh discretisation using any of the following methods: Regular is used when opposite sides of a Volume have the same number of mesh divisions. Allow Transition pattern allows standard mesh patterns on regular Volumes when the mesh divisions are non uniform. Allow Irregular mesh allows irregular meshing when regular or transition meshing is not possible. (Only applicable for tetrahedral elements) Automatic uses the default mesh divisions (File > Model properties menu item), or the divisions specified in an assigned Line mesh or Surface mesh. Local x, y, z divisions allow mesh refinement to be achieved Irregular Mesh used for irregular Volumes. Element size defines the maximum size of the elements on the Volume boundary Lines for which no adjoining volumes are present and when no Line attributes have been assigned. topics.title: Element Orientation (default method)
topics.text: Element Orientation (default method) Line elements are orientated according to the following rules: If the beam is curved then the node is placed in the same plane as the existing three nodes, i.e. the node position is calculated as p + z x x2 where p is the position vector to the first node, z is the vector calculated from z = x2 x x3 where x2 and x3 are vectors from the first node to the second and third nodes respectively. If the beam is straight and parallel to the global x axis then the node is placed in the xy plane and the position calculated as p + x x Y where x is a vector from the first node to the second node and Y is a unit vector along the global y axis. If the beam is straight and not parallel to the global X axis then the node position is calculated as p + z x x where z is the vector calculated from z = X x x where X is a unit vector along the global X axis and x is a vector from the first to the second node.

topics.title: Import / Define Laminae (FiberSIM Solids and Shells)
toc_path: Import / Define Laminae (FiberSIM Solids and Shells)
headings: Import / Define Laminae (FiberSIM Solids and Shells)
topics.text: Import / Define Laminae (FiberSIM Solids and Shells) Defines a composite stack for draping based upon FibreSIM XML data. Location of FibreSIM xml file is used to import each lamina individually. Default material to use for laminae is populated from any materials previously added to the Attributes treeview. Default fibre volume fraction for laminae is the proportion of the volume of a lamina that is fibre with the remaining portion being the resin. For example, a volume fraction of 1 means 100% fibre and no resin, 0.55 means 55% fibre and 45% resin. Layer to layer relative offset should be set to match the lamina layup stacking method as defined by the creator of the FibreSIM XML file. Default - Typically FibreSIM XML files are defined with a stack of layers sitting together at the tooling surface level. In this case the Default option would be used unless investigation of the FibreSIM XML file suggested otherwise. Grouped - FiberSIM XML files have sometimes been found to contain stack data that is grouped such that the lowest two layers are set at tooling surface level, the next two layers are offset from tooling level by the actual thickness of the previous two layers, and the next two layers offset from the previous pair by the previous pairs's thickness and so on. In this case a Grouped size of 2 would be selected. If lamina were in sets of 3 a grouped size of 3 would apply. General - Should a FibreSIM XML file ever contain stack data that is grouped in non-repetitive sets such that layer 1 was at tooling surface level, layer 2, was offset from layer 1, and layers 3 and 4 were offset from layer 2, for example, then this option would be used. Extend FiberSIM grid - Extends the FiberSIM grid to ensure the edges of the component are fully enclosed by the draping grid. Note that FiberSIM grids are not automatically trimmed at Surface boundaries. Drape locking angle - A locking angle may be specified so that if an imported grid has a skew angle greater than that specified, an error is generated . See also: Composites Composites

topics.text: Assign Section This dialog is displayed when a geometric line attribute that contains a set of multiple varying sections is assigned to a selection of lines on the model. Global axis aligns sections to the global X , Y or Z axis. Local axis aligns sections to a pre-defined local coordinate system Path reference aligns sections to a pre-defined reference path Create path from selection creates a path from previously selected lines, arcs or splines and aligns the sections to that path. Starting offset distance offsets the first section a specified distance from the start of the selected line or reference path. Notes If the lines being assigned the geometric line attribute do not all lie in a global axis a reference path must be used. See also: Reference paths Reference paths

topics.title: Point Mesh Assignment (Manual method)
topics.text: Point Mesh Assignment (Manual method) There are two types of Point Mesh assignment: Non-Structural Mass Elements and Mesh Spacing attributes are assigned to a single Point. Joint elements are assigned to two Points. These Points may be coincident (if one is made unmergeable) or non-co-incident. When joint elements are to be assigned to many pairs of points use selection memory selection memory to define the set of slave points.

topics.title: Element Orientation
topics.text: Element Orientation Point meshes require the local element axes to be defined using one of the following methods: Follow point axes (Default selection) Adopt the axes assigned from the Local Coordinate (if any) assigned to the point. Ignore local coords assigned to point When joints are defined between non-coincident points the local x-axis is orientated from Master (Point 1) to Slave (Point 2) and the element local z is then defined in the XZ plane unless the local x axis is aligned to the global Z axis in which case the element local z axis is aligned with the global Y axis. When non-structural mass, mesh spacing or joints between coincident points are assigned a Point Mesh the local axes are aligned to the global axes. This method is also used when no Local Coordinate is assigned. By point in selection memory - A Point previously added to selection memory selection memory is used to define the xy-plane. By specified local coordinates The element axes are defined using a previously defined local coordinate. Align joint to local axes - The Advanced button provides the means to align the local axes of the joint to specified local coordinate axes. For example joint x to match local coordinate x, or joint y to match local coordinate x etc.

topics.title: Point Mesh Spacing
topics.text: Point Mesh Spacing Point mesh spacing is used to define the target mesh size for irregular meshing using a background grid background grid . The element size specifies the actual element size at the Point if the stretching parameters are used at the default settings. The stretching parameters control the element distortion in the directions specified by the stretching vectors. For example if the following data was input: 1st stretching parameter = 1 1st stretching vector = [1 0 0] 2nd stretching parameter = 2 2nd stretching vector = [0 1 0] The above would lead to a mesh in which the elements were twice as long in the y direction as in the x direction. See also: About Meshing About Meshing

topics.title: Isotropic (Attributes menu)
topics.text: Isotropic (Attributes menu) Defines an Isotropic Elastic material which can also include the properties Plastic, Creep, Damage and/or Viscous. Elastic specifies linear elastic material properties. Isotropic, orthotropic and anisotropic sub - types are available. Orthotropic material orientation is specified as global, relative to a local coordinate system or relative to the feature local axis system. Plastic specifies yield behaviour. von Mises, modified von Mises, Hill, Hoffman, Tresca, Drucker - Prager, Resultant, and User - defined sub - types are available. Creep specifies creep parameters. Must be used in conjunction with an elastic material dataset. Creep can be combined with von Mises, Hill, modified von Mises and Hoffman plasticity models. It is not possible to combine creep with any other material. Damage specifies damage model parameters. Must be used in conjunction with an elastic material dataset. Viscous enables the viscoelastic material behaviour to be represented by a viscoelastic shear modulus and a decay constant. Viscoelasticity imposed in this way acts like a spring - damper in parallel with the elastic - plastic, damage and creep response. Two - phase material properties are used with two-phase elements to define soil in a saturated or partially saturated state, for use in an undrained or consolidation analysis. See also: Isotropic/Orthotropic Materials Isotropic/Orthotropic Materials

topics.title: Plastic Properties
topics.text: Plastic Properties Select a material model from the drop - down list to model ductile yielding of nonlinear elasto - plastic materials such as metals, concrete, soils/rocks/sand. Click on each model name for more information. Stress Resultant Stress Resultant (model 29) Applicable to certain beam and shell elements Tresca Tresca (model 61) Represents ductile behaviour of materials which exhibit little volumetric strain (for example, metals and undrained clays). Incorporates isotropic hardening. Stress Potential Stress Potential general nonlinear properties based on von-Mises or modified von-Mises criterion including hardening. Optimised implicit von Mises Optimised implicit von Mises (model 75) Represents ductile behaviour of materials which exhibit little volumetric strain (for example, metals). Especially for explicit dynamics. Modified Mohr Coulomb Modified Mohr Coulomb This model applies a tensile and/or a compressive cut-off to the standard Mohr-Coulomb model. In tension this prevents unrealistic tensile stresses developing in materials such as soil or rock. In compression the cut-off results in irreversible deformations once the maximum compressive stress is exceeded. The cut-off can be applied to either a single principal stress component or to the mean pressure. Mohr-Coulomb Mohr-Coulomb (model 65) with non-associative flow. Represents materials which exhibit volumetric plastic strain but no volumetric strain during shear. (for example, granular materials such as rock and soils). Incorporates isotropic hardening. Drucker-Prager Drucker-Prager (model 64) Represents ductile behaviour of materials which exhibit volumetric plastic strain (for example, granular materials such as concrete and soils). Incorporates isotropic hardening. See Concrete Models (Nonlinear) Concrete Models (Nonlinear) for material models that model both cracking and crushing behaviour of concrete. Notes Consult the Element Reference Manual to check which material models can be used for the elements used. Optional properties may be added by clicking on a check box and entering the required data. See also: About Isotropic and Orthotropic Materials About Isotropic and Orthotropic Materials

headings: Multiple Curve Definition (for Piecewise Linear Elastic (Axial force dependent) Material)
topics.text: Multiple Curve Definition (for Piecewise Linear Elastic (Axial force dependent) Material) This sub dialog allows any number of Force/Displacement (Moment/Rotation) curves to be optionally specified in a piecewise linear way for a stated axial force using either real numbers or variations, where each curve can be of a separate length. As coordinates are defined a dynamic display of the curve is produced. A dotted line is used to identify the extrapolated regions outside of the defined force/displacement curve. A set of defined force/displacement (moment/rotation) curves will be automatically interpolated by Modeller to arrive at suitable force/displacement (moment/rotation) values for the particular axial force imposed upon the assigned joint during an analysis.
