As coordinates are defined a dynamic display of the curve is produced. A dotted line is used to identify the extrapolated regions outside of the defined force/displacement curve. A set of defined force/displacement (moment/rotation) curves will be automatically interpolated by Modeller to arrive at suitable force/displacement (moment/rotation) values for the particular axial force imposed upon the assigned joint during an analysis.

topics.title: Creating a curve definition
topics.text: Creating a curve definition The dialog can be used to create any number of Force/Displacement curves. The curves can be defined by coordinate input or spreadsheet import. After the values defining a curve have been specified, press the Add button if more curve definitions are to be defined, or press the OK button to complete all definitions. Stiffness factor outside the range This governs how force/displacement values should be interpolated when they fall outside the range of those defined. A factor of 1 (the default) keeps the same slope as the adjacent force/displacement line segment. A factor of 0 keeps the force the same. Axial force defines the axial force for which the curve defined is valid. The preview window shows the active curve with a green line, and all the inactive curves in the background in grey.Previously defined curve definition data can be accessed using the drop-down list and up/down control alongside the Curve name. Notes A force/displacement curve can be defined for the axial component axis (denoted 'u' on the parent dialog) of an axial force dependent piecewise linear elastic material. If multiple curves defining the behaviour of the axial component are defined for various values of axial force, the behaviour between the singular points on each curve that matches the axial force it was defined for will be cross-interpolated between both bounding piecewise linear curves. This behaviour is complex, and it is therefore recommended that only a single curve is defined for the axial component (u). When clicking the Add button the current data in the grid is validated before adding the new curve. Any errors in the grid data must be corrected before a new curve can be added. When defining a number of displacement/force (moment/rotation) curves, they remain in the order they were defined regardless of the controlling axial force, but on clicking the OK button to close the curve definition dialog and return to the main dialog , the curves are sorted into ascending order by the controlling axial force values. If more than one curve is defined, the Delete button will delete the active curve. It is possible to zoom in progressively on a part of the graph by boxing with the mouse. To un-zoom by one step, right-click in the graph area. Whilst variations may be used to define curve segments a force response curve that contains them cannot be visualised. It is possible to define segments with negative stiffness/gradient on the force-displacement curve to the positive side of the displacement origin. However, the curve cannot extend below the force level at this origin as the force-displacement relationship would then become non-unique because of the curve data defined (or extrapolated) for negative displacements. This is also true for forces on the negative side of the displacement origin; in this case the curve cannot extend above the force at the displacement origin. When clicking the Add button the current data in the grid is validated before adding the new curve. Any errors in the grid data must be corrected before a new curve can be added. When defining a number of displacement/force (moment/rotation) curves, they remain in the order they were defined regardless of the controlling axial force, but on clicking the OK button to close the curve definition dialog and return to the main dialog , the curves are sorted into ascending order by the controlling axial force values. If more than one curve is defined, the Delete button will delete the active curve. It is possible to zoom in progressively on a part of the graph by boxing with the mouse. To un-zoom by one step, right-click in the graph area. Whilst variations may be used to define curve segments a force response curve that contains them cannot be visualised. It is possible to define segments with negative stiffness/gradient on the force-displacement curve to the positive side of the displacement origin. However, the curve cannot extend below the force level at this origin as the force-displacement relationship would then become non-unique because of the curve data defined (or extrapolated) for negative displacements. This is also true for forces on the negative side of the displacement origin; in this case the curve cannot extend above the force at the displacement origin. After the values defining a curve have been specified, press the OK button to complete the definition. Stiffness factor outside the range This governs how force/displacement values should be interpolated when they fall outside the range of those defined. A factor of 1 (the default) keeps the same slope as the adjacent force/displacement line segment. A factor of 0 keeps the force the same. Notes It is possible to zoom in progressively on a part of the graph by boxing with the mouse. To unzoom by one step right - click in the graph area. Whilst variations may be used to define curve segments a force response curve that contains them cannot be visualised. Rotations should be defined in radians. It is possible to define segments with negative stiffness/gradient on the force-displacement curve to the positive side of the displacement origin. However, the curve cannot extend below the force level at this origin as the force-displacement relationship would then become non-unique because of the curve data defined (or extrapolated) for negative displacements. This is also true for forces on the negative side of the displacement origin; in this case the curve cannot extend above the force at the displacement origin. topics.title: General settings for all joints
topics.text: General settings for all joints Analysis category Shows the analysis category analysis category in use. Assignment to defines / shows the feature(s) to which the joint material has been defined. Options (according to joint type selected are 'Points', 'Points and line ends' (meaning rigid zones), 'Lines', and 'Surfaces'. Once assigned to a feature type, the joint cannot be assigned to different feature types. Joint type selection of a joint type adds the properties that need to be defined for each freedom for that joint type to the tabular grid on the dialog. Mass position (when required) options are used to specify that the joint mass will be 'Between nodes', or 'At first node', or 'At second node' Axial direction / Coupled axis / Normal direction (according to joint material type and dialog selections made) can specified to be local x, y or z axis. For 'Coupled axis' an Uncoupled option is also available. Additional Cylindrical , Thermal expansion , Damping , Varying friction coefficient and Compound hysteresis options are selectable according to joint type. Note that selection of one of the 'Assignment to' options controls the expected units for each degree of freedom as displayed in the tooltip when the cursor is hovered over an input cell. When defining a new joint material 'Point' or 'Point and line ends' is the default, again according to joint type. When pre-version 15 models are being edited no selection is automatically made and for these models there is no requirement to make a selection.

topics.text: Settings Specify a p-y curve for Cohesionless soil or Cohesive soil Description (For cohesionless soil only) options are: Sand, Sand silt, Silt, Gravel, or User-defined. Relative density (For cohesionless soil only) options are Very loose, Loose, Medium dense, Dense, or Very dense. Curves based on options are API RP2A-WSD, DNV-OS-J101, ISO 19902:2007 or JTS 167-4-2012. The soil parameters grid is populated according to the soil type and Code of Practice selected. These parameters are generally self-explanatory. Unit weight of soil - dry ( g d ) Unit weight of soil - saturated ( g s ) Curve fitting factor (r f ) - for DNV-OS-J101 only. Ratio of zone of influence radius to pile radius - for DNV-OS-J101 only. Residual adhesion ratio - (t res /t max - for DNV-OS-J101 only. Undrained shear strength (s u ) - for cohesive soils only. Strain at one-half maximum stress (epsilon c ) Dimensionless empirical constant (J) - for cohesive soils only. Overconsolidation ratio (OCR - DNV only) - for cohesive soils only. Angle of internal friction of soil ( f )- for cohesive soils only. Poisson's ratio of soil ( n ) - for DNV-OS-J101 only and cohesive soils only. P-Multiplier - Define a suitable value for a pile according to its position in a pile group with respect to any applied transverse loading. Because of "shear zone" effects within piles in groups, the leading row of piles has the highest resistance of any of the rows in the group to any applied transverse loading, and may be only slightly less resistant than a single isolated pile under the same loading. The piles in the other rows have lower resistance. As an example, in AASHTO LRFD 9th Edition, Table 10.7.2.4-1, the following the P-Multipliers are defined: P-Multipliers, Pm Pile centre to centre spacing (in the direction of loading) Row 1 Row 2 Row 3 and higher 3 pile diameters 0.8 0.4 0.3 5 pile diameters 1.0 0.85 0.7 Refer to the requirements of a selected code for additional guidance. Note that square and H-piles, as a result of both increased side shear and direct stress components of soil resistance, have more resistance to lateral loading than circular piles. When using User defined cohesionless soil, the following parameters are offered, named according to the nomenclature used in the selected code of practice: Shaft friction factor (open) (Beta) Shaft friction factor (closed) (Beta) or Angle of soil friction on the pile wall (δ, degrees) Limiting shaft friction value (t lim ) or Limiting unit skin friction (f l ) End bearing factor (N q ) or Bearing factor (N q ) Limiting unit end bearing value (q lim ) or Limiting tip resistance (q l )

topics.title: Tension or Compression Bar material
topics.text: Tension or Compression Bar material Tension-only or compression-only bar material can be defined in the tension or Compression Bar dialog, which is accessed from the Attributes> Material> Tension / Compression Only (Bar)... menu item. Bar materials can be defined by entering properties directly, or by selecting the From library option and choosing a material type, for a region or country (when applicable), for design code or standard (when applicable), and for a grade of material (when applicable). For some materials in some regions a user-defined grade can also be specified, using the Advanced define drop-down item. An example of this would be for Concrete, USA, AASHTO LRFD 7th, where a compressive strength, weight, and aggregate correction factor can be defined. Values displayed or calculated for each chosen or defined material type are isotropic material properties. The units will default to those chosen on model startup but may be changed if desired. Values can be modified and other material properties can be defined once the material is added to the Attributes Treeview. Note that the attribute name provided, or a name that is manually defined, will also automatically include a description formed from the selections made, when added to the Attributes Treeview. Pick the material type and options required from the drop down list, and click OK or Apply to add the material properties to the Attributes Treeview. Assign the material attribute to the appropriate features in the model. See also: Piecewise Linear Bar Material Model Piecewise Linear Bar Material Model

topics.title: Damage Properties
topics.text: Damage Properties Damage is assumed to occur in a material by the initiation and growth of cavities and micro - cracks. The damage model allows parameters to be defined which control the initiation of damage and post damage behaviour. In LUSAS a scalar damage variable is used in the degradation of the elastic modulus matrix. This means that the effect of damage is considered to be non - directional or isotropic. Two LUSAS damage models are available (Simo and Oliver) together with a facility for a user - supplied model. See also: About Isotropic and Orthotropic Materials About Isotropic and Orthotropic Materials Damage Properties Damage Properties

topics.title: Viscous Properties
topics.text: Viscous Properties Viscoelasticity can be coupled with the linear elastic and non - linear plasticity, (isotropic or orthotropic), creep and damage models available in LUSAS. The model restricts the viscoelastic effects to the deviatoric component of the material response. This enables the viscoelastic material behaviour to be represented by a viscoelastic shear modulus Gv and a decay constant b . Viscoelasticity imposed in this way acts like a spring - damper in parallel with the elastic - plastic, damage and creep response. Coupling of the viscoelastic and the existing nonlinear material behaviour enables hysteresis effects to be modelled. See also: About Isotropic and Orthotropic Materials About Isotropic and Orthotropic Materials Viscous Properties Viscous Properties

topics.title: Set Active Combination or Envelope
topics.text: Set Active Combination or Envelope When selecting a primary component of interest for investigating results for a particular effect, either ‘Raw components’ or ‘Derived components’ may be used. Raw components are those calculated for each element type by LUSAS Solver, as for example, Fx, Fy,and Mz, for a 2D thick beam. Derived components are those created by LUSAS Modeller by mathematically manipulating the raw components, and include components such as absolutes, equivalents, principals, Wood-Armer, User Defined Results and others. When a derived component is used as a primary component, or when a derived component is inspected when choosing the 'Max/min each component individually' option for particular situations involving smart combinations and envelopes, LUSAS Modeller will automatically suppress the listing of particular derived components in the Component drop-down list that could produce misleading results as the unwary could get an answer that could be misunderstood or misinterpreted when reporting on results involving those components. This can be overridden. See Raw and Derived Components Raw and Derived Components for details. On the dialog: Max / min primary component with coincident effects Views coincident effects for each results component as set in the Layers Treeview based upon the chosen primary results component selected from the Entity and Component drop-lists on this dialog . Results may be transformed to a consistent direction using the Set... button. Note that if the results component being displayed is a derived component, no results will be available unless 'Allow derived components' is selected. See below. Allow derived components (When present on a dialog) Adds Entities and corresponding derived results components to the drop-lists. The ability to access derived components must be used with caution because erroneous results can be obtained in some situations. See Raw and Derived Components Raw and Derived Components for details. Change existing drawing layers to above component Changes any results component previously specified (and displayed as one of the drawing layers) to be that of the results component chosen on this dialog. Max / min each component individually Views optimised effects for each results component as set in the Layers Treeview, such that each displayed component is optimised individually. Note that if the results component chosen is a derived component, no results will be available unless 'Allow derived components' is selected. See below. Allow derived components (When present on a dialog) The ability to access derived components must be used with caution because erroneous results can be obtained in some situations. See Raw and Derived Components Raw and Derived Components for details.

topics.title: Loadcases
topics.text: Loadcases The loadcases that the slice/graph is to report on can be specified by selecting either: <Current active loadcase name> - reports for this loadcase name only. See note. Active - reports for the active loadcase only. See note. All - reports for all loadcases. Specified - reports for a specified named loadcase, when the graph is viewed or created, or used in a report. Create new window for each loadcase - when checked, displays each graph in a separate window. Unchecked, all graphs are displayed within one window. Note Graphing of data for <Current active loadcase name> will graph only that loadcase. By setting the Active loadcase option will allow multiple graphs to be created or included in separate reports, simply by changing the Active loadcase in the Analyses Treeview, before each graph or report is created.

Selection - reports for only those previously selected elements at the graph is created <Group name(s)> - (if present) lists available group names. New... - allows creating a group name of selected visible items, or an empty group, as part of the graphing process See also: Results on Sections Through a Model Results on Sections Through a Model

topics.title: Graph Through 2D
topics.text: Graph Through 2D Arbitrary line sections may be taken through any surface of a two dimensional model or on a slice cut through a three dimensional solid model. The process of cutting a slice will generate two graph datasets in the Utilities Treeview; the first containing the distance along the line section and the second containing the specified results along the line. Lines showing the location of the slice sections are shown on the model and are saved with the model. Slices on a surface can also be defined by a selected line, or (for more advanced use) the projection of a line or a surface to intersect with a surface in the model.

topics.title: By cursor
topics.text: By cursor Signifies that an arbitrary section line will be defined. Snap to grid defines a section line at a precise location. Useful if wanting to create graphs at regular intervals along a model. See notes. Grid size used in conjunction with snap to grid. Controls the spacing of the grid points. Maximum utilisation Grid offset positions the slice section a specified distance offset from the selected grid points Generate new annotation line Additionally marks the automatically drawn slice section location with a line held in the Annotation layer. This legacy option allows annotation lines to be re-selected if a model is reloaded at a later date in order to view results at the same location. It is effectively superseded by slice section lines now being automatically shown on a model (unless turned-off in the Utilities properties dialog).

topics.title: Notes
topics.text: Notes The 'Snap to grid', 'Grid size' and 'Grid offset' options are not available for models of Analysis category '3D' when they are viewed in a non-primary view - that is when they viewed along anything other than the X, Y or Z axis. The Graph through 2D option is not available when a model is being viewed using the perspective facility. If active, press the perspective button to revert to a non-perspective view. topics.title: Layout Grid Labels
topics.text: Layout Grid Labels Grid labels can be specified for the layout grid lines in the X, or radial direction, and in the Y, or circumferential direction. Labels can be alphabetic or numeric, and be positioned at the top end, bottom end, top and bottom (both) ends or neither end of each grid line. Alphabetic labels will be auto generated as 'A', 'B', C' etc and increment to 'AA', AB' etc. An option to reverse the direction of the labelling is provided. By default labels are drawn flat to screen. An option to draw them flat to grid (in the plane of the grid) is also available. See also: Layout Grid Layout Grid

Anchor point An annotation can be located with respect to the model, or to the window (page). Coordinate locations are taken from the bottom left corner of the window in working mode, or the page in page layout Arrow head Enable the size and shape of the arrow head to be adjusted. Visibility The annotation can be made visible on all windows or just the current one. Choose Pen Enables the line colour and thickness to be modified. Name An identifier for the item. topics.title: Section Details - for arbitrary section
topics.text: Section Details - for arbitrary section This dialog shows calculated properties (or illustrative section properties for any section defined with two or more different materials) for a defined section. A black section axis is drawn at the centroid of the section. Symbols showing the centroid, shear centre, plastic neutral axis, the (view) origin about which the section was drawn and fibre locations that are automatically created for extreme positions within each quadrant are also shown. For sections comprising two or more materials, note that the material attributes in the Arbitrary Section's treeview that are used in the calculation of section properties are not saved to the Attributes Treeview of the model for which the arbitrary section may be intended. When a geometric line attribute (that references the section) is assigned to a line on a model, a material attribute appropriate to the reference material using a mass density suitable for the section as a whole must be assigned to any line of the model to which the geometric line attribute is assigned. topics.title: Section Through 3D
topics.text: Section Through 3D Slice sections may be cut at arbitrary positions through the model using the cursor to define either a horizontal or vertical slice in the View window. Slices may be generated in any plane by rotating the model to the desired orientation before a section is cut. By default the location of an arbitrary slice section through a model is not saved with the model. However, when cutting a slice section through the model an option to create an annotation polygon is provided. This annotation polygon effectively defines the location and orientation of the cutting plane and does get saved with the model. Annotation polygons may be re-selected if a model is reloaded at a later date in order to view results at the same location. Slice sections can also be created using surfaces that are created at slice section locations. These surfaces do not have to surround a model, they must simply be defined in the orientation of the cutting plane required. To use a saved cutting plane or a surface defining a cutting plane instead of indicating the cut using the cursor, the annotation polygon or surface should be selected before choosing the Utilities> Slice Through 3D menu item, and By selected polygon / surface option. By cursor signifies that an arbitrary section plane will be defined. A slice section created using this method is not saved if the model is subsequently saved. The created slice plane will be normal to the screen view so the model should be manipulated to a suitable view prior to choosing this option. Snap to grid defines a section plane at a precise location. Useful if wanting to create sections at regular intervals along a model. Grid size used in conjunction with snap to grid Generate new annotation polygon signifies that an arbitrary section plane will be defined but the location and orientation of the cutting plane is marked by a polygon drawn in the Annotation layer. A polygon (and hence slice section) created using this method is saved if the model file is subsequently saved. By selected polygon / surface used to plot results through previously defined (and hence saved) polygon and surface locations. See also: Results on Sections Through a Model Results on Sections Through a Model

A polygon (and hence slice section) created using this method is saved if the model file is subsequently saved. By selected polygon / surface used to plot results through previously defined (and hence saved) polygon and surface locations. topics.title: Surface Function Variation
topics.text: Surface Function Variation A Surface function variation consists of a single function in terms of the parametric coordinates of the Surface u and v. The value of the variation at any point on the Surface is given by finding the parametric coordinates of the point within the Surface and substituting them into the specified function. Surface function variations are only allowed for 3 and 4 sided Surfaces. The example shown here defines a variation using the function max(4,10*u) in terms of the local Surface x direction parametric distance. The max function takes two arguments and returns the maximum of both arguments. In this case, 4 is the maximum value until u exceeds 0.4. See also: Variations Variations

topics.title: Profile Variations
topics.text: Profile Variations Profile variations allow modelling of the variation of (primarily, but not exclusively) material properties at any location in a model. They are defined by selecting the Utilitites > Variation menu item. A single profile variation is defined by distance against value, however, any number of profiles in-plane or out-of-plane may be grouped to form a profile set variation. When used to define particular material properties in a supported material model, material properties for elements in any region of a model can be calculated by LUSAS Modeller by interpolating between the distance and values defined for each element between each profile variation location. A typical use is modelling the variation of soil properties with depth, as obtained by borehole data.

topics.title: Direction definition

The local coordinate attribute is stored in the profile set variation so changing the local coordinate attribute definition changes the variation definition, and similarly if the vertical axis changes. Global coordinates provides 'Positive X or Y or Z' or 'Negative X or Y or Z' options to indicate which axis is to be used to define the direction. (Defined cartesian local coordinates) provides 'Positive X or Y or Z' or 'Negative X or Y or Z'options to indicate which axis is to be used to define the direction. topics.title: Defining a profile variation
topics.text: Defining a profile variation A profile variation is defined by pressing the New button and entering distance and value data that describes the line profile. Previously defined data can be edited by pressing the Edit button. Any previously defined profiles are shown in the list box. The Add to '>>' and Remove from '<<' buttons include or exclude a profile from a set. For a 2D analysis category any number of profiles can be specified together with the x,y coordinates for each profile origin, the z coordinate is not shown and defaults to zero. For a 3D analysis category x,y, and z coordinates must be specified for each profile origin. The same profile variation may be used any number of times in the profile set definition but no profiles can have the same origin. See Variations: Profile variation types and calculations made Variations: Profile variation types and calculations made for more details.

topics.title: Evaluation outside range

Extend start value continues the extreme data point at a constant value Linear extrapolation extrapolates the extreme two data points as a straight line.

topics.title: Surface Interpolation Variation by Boundary
topics.text: Surface Interpolation Variation by Boundary Defines a set of interpolation values by specifying variations around the Surface boundary Lines. A variation must be specified for each Line in the Surface definition. If no variation is required along a Line, a constant order variation must be specified. Care must be taken to ensure that interpolation values at corner points are common to both variations meeting there otherwise strange results may occur. Variations are defined in the same direction on opposite sides of the Surface (see the following example) and use the Line order in the Surface definition on which to base the variation direction. Individual Line directions have no effect on variation directions. See also: Variations Variations

topics.title: Surface Interpolation Variation by Grid
topics.text: Surface Interpolation Variation by Grid Defines a full grid of interpolation values by specifying numbers of equal divisions in Surface local X and Y directions and interpolation values at each resulting grid position. Surface grid interpolation can only be used on 3 and 4 sided Surfaces. Care must be taken to supply the correct number of interpolation values for the type of interpolation chosen (see table below). Values are specified along the local X axis first, then along each line of grid positions parallel to the x axis in turn. Interpolation order can be different in each direction. topics.title: Path Definition
topics.text: Path Definition The path definition dialog is accessed by using the Utilities> Reference Path menu item. It allows reference paths to be defined or copied and pasted from a spreadsheet. It also shows path geometry and allows specification of line segment type when a reference path has been generated using lines, arcs or splines in Modeller. A reference path defines a route through a model that provides a concept of distance to each point in the model. Those distances can be used in the definition of a varying section, such that when the section is assigned to lines, the path is used to interpret which part of the section is appropriate to each line. Bridge engineers refer to this reference path concept as chainage. Paths created using this dialog are stored and viewed in the Utilities Treeview. Like other utilities, paths are not directly assignable to geometry and can only be edited using this dialog.

topics.text: Defining a path by coordinate input Path information can be defined by adding rows to a table and specifying the coordinates of each defining point along the path. Values are entered in global coordinates. As the coordinates are entered the path that they define is visualised in the adjacent graphs. Type Clicking on the drop-list button in this cell of the table allows the type of line to be specified. Options are Straight, Arc Bulge, Arc Centre, Spline, Parabola Bulge, and Spline Continued. Insert , Delete and Reverse buttons provide the means to create a new row above a selected row, to delete selected rows, and to reverse the order of all of the rows in the table. Use the tab key to create a new row at the bottom of the table.

topics.title: Transverse direction
topics.text: Transverse direction The transverse direction defines the orientation of the plane of points of equal distance along the path. One example of use would be for straight or skewed grid or grillage models. For this type of modelling a single reference path can be used in conjunction with one of the following settings to offset multiple varying section line attributes appropriately for each longitudinal beam member. Options are: Perpendicular to path - the plane of constant distance is normal to the path tangent in both local y and z directions Skew angle - is defined as the horizontal angle between the orthogonal plane and the plane of equal distance. Local coordinate - as skew angle, but where the skew angle is read from an existing local coordinate system. For more information on transverse direction options see Reference paths Reference paths .

topics.title: Sampling points
toc_path: Defining a Tendon Profile - Advanced options
headings: Defining a Tendon Profile - Advanced options
topics.text: Sampling points For each line segment (that is for each line, arc or spline) of each tendon profile, the number and location of tendon sampling points are calculated according to values specified on the Sampling Points dialog. Tendon sampling points are the locations along a tendon profile at which equivalent tendon loads are calculated and applied to the model. The calculation of the equivalent tendon loads is based upon an underlying piecewise linear curve that is defined by the sampling point settings made. Note that the original points used to define the line, arc or spline have no bearing on any calculations that are carried out. They are simply used to ensure a good tendon profile is obtained. Minimum total number specifies the minimum number of sampling points that will be accepted throughout the tendon profile. Minimum per profile segment specifies the minimum number of sampling points that will be accepted per line segment of the tendon profile. Maximum deviation specifies the maximum offset distance (in modelling units) from the line segment of the tendon profile to the adjacent line of the generated piecewise linear curve that will be accepted along each line segment of the tendon profile. Maximum angular deviation specifies the maximum angle of deviation between segments that will be accepted. From the Minimum total number, Minimum per profile segment and Maximum deviation value entries specified a calculated number of sampling points for each line segment will be arrived at. The Maximum angular deviation value will introduce additional sampling points in line segments where the line segment curvature is high. Note that the maximum deviation distance is input and displayed in current model units. Consistently with other inputs in Modeller, changing the units after entering a value changes the meaning, not the numerical value that was previously input.

topics.text: Other options Pre-solutions for concrete stress calculations - The number of times the model should be solved to calculate prestress effects. For the first solve (the pre-solution), the stress at transfer is assumed to be zero, all time-dependent losses are assumed to be zero, and the prestress loads calculated accordingly. In the second (or subsequent) solve, the stress at transfer is calculated using the eccentricity of each sampling point, and the forces that are read from the results of the corresponding loadcase in the first (or previous) solution. The default number of pre-solutions is 1. See also: Defining a Tendon Profile Defining a Tendon Profile

topics.title: General - Branch types
topics.text: General - Branch types Nonlinear and transient By default, a nonlinear and transient analysis branch continues the nonlinear and transient behaviour of the parent analysis, even if no new control chapter is created. This behaviour may be modified by attaching nonlinear and transient controls to the loadcases in the branch. In this context, those loadcases then behave exactly like stages. This option is appropriate, for example, to “fork” an analysis in two different directions, based perhaps on different loading, or different convergence criteria. When this option is selected, a nonlinear options “cog” is added to the treeview, within the branch, and the user may use this to, for example, switch geometric and material nonlinearity on and off. Linear Used to create linear loadcases inside the analysis branch that behave exactly like those in a normal linear analysis, except that the supports, materials, geometric assignments and stiffness matrix are inherited from the nonlinear controls of the parent loadcase. This option is appropriate, for example, for considering a moving load analysis on a structure during its staged construction. For this option, no controls can be defined and assignment of nonlinear facilities (such as activate/deactivate) is not permitted. Phi-c Reduction This is used to perform multiple phi-c analyses on the same structure, considering different areas of the model, and/or different input settings. A single loadcase is created inside the new analysis branch. Eigen analysis Choosing this option (and making appropriate selections on the eigenvalue control dialog) creates an eigenvalue control for a single loadcase inside the new analysis branch. Use this option, for example, to perform a buckling check on a structure during staged construction.

topics.title: Modal Damping Control
topics.text: Modal Damping Control Modal Damping is used to compute the damping factors for each eigenmode and output these as a table in the output file. These values may then be used in a subsequent dynamic analysis if desired. By default viscous damping for all modes is computed from the mass and stiffness Rayleigh damping constants specified in the material properties. These values may be overridden for specified modes by entering a default damping factor. Viscous/Structural allows specification of viscous or structural damping. Use distributed damping for provides for three options: When All modes is selected material damping will be used to compute the modal damping factors. If Specified modes is chosen the mode numbers for which the material damping is to be used should be entered in the Specified modes table. All other modes will use the default damping constant. If No modes is selected no additional damping will be carried out. Damping ratio for modes not using distributed damping enables a damping factor to be used for all modes not specified in Specified modes table when Specified modes is chosen from Use distributed damping for combo. See also: Dynamic (Transient) Analysis Dynamic (Transient) Analysis

topics.title: Maximum number of iterations
topics.text: Maximum number of iterations Subspace iteration (default = 10) Defined as the absolute value of (current eigenvalue - previous eigenvalue)/current eigenvalue. This must be satisfied for all eigenvalues before convergence is assumed. Inverse iteration (default = 30) this measure is defined as the tolerance for mass orthogonality. Lanczos (default = 100) this parameter defines the number of steps to be carried out. The inverse iteration procedure should always converge quickly since the shift point is automatically updated to improve convergence if this is not the case. The maximum number of iterations should therefore be set at 30 to act merely as a safety measure since this should never be required by the algorithm.

headings: Use P-Delta stress stiffness for 2-noded beams
topics.text: Use P-Delta stress stiffness for 2-noded beams Requires Buckling Load solution to be set on the parent dialog. This option is only applicable to beam elements of the BMI and BMX families. When selected, the 2-noded beams of these element families are formulated using P-Delta stress stiffness When selected, the 3-noded beams of these element families are formulated using Total Lagrangian stress stiffness If not selected all 2 and 3-noded beams of these element families are formulated using Co-Rotational stress stiffness For buckling load assessment this option works at its best when a member is represented by a line meshed with one beam element . For situations where more than one element is used a co-rotational stiffness formulation will give a better performance in general. topics.title: Solution type
topics.text: Solution type Frequency analysis extracts the natural modes of vibration of a structure. Frequency (complex) is used when joint or material damping has been specified for a model. For this, resultant displacement results of the real and imaginary components are displayed within Modeller. Buckling load A linear buckling analysis which may be applied to relatively ‘stiff’ structures to estimate the maximum load that can be supported prior to structural instability or collapse. Eigenvalues of stiffness analysis Used to perform an eigenvalue analysis of the stiffness matrix at a selected stage of an analysis. This facility may be used in conjunction with a nonlinear analysis nonlinear analysis to predict structural instability or bifurcation points during a geometrically nonlinear analysis. Include modal damping (available for Frequency options only) is used to output the overall damping factors for each eigenmode and output these as a table in the output file. These values may then be used in a modal dynamic or spectral (harmonic/IMD) analysis if desired.

topics.text: Eigenvalues required and type of eigensolver available The Subspace ( QL and Jacobi ), Lanczos and Fast Block Lanczos solvers are available to compute either the maximal or minimal eigenvalues, while the Inverse iteration, Lanczos and Fast Block Lanczos solvers may be used to compute the eigenvalues or frequencies that exist within a specified eigenvalue or frequency range of interest. See Eigenvalue analysis Eigenvalue analysis for further information. Eigenvalue normalisation may be performed with respect to the global mass matrix, stiffness matrix, or to unity.

topics.title: Enter the required control values
topics.text: Enter the required control values Eigenvalues required (Minimum, Maximum or Range) Must be less than or equal to the number of free nodal variables for the structure. The range can be specified for Frequency or Eigenvalue. Eigenvector normalisation Chooses between eigenvector normalisation with respect to the global mass matrix, stiffness matrix or to unity. (Default is unity for buckling, and mass for frequency. Maximum and minimum frequency/eigenvalue range points and the number of eigenvalues required (range) All eigensolutions are searched for unless you request a smaller number of solutions by specifying the number of eigenvalues. Note the Eigenvalue/Frequency Range facility cannot be used if constraint equations have been defined, unless the Fast Block Lanczos solver is used. Shift to be applied (Minimum/Maximum) Used to overcome numerical problems when rigid body modes are present. (Default = 0 i.e. no shift.) Number of starting iteration vectors (Subspace only) Default is the lowest of: 2 * number of Eigenvalues 8 + number of Eigenvalues The number of structural degrees of freedom Note that entering zero (0) will force LUSAS to use the default value.

Maximum and minimum frequency/eigenvalue range points and the number of eigenvalues required (range) All eigensolutions are searched for unless you request a smaller number of solutions by specifying the number of eigenvalues. Note the Eigenvalue/Frequency Range facility cannot be used if constraint equations have been defined, unless the Fast Block Lanczos solver is used. Shift to be applied (Minimum/Maximum) Used to overcome numerical problems when rigid body modes are present. (Default = 0 i.e. no shift.) Number of starting iteration vectors (Subspace only) Default is the lowest of: 2 * number of Eigenvalues 8 + number of Eigenvalues The number of structural degrees of freedom Note that entering zero (0) will force LUSAS to use the default value.

topics.title: Fourier Analysis
topics.text: Fourier Analysis A Fourier analysis is used to solve problems in which axisymmetric structures are subjected to non axisymmetric loading, provided that the displacements are small and linear theory applies. Notes All loads for a static analysis will be decomposed into the defined harmonic components. If a dynamic, eigenvalue or harmonic response analysis is required the harmonic series should only contain 1 term. CL loads in locals Applies concentrated loads concentrated loads in the local cylindrical coordinate system local cylindrical coordinate system . See also: Fourier Analysis Fourier Analysis

topics.title: Restarts
topics.text: Restarts When carrying out incremental analysis, such as nonlinear, transient dynamic or staged construction analyses, the restart facility can be used to continue the solution of an analysis which failed to finish, for whatever reason, and re-solve (normally requiring an alternative strategy) from a chosen 'safe' increment. It can also be used to start a new incremental analysis which inherits the stress-state and deformations from any completed loadcase or 'stage' of a prior incremental analysis. When the restart facilty is chosen, and dependent upon the 'Restart file' increment specified, all specified increments (or loadcases) created up to the point of failure can be accessed when specifying an initial state for a new (continuation) analysis. Save a restart at the end of this control Saves a restart (for the increment or time-step, or loadcase completed) to allow another analysis to continue a solution from this point forward. For more information see Specifying an initial state for an analysis Specifying an initial state for an analysis See also: LUSAS Analysis Types LUSAS Analysis Types Nonlinear Analysis Nonlinear Analysis Thermal/Field Analysis Thermal/Field Analysis Dynamic (Transient) Analysis Dynamic (Transient) Analysis Viscous Analysis Viscous Analysis

topics.title: Arc Length (Automatic Incrementation)
topics.text: Arc Length (Automatic Incrementation) Stiffness ratio to switch to arc - length Stiffness parameter value at which the solution will switch from a constant load level to an arc - length procedure (default = 0.4) By default, the loading remains constant during the iteration process. When Use arc length control is ticked the loading varies during the iterations according to either of the two Arc - length methods, Crisfield’s or Rheinboldt’s. See Incremental Procedures Incremental Procedures . Relative displacement arc - length procedure Only to be used with interface elements to provide an alternative arc - length procedure if convergence problems occur. See Theory Manual for details. Guide arc - length procedure with current stiffness Used in situations where unwanted unloading is occurring in the presence of bifurcations. See Theory Manual for details. Use root with lowest residual norm Only required to select the best solution path when severe snap back is occurring. See Theory Manual for details. Arc - length restart load factor The incremental - length value required to restart an analysis under arc - length control. When applying a restart with the structure near to collapse, it is advisable to use arc - length control (isurfc=1). If the load - deflection response is very flat, it is impractical to restart (as normal) by specifying a load factor, slamda. Instead, it is better to specify an ‘arc - length increment’, dellst. An appropriate value for dellst can be obtained by looking at output values of the arc length in the iterative log or output file, of prior arc - length increments, deltl. If dellst is nonzero this value will be used for the new load increment instead of slamda no matter what value of slamda is specified. Arc - length restart load change The maximum value of dellst for subsequent increments (default is calculated as delsmx =2*dellst). If the Arc - length restart load factor is nonzero this value will be used to limit the size of subsequent increments instead of Max change in load factor no matter what value of dlamdx is specified.

topics.title: Termination Criteria
topics.text: Termination Criteria Terminate on value of limiting variable Terminates the solution when the value of a named freedom is reached. For example, if a Point is selected prior to choosing to specify nonlinear controls, a limiting displacement of 1 in the local y direction (v) could be specified for that point, which once reached would cause the analysis to terminate. Note that only Points currently selected with the cursor will appear in the drop-list and that if more than one termination criteria has been specified, termination will occur following the first criterion to be satisfied. Minimum change in incremental load Terminates the solution when the specified value of minimum change of incremental load is reached. For arc-length the default value is 1-0E-15.For standard incrementation if 1E-15 was entered, this is multiplied by a hard-coded value of 1.0E-9 to give a resulting value used of 1E-6.

topics.title: Step Reduction
topics.text: Step Reduction Defines how a load increment will be reduced if convergence difficulties occur. The 'Allow step reduction' option sis ticked by default to apply automatic step reduction with the following settings: Maximum step reductions The maximum number of times a step reduction can occur on a single increment. If input as zero step reduction will be suppressed. Load reduction factor Used to reduce the load increment on a step reduction. Load increase factor Used to increase the original load increment if the Maximum step reductions have failed to achieve a solution. If the maximum number of step reductions has failed to lead to convergence then a final attempt is made to achieve a solution by increasing the original increment using the Load increase factor . This procedure has the potential to ‘step over’ a difficult point in an analysis (e.g. a bifurcation point) so that the solution can continue. See also: Nonlinear Analysis Nonlinear Analysis

topics.title: Nonlinear convergence
topics.text: Nonlinear convergence Specifies at which stage the iterative corrections can be assumed to have restored the structure to equilibrium. Maximum absolute residual The limit for the maximum absolute value of any residual (mar). Root mean square of residual The limit for the square root of the mean value of the squares of all residuals (rms). Displacement norm The limit for the sum of the squares of the iterative displacements as a percentage of the sum of the squares of the incremental displacements (dtnrm). Only translation degrees of freedom are considered by default Residual work norm The limit for the work done by the residuals acting through the iterative displacements as a percentage of the work done by the loads on iteration zero of the increment (wdnrm). Euclidean pressure norm description needed. Increment Euclidean pressure norm description needed. For Residual force norm , Incremental displacement norm and Displacement norm only translation degrees of freedom are considered by default but all degrees of freedom can be included by specifying Option 187. Nonlinear iterative acceleration With respect to the line searc options available: Line searches are carried out if the absolute value of the Line search tolerance parameter on the nonlinear iterative log exceeds the Line search tolerance factor . The aim is to make the Line search tolerance parameter reasonably small on each iteration to speed convergence and prevent divergence. The selection of line search parameters is problem dependent and largely a matter of experience. However, a maximum of 3 to 5 line search iterations with a tolerance of 0.3 to 0.8 is usually sufficient (the closer the tolerance is to unity, the more slack the minimum energy requirement). See Iterative Acceleration Iterative Acceleration .

topics.title: Direct Method Influence Grid Settings
topics.text: Direct Method Influence Grid Settings These settings control the density of the virtual grid of points that is to be loaded with a unit point load as part of an influence analysis. Match nodes in search area (line beam models only) - with this option selected, the nodes in the DMI grid are created by projecting the nodes in the search area specified (or all the nodes in the model if no search area was specified) onto the line path that specifies the centreline of the DMI grid and then translates them in the transverse direction each side of the path. The DMI grid is updated automatically when the mesh changes. Specify grid - allows a user-defined loading grid to be generated based upon longitudinal and transverse settings.

topics.title: Transverse spacing
topics.text: Transverse spacing Minimum number Minimum number of load locations (default is 20 when a Search area is set to Whole model, and 2 when a reference path is being used on a line beam model). Note that when modelling line beams with geometric properties representing loadable slabs, the minimum number should always be set to 2 for a faster solution. Note that increasing this minimum number will not improve accuracy. Maximum spacing Maximum spacing between load locations (default is 1.5). Loading grid examples for line beam models Loading grid created by matching nodes in the search area. Loading grid created from either minimum or maximum number or spacing values Notes The default value for the maximum spacing (in both longitudinal and transverse directions) is 1 foot if the model units are imperial. If one of the global axes (X, Y or Z) has been selected as the centreline of the grid on the Direct Method Influence dialog, then the extents of the model will be calculated. topics.title: Direct Method Influence Analysis
topics.text: Direct Method Influence Analysis A Direct Method Influence Analysis requires Direct Method influence attributes Direct Method influence attributes to be defined and assigned to a line beam, frame, grillage, or slab and deck model. The locations at which a prescribed load will be applied to nodes or points on the model also need to be specified. Influence attributes are defined and assigned from the Attributes> Influence menu. Load locations are defined on the Direct Method Influence dialog, which is displayed either when a Direct Method Influence attribute is first assigned to a node or point on the model, or when the Analyses> Direct Method Influence Analysis menu item is selected or edited. Previously defined settings can be accessed and edited from the context menu for each Direct Method Influence entry in the Analyses Treeview. Materials, sections, supports and other attributes for a DMI analysis are taken from the base analysis base analysis . Because of this, it is a requirement of a DMI analysis that the base analysis is a simple linear static analysis.

topics.title: Load locations
topics.text: Load locations Search area - A search area search area can be used to limit the features to which the prescribed load is considered to be applied so that the effect of the load on other features in the model may discounted. If a search area is not specified the default loading area is Whole model . Nodes in search area - restricts the application of the applied load to just those mesh nodes within the search area, or to the whole model, as appropriate. For shell/plate/grillage models, it is recommended that the DMI analysis should be defined with the ‘Nodes in the search area’ selected. For line beam models where the geometric beam section represents a loadable top slab, it is recommended that the Grid option be used instead, specifying Grid settings to automatically create grid points to match the longitudinal positions of the nodes in the search area. Grid - predominantly used with line beam models where the geometric beam section represents a loadable top slab. For this, a defined grid of points is used to represent the loadable region of the slab. The Grid method also provides the means to define a grid of points that can be used as an alternative to the nodes or points present in a shell or plate model that are used in an influence analysis. For a model with a very fine mesh, loading a grid having fewer points will reduce the solution time. For line beam models the use of a reference path reference path using lines representing the centreline of a loaded region of a structure is recommended if the grid loading method is used. For plate and shell models a reference path may represent the centreline of a carriageway on which a loading grid would be positioned. See the worked example 'Vehicle Load Optimisation of a Box Beam Bridge', which provides more details on the use of a loading grid. Centreline - the centreline of the grid can be defined with reference to a previously defined Path or the X , Y or Z global axes. For most types of modelling the use of a reference path reference path is recommended. Specifying X, Y or Z causes the grid to be created along each of those axes at X=0, Y=0 or Z=0. Transverse width - the width of the loadable grid to be generated. Grid settings control the number of load locations within this defined width. Grid settings Grid settings - These control the density of the grid of points that will be loaded. Longitudinal and transverse values can be specified. If one of the global axes has been selected as the centreline of the grid, then the overall extent of the model will be calculated and a suitable grid generated to encompass the whole model.
topics.search_text: Load locations Direct Method Influence Analysis Direct Method Influence Analysis Load locations dlg6anal idd direct method influence analysis.htm Load locations Search area - A search area search area can be used to limit the features to which the prescribed load is considered to be applied so that the effect of the load on other features in the model may discounted. If a search area is not specified the default loading area is Whole model . Nodes in search area - restricts the application of the applied load to just those mesh nodes within the search area, or to the whole model, as appropriate. For shell/plate/grillage models, it is recommended that the DMI analysis should be defined with the ‘Nodes in the search area’ selected. For line beam models where the geometric beam section represents a loadable top slab, it is recommended that the Grid option be used instead, specifying Grid settings to automatically create grid points to match the longitudinal positions of the nodes in the search area. Grid - predominantly used with line beam models where the geometric beam section represents a loadable top slab. For this, a defined grid of points is used to represent the loadable region of the slab. The Grid method also provides the means to define a grid of points that can be used as an alternative to the nodes or points present in a shell or plate model that are used in an influence analysis. For a model with a very fine mesh, loading a grid having fewer points will reduce the solution time. For line beam models the use of a reference path reference path using lines representing the centreline of a loaded region of a structure is recommended if the grid loading method is used. For plate and shell models a reference path may represent the centreline of a carriageway on which a loading grid would be positioned. See the worked example 'Vehicle Load Optimisation of a Box Beam Bridge', which provides more details on the use of a loading grid. Centreline - the centreline of the grid can be defined with reference to a previously defined Path or the X , Y or Z global axes. For most types of modelling the use of a reference path reference path is recommended. Specifying X, Y or Z causes the grid to be created along each of those axes at X=0, Y=0 or Z=0. Transverse width - the width of the loadable grid to be generated. Grid settings control the number of load locations within this defined width. Grid settings Grid settings - These control the density of the grid of points that will be loaded. Longitudinal and transverse values can be specified. If one of the global axes has been selected as the centreline of the grid, then the overall extent of the model will be calculated and a suitable grid generated to encompass the whole model.

topics.title: Results file scope
topics.text: Results file scope Following results calculation for the whole model, the results that are written to a results output file can be restricted to be those only for any assigned influences (loadcases), or for those assigned influences (loadcases) and an additional subset of elements (those part of a group) within a model. Restricting the results output produces smaller results files more quickly than would be created for a whole model, but note that if subsequent influence assignments are made to the model a Direct Method Influence analysis would have to be solved again because results for those influence locations would not be present in the previously calculated results file. Assignments only calculates and writes results to a results file for only the assigned influences in the model. Assignments and additional group calculates and writes results to a results file for only the assigned influences in the model, and also for those elements within the chosen group. topics.title: Direct Method Influence Loading Settings
topics.text: Direct Method Influence Loading Settings These settings provides the means to specify the magnitude and direction of the loading applied to a grid of points used for an influence analysis. Magnitude Specifies the magnitude of the loading. The default loading is 1e3 if the model units are metric, and an equivalent rounded value if the model units are imperial. The default value of 1e3 is used in preference to unity so that any factoring or scaling of the loading (depending on the unit system in use) does not cause the order of magnitude of displacement to fall below a tolerance used in the vehicle load optimisation software. Load direction This can be either the X , Y , or Z global axis, or the Vertical axis (as defined by the Tools> Vertical axis menu item. The default loading direction is the Vertical axis. topics.text: Choose Loadcases to Solve The 'Choose Loadcases to Solve' dialog is accessed via the context menu for any analysis entry in the Analyses Treeview or from the context menu for any loadcase within that analysis. It allows particular loadcases to be selected for solving using the Solve now button. It can also be accessed from the Export Solver datafile dialog when specifying selected loadcases to be tabulated. The checkbox alongside each loadcase name shows whether a loadcase will be solved (it is checked) or not solved (it is unchecked). A red cross on the loadcase symbol for a loadcase entry in the Analyses Treeview shows the loadcase has been turned off for solving. Note The first loadcase in each analysis cannot be turned off because it will contain support conditions on which other loadcases rely. Using the Windows dialog context menu item Select all and then checking or unchecking a loadcase entry in the dialog will apply that choice to all loadcases listed in the dialog. topics.title: Solve now
topics.text: Solve now The Solve now dialog appears when the Solve now toolbar button is pressed. It provides information regarding the status of the Analyses that have been defined and allows particular analyses or tasks to be selected for solving. The checkbox alongside each analysis name or task shows whether an analysis needs to be solved (it is checked) or not solved (it is unchecked). Descriptive text alongside each analysis name or task shows the reason why it needs to be solved or not. Typical entries are: "Needs solving" - No results are available on disk. "Needs solving" - <Reference to reason why it needs solving> Results might expected to have changed. "Results are up to date" - Results are available on disk. If OK is pressed any valid existing results files will be loaded, even if not selected on the dialog as needing to be solved. "Prestress loading is out of date" - meaning that changes have been made requiring a re-solve to re-calculate the revised tendon forces. No solving will take place unless the checkbox adjacent to an analysis listed is checked to deliberately force a re-solve for that analysis.

topics.title: Loadcase settings
topics.text: Loadcase settings In the calculation of target values each included loadcase can be marked as having a Constant factor meaning that the loadcase is used by the optimisation algorithm with a constant load factor, or marked as having a Calculated factor meaning that the loadcase will be factored by the optimisation algorithm to try to achieve the defined target values. For a loadcase marked as having a calculated factor this must be set as either Positive , or Allow negative . For loadcases marked as having a constant factor this choice is not available. Loadcases marked as having a calculated factor may have an Importance level assigned to them (a weighting) but only in an optimised solution. A default value of 1.0 is applied for each if an importance level is not specified. Notes Loadcases marked as having a Constant factor are considered in the optimisation, but not modified by it. There may also be other loadcases in the model which form no part of the optimisation. Loadcases marked as having a Calculated factor may be factored, for both exact and non-exact solutions. There is no restriction on multiple combinations and envelopes that reference the same loadcase, or indeed that reference loadcases that are included in their own right. As a result there may be some permutations of loadcases for which a particular analysis solution cannot be found. Detecting a potential problem in advance of solving is not practical, so if this should occur any error is reported after a solution has been attempted. When a target values analysis is carried out LUSAS cannot verify that superposition holds when combinations contain loadcases from different analyses or when nonlinear behaviour is being considered. This may occur if lift-off supports are present, or when geometric or material changes take place between analyses. topics.title: Solution types
topics.text: Solution types The choice of solution type is made on the main page of the Target Values dialog. The type of solution that can be chosen is dependent upon the number of lines selected and the number of equality conditions as seen in the Condition column on the Targets grid. The solution type can be set to be: Exact This requires the number of equality conditions (as seen in the Condition column on the Targets grid) to be the same as the number of loadcases that are defined as requiring a Calculated factor on the Loadcases tab. No inequality conditions can be defined for the exact method. Using this option, only one solution is possible. Note that the exact solution for a given set of target values may produce negative factors for some loading arrangements. If this occurs an optimised solution should be investigated where all of the points of interest are permitted to move a small distance to try and achieve a better solution. In the case of Points being used to restrict displacement in a bridge deck this would amount to specifying a distance that would slacken the cables. Optimised (an under-determined solution) requires the number of equality conditions (as seen in the Condition column on the Targets grid) to be less than the number of number of loadcases that are defined as requiring a Calculated factor on the Loadcases tab. Any number of targets specifying inequality conditions can be defined. For this option a range of solutions is possible provided that they are not mutually exclusive. For this option a range of solutions is possible. Options to minimise or maximise the calculated factors for a variety of in-built or specified criteria are provided on the optimisation criteria page. Best fit (discrete least squares) and Best fit (Chebyshev) (both over-determined solutions) require the number of equality conditions (as seen in the Condition column on the Targets grid) to be greater than or equal to the number of loadcases number of loadcases that are defined as requiring a Calculated factor on the Loadcases tab. Any number of targets specifying equality or inequality conditions can be defined. For this approach no unique solution is guaranteed. Discrete least squares provides positive and negative load factors. No inequality conditions can be stated for this option. Chebyshev will always produce positive load factors. Inequality conditions can be stated for this option.

topics.title: Incrementation
topics.text: Incrementation Automatic/manual incrementation Specifies the incremental loading incremental loading method. For automatic incrementation the following parameters may also be set: Starting load factor (default = 1.0 on first increment, default = 0.0 on subsequent increments) This is the factor by which the reference load level will be multiplied for the predictor, or first iteration, of the next load increment. This load level will remain constant if constant load level is used (i.e. no arc - length control ). Must be nonzero at the first increment but may subsequently be respecified as zero if the new load factor is to be computed from the previous convergence history (i.e. using the iterations per increment value). Maximum (absolute) change in load factor (on iteration zero of any load increment) Limits the rate of change of load in an increment. If zero is input, no limit is applied. This parameter is used when the load level is automatically adjusted following consideration of the iterations desired for convergence against those achieved. The default value is 2.0*( Max total load factor - Starting load factor ); Max total load factor is the total load factor at the end of the previous increment. Maximum total load factor Will terminate at the specified value for analyses that are controlled by non arc - length automatic incrementation. Note that if more than one termination criteria has been specified, termination will occur following the first criterion to be satisfied. Adjust load based on convergence history By default, uniform incrementation will be applied. That is, for each increment the starting load factor will be multiplied by the specified load components and added to the previous level. Alternatively, variable incrementation may be requested. In this case the starting load factor will be automatically varied according to the iterative performance of the solution. The variation is a function of the required number of iterations and a specified desired iterative performance. Thus, where the number of iterations taken is less than the desired value the incremented load factor will subsequently be increased, and conversely, if the number of iterations is greater than the desired value, it will be decreased. Iterations per increment The loading variable (load or arc - length) is varied according to the number of iterations taken to converge on the preceding step. If the number of iterations taken for convergence exceeded the desired number, specified by the iterations per increment value, then the loading variable is decreased; conversely, if the number of iterations taken to converge was less than the desired number, the step length is increased. Hence the rate of change of loading variable is adjusted depending on the degree of nonlinearity present. If zero is input, the load variable will remain constant. Displacement reset step Used to establish an initial equilibrium state, such as for a geotechnical analysis. See geostatic analysis control. geostatic analysis control.

topics.title: Solution Strategy
topics.text: Solution Strategy The convergence criteria specifies to what extent the numerical iterative procedure has reached the true equilibrate state. The specification of convergence therefore involves two considerations: Type of convergence criterion Convergence tolerance. The solution has converged if the values of all the following criteria computed after an iteration are less than those specified. If a parameter is input as zero, the corresponding criteria is ignored. Maximum number of iterations for each load increment if convergence is not achieved Residual force norm The limit for the sum of the squares of all residual forces as a percentage of the sum of the squares of all external forces, including reactions (rdnrm). By default only translation degrees of freedom are considered Incremental displacement norm The limit for the sum of the squares of the iterative displacements as a percentage of the sum of the squares of the total displacements (dpnrm). By default only translation degrees of freedom are considered. See also: Nonlinear Analysis Nonlinear Analysis

topics.text: Create Loadcases (from a Basic Combination) The Create Loadcases dialog is accessed via the context menu for the Post processing folder in the Analyses Treeview. It allows particular basic combinations to be selected for expanding into separate loadcases containing loadings factored by the values used in the basic combination. topics.title: Graph Through 2D
topics.text: Graph Through 2D Arbitrary line sections may be taken through any surface model or on a slice cut through a three dimensional solid model. The process of cutting a slice will generate two graph datasets, the first containing the distance along the line section and the second containing the specified results along the line. The graph datasets are plotted automatically using the Graph Wizard Graph Wizard . The graph through 2D section line can be defined: By cursor using either a freehand start and finish point or to fixed points defined using the Snap to grid option in conjunction with the Grid size value. Generate new annotation line creates a line that is saved with the model to show the location of section slice and to allow re-selection for re-graphing along the same section. By selected line is used if a previous annotated section line is present and a graph for results along this line is to be re-calculated. The line should be selected prior to accessing this dialog. Note. Sometimes, dependent upon model size, the grid points are too close together to be usable. In these cases simply increase the grid size so that individual grid points can be selected. topics.title: Contour Appearance Settings
topics.text: Contour Appearance Settings A contour style or appearance is governed by settings made on this dialog. Filled / Lines Contours may be drawn using colour fill, or contour lines or both. Click here for examples Click here for examples . When both filled and line contours are drawn, LUSAS colours the lines using a single colour to emphasise the contours. This is especially useful where the plot will ultimately appear in black and white, or where the output device supports less colours than the screen. Name The name given for the contour style. This can be renamed to suit. Width For a line beam model, specifying a width changes the width of the contour that is drawn along each line of the model. For shell or volume models, if the Gauss point display option has been chosen on the contour properties dialog, the width setting changes the size (diameter) of the contour colour filled circle shown at each gauss point. Labels Adds labels to the contour lines. Multicolour (For line contours only) Use the contour colour for the contour line label. Unchecked, black is used as the label colour. Interval defines the frequency in millimetres on the display at which labels are displayed on each contour line Angle defines the orientation of the contour label. Use the Font button to set the font size and style used for line contour labels. Pen Sets the pen used to draw the line contours when automatic colouring is not selected.

topics.title: Setting an Automatic Contour Range
topics.text: Setting an Automatic Contour Range Selecting Automatic range calculates contour levels automatically according to either one of the following specification: Number of boundaries Specifies the number of contours to be plotted, with smoother contours obtained by specifying a greater number of boundaries. LUSAS calculates the contour levels to fit the number of contours specified. Interval Sets an interval between adjacent contours. The number of contours required are set automatically. The contour levels may be further controlled by setting certain fixed contour values: Value to pass through Fixes one contour level such that it passes through a specified value. All other contour values are adjusted to keep the current range and interval. Maximum, Minimum Specifies maximum and minimum values of a contour range. Results lying outside this range will be lumped and contoured together. LUSAS calculates the maximum and minimum contour values automatically if not specified. Symmetric about zero Centres the contour range about a value of zero.

topics.title: Defaults
topics.text: Defaults Pressing the Defaults button resets the currently edited contour style to its default setting. In doing so, note that settings made for the four other contour styles are unaffected. Notes Fixing the contour levels is important before creating animation sequences which display a contour plot so that the same levels are used for all animation frames. It is also useful to fix the contour levels when comparing results from different loadcases or increments. The Contour key created is part of the Annotation layer in the Layers Treeview. After initial selection it may be dragged to a new position using the mouse. The font and text colour can be changed from the properties box which is accessed by selecting the annotation and using the right-hand mouse button. It is often useful to adjust the colour palette so that low stress contours are set to white. This avoids excessive use of single colour ink when printing on colour plotters. Labelled contours in conjunction with a single colour contour plot is a useful alternative when plotting on a black and white printer or if the plot is to be photocopied. See also: Visualising the Results Visualising the Results

topics.title: Contour Appearance
topics.text: Contour Appearance Five contour appearence 'styles' can be used as supplied or be customised to plot contours for different uses in order to suit project needs. These are, and comprise: Classic - 9 contour boundaries (lines), passing through zero, created from 10 seed colours, producing 10 contoured regions. This mimics the default legacy style that used a limited contour range. Smooth - 200 contour boundaries, passing through zero, created from 10 seed colours, providing smoothed contours. Design - A manually set range of 4 values from 0.7 to 1.0. Suitable for plotting contours of utilisation factors as produced by LUSAS design checking software options. Red/Blue - 1 boundary line, passing through zero, symmetric about zero, created from 2 seed colours. Useful for visualising positive and negative regions of interest in different colours (e.g. viewing of positive or negative displacement of influence shapes for loading purposes). Fade - 200 colour boundaries, passing through zero, created from two seed colours (white and red), providing smoothed single colour fading contours.

topics.title: Annotating the model view window
topics.text: Annotating the model view window Contour key When selected, displays a key within the model view window representing the contour levels in use for that window. Pressing the Set button enables the Contour appearance settings dialog Contour appearance settings dialog which allows for: Positioning of the key/annotation to be set with respect to paper edges. Specifying the number of Significant figures or Decimal places . Display of the loadcase ID. Display of maximum /minimum values and nodal position at which these values occur. The appearance to be changed to draw outlines around the contour colours, or to change the order of the contour colours, such as to place red uppermost in the key (in the case of the 'Classic' range of colours). Deform This check box is available for selection if a Deformed mesh layer is not displayed, and if selected, displays contours on the deformed shape that would otherwise be seen if the Deformed mesh layer were displayed. Ghost fleshing This check box option is on by default, and is only valid when the fleshing toolbar button is 'on 'and a stress or strain top/middle/bottom result is chosen (on the 'Contour Results' page). A ghost fleshed thickness is drawn across each element as a shaded transparent white, helping to identify the location of the results within a fleshed surface. When fleshing is off, results are drawn at the nodal plane, with no ghost fleshing.
