topics.title: Contour results
topics.text: Contour results Defines a contour display using a specified modelling or results type. Modelling contours can be plotted for specified components by selecting a particular material, geometric or loading attribute assignment. Plotting modelling contours is especially useful when an attribute value changes across the model as, for example, when changes of thickness have been defined using a variation variation . Results contours can be plotted for specified results components. All contours are taken from the active loadcase active loadcase of the current window.

topics.title: Modelling / Results Selection
topics.text: Modelling / Results Selection Entity The modelling or results type to display from the list of available options. Component For results contours this can be selected directly from the drop-down list. See the Key to Results Tables Key to Results Tables in Appendix K of the Element Reference Manual for component definitions. User-defined results components will appear at the bottom of the drop-down list. For modelling contours, the component is selected by choosing the material, geometric or loading attribute of interest in the side panel. Display The method to be used to display the contours. Options include: Averaged nodal By default, averaged nodal contours are drawn respecting discontinuities formed by geometry orientation, geometric assignments and material assignments. Default averaging settings can be changed on the Model Properties - Options (Averaging) Model Properties - Options (Averaging) dialog. Gauss points For these, contour value coloured circles are drawn at gauss points for surface and volume elements. Unaveraged nodal Unaveraged nodal contours draw results on an element-by-element basis, and will show inter-element discontinuities. This is useful for checking possible mesh discretisation errors and for displaying results across geometry or material discontinuities (if averaging for these situations has been otherwise enabled). Internal points (if thick beam elements are in use) Internal locations along each element at which results can be obtained. Inspection locations (if defined) For these, contour value coloured circles are drawn at those inspection locations that have only a single value (i.e. for continuous results or where averaging has been successful). At inspection locations that resolve to multiple values (because averaging is inappropriate), no contour value coloured circle is drawn, and instead an ‘invalid’ symbol appears. Feature maximum , Feature minimum , and Feature extreme For these, the whole of each feature (line, surface etc) will be drawn in the same contour colour and in a colour that relates to the single highest value found in any node / element within that feature. 'Feature extreme' contours the value with the largest magnitude and preserves its sign. Transform Sometimes it may be necessary to transform the results, for example if the elements in a model are orientated such that their local axes vary from one another. Numerous options are available by pressing the Set... button. See Results Transformation Results Transformation for details. When section slices have been created through a solid model the following options are also available: Display on slice(s) Displays contours of results on the section slice(s) Draw in slice local direction

topics.title: Envelopes and smart combinations
topics.text: Envelopes and smart combinations These options are only available when an envelope or a smart combination is set active. When viewing 'Max' results for an active envelope or a smart combination: Show maximum only Display contours of maximum values. (Only available if the 'Max' envelope or smart combination is set active) Show minimum only Display contours of minimum values. (Only available if the 'Min' envelope or smart combination is set active) Show extreme Display contours of extreme values by considering both the maximum and minimum value at each location, taking the larger absolute numerical value in each case, and preserving the sign of whichever value is used. topics.title: Diagram Display
topics.text: Diagram Display Label values Labels the diagram with the results values. Peaks only labels maximum and minimum values whenever there is a positive or negative change of gradient of the curve representing the diagram of interest. Label only if selected Labels diagrams of selected elements only, and improves clarity. Label in plane Labels values in the plane of the diagram, as opposed to labelling the values flat to the plane of the screen. Deform Draws the diagrams on the deformed shape i.e. the shape of the structure when subjected to applied load or due to mode of vibration. The deformed shape may be scaled by specifying a magnitude or a scale factor (click on the Scale tab). Lines between elements Draws orthogonal lines from each nodal position to intersect with the line of the diagram at that location. Can be included or omitted as a personal preference. Orientate by element axes draws the diagram in the orientation of the component selected. This is only available for beam element components that can be plotted in y and z element axes such as Fy, Mz etc. Other components including user results components can only be plotted flat on the screen/page. Orientate flat to screen/page draws all diagrams flat on the screen regardless of model orientation.

topics.title: Style
topics.text: Style % of element length Draws the diagrams at a specified percentage of the element length, for improved clarity. The Label font button defines the font size and style used to label the diagrams. The Angle specifies the rotation of the displayed text. The Significant figures and Decimal places counter enables the number of significant figures in the values display to be adjusted. Show trailing zeros includes the required number of zeros for a chosen number of significant figures. The pen used to draw the diagram lines and labels may be changed by specifying a different pen number, or by clicking on the Choose Pen button. Pen for maximum / Pen for minimum (only available when an envelope or a smart combination is set active). Here, a different pen colour can be specified for the selected Maximum or Minimum loadcase. By default Maximum loadcase values are drawn in red, and Minimum loadcase values are drawn in blue. Use for labels too uses the diagram line colour for labels, Unchecked, labels are drawn in black. Tips The default font used may be set from the Defaults Defaults tab of the model properties dialog. Label only small portions of the model by only choosing 'Label only if selected' to improve clarity. Use Groups Groups to limit the visible model. Setting an angle for text labels usually prevents labels from overwriting each other. An angle of 30 or 45 degrees is recommended. See also: Visualising the Results Visualising the Results

topics.title: Initial deformations / cable sag
topics.text: Initial deformations / cable sag Exaggerate initial deformations (Off by default) Initial deformations may be inherited from a previous analysis, as for example with an initial imperfection in a girder system generated from an eigenvalue buckling mode, used for a full nonlinear buckling analysis. See Specifying an Initial State for an Analysis Specifying an Initial State for an Analysis for details. In such a case, usually the initial deformation is not exaggerated (displayed at a scale of 1:1), so that it is not distracting when examining deformations in the current (e.g. nonlinear buckling) analysis. However the initial deformation can be exaggerated by turning on this check-box. Note. When displaying deformed mesh plots of contact analyses the exaggeration factor should be set to unity to avoid producing misleading or overlapping results. See also: Visualising the Results Visualising the Results Deformed Mesh Plots Deformed Mesh Plots About Results About Results About Loadcases About Loadcases

topics.title: Viewing Results in a Consistent Direction
toc_path: Viewing Results in a Consistent Direction
headings: Viewing Results in a Consistent Direction
topics.text: Viewing Results in a Consistent Direction If the elements in a model are orientated such that their local axes vary from one another (and note for surfaces they may also vary from the surface orientation), or if an alternative coordinate system is required, the results may be transformed to a consistent direction. Results displayed on contour, values or vector layers in a particular view window can be transformed using the Transform Set... button on the layer properties dialog for each layer. Results plotted using the graph wizard, or obtained using the print results wizard, or the report writer can be transformed using the Transform Set... button on their respective dialogs. Results may be transformed to the following directions: No transformation applied (consult Solver manual) Results may be in global and/or element local axes according to element formulation. Depending upon the type of model and elements used, a results transformation may be required. Local axes or element/node Transforms nodal results (displacements, reactions etc.) according to the local transformed freedoms or element results (stresses, strains etc.) to element local directions. Local coordinate of parent feature Transforms element results according to the local axes of the line, surface or volume feature. Global axes Transforms nodal or element results to the global axes. Material Transforms element results to the local element material direction. Assigned results transformation attribute Transforms element results to directions specified by any assigned results transformation attributes results transformation attributes . Specified local coordinate Transforms results to a consistent direction using a local coordinate local coordinate . Shell plane for resultants enables the local coordinate plane which is aligned with the plane of the shell elements to be defined for shell moments and shear forces when using cylindrical or spherical coordinates. See Shell plane for resultants Shell plane for resultants . Reference path Transforms nodal or element results relative to the angle or route of a reference path reference path . Notes Different drawing layers can each have different Results Transformation settings. Beam and bar elements always have their local x direction along the length of the element. For plates and shells the normal direction is defined by the local element z axis and this cannot be transformed. A results transformation only applies to the orientation of the local element x and y directions in the plane of the shell element. Top/Middle/Bottom, Wood Armer top and bottom, and sign conventions rely on the element z axis. When viewing Wood Armer results a transformation is used to set the direction of the X reinforcement. A skew angle may then be set independently to define the Y reinforcement direction. The default skew angle is 90 degrees. When viewing shell moments and shear stresses using a cylindrical or spherical local coordinate the shell plane for resultants needs to be defined as theta/z, r/theta or r/z. Using the transformation options for joint elements has no effect. With the exception of the No transformation applied option the type of transformation used is written to the Contour key. See also: Results Transformation Results Transformation

topics.text: General notes When considering the load factors for permanent loads due to superimposed deformations from table 3.4.1-3, currently 'Non-segmental concrete superstructures' is the only option included. The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility gives two options for creation of traffic loads: 'Patterns and global factors', and 'Patterns only'. headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to AASHTO 7th Edition
topics.text: Earth pressure When considering horizontal earth pressure each of the three cases in Table 3.4.1-2 (Active, At-Rest and AEP for anchored walls) is given a separate entry in the load type droplist. This is to allow for different γp load factors to apply to different walls within the model. The following modified designations apply: EHac = Horizontal Earth Pressure, Active EHar = Horizontal Earth Pressure, At-Rest EHaep = Horizontal Earth Pressure, AEP for anchored walls For vertical earth pressure from Table 3.4.1-2 buried structures are not considered. The remaining three cases are given a separate entry in the load type droplist. The following modified designations apply: EVos = Vertical Earth Pressure, Overall Stability EVrwa = Vertical Earth Pressure, Retaining Walls and Abutments EVrf = Vertical Earth Pressure, Rigid Frames When considering vertical earth pressure in Table 3.4.1-2 the options are limited to Overall Stability, Retaining Walls & Abutments and Rigid Frames. Rigid Buried Structure and Flexible Buried Structures are not considered.

topics.title: Vehicle loads
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to AASHTO 7th Edition
headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to AASHTO 7th Edition
topics.text: Vehicle loads The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility output creates separate load cases for each of the following: LNN = Notional design load LLP = Strength II (Permit) unfactored LLF = Fatigue Deflection In the foregoing, the appropriate multiple presence factor, m, and the dynamic load allowance (IM) in Table 3.4.1-1 have been applied in the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation and so are excluded from the load types. The deflection output from VLO is not considered in combination with any other load and so is not assigned a load type. As described in Article 3.4.1 two values are provided for the force effect due to uniform temperature (TU). The user can chose from options to create load combinations to consider: Deformations Other effects Both deformations and other effects Values of  LL as applied to live loads in Service III can be 1.0 or 0.8 depending on how time dependent losses are calculated. The default value of  LL is taken as 1.0 as this is suitable where refined estimates of time-dependent losses as specified in Article 5.9.3.4 are used in the prestress calculations. For each combination option a separate folder is created for combinations to differentiate between deformations and other effects. It should be noted that if the Uniform Temperature (TU) load type is not used the same combinations are created for the deformations case and the other effects case. When considering centrifugal force or braking force (Articles 3.6.3 and 3.6.4) the co- existent vertical loads should be defined in the same load case and the appropriate load type assigned to the load case. The co-existent vertical effects should have the appropriate multiple presence factor, m, applied but not the load factor,  i, as this is applied in the design combination wizard. By default Earthquake effects (EQ) load types are considered as mutually exclusive. When considering the seismic effects on 2 principle axes as per Article 3.10.8 the effects in the two directions should be considered in the same loadcase. Fatigue load combinations do not consider centrifugal forces in combinations generated by the design combination wizard. See also: Design Combination Options - AASHTO LRFD 7th Design Combination Options - AASHTO LRFD 7th Design Combinations Design Combinations

The co-existent vertical effects should have the appropriate multiple presence factor, m, applied but not the load factor,  i, as this is applied in the design combination wizard. By default Earthquake effects (EQ) load types are considered as mutually exclusive. When considering the seismic effects on 2 principle axes as per Article 3.10.8 the effects in the two directions should be considered in the same loadcase. Fatigue load combinations do not consider centrifugal forces in combinations generated by the design combination wizard. The default value of  LL is taken as 1.0 as this is suitable where refined estimates of time-dependent losses as specified in Article 5.9.3.4 are used in the prestress calculations. topics.text: Vehicle loads The alternative values of  fL for dead and superimposed dead loads to BD 37/01 Table 1 are not considered. Local effects from loads due to vehicle collision with parapets (Clause 6.7.1) are not considered. The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility creates separate load cases for each of the following using combinations of HA loading and HB loading as appropriate: ULS combination 1 ULS combination 2 and 3 SLS combination 1 SLS combination 2 and 3 In the combinations listed above the appropriate lane factor, β, and load factor,  fL, have been applied in the Vehicle Load Optimisation facility. Therefore in the load combination wizard a load factor of 1.0 is assigned in all cases. When considering secondary live loads, the associated primary live load should be defined in the same load combination as the secondary load for the following loads: Centrifugal load Longitudinal load (note two load types are available depending on whether the primary load is HA or HB) Accidental skidding These load combinations are then assigned the appropriate load type. For ULS Combination 2 it should be noted that the 'Wind: in service (Ws)' has three possible values depending on whether or not traffic load effects are included and if the effect of wind in relieving. On the Advanced option dialog the load factor for the case with traffic load is shown. The case of wind without traffic load and the relieving effect of wind with or without traffic is considered but is not shown on the dialog. For erection stage combinations, loads due to 'Differential Settlement' are not included as it is assumed that this has not yet occurred. See also: Design Combination Options - BD37/01 Design Combination Options - BD37/01 Design Combinations Design Combinations

topics.text: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to CS 454 The requirements for load combinations used in the assessment of highway bridges in the UK are implemented in accordance with the requirements of: CS 454 Revision 0 - Design Manual for Roads and Bridges CS 454 Revision 0, Volume 3, Section 4, Part 3 – The Assessment of Highway Bridges and Structures June 2019, Highways England; Transport Scotland; Welsh Government; Department for Infrastructure Northern Ireland. The combinations are based on the requirements of Table 3.4 except for cast iron bridges which are taken from Table A.1. Option verifications such as serviceability limit state (3.2.1) and fatigue (3.2.2) are not considered. The γf3 factor (as per clause 3.7) is applied to each load. This is different from the code requirements where it is applied to the effects of the assessment loads. This is acceptable for cases where the principle of superposition applies. The partial factor for accidental vehicle loading is taken as 1.5. The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility gives separate options for the implementation of CS 454 – one option for 'ALL Model 1' and a separate one for 'ALL Model 2'. Both options are accommodated using a single entry in the design combinations. topics.text: Traffic loads The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility creates separate load cases for each of the following using combinations of Group 1a – LM1, Group 4 – LM4 and Group 5 – LM3 as appropriate: Traffic Load – characteristic Traffic Load – combination Traffic Load – frequent When using these load types it should be noted that the ψ factors and  adjustment factors are applied in the Vehicle Load Optimisation facility. Subsequently, when using the design combination wizard, the appropriate partial factor for variable loads,  Q , is applied. In order to ensure that each of the different ultimate and serviceability limit state combinations can be generated, each of the traffic load types (characteristic, combination, frequent, quasi-permanent) must be assigned. Horizontal forces to clause 4.4 are not included in the Vehicle Load Optimisation. When these load types are included they are combined with the traffic load type 'Traffic Load – frequent' (assuming this load type is defined). This is why the 'Traffic Load – frequent' has a  Q factor applied to it. Note that if the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation creates a “Traffic Load – frequent” based on LM4 Crowd loading this will still be combined with the horizontal force load types. The horizontal loads, gr2, are only ever considered as a leading action. Footway and cycle track loading to clause 5.3.2 is not considered as part of the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation . No load type exists or it. Load combinations with Footway and cycle track loading should be created outside of the load combination wizard.

topics.text: Wind and other actions The  Q for wind loads is taken as 1.70. The reduced value of  Q = 1.55 from NA to IS EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 1] Table NA.9 Note 6 is not considered. There appears to be an error in NA to IS EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 1] Table NA.7. For the wind load F* w the load component “During execution” is applied. However F* w is defined as Wind force compatible with road traffic (Clause A2.1.2). It is thought that the “During execution” reference possibly applies to the snow load in Table NA.A2.1. This interpretation would be consistent with the base EN 1990 document Table A2.1. There appears to be an error in NA to IS EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 1] Table NA.7. However in the case of the Irish National annex F w is used instead of F* w . Note that F w is defined as “Wind load (general symbol)”. Cl. A2.2.2 (5) notes that: " No wind action greater than the smaller of F W* and  0 F Wk should be combined with Load Model 1 or with the associated group of loads gr1a '. This requirement is not fully implemented in the current implementation as the governing group of loads are not identifiable from the Vehicle Load Optimisation output. Currently it is assumed that the loadcase from the Vehicle Load Optimisation is for a group of loads gr1a and that this will always be included with the load type 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Road Traffic'. The user must check which of F W* or  0 F Wk is smaller and assign this value to 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Road Traffic' – note the inclusion of the  0 parameter in the latter case. The characteristic value of the wind F Wk is assigned to the 'Qwt | Wind Persistent' load type and is this is used in combinations without the loadcase from the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation .

For the wind load F* w the load component “During execution” is applied. However F* w is defined as Wind force compatible with road traffic (Clause A2.1.2). It is thought that the “During execution” reference possibly applies to the snow load in Table NA.A2.1. This interpretation would be consistent with the base EN 1990 document Table A2.1. There appears to be an error in NA to IS EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 1] Table NA.7. However in the case of the Irish National annex F w is used instead of F* w . Note that F w is defined as “Wind load (general symbol)”. Cl. A2.2.2 (5) notes that: " No wind action greater than the smaller of F W* and  0 F Wk should be combined with Load Model 1 or with the associated group of loads gr1a '. This requirement is not fully implemented in the current implementation as the governing group of loads are not identifiable from the Vehicle Load Optimisation output. Currently it is assumed that the loadcase from the Vehicle Load Optimisation is for a group of loads gr1a and that this will always be included with the load type 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Road Traffic'. The user must check which of F W* or  0 F Wk is smaller and assign this value to 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Road Traffic' – note the inclusion of the  0 parameter in the latter case. The characteristic value of the wind F Wk is assigned to the 'Qwt | Wind Persistent' load type and is this is used in combinations without the loadcase from the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation .

topics.title: Traffic loads
toc_path: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Highway Bridges) to Italy National Annex
headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Highway Bridges) to Italy National Annex
topics.text: Traffic loads The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility creates separate load cases for each of the following using combinations of Group 1a – LM1, Group 4 – LM4 and Group 5 – LM3 as appropriate: Traffic Load – characteristic Traffic Load – combination Traffic Load – frequent When using these load types it should be noted that the ψ factors and  adjustment factors are applied in the Vehicle Load Optimisation. Subsequently when using the load combination wizard the appropriate partial factor for variable loads,  Q , is applied. Horizontal forces to clause 4.4 are not included in the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation . When these load types are included they are combined with the traffic load type “Traffic Load – frequent” (assuming this load type is defined). This is why the “Traffic Load – frequent” has a  Q factor applied to it. Note that if the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility creates a “Traffic Load – frequent” based on LM4 Crowd loading this will still be combined with the horizontal force load types. The horizontal loads, gr2, are only ever considered as a leading action. Footway and cycle track loading to clause 5.3.2 is not considered as part of the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation . No load type exists for it. Load combinations with Footway and cycle track loading should be created outside of the load combination wizard.

toc_path: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Highway Bridges) to Recommended Values
headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Highway Bridges) to Recommended Values
topics.text: General notes For the Ultimate limit state, and for the three sets of factors applicable, namely: Set A for static equilibrium, Set B for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions, and Set C for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions, only Set B and Set C have been implemented to date. The implementation is currently limited to persistent combinations. Transient combinations (including the execution stage) are not considered. When considering settlement, only a load type for settlement using linear elastic analysis is permitted.

topics.text: Snow load The snow load, Q Sn,k , in Table A2.1 is considered for the execution stage. Snow load is not considered for the Persistent stage since Clause 1.1 (8) of BS EN 1991-1-3:2003 [Ref. 11] notes that snow loads on bridges is considered a specialist aspect and guidance is not provided in that document. Additionally as per cl. A2.2.2 (3) & (4) of BS EN 1990: 2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 1] snow loads need not be considered with traffic loads unless specified for a particular geographical area. Any such situations will be considered it the appropriate National annex.

headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Highway Bridges) to UK National Annex
topics.text: Traffic loads The Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation facility creates separate load cases for each of the following using combinations of Group 1a – LM1, Group 4 – LM4 and Group 5 – LM3 as appropriate: Traffic Load – characteristic Traffic Load – combination Traffic Load – frequent When using these load types it should be noted that the ψ factors and  adjustment factors are applied in the Vehicle Load Optimisation facility. Subsequently, when using the load combination wizard, the appropriate partial factor for variable loads,  Q , is applied. In order to ensure that each of the different ultimate and serviceability limit state combinations can be generated, each of the traffic load types (characteristic, combination, frequent, quasi-permanent (and possibly infrequent)) must be assigned. Horizontal forces to clause 4.4 are not included in the Vehicle Load Optimisation. When these load types are included they are combined with the traffic load type 'Traffic Load – frequent' (assuming this load type is defined). This is why the 'Traffic Load – frequent' has a  Q factor applied to it. Note that if the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation creates a 'Traffic Load – frequent' based on LM4 Crowd loading this will still be combined with the horizontal force load types. The horizontal loads, gr2, are only ever considered as a leading action. Footway and cycle track loading to clause 5.3.2 is not considered as part of the Vehicle Load Optimisation. No load type exists or it. Load combinations with Footway and cycle track loading should be created outside of the load combination wizard.

topics.text: Wind actions The  Q for wind loads is taken as 1.70. The reduced value of  Q = 1.55 from NA to BS EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 2] Table NA.A2.4(B) Note 5 is not considered. There appears to be an error in NA to BS EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 [Ref. 2] Table NA.A2.1. For the wind load F* w the load component “During execution” is applied. However F* w is defined as Wind force compatible with road traffic (Clause A2.1.2). It is assumed that the “ During execution” reference possibly applies to the snow load in Table NA.A2.1. This interpretation would be consistent with the base EN 1990 document Table A2.1. Cl. A2.2.2 (5) notes that: " No wind action greater than the smaller of F W* and  0 F Wk should be combined with Load Model 1 or with the associated group of loads gr1a" . This requirement is not fully implemented in the current implementation as the governing group of loads are not identifiable from the Vehicle Load Optimisation output. Currently it is assumed that the loadcase from the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation is for a group of loads gr1a and that this will always be included with the load type 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Road Traffic'. The user must check which of of F W* or  0 F Wk is smaller and assign this value to 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Road Traffic' – note the inclusion of the  0 parameter in the latter case. The characteristic value of the wind F Wk is assigned to the 'Qwt | Wind Persistent' load type and is this is used in combinations without the loadcase from the Vehicle Load Optimisation Vehicle Load Optimisation .

Pattern loading is not taken into account. Prestressing actions are not covered by the National Annex so are not included in any of the combinations generated using the Design Combination wizard. Combinations involving prestressing actions must be created by the user. EN 1991-1-1 Cl. 3.3.2 (2) notes that: "When the imposed load is considered as an accompanying action, in accordance with EN 1990, only one of the two factors  (EN 1990, Table A1.1) and  n (6.3.1.2 (11)) shall be applied." Since the reduction factor,  n is not considered as part of the load combination wizard, accompanying actions will always be factored by ψ. If the  n factor is applied to loads manually a further reduction by ψ will also be applied, which would be non-compliant with this clause.

topics.text: General notes For the Ultimate limit state, and for the three sets of factors applicable, namely: Set A for static equilibrium, Set B for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions, and Set C for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions, only Set B has been implemented to date. Pattern loading is not taken into account. Prestressing actions are not covered by the National Annex, so are not included in any of the combinations generated using the Design Combination wizard. Combinations involving prestressing actions must be created by the user. EN 1991-1-1 Cl. 3.3.2 (2) notes that: "When the imposed load is considered as an accompanying action, in accordance with EN 1990, only one of the two factors  (EN 1990, Table A1.1) and  n (6.3.1.2 (11)) shall be applied." Since the reduction factor,  n is not considered as part of the load combination wizard, accompanying actions will always be factored by ψ. If the  n factor is applied to loads manually a further reduction by ψ will also be applied, which would be non-compliant with this clause.

topics.text: General notes For the Ultimate limit state, and for the three sets of factors applicable, namely: Set A for static equilibrium, Set B for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions, and Set C for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions, only Set B has been implemented to date. Pattern loading is not taken into account. Prestressing actions are not covered by the National Annex so are not included in any of the combinations generated using the Design Combination wizard. EN 1991-1-1 Cl. 3.3.2 (2) notes that: "When the imposed load is considered as an accompanying action, in accordance with EN 1990, only one of the two factors  (EN 1990, Table A1.1) and  n (6.3.1.2 (11)) shall be applied." Since the reduction factor,  n is not considered as part of the load combination wizard, accompanying actions will always be factored by ψ. If the  n factor is applied to loads manually a further reduction by ψ will also be applied. The option of applying reduction factor, kFi, to structures in reliability class 1, as per clause NA.A1.3.1(1), has not been implemented due to the limited nature of its use. When considering accidental combinations [Ref. 1] Table NA.A1.3 refers to EN 1991-1-2 [Ref. 3] (actions on structures exposed to fire). [Ref. 3] clause 4.3.1 (2) allows the use of the frequent or quasi-permanent value of the action. The note to this clause recommends the use of the quasi-permanent value but the choice is to be determined from the National annex. As implemented the frequent value has been conservatively used. The intent of [Ref. 1] Note 1 to Table NA. A1.3 is unclear, so the implementation has been made on the basis of it applying to all accidental actions, which would be non-compliant with this clause. See also: Design Combination Options - EN1990 - 2002 (Buildings) to Norway National Annex Design Combination Options - EN1990 - 2002 (Buildings) to Norway National Annex Design Combinations Design Combinations

topics.text: General notes For the Ultimate limit state, and for the three sets of factors applicable, namely: Set A for static equilibrium, Set B for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions, and Set C for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions, only Set B has been implemented to date. Pattern loading is not taken into account. Prestressing actions are not included in any of the combinations generated using the wizard. Combinations involving prestressing actions must be created by the user. EN 1991-1-1 Cl. 3.3.2 (2) notes that: "When the imposed load is considered as an accompanying action, in accordance with EN 1990, only one of the two factors  (EN 1990, Table A1.1) and  n (6.3.1.2 (11)) shall be applied." Since the reduction factor,  n is not considered as part of the load combination wizard, accompanying actions will always be factored by ψ. If the  n factor is applied to loads manually a further reduction by ψ will also be applied. BS EN 1990: 2002+A1:2005 clause 6.3.1.2(10) permits the use of a reduction factor for imposed load categories A-D based on the loaded area. This reduction factor is member specific and therefore cannot be included in the combinations. It may however be manually accounted for by using the ' Distributed to perimeter Distributed to perimeter ' load and the area reduction factor which can be defined as an expression in terms of 'A' the area supported by each edge of the surface to which the attribute is assigned. BS EN 1990: 2002+A1:2005 clause 6.3.1.2(11) permits the use of a reduction factor for imposed load categories A-D where multiple storeys are loaded. The reduction factor is only applicable to columns and walls and accounts for the fact that not all storeys will be loaded to the maximum values simultaneously. This factor is not accommodated in the design combinations meaning that and a separate set of combinations for column design will need to be created manually applying the adjustment factor as required.

topics.text: General notes For the Ultimate limit state, and for the three sets of factors applicable, namely: Set A for static equilibrium, Set B for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions, and Set C for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions, only Set B has been implemented to date. Pattern loading is not taken into account. Prestressing actions are not covered by the National Annex so are not included in any of the combinations generated using the wizard. Combinations involving prestressing actions must be created by the user. EN 1991-1-1 Cl. 3.3.2 (2) notes that: "When the imposed load is considered as an accompanying action, in accordance with EN 1990, only one of the two factors  (EN 1990, Table A1.1) and  n (6.3.1.2 (11)) shall be applied." Since the reduction factor,  n is not considered as part of the load combination wizard, accompanying actions will always be factored by ψ. If the  n factor is applied to loads manually a further reduction by ψ will also be applied.

topics.text: General notes For the Ultimate limit state three sets of factors are supplied as follows: Set A is for static equilibrium Set B is for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions Set C is for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions Only Set B and Set C have been implemented to date. The implementation is limited to persistent combinations. Transient combinations (including the execution stage) are not currently considered. When considering settlement, Table A2.4(B) (and the corresponding tables in the National annexes) give two possible values of γ Gset with the value used dependent upon whether a linear elastic analysis or non linear analysis is used. In the current implementation, the user is limited to choosing a load type for settlement using linear elastic analysis only.

The implementation is limited to persistent combinations. Transient combinations (including the execution stage) are not currently considered. When considering settlement, Table A2.4(B) (and the corresponding tables in the National annexes) give two possible values of γ Gset with the value used dependent upon whether a linear elastic analysis or non linear analysis is used. In the current implementation, the user is limited to choosing a load type for settlement using linear elastic analysis only.

headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Railway Bridges) to Ireland National Annex
topics.text: Wind loads [Ref 1] Clause A2.2.4 (4) notes that: ' No wind action greater than the smaller of F W** and  0 F Wk should be combined with traffic actions. '. Furthermore clause A2.2.4 (3) identifies groups of loads that wind loads do not act with. These requirements are not fully implemented in the current implementation. Rather, the rail traffic load from the Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation is combined with the load type 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Rail Traffic'. The user must check which of F W** or  0 F Wk is smaller and assign this value to 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Rail Traffic' – note the inclusion of the  0 parameter in the latter case. The characteristic value of the wind F Wk is assigned to the 'Qwp | Wind Persistent' load type and is this is used in combinations without the loadcase from the Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation .

headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to EN 1990 (Railway Bridges) to Recommended Values)
topics.text: General For the Ultimate limit state three sets of factors are supplied as follows: Set A is for static equilibrium Set B is for design of structural members not involving geotechnical actions Set C is for design of structural members involving geotechnical actions Only Set B and Set C have been implemented to date. The implementation is limited to persistent combinations. Transient combinations (including the execution stage) are not currently considered. When considering settlement, Table A2.4(B) (and the corresponding tables in the National annexes) give two possible values of γ Gset with the value used dependent upon whether a linear elastic analysis or non linear analysis is used. In the current implementation, the user is limited to choosing a load type for settlement using linear elastic analysis only.

topics.text: Wind loads Clause A2.2.4 (4) notes that: ' No wind action greater than the smaller of F W** and  0 F Wk should be combined with traffic actions. '. Furthermore clause A2.2.4 (3) identifies groups of loads that wind loads do not act with. These requirements are not fully implemented in the current implementation. Rather, the rail traffic load from the Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation is combined with the load type 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Rail Traffic'. The user must check which of F W** or  0 F Wk is smaller and assign this value to 'Qwt | Wind compatible with Rail Traffic' – note the inclusion of the  0 parameter in the latter case. The characteristic value of the wind F Wk is assigned to the 'Qwp | Wind Persistent' load type and is this is used in combinations without the loadcase from the Rail Load Optimisation Rail Load Optimisation .

headings: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to IRC: 6-2017
topics.text: Implementation Notes for Design Combinations to IRC: 6-2017 The requirements for load combinations used in the assessment of highway bridges in the India are implemented in accordance with the requirements of: IRC: 6-2017 IRC: 6-2017 – Standard Specifications and Code of Practice for Road Bridges - Section: II - Loads and Load Combinations (Seventh Revision), Indian Roads Congress, New Delhi, Mar 2017. [Ref. 1] Reference should also be made to: IRC: 112-2011 IRC: 112-2011 – Code of Practice for Concrete Road Bridges, Indian Roads Congress, New Delhi, Nov 2011. [Ref.2 ] The load combinations are based on the limit state design approach as set out in [Ref 1] Annex B. Construction stage load combinations are not considered. Partial safety factors for prestress are based on those given in [Ref 2]. Requirements are taken as per clause 7.9.5 and assume post-tensioning with bonded tendons. This gives values of: 1.0 at ULS 0.9 for inferior case at SLS 1.1 for superior case at SLS Note that carriageway loading and the associated live load should be included in the same loadcase. Footway loading should be included in a different loadcase. See also: Design Combination Options - IRC: 6-2017 Design Combination Options - IRC: 6-2017 Design Combinations Design Combinations

topics.title: Reliability class
toc_path: Design Combination Options - EN1990 - 2002 (Buildings) to Finland National Annex
headings: Design Combination Options - EN1990 - 2002 (Buildings) to Finland National Annex
topics.text: Reliability class A single reliability class can be selected each time the Design Combination wizard is run. If different reliability classes are required for different parts of the structure the Design wizard should be run again and the appropriate loadtypes included and the option to 'Add' combinations selected. If the 'Create an envelope for each combination type' is checked for both the initial and subsequent run, all combinations will be included in a single envelopes. Mixing of different reliability class factors within a single combination are outside the scope of the combination wizard. The default reliability class is RC2.

topics.title: Safety class
toc_path: Design Combination Options - EN1990 - 2002 (Buildings) to Sweden National Annex
headings: Design Combination Options - EN1990 - 2002 (Buildings) to Sweden National Annex
topics.text: Safety class A single safety class can be selected each time the Design Combination wizard is run. If different safety classes are required for different parts of the structure the Design wizard should be run again and the appropriate loadtypes included and the option to 'Add' combinations selected. If 'Create an envelope for each combination type' is checked for both the initial and subsequent run, all combinations will be included in a single envelopes. Mixing of different safety class factors within a single combination are outside the scope of the combination wizard. The default safety class is 2.

topics.title: Frequency PSD
topics.text: Frequency PSD Defines a Frequency Power Spectral Density for use in spectral or frequency response analyses. Frequency PSD may be referenced from IMD loadcases or from the modal expansion option of the Graph Wizard. Frequency/Amplitude The value of PSD used in response calculations is interpolated from the frequency/PSD values defined by the PSD. Interpolation schemes A range of linear and logarithmic interpolation schemes are provided, in accordance with typical PSD specifications. Notes Use the Tab key to enter new lines of data. If the current results file is opened as read only then attributes may be defined but they will be lost when the results file is closed. More copious PSD tables are more easily defined using a command file, or by copying and pasting the data from a text file or spread sheet. Command files can be used to store a library of frequently used PSDs. Defined Frequency PSD are stored in, and may be edited from, the Utilities Treeview. See also: Interactive Modal Dynamics Interactive Modal Dynamics

topics.title: Design Combinations - Advanced Options
topics.text: Design Combinations - Advanced Options The Advanced options dialog of the Design Combinations wizard provides a design code-specific editable tabular listing of the load types and the associated factors to be considered. Load types are separated into Permanent actions and Variable actions, and factors for table entries can be edited. Load types can be set to be mutually exclusive, or not. When mutually exclusive is set to 'Yes', loadcases that have the same load type assigned are not included in a combination simultaneously. For example two loadcases may be created to analyse wind load in different directions. Setting 'wind load' to be mutually exclusive would create two sets of combinations, rather than combining the wind effects together. A defaults button sets all factors (if edited) back to the design codes values. See also: Design Combinations Design Combinations

topics.title: Fatigue Properties
topics.text: Fatigue Properties A fatigue loadcase may be added to the Analyses Treeview using the Analyses > Fatigue menu item, or by right - clicking the Loadcases folder in the Analyses Treeview and selecting New > Fatigue from the context menu.Double - click on the fatigue loadcase to edit its properties. Right - click on the loadcase and choose Set Active from the context menu to visualise results from the fatigue calculations. A S-N curve and fatigue loading spectra are required to carry out fatigue analysis. The S - N curve is used to define the number of cycles to failure at various stress levels. The fatigue loading spectrum defines the loading sequence in terms of the number of cycles of each loadcase that are to be applied to the structure. A load factor may be applied to each loadcase if required. The damage is computed for each loadcase and combined using Miners rule to give the total damage to the structure for the specified loading spectrum. The results entity specified in this dialog is used to calculate the fatigue life.

A S-N curve and fatigue loading spectra are required to carry out fatigue analysis. The S - N curve is used to define the number of cycles to failure at various stress levels. The fatigue loading spectrum defines the loading sequence in terms of the number of cycles of each loadcase that are to be applied to the structure. A load factor may be applied to each loadcase if required. The damage is computed for each loadcase and combined using Miners rule to give the total damage to the structure for the specified loading spectrum. The results entity specified in this dialog is used to calculate the fatigue life.

topics.title: Creating a Fatigue Loadcase
topics.text: Creating a Fatigue Loadcase Fatigue loadcases can be formed from different results files if those files are open. Click in the drop - down list to select the results file. To include a results load case select it in the Available list of loadcases and click the >> button to add it to the Included list on the right. Use the Shift key to select multiple results cases. Select a results case in the Included list on the right, then specify the factor or cycles to failure. Fatigue loadcases may include results from combinations or envelopes as necessary. Loadcases selected for inclusion in the combination can be filtered prior to being included by using the Step option. For example, entering a step value of 2 will include the first loadcase and every second loadcase in the selection.

Loadcases selected for inclusion in the combination can be filtered prior to being included by using the Step option. For example, entering a step value of 2 will include the first loadcase and every second loadcase in the selection.

topics.title: Defining fatigue parameters
topics.text: Defining fatigue parameters For each included loadcase load factors and cycles to failure need to be defined. S-N curve and log data is also required and is defined on the S-N tab . S-N curves contain the variation in stress/strain values with the number of cycles to failure and are defined on a Log Log scale. An S - N curve is used to calculate the number of cycles to failure for each loadcase. Miner's rule is then used to combine the damage for each loadcase to give the total damage to the structure for the specified loading sequence. Fatigue loadcases are saved with the model data. Double-click on the fatigue loadcase to edit its properties.

topics.text: Setting the Active Loadcase Results are always visualised using the active loadcase. To make a loadcase active right - click on the loadcase in the Analyses Treeview, and choose Set Active… from the context menu. The results component on which to decide which factor to use must be specified. The Set Active… button enables the primary results component on which to decide which factor to use to be specified. topics.title: Defining an IMD Loadcase
topics.text: Defining an IMD Loadcase Interactive modal dynamics (IMD) is the investigation of various dynamic responses using the results from an eigenvalue analysis. Defining an IMD loadcase involves setting any or all of the following: Excitation Excitation The form of dynamic excitation must be specified to allow the modal forces to be calculated. To define an IMD Loadcase for Point excitation requires pre-selection of a node of interest, or specification of a node number at the time of definition. Click on the Set button to define the parameters for the specified excitation type. Results Results Sets the type of calculations (analysis) to be carried out. Click on the Set button to define the parameters for the specified results type. Damping Damping Sets the modal damping ratios, either user specified or LUSAS calculated values may be used. Modes Specifies the eigenvalue modes to be considered in the calculations. An IMD analysis may be performed on all of the modes from an eigenvalue analysis ( Use all modes ) or, by pressing the Select modes... button, on selected modes. Modes not selected are ignored in the modal analysis. Modes from multiple results files may be selected. Notes Excitation settings of displacement or velocity are disallowed for modal response calculations in the time domain. Generally, if the supports do not move together large mass point displacement, velocity or acceleration excitation may be the most appropriate. If all the supports move together support motion excitation may be the most appropriate. For Point Displacement, Velocity and Acceleration excitation, the displacement response is absolute and not relative to supports. Only Support motion excitation is applicable for spectral analyses.

topics.title: Defining a new loadcase
topics.text: Defining a new loadcase Analysis Reports on the analysis to which the loadcase has been assigned. For models with more than one analysis entry present in the Analyses Treeview the analysis to which the loadcase will be added needs to be selected. Type Reports on the loadcase type. This is only availble for Bridge and Civil software products when Design Combinations have been specified. Selecting the Automatically add gravity to this loadcase option will, at the time of solving the model, apply a constant body force load equal to the value of gravity to all elements that are active in the loadcase. Note that no visualisation of this gravity loading is available on the model for gravity defined in this manner. However, the general loadcase symbol will change to include a loading arrow symbol to show that gravity is automatically being considered for a particular structural loadcase. Name The loadcase name.

topics.title: Analysis Control Parameters
topics.text: Analysis Control Parameters Loadcase properties enable analysis control parameters to be set if required, for example nonlinear or Eigenvalue controls may be defined. If no control properties are defined, a linear elastic analysis is performed. Analysis control parameters can be set to change throughout an analysis by specifying separate loadcases using different control parameters. These loadcases are the pre - processing loadcases and will not necessarily correspond to post - processing load increments/time steps due to the use of automatic load incrementation. Nonlinear Nonlinear and Transient Transient Used to define nonlinear, and/or transient (dynamic, thermal or consolidation) analyses. Must be specified on the first loadcase if it is to be respecified on a subsequent loadcase. It is not possible to change between thermal and dynamic during the course of an analysis. Eigenvalue Eigenvalue Used to define natural frequency, eigenvalue buckling and stiffness analyses. Can be specified on any loadcase, but only once. Fourier Fourier Used to define Fourier analyses. Must be used if Fourier elements have been used. Can only be specified on loadcase 1.

topics.title: Defining and Setting Combination Properties
topics.text: Defining and Setting Combination Properties To include a results loadcase select it in the Available panel and click the Add to >> button to add it to the Included list on the right. Use the Shift key to select multiple items. Use the Ctrl key to select/deselect individual items. Use the View button for a selected loadcase in the Available or Included panel to view the definition dialog for that loadcase. Where the selected loadcase is a combination or envelope, the definition dialog will have the same 'View' button, allowing recursive viewing of the loadcases used in each higher definition. Adding and removing of loadcases from the one being currently viewed is supported, as is changing of any factors associated with that loadcase, but renaming of the loadcase or viewing details of other loadcases by making selections from the Name combo is prevented. Loadcases selected for inclusion in the combination can be filtered prior to being included by using the Step option. For example, entering a step value of 2 will include the first loadcase and every second loadcase, for a selected analysis, in the selection. The tabular format of the 'Included' list allows the factor for each loadcase / results case to be modified. The table data may also be copied and pasted to and from a spreadsheet for external editing.

topics.title: Options
topics.text: Options Method provides the means to specify a combination method Factored (the default option) - The sum of all included loadcases, where each loadcase is multiplied by its specified load factor. For example: (Loadcase 1 x Factor 1 + Loadcase 2 x Factor 2...) etc. Average Combination - The average of the sum of all included loadcases, where each loadcase is multiplied by its specified load factor. For example: (Loadcase 1 x Factor 1 + Loadcase 2 x Factor 2...) etc. / number of included loadcases SRSS Combination A combination of the square root of the sum of the squares of all included loadcases, where each loadcase is multiplied by its specified load factor. For example: The square root of {(Loadcase 1 x Factor 1) 2 + (Loadcase 2 x Factor 2) 2 ... } etc. Absolute Combination The absolute sum of all included loadcases where each loadcase is multiplied by its specified load factor. For example: The absolute value of (Loadcase 1 x Factor 1) + The absolute value of (Loadcase 2 x Factor 2) + etc. Notes Results can be combined from different analyses. Only analyses with loadcases that are suitable for combining will be listed in the 'Available' panel. The Combination created is saved with the model data.

topics.title: Options
topics.text: Options The Loadcases to consider option enables a combination to be created from the specified number of loadcases with the most adverse effects. The loadcases to consider may not be greater than the total number of loadcases included in the combination. All loadcases are considered by default. The Variable loadcases option enables a combination to be created from loadcases with only the specified number of variable factors included to create the most adverse effects. The number of variable loadcases must not be greater than the number of loadcases to consider. By default the variable factor is considered for all loadcases. Different factors for beneficial and adverse (or permanent and variable effects) may be specified for each combined results loadcase. The Beneficial load factor and Adverse load factor names may be optionally displayed as Permanent load factor and Variable load factor if the check box on the Combination and envelope options dialog has been selected. Note that Beneficial load factor = Permanent load factor. Adverse load factor = Permanent load factor + Variable load factor. For example, specifying a Beneficial load factor of 0.9, and an Adverse load factor of 1.1, causes the same effect as specifying a Permanent load factor of 0.9, and a Variable load factor of 0.2. For permanent and variable load factors: A permanent load factor is always applied A variable load factor is only applied if the effect is adverse. This means a maximum smart combination (Max) will assemble results from the loadcases selected using just the permanent factors for negative load effects, and using a summary of permanent and variable factors for positive load effects, and a minimum smart combination (Min) will assemble results from the loadcases selected using just the permanent factors for positive load effects, and using a summary of permanent and variable factors for negative load effects. Notes Results can be combined from different analyses. Only analyses with loadcases that are suitable for combining will be listed in the 'Available' panel. Combinations may include results from other combinations or envelopes as necessary. If a smart combination is to include another envelope or smart combination both the (Max) and (Min) loadsets should be included in the definition. For a smart combinations the load factor column names will depend upon whether permanent and variable or beneficial and adverse factors are being viewed. The combination created is saved with the model data. Double - click on the combination loadcase to edit its properties.

The Beneficial load factor and Adverse load factor names may be optionally displayed as Permanent load factor and Variable load factor if the check box on the Combination and envelope options dialog has been selected. Note that Beneficial load factor = Permanent load factor. Adverse load factor = Permanent load factor + Variable load factor. For example, specifying a Beneficial load factor of 0.9, and an Adverse load factor of 1.1, causes the same effect as specifying a Permanent load factor of 0.9, and a Variable load factor of 0.2. For permanent and variable load factors: A permanent load factor is always applied A variable load factor is only applied if the effect is adverse. This means a maximum smart combination (Max) will assemble results from the loadcases selected using just the permanent factors for negative load effects, and using a summary of permanent and variable factors for positive load effects, and a minimum smart combination (Min) will assemble results from the loadcases selected using just the permanent factors for positive load effects, and using a summary of permanent and variable factors for negative load effects. Notes Results can be combined from different analyses. Only analyses with loadcases that are suitable for combining will be listed in the 'Available' panel. Combinations may include results from other combinations or envelopes as necessary. If a smart combination is to include another envelope or smart combination both the (Max) and (Min) loadsets should be included in the definition. For a smart combinations the load factor column names will depend upon whether permanent and variable or beneficial and adverse factors are being viewed. The combination created is saved with the model data. Double - click on the combination loadcase to edit its properties.

topics.title: Load curve Properties
topics.text: Load curve Properties Load curves can be used to describe the variation of the loading in nonlinear, transient and Fourier analyses. For example, in a transient problem the loading changes with time, in a nonlinear problem the loading level varies with load increment and in a Fourier analysis the loading varies with angle. New load curves may be added to the Analyses Treeview using the Utilities menu. Double-click on a load curve to edit its properties.

topics.title: Setting the Load Curve Parameters
topics.text: Setting the Load Curve Parameters User-defined Allows a user-defined load curve to be specified. Modeller will linearly interpolate between the defined values. Standard curve Select sine, cosine or square wave input and specify values for peak (amplitude), frequency and phase angle. Variation Specify a previously defined line variation variation to use as a user-defined load curve. For this, units of x-distance are interpreted as units of time, and units of y-value are interpreted as load factor. Specifying a Termination time cuts-off the variation-generated load curve loading at that time. Specifying a Sampling increment samples along the time axis, and uses those values and the corresponding load curve factors to define the load curve output written to the Solver data file. For each of the above options: Activation time specifies at what time along the defined load curve the corresponding value of loading for that time will be applied. Scaling factor scales the loading that is assigned using the defined load curve by factor specified. Load curves are defined with respect to a chosen analysis and given a unique name. Load curve parameters are illustrated in the following image. Note that in a transient or time based analysis the x-axis represents time. In a nonlinear the x-axis represents load increment. In a fourier analysis the x-axis represents angle.

topics.title: Envelope
topics.text: Envelope Envelopes may be added to the Analyses Treeview by using the Analyses menu, or by right - clicking the Structural analysis or Thermal analyses folder (if present) in the Analyses Treeview and selecting New > Envelope from the context menu. Enveloping is used to perform results processing on maximum and minimum values of results loadcases. This is done by creating two loadcases, one for the maximum values and one for the minimum of the specified loadcases.

This is done by creating two loadcases, one for the maximum values and one for the minimum of the specified loadcases.

topics.title: Defining and Setting Envelope Properties
topics.text: Defining and Setting Envelope Properties The Type field is not currently used. Loadcases can be enveloped from different analyses and different results files if those files are open. Click in the drop - down list to select the results file. To include a loadcase select it in the Available panel click the >> button to add it to the Included list on the right. Use the Shift key to select multiple loadcases. Use the Ctrl key to select/deselect individual items. Use the View button for a selected loadcase in the Available or Included panel to view the definition dialog for that loadcase. Where the selected loadcase is a combination or envelope, the definition dialog will have the same 'View' button, allowing recursive viewing of the loadcases used in each higher definition. Adding and removing of loadcases from the one being currently viewed is supported, as is changing of any factors associated with that loadcase, but renaming of the loadcase or viewing details of other loadcases by making selections from the Name combo is prevented.. Envelopes may include loadcases, combinations or other envelopes as necessary. Loadcases selected for inclusion in the envelope can be filtered prior to be included by using the Step option. For example, entering a step value of 2 will include the first loadcase and every second loadcase, for a selected analysis, in the selection.

topics.title: S-N Curve
topics.text: S-N Curve S - N curves are required for Fatigue analysis. The S - N curve is used to calculate the number of cycles to failure for each loadcase. The damage for each loadcase is then combined to give the total damage to the structure for the specified loading sequence. Notes Use the Tab key to enter new lines of data. If plotting the number of cycles to failure, then the number of cycles entered in the loading spectrum should sum to unity. If the current results file is opened as read only then an S-N curve may be defined but it will be lost when the results file is closed. More copious S - N Curve tables are more easily defined using a command file, or by copying and pasting the data from a text file or spread sheet. Command files can be used to store a library of frequently used S - N Curves. Defined S - N Curves are stored in, and may be edited from, the Utilities Treeview. See also: Fatigue Calculations Fatigue Calculations

topics.text: Point Excitation Force/Displacement/Velocity/Acceleration Specifies the excitation type. Node number Specifies which node is to receive the excitation. topics.title: Frequency Response
topics.text: Frequency Response Type The response variable type to be plotted against the specified frequency range. See Modal Dynamics for examples of typical graphs. Type can be set to: Real, Imaginary, Amplitude, Phase, Value or PSD. Real , Imaginary , Amplitude and Phase permit entering of a specific frequency Value permits entering a specific frequency and phase angle PSD Power Spectral Density. A excitation PSD profile can be defined or a pre - defined excitation PSD profile may be referenced. The PSD response is simply the square of the FRF amplitude multiplied by the excitation PSD, at each selected frequency. The RMS value of this PSD is the square - root of the area under this response PSD. Frequency Specify a frequency at which the modal response will be calculated. Response calculations are only valid for a frequency range defined by the available eigenvectors. Phase angle Calculates the response at a particular phase angle shift. Scale Defines the scale of the PSD input. Details can be entered in the data grid. See also: Interactive Modal Dynamics Interactive Modal Dynamics

topics.title: PSD Response
topics.text: PSD Response Evaluation of the RMS response is based on trapezoidal numerical integration of the response PSD, using the specified frequency points. Care is needed to ensure that the frequency resolution is fine enough to integrate sharp resonant peaks adequately. Adjustment of start and end frequencies allow calculations of RMS levels within arbitrary frequency bands. Frequency start /end /step Specify the frequency range for the PSD modal analysis. The PSD sampling frequencies should coincide with the sampling frequencies from the solution. Frequency PSD Specify a previously defined Frequency PSD dataset. See also: Interactive Modal Dynamics Interactive Modal Dynamics

topics.title: Real and/or Imaginary Loading
topics.text: Real and/or Imaginary Loading A load vector is extracted from the eigenvalues (loadcases) specified. In this case the modal forces are complex and therefore the modal forces are stored in two arrays - one for the real component and one for the imaginary. (For excitation types other than these the imaginary components will always be zero). Note that it will be assumed that all applied forces are in phase. The chosen load vector need not be in the same results file as the eigenvectors used for the response calculation - typically only one load vector will be stored with the modes. See also: Interactive Modal Dynamics Interactive Modal Dynamics

headings: Response Spectrum - User-defined (for IMD loadcase use)
topics.text: Response Spectrum - User-defined (for IMD loadcase use) Response spectrum data for use with IMD loadcases is defined by selecting the Utilities > Response Spectrum menu item. Response Spectrum datasets are referenced from IMD loadcases when calculating spectral response. Frequency / Period versus Displacement / Velocity / Acceleration / Gravity The value of the frequency used in spectral calculations is interpolated from the frequency-amplitude or period-amplitude values defined. The type of values entered, i.e. displacement, velocity, acceleration or acceleration/gravity should match the type of support motion which is used to excite the structure. Spectral curve damping Defines the damping inherent in the response spectrum. A default value is 0% is initially set. Notes More copious Response Spectrum tables are more easily defined using a command file, or by copying and pasting the data from a text file or spreadsheet. Command files can be used to store a library of frequently used Response Spectrum datasets. Defined Response Spectrum datasets are stored in, and may be edited from, the Utilities treeview. Response Spectrum datasets are referenced from IMD loadcases when calculating spectral response. Frequency / Period versus Displacement / Velocity / Acceleration / Gravity The value of the frequency used in spectral calculations is interpolated from the frequency-amplitude or period-amplitude values defined. The type of values entered, i.e. displacement, velocity, acceleration or acceleration/gravity should match the type of support motion which is used to excite the structure. Spectral curve damping Defines the damping inherent in the response spectrum. A default value is 0% is initially set. Notes More copious Response Spectrum tables are more easily defined using a command file, or by copying and pasting the data from a text file or spreadsheet. Command files can be used to store a library of frequently used Response Spectrum datasets. Defined Response Spectrum datasets are stored in, and may be edited from, the Utilities treeview. topics.title: Type of spectral response
topics.text: Type of spectral response The method of combining the modes to obtain the maximum structural effects are: CQC The complete quadratic combination of the results from all the selected modes. SRSS The square root of the sum of the squares of the results from all the selected modes. Absolute Sum The absolute sum of the results from all the selected modes.

topics.title: Support Motion
topics.text: Support Motion Parameters for defining a Support motion excitation: Displacement/Velocity/Acceleration Specifies the support motion type. When performing a spectral analysis, the support motion type should match the spectral response data i.e. frequency against displacement, velocity, or acceleration. Acceleration is usually used for earthquake analyses. Vector Specifies the excitation direction as a component in either the X, Y, or Z direction. User specified Used to specify a support motion in a user-defined direction. Note that specifying a user direction re-orientates and factors the input motion according to a vector, which unless adjusted, will amplify (scale) the motion. For instance. if you wish to apply a spectral curve at 45 degrees in the horizontal plane, you should use a vector which is specified as (0.707, 0.707, 0), otherwise if (1.0,1.0,0) is specified a motion of 1.414 times the specified motion at an angle of 45 degrees will be obtained. Frequency domain response motion type Normally displacement response is relative to the supports and not absolute. In the frequency domain, (when results are set to Frequency), the displacement response may be specified as relative or absolute. If absolute is chosen then the motion of the support is added to the structural motion to give motion with respect to ground. This is useful for comparison with measured data. See also: Interactive Modal Dynamics Interactive Modal Dynamics

topics.title: User Defined Results
topics.text: User Defined Results User-defined results components can be defined by creating expressions based upon results entities, components, model data and other user-defined results component calculations. User defined results expressions are normally created after a solve has been done and with results loaded, but they can also be defined as part of the modelling process after all relevant features have been assigned an element mesh. The user-defined results table contains the following column headings: Entity - Clicking on the drop-list button in this cell lists all entities available for the particular results file loaded. By selecting a particular results entity a list of variables that are valid for that entity are presented for selection when clicking in the Expressions column Expression - Clicking on the launch dialog button in this cell displays a dialog populated with valid variables for the selection made in the Entity field. By use of these variables and usual arithmetic syntax a user-defined results expression can be built. Name - a name for the calculation should be entered. This will appear in the Component drop-down on a Contour, Values or Diagram properties dialog and also in the user-defined component section of the User Defined Results Expression variables listing. Description - a longer piece of explanatory text. The description will appear alongside the name in the user-defined component section of the Expression variables listing. In addition the following buttons can be used: Add - adds a new row to the table beneath existing rows Delete - deletes a selected row Copy to Clipboard - copies contents of selected cells to clipboard Insert from Clipboard - pastes contents of clipboard into selected cells After definition, the user-defined results components created can be selected by name from the Component drop-down list on the Contours, Values, and Diagrams layers properties dialogs. See also: User Defined Results User Defined Results

topics.title: Animating the Active Loadcase
topics.text: Animating the Active Loadcase The active loadcase can only be animated for results loadcases Deformation function (the type of animation cycle) can specified to be Sine , Square , Saw Tooth or Ramp . The deformation function is applied over the number of frames in the animation and can be specified to be over a positive range (from 0 to 1) or from negative to positive (-1 to 1) A greater number of frames increases the smoothness of the animation sequence, takes longer to create, and ultimately produces a larger file than fewer frames. Specifying a deformation factor is recommended since a specified magnitude will deform each frame by the same amount leading to ambiguous results.

topics.title: Animating Load History
topics.text: Animating Load History The load history can be animated for both model or results loadcases. All loadcases animates all available results loadcases. Final increment animates all available results loadcases using only the last increment of each nonlinear results loadcase. This is useful for animating the actual effect of a fully applied load factor rather than viewing the incremental steps taken to achieve it. Specified allows a user-defined selection of model or results loadcases for animation. Loadcases selected for inclusion in the animation can be filtered prior to be included by using the Step option. For example, entering a step value of 2 will include the first loadcase and every second loadcase in the selection.

topics.title: Usage:
topics.text: Usage: Choose whether to animate Model or Results file loadcases. If more than one results file is loaded, choose a results file from the drop - down list. From the left 'Available' panel select a loadcase, or hold down the Shift key to select multiple loadcases, (filter the selection using the step option, if required) and click on the 'Add to' >> button to include them. The right 'Included' panel shows which loadcases will be used. If required, select another results file from the drop - down list, and add further loadcases. Press the Finish button to create the animation See also: Creating Animation Sequences Creating Animation Sequences
