topics.text: Long term losses Include When set to 'Yes', prestress loss calculations are based upon approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses. When sete to 'No', only short term losses are calculated, with elastic shortening based upon calculated losses. Age of concrete at time of prestressing [t i ]. This value is used for the calculation of losses due to creep to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. Strength of concrete at time of prestressing [f’ ci ]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to creep to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. f’ ci is defined as the “ specified compressive strength of the concrete at the time of initial loading or prestressing; nominal concrete strength at time of application of tendon force (ksi)” . According to clause 5.4.2.3.2, f’ci may be taken as 0.8f’c if concrete age at time of initial load is unknown at design stage. Gross area of concrete section [A c ], and Moment of inertia of gross concrete section , [I c ]. These values are used for the calculation of losses due to shrinkage, to clause 5.9.5.4.3a, and creep, to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. Where the concrete section varies, suitable intermediate values may be required. Volume to surface ratio [V/S]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to shrinkage to clause 5.9.5.4.3a, and creep, to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. Details on how the ratio should be calculated are given in clause 5.4.2.3.2. No of days shrinkage [t]. This value is used for the calculation of losses due to shrinkage to clause 5.9.5.4.3a. t is defined as the “ number of days between end of curing and time being considered for analysis of shrinkage effects ”. The default value is based on the design life for a bridge, which is 75 years according to clause 1.2. Relative humidity [H]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to shrinkage, to clause 5.9.5.4.3a, and creep, to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. H is defined as the “ average ambient mean relative humidity (percent) ” and guidance can be found in Figure 5.4.2.3.3-1. No of days creep [t]. This value is used for the calculation of losses due to creep to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. t is defined as the “no of days between application of load and time considered for creep calculation”. The default value is based on the design life for a bridge, which is 75 years, according to clause 1.2. Modulus of elasticity of concrete [E c ]. This value is used for the calculation of losses due to creep to clause 5.9.5.4.3b. E c may be calculated for a given concrete grade from the equation in clause 5.4.2.4. Change in stress due to loads after transfer [Δ fcd ]. This value is used for the calculation of the creep losses according to equation 5.9.5.4.3b-1, and is defined in the code as the “ change in concrete stress at centroid of prestressing strands due to long-term losses between transfer and deck placement, combined with deck weight and superimposed loads ”. In fact, a value appropriate to the concrete adjacent to the tendon in question may be used. Δ fcd is generally negative since applied loads and long-term losses oppose the initial prestress that dominates f cgp . Low relaxation strands When set to 'Yes', the relaxation loss Δf pR1 = 1.2ksi is assumed according to clause 5.9.5.4.2c, and the grid entries 'Yield stress of tendon' and 'Factor accounting for type of steel' are unavailable. If this assumption is deemed inappropriate, selecting 'No' will add the entries 'Yield stress of tendon' and 'Factor accounting for type of steel' to the grid and permit specification of suitable values. Yield stress of tendon [f py ]. (Option only available with 'Low relaxation strands' set to 'Yes'.) This value is used for the calculation of relaxation losses according to equation 5.9.5.4.2c-1. f py is defined as “yield stress of prestressing steel.”. Suitable values may be based on clause 5.4.4.1. Factor accounting for type of steel [K L ]. Option only available with 'Low relaxation strands' set to 'Yes'. This value is used for the calculation of relaxation losses according to equation 5.9.5.4.2c-1, when the assumption of Δf pR2 = Δf pR1 = 1.2ksi is deemed inappropriate. K L is defined as “factor accounting for type of steel, taken as 30 for low relaxation strands and 7 for other prestressing steel, unless more accurate manufacturer’s data is available.”.

This value is used for the calculation of the creep losses according to equation 5.9.5.4.3b-1, and is defined in the code as the “ change in concrete stress at centroid of prestressing strands due to long-term losses between transfer and deck placement, combined with deck weight and superimposed loads ”. In fact, a value appropriate to the concrete adjacent to the tendon in question may be used. Δ fcd is generally negative since applied loads and long-term losses oppose the initial prestress that dominates f cgp . Low relaxation strands When set to 'Yes', the relaxation loss Δf pR1 = 1.2ksi is assumed according to clause 5.9.5.4.2c, and the grid entries 'Yield stress of tendon' and 'Factor accounting for type of steel' are unavailable. If this assumption is deemed inappropriate, selecting 'No' will add the entries 'Yield stress of tendon' and 'Factor accounting for type of steel' to the grid and permit specification of suitable values. Yield stress of tendon [f py ]. (Option only available with 'Low relaxation strands' set to 'Yes'.) This value is used for the calculation of relaxation losses according to equation 5.9.5.4.2c-1. f py is defined as “yield stress of prestressing steel.”. Suitable values may be based on clause 5.4.4.1. Factor accounting for type of steel [K L ]. Option only available with 'Low relaxation strands' set to 'Yes'. This value is used for the calculation of relaxation losses according to equation 5.9.5.4.2c-1, when the assumption of Δf pR2 = Δf pR1 = 1.2ksi is deemed inappropriate. K L is defined as “factor accounting for type of steel, taken as 30 for low relaxation strands and 7 for other prestressing steel, unless more accurate manufacturer’s data is available.”.

topics.text: Defining AASHTO LRFD 5th to 9th Edition Tendon Properties with losses based upon time inputs and calculated stresses Tendon properties relating to loss calculations need to be defined. Other values required to carry out loss calculations are obtained from the tendon loading definition tendon loading definition , concrete materia concrete materia l and age age assignments, and the time management time management module. It should be noted that AASHTO 8th and 9th edition differ from the 7th edition due to two modifications - the Concrete modulus of elasticity (eqn 5.4.2.4-1) and the coefficient for time dependency which is used for creep and shrinkage (eqn 5.4.2.3.2-5). References cited below are to 'AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications 7th Edition' unless otherwise stated. topics.text: General Tendon area [A p ]. The cross-sectional area of the tendon (or total area if a group is being represented by a single load assignment). In general, for internal prestressing, tendons of modest size are advisable to avoid difficulties in housing and anchoring larger tendons with the attendant increase in thickness of members and in the weight of reinforcement. 19 No 0.6” strand (A p =4.123in²) is considered to be a practical upper limit per tendon. The prestress loading facility allows tendons of larger area to be defined. Modulus of elasticity for tendon [E p ]. Refer to clause 5.4.4.2. The default value is 28,500ksi, representing strand.

topics.text: Post-installation losses Include When set to 'Yes', prestress calculations include losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses, i.e.elastic shortening, creep, shrinkage and relaxation. When set to 'No', only installation losses are calculated, i.e. friction and anchorage. Tensile strength of tendon [f pu ]. This value is used for the calculation of relaxation losses according to commentary eqn C5.9.5.4.2c-1. f py is calculated from f pu for use in that equation, using from Table 5.4.4.1-1, i.e. F py =k p *f pu where k p =0.85 or 0.9 for low relaxation strand . Suitable values for f pu are stated in table 5.4.4.1-1. Low relaxation strands When set to 'Yes', the relaxation loss is calculated using f py (as described above) and K' L = 45 from the commentary clause C5.9.5.4.2c. When set to 'No', the relaxation loss is calculated using f py =0.9f py (as described above) and K' L = 10. The approximations of clause 5.9.5.4.2c, such as the use of a single value of 1.2ksi are not used for time-dependent calculations.

topics.title: Creep loss
toc_path: With losses based upon time inputs and calculated stresses
Defining AASHTO LRFD 5th to 9th Edition Tendon Properties with losses based upon time inputs and calculated stresses
headings: Defining AASHTO LRFD 5th to 9th Edition Tendon Properties with losses based upon time inputs and calculated stresses
topics.text: Creep loss Creep loss can be calculated by one of two available methods, described below. It may be appropriate to compare the two approaches for structures which have a high sensitivity to creep loss. Using article 5.4.2.3.2 This option calculates creep losses using eqn 5.4.2.3.2-2 to determine k s (the factor for the effect of the volume-to-surface ratio of the component), rather than using the alternative commentary clause. Eqn 5.4.2.3.2-2 leads to values of k s ≥1.0 and, in tests, gave creep losses in the expected range. This option is fully compliant with AASHTO 8th and 9th but is using an approach described in the commentary as 'an approximation' for the value of k s . Using commentary and 2nd Edition This option calculates creep losses using the commentary clause C5.4.2.3.2-2 to determine k c , which is used in place of k s . The commentary may lead to values of k c <1.0 for sections thicker than 1.5" and, in tests, gave creep losses somewhat lower than the expected range. Comparison with the 2nd edition identified the original use of k c with a 3.5 multiple in the creep coefficient, rather than 1.9 as in later editions. Accordingly this option adopts the 3.5 multiple, also capping the ratio V/S at a notional thickness of 6", and has been found also to give creep losses in the expected range for the tests undertaken; less conservative than those arising from the use of article 5.4.2.3.2 above for all sections >1" thick. This option is therefore not fully compliant with AASHTO 5th to 7th but may be deemed to be a more accurate approach.

topics.text: Shrinkage loss Shrinkage loss can be calculated by one of two available methods, described below. It may be appropriate to compare the two approaches for structures which have a high sensitivity to shrinkage loss. Using equation 5.4.2.3.2-2 This option calculates shrinkage losses using eqn 5.4.2.3.2-2 to determine k s (the factor for the effect of the volume-to-surface ratio of the component), rather than using the alternative commentary clause. Eqn 5.4.2.3.2-2 leads to values of k s ≥1.0 and, in tests, gave shrinkage losses ranging from those in the expected range to those somewhat larger. This option is fully compliant with AASHTO 8th and 9th but is using an approach described in the commentary as " an approximation " for the value of k s . Using commentary This option calculates shrinkage losses using the commentary clause C5.4.2.3.2-2 to determine k s , capping the ratio V/S at a notional thickness of 6". The commentary may lead to values of k s <1.0 for sections thicker than 1.5" and, in tests, gave shrinkage losses ranging from those in the expected range to those somewhat lower. This option is fully compliant with the commentary approach set out in AASHTO 8th and 9th, and therefore may be deemed to be a more accurate approach, however, caution is recommended.

headings: Defining AASHTO LRFD 5th to 9th Edition Tendon Properties with losses based upon time inputs and calculated stresses
Notes on post-installation losses calculated to section 5.9
topics.text: Notes on post-installation losses calculated to section 5.9 Elastic losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of article 5.9.5.2.3b, using the modulus of elasticity for concrete amended for aggregate type as per article 5.4.2.4 and amended for age and cement type using the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 clause 2.1.6.3. The simplified formula of equation 5.9.5.2.3b-1 is not used, instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used. Creep losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of article 5.9.5.4. Equations 5.9.5.4.2b-1 and 5.9.5.4.3b-1 are not used directly; instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution, and allowing calculation of creep loss at any stage in the analysis is adopted. The creep coefficient can be based purely upon article 5.4.2.3.2, with the factor for the effect of volume-to-surface ratio (k s ) calculated using equation 5.4.2.3.2-2 or based upon the commentary C5.4.2.3.2-1 and AASHTO 2nd edition as described earlier. In either case, coefficients k f and k td for creep are evaluated using the f' ci amended for aggregate type as per article 5.4.2.4 and amended for age and cement type using the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 clause 2.1.6.1. Shrinkage losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of article 5.9.5.4. Equations 5.9.5.4.2a-1 and 5.9.5.4.3a-1 are not used directly; instead a generalised approach allowing calculation of shrinkage loss at any stage in the analysis is adopted. The factor for the effect of volume-to-surface ratio (k s ) may be calculated using either equation 5.4.2.3.2-2 or commentary C5.4.2.3.2-2 as described earlier. In either case, coefficients k f and k td for shrinkage are evaluated using the approximation f' ci =0.8*f'_c as f' ci is not properly defined in the context of shrinkage. Relaxation losses are evaluated using the commentary C5.9.5.4.2-c1. By comparison to source documents ACI435, AASHTO 2nd article 5.9.5.4.4b and NCHRP Report 496 eqn 63, the total relaxation loss at each stage of construction at each location along the tendon is calculated using: where t is the time since tensioning in days. The equation cited here differs from that in C5.9.3.4.2-1, retaining the factor of 24 hours to convert from days to hours as per the source documents and previous LRFD editions. (24t+1) is used to avoid a math error for t=0, and reference is made to source documents and the log quotient rule in order to give what is understood to be a correct rendering. When the AASHTO 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be combined with either the corresponding AASHTO 8th to 9th Concrete (Nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material or the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 creep and shrinkage material in order to obtain the corresponding deformations at each time step in the analysis. The program will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , the corresponding AASHTO 5th to 7th "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter approach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. The simplified formula of equation 5.9.5.2.3b-1 is not used, instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used. Creep losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of article 5.9.5.4. Equations 5.9.5.4.2b-1 and 5.9.5.4.3b-1 are not used directly; instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution, and allowing calculation of creep loss at any stage in the analysis is adopted. The creep coefficient can be based purely upon article 5.4.2.3.2, with the factor for the effect of volume-to-surface ratio (k s ) calculated using equation 5.4.2.3.2-2 or based upon the commentary C5.4.2.3.2-1 and AASHTO 2nd edition as described earlier. In either case, coefficients k f and k td for creep are evaluated using the f' ci amended for aggregate type as per article 5.4.2.4 and amended for age and cement type using the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 clause 2.1.6.1. Shrinkage losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of article 5.9.5.4. Equations 5.9.5.4.2a-1 and 5.9.5.4.3a-1 are not used directly; instead a generalised approach allowing calculation of shrinkage loss at any stage in the analysis is adopted. The factor for the effect of volume-to-surface ratio (k s ) may be calculated using either equation 5.4.2.3.2-2 or commentary C5.4.2.3.2-2 as described earlier. In either case, coefficients k f and k td for shrinkage are evaluated using the approximation f' ci =0.8*f'_c as f' ci is not properly defined in the context of shrinkage. Relaxation losses are evaluated using the commentary C5.9.5.4.2-c1. By comparison to source documents ACI435, AASHTO 2nd article 5.9.5.4.4b and NCHRP Report 496 eqn 63, the total relaxation loss at each stage of construction at each location along the tendon is calculated using: where t is the time since tensioning in days. The equation cited here differs from that in C5.9.3.4.2-1, retaining the factor of 24 hours to convert from days to hours as per the source documents and previous LRFD editions. (24t+1) is used to avoid a math error for t=0, and reference is made to source documents and the log quotient rule in order to give what is understood to be a correct rendering. When the AASHTO 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be combined with either the corresponding AASHTO 8th to 9th Concrete (Nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material or the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 creep and shrinkage material in order to obtain the corresponding deformations at each time step in the analysis. The program will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , the corresponding AASHTO 5th to 7th "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter approach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. See also: Defining a Tendon Profile Defining a Tendon Profile Defining Tendon Loading Defining Tendon Loading Prestress Loading Prestress Loading

Other values required to carry out loss calculations are obtained from the tendon loading definition tendon loading definition , concrete materia concrete materia l and age age assignments, and the time management time management module. It should be noted that AASHTO 8th and 9th editions differ from AASHTO 7th edition due to two modifications - the Concrete modulus of elasticity (eqn 5.4.2.4-1) and the coefficient for time dependency which is used for creep and shrinkage (eqn 5.4.2.3.2-5). Clauses referred to AASHTO 8th and 9th editions of the form 5.9.3... are referenced as 5.9.5... within AASHTO 7th Edition. topics.text: Tendon details Tendon area [Ap] The cross-sectional area of the tendon (or total area of a group of strands if a group is being represented by a single load assignment). In general, for internal prestressing, tendons of modest size are advisable to avoid difficulties in housing and anchoring larger tendons with the attendant increase in thickness of members and in the weight of reinforcement. 19 No 15mm strands (Ap=2850mm²) or 27 No 13mm strands (Ap=2700mm²) might be a practical upper limit per tendon. The prestress loading facility allows tendons of larger area to be defined. Modulus of elasticity [Ep]. Refer to 4.3.2.2 and Figure 3. The default value is assumed to be 200kN/mm², representing wire and strand to BS5896 sections 2 and 3.

topics.title: Instantaneous losses
toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining BS5400-4:1990 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining BS5400-4:1990 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Instantaneous losses Wobble factor [K]. Losses due to unintentional variation from the specified profile are calculated from clause 6.7.3.3 eqn 31, in which K is the constant depending on the type of duct employed, the nature of its inside surface, the method of forming it and the degree of vibration employed in placing the concrete. The value of K should generally be taken as not less than 33 x10-4 per metre length, but where strong rigid duct formers are used closely supported so that they are not displaced during the concreting operation, the value of K may be taken as 17x10-4/m. Other values may be used as established for the project in question. It should be noted that this K does not correspond to the similar coefficient in EN1992-1-1:2004 exp 5.45 because the Eurocode value is multiplied by the coefficient of friction whereas K is not. The value is also used in the reverse friction loss calculation associated with anchorage slip losses (clause 6.7.2.6). Duct friction coefficient [μ]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction according to clause 6.7.3.4 eqn 32. Μ may be taken as 0.55 for steel moving on concrete, 0.3 for steel moving on steel or 0.1 for strand moving on rigid steel spacers coated with molybdenum disulphide. The value is also used in the reverse friction loss calculation associated with anchorage slip losses (clause 6.7.2.6).

topics.title: Long term losses
toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining BS5400-4:1990 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining BS5400-4:1990 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Long term losses Include When set to 'Yes', prestress loss calculations are based upon approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses. When set to 'No', only short term losses are calculated, with elastic shortening based upon calculated losses. Relaxation loss According to clause 6.7.2.2, the loss of force in the tendon allowed for in the design should be the maximum relaxation after 1000h duration, for a jacking force equal to that imposed at transfer, as given by the appropriate British Standard. No reduction in the value of the relaxation loss should be made for a tendon which has been preloaded or over-tensioned. The relaxation loss is therefore taken as the percentage of the prestress force as entered here.. Shrinkage Coefficient The basic shrinkage is taken from Table 29 with the loss calculated as described in clause 6.7.2.4, and typically takes a value of 200x10-6 for post-tensioning with transfer at between 7 days and 14 days after casting with normal exposure (70% relative humidity) or 70 x10-6 for humid conditions (90% RH). For other ages of concrete at transfer, for other conditions of exposure or for massive structures, some adjustment to these figures will be necessary, in which case reference should be made to Appendix C or specialist literature. Creep coefficient In accordance with clause 6.7.2.5, it is assumed that crep is proportional to stress in the concrete for stress up to one-third of the cube strength at transfer. For post-tensioning at between 7 days and 14 days after concreting and for humid or dry conditions where the cube strength at transfer fci>40N/mm², the creep of the concrete per unit length should be taken as 36x10-6 per N/mm². For lower values of cube strength at transfer the creep per unit length should be taken as 36x10-6 x 40/fci per N/mm². Stress at transfer This value is used for the calculation of elastic shortening losses, according to clause 6.7.2.3, and, when long-term losses are requested, for the creep component of long term losses to clause 6.7.2.5. Creep losses are based on a single value for each tendon, and the elastic shortening losses are based on a single value for each member (calculated from the values given for all the applicable tendons). The value entered for here should be the stress in the concrete adjacent to the tendon in question, immediately after tensioning and anchoring, due to total prestressing forces and self weight, averaged along the length of the tendon. Variations in stress arising from permanent actions applied after prestressing (generally, but not exclusively, leading to elastic gains) are not incorporated into the calculation of initial elastic shortening loss..

topics.text: Installation losses Unintentional angular displacement [k]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction, according to clause 4.3.3.2 eqn 4.3-1, for the component sometimes referred to as “wobble” loss and also in determining anchorage losses. k describes the “unintentional angular displacement” for internal tendons in radians per unit length. The commentary to clause 4.3.3.2, part (a), gives the range 0.005 < k <0.01 rad/m for the case of bonded internal tendons made from prestressing steel. Duct friction coefficient [μ]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction according to clause 4.3.3.2 eqn 4.3-1, and also in determining anchorage losses. Suitable values may be found in the commentary to clause 4.3.3.2; the default value μ = 0.19 is for internal tendons made up of strand filling roughly half of the duct.

topics.text: Post-installation losses Include When set to 'Yes', prestress calculations include losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses, i.e. elastic shortening, creep, shrinkage and relaxation. When set to 'No', only installation losses are calculated, i.e. friction and anchorage. Tensile strength of prestressing steel [f ptk ] This value is not used for loss calculations but is used to provide an improbable data check on prestressing forces specified in any tendon loading attribute in which this tendon property is utilised. Notes on post-installation losses calculated to CEB-FIP Model Code 1990
topics.text: Notes on post-installation losses calculated to CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 Elastic losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of clause 4.3.3.1, using the reduced modulus of elasticity for concrete (accounting for initial plastic strain) from expression 2.1-17, based on strength class (clause 2.1.4.2), aggregate type (table 2.1.5), amended for age (exp 2.1-57) and cement type (clause 2.1.3). A comprehensive summation using concrete stresses derived from an initial solution of the model is used. Creep and shrinkage losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of 2.1.6.4.3 (a), (b) and 2.1.6.4.4. The effects of temperature during curing may be taken into account by utilising a modified age at loading in the age age attribute. A comprehensive summation using concrete stresses derived from an initial solution of the model and allowing calculation of creep and shrinkage losses at any stage in the analysis is adopted. When the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be combined with the use of the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material in order to obtain the corresponding deformations at each time step in the analysis. LUSAS will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter approach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. See also: Defining a Tendon Profile Defining a Tendon Profile Defining Tendon Loading Defining Tendon Loading Prestress Loading Prestress Loading

Defining DD EN1992-1-1:1992 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining DD EN1992-1-1:1992 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Tendon details Tendon area [A p ]. The cross-sectional area of the tendon (or total area of a group of strands if a group is being represented by a single load assignment). In general, for internal prestressing, tendons of modest size are advisable to avoid difficulties in housing and anchoring larger tendons with the attendant increase in thickness of members and in the weight of reinforcement. 19 No 15mm strands (A p =2850mm²) or 27 No 13mm strands (A p =2700mm²) might be a practical upper limit per tendon. The prestress loading facility allows tendons of larger area to be defined. Modulus of elasticity of tendon [E s ] . Refer to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 3.3.4.4 (2). The default value for the modulus of elasticity, E s , is assumed to be 190kN/mm², representing strand. Values typically fall in the range of 185kN/mm² to 210kN/mm². Concrete stress at transfer [σ co ]. This value is used for the calculation of elastic shortening losses to DD ENV1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(6) and, when long-term losses are requested, the creep component of time-dependent losses to clause 4.2.3.5.5(9) eqn 4.10. Creep losses are based on a single value of σ co for each tendon (combined with Δσ cg below, defined as appropriate), and the elastic shortening losses are based on a single σ co value for each member (calculated from the values given for all the applicable tendons). The value entered for σ co here should be the stress in the concrete adjacent to the tendon in question, immediately after tensioning and anchoring, due to total prestressing forces and self weight averaged along the length of the tendon. Variations in stress arising from permanent actions applied after prestressing (generally but not exclusively leading to elastic shortening gains) are not incorporated in the calculation of initial elastic shortening loss.

topics.title: Instantaneous losses
toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining DD EN1992-1-1:1992 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining DD EN1992-1-1:1992 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Instantaneous losses Modulus of elasticity of concrete at transfer [E cm(t) ]. This value is used for the calculation of elastic shortening losses to DD ENV1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(6). This is the secant modulus of elasticity for concrete, adjusted for concrete age at the time of application of the load, under the provisions of DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 3.1.2.5.2(4). There are no formulae for the strength of concrete developing with time in DD ENV 1992-1-1, therefore reference may be made to the CEB-FIP Model Code 1990, clauses 2.1.6.1 and 2.1.3.2, or EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 3.1.2. A likely range of values would be 24-37kN/mm². Unintentional angular displacement [k]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction, according to DD ENV1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(8), for the component sometimes referred to as “wobble” loss. It is also used in the calculation of anchorage losses. k is defined as “ unintentional angular displacement (per unit length) related to the profile of the tendons ". Clause 4.2.3.5.5(8) gives a range of 0.005 < k <0.01 /m. Duct friction coefficient , μ. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction, according to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(8). It is also used in the calculation of anchorage losses. Suitable values may be found in clause 4.2.3.5.5(8); the default value μ = 0.19 is for internal tendons made up of strand filling roughly half of the duct.

topics.title: Long term losses
toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining DD EN1992-1-1:1992 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining DD EN1992-1-1:1992 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Long term losses Include When set to 'Yes', prestress loss calculations are based upon approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses. When set to 'No', only short term losses are calculated, with elastic shortening based upon calculated losses. Relaxation loss [ρ t ]. This value is used for the calculation of Δ σpr , the absolute value of relaxation loss, which is incorporated into the time dependent loss calculation of DD ENV 1992-1-1 eqn 4.10. According to clause 4.2.3.4.1(2), the long term value of the relaxation loss may be assumed to be three times the relaxation losses after 1000h, which may in turn be taken from Figure 4.8, dependent upon the ratio of the applied prestress to the tensile strength of the tendons and the type of prestressing steel in use. Typical values for class 2 (strand) would therefore be (from Figure 4.8); σ p /f pk = 0.6; ρ1000 = 1%; ρ∞ = 3% σ p /f pk = 0.7; ρ1000 = 2.5%; ρ∞ = 7.5% σ p /f pk = 0.8; ρ1000 = 4.5%; ρ∞ = 13.5% Shrinkage strain [ε s (t,t0)]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to shrinkage according to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(9). ε s (t,t0) is “the estimated shrinkage strain, derived from the values in Table 3.4 for final shrinkage (see also 2.5.5 and Appendix 1)” and should be specified “per mil” (‰) in accordance with the code (rather than actual strain). Creep coefficient [φ(t,t0)]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to creep, according to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(9). Clause 1.7.4 describes φ(t,t0) as the “Creep coefficient, defining creep between times t and t0, related to elastic deformation at 28 days”. Clause 4.2.3.5.5(9) refers to clause 2.5.5 that in turn refers to clause 3.1 or (for greater accuracy) Appendix 1. If greater accuracy is not required, a value for φ(∞,t0) may be obtained from Table 3.3, dependent upon notional size, relative humidity and maturity of the concrete when the load is first applied. Secant modulus of elasticity of concrete [E cm ]. This value is used for the calculation of time-dependent losses according to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(9). Equation 4.10 requires a modular ratio, α = E s /E cm , where E cm can be obtained from Table 3.2. A likely range of values would be 29-37kN/mm². Change in stress due to loads after transfer Δσ cg . This is used to adjust the concrete stress at transfer, σ co , to account for stress in the concrete due to permanent loads applied after prestressing. σ co + Δσ cg gives the concrete stress appropriate for the calculation of the creep component of time-dependent losses according to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(9), eqn 4.10 that is σ co + Δσ cg = (σ cg + σ cpo ). Δσ cg is typically negative, since applied loads oppose the prestress that dominates σ co . Area of concrete section [Ac] and Second moment of area – concrete [Ic]. These values are used for the calculation of time-dependent losses, according to DD ENV 1992-1-1 clause 4.2.3.5.5(9) eqn 4.10. Where the concrete section varies, suitable intermediate values may be required. If the member is a standalone beam element the area of the beam should be used. If the beam member represents part of a larger structure (for example a certain width of slab) then only the area of the portion represented by this particular beam member should be used. Please note that the prestress loading facility is designed to work for a single beam member, not for a subdivided portion of slab or wide beam element, so using it in any other way is at the engineer’s judgement.

toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining EN 1992-1-1:2004 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining EN 1992-1-1:2004 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Tendon details Tendon area [A p ]. The cross-sectional area of the tendon (or total area of a group of strands if a group is being represented by a single load assignment). In general, for internal prestressing, tendons of modest size are advisable to avoid difficulties in housing and anchoring larger tendons with the attendant increase in thickness of members and in the weight of reinforcement. 19 No 15mm strands (A p =2850mm²) or 27 No 13mm strands (A p =2700mm²) might be a practical upper limit per tendon. The prestress loading facility allows tendons of larger area to be defined. Modulus of elasticity for tendon [E p ]. Refer to EN 1992-1-1:2004 clause 3.3.6. The default value for the modulus of elasticity, E p is assumed to be 195GPa, representing strand. Values typically fall in the range of 185GPa to 210GPa. Concrete stress at transfer [Δσ c (t)]. This value is used for the calculation of elastic shortening losses, according to EN1992-1-1 clause 5.10.5.1(2), and, when long-term losses are requested, for the creep component of time-dependent losses, to clause 5.10.6(2). Creep losses are based on a single value of Δσ c (t) for each tendon (combined with Δσ cg below as appropriate), and the elastic shortening losses are based on a single Δσ c (t) value for each member (calculated from the values given for all the applicable tendons). The value entered for Δσ c (t) here should be the stress in the concrete adjacent to the tendon in question, immediately after tensioning and anchoring, due to total prestressing forces and self weight, averaged along the length of the tendon. Variations in stress arising from permanent actions applied after prestressing (generally, but not exclusively, leading to elastic shortening gains) are not incorporated into the calculation of initial elastic shortening loss.

topics.title: Instantaneous losses
toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining EN 1992-1-1:2004 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining EN 1992-1-1:2004 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Instantaneous losses Modulus of elasticity for concrete at transfer [E cm (t)]. This value is used for the calculation of elastic shortening losses, according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.5.1(2). E cm (t) is defined as “the secant modulus of elasticity of concrete at time t”. From clause 5.10.3, time t=t 0 (immediately after tensioning and anchoring) should be used for this calculation. Thus E cm from Table 3.1 may need to be adjusted according to clause 3.1.3(3). A likely range of values would be 26-39MPa. Unintentional angular displacement [k]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction, according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.5.2, for the component sometimes referred to as “wobble” loss and also in determining anchorage losses. k describes the “unintentional angular displacement” for internal tendons in radians per unit length. Clause 5.10.5.2(3) gives the range 0.005 < k <0.01 rad/m. Duct friction coefficient [μ]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.5.2(1), and also in determining anchorage losses. Suitable values may be found in Table 5.1; the default value μ = 0.19 is for internal tendons made up of strand filling roughly half of the duct.

topics.title: Long term losses
toc_path: With approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
Defining EN 1992-1-1:2004 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
headings: Defining EN 1992-1-1:2004 Eurocode 2 Tendon Properties with approximate losses, requiring input of estimated stresses
topics.text: Long term losses Tensile strength of prestressing steel [f pk ] This value is used for the calculation of Δ σpr , the absolute value of relaxation losses to EN1992-1-1 clause 3.3.2(7) and incorporated into the time dependent loss calculation of clause 5.10.6(2). Relaxation Class This is used along with f pk to calculate relaxation losses. Classes 1, 2 and 3 are defined in EN1992-1-1 clause 3.3.2(4). Relaxation loss at 1000 hours [ρ 1000 ]. This is used, along with f pk and the Relaxation Class, to calculate relaxation losses. Typical values may be found in clause 3.3.2(6) and the default value is based on low relaxation strand (Class 2). Time after tensioning (for relaxation calcs) [t]. This is used, along with f pk , Relaxation Class and ρ 1000 to calculate relaxation losses. According to EN1992-1-1 clause 3.3.2(8), long term (final) values of the relaxation losses may be estimated for a time (t) equal to 500 000 hours (i.e. around 57 years). Shrinkage strain [ε cs ]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to shrinkage, according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.6(2). The value should be calculated from clause 3.1.4(6), depending on notional size, relative humidity, concrete strength and cement class, and should be specified “ per mil” (‰) in accordance with the code (rather than actual strain). Creep coefficient [φ(t,t0)]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to creep, according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.6(2). The value should be calculated from clause 3.1.4(2), dependent upon the same parameters as the shrinkage strain plus the maturity of the concrete when the load is first applied. Values may be taken from Figure 3.1. Secant modulus of elasticity for concrete [E cm ]. This value is used for the calculation of time-dependent losses according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.6(2). The clause refers explicitly to obtaining E cm from Table 3.1. A likely range of values would be 27-44MPa. Change in stress due to loads after transfer [Δσ cg ]. This is used to adjust 'Concrete stress at transfer' according to the permanent loads applied after transfer, to give the concrete stress appropriate for the calculation of the creep component of time-dependent losses, according to EN1992-1-1 clause 5.10.6(2), that is, σ c,QP = Δσ c (t) + Δσ cg . Note that Δσ cg is typically negative since applied loads oppose the prestress that dominates Δσ c (t). Area of concrete section [Ac], Second moment of area – concrete [I c ].The area and second moment of area of the concrete member to which the prestress forces will be applied. These values are used for the calculation of time-dependent losses, according to EN1992-1-1:2004 clause 5.10.6(2). Where the concrete section varies, suitable intermediate values may be required. If the member is a standalone beam element the area of the beam should be used. If the beam member represents part of a larger structure (for example a certain width of slab) then only the area of the portion represented by this particular beam member should be used. Please note that the prestress loading facility is designed to work for a single beam member, not for a subdivided portion of slab or wide beam element, so using it in any other way is at an engineer’s judgement.

topics.text: Defaults The Defaults button sets all previously entered values to those specified when the dialog was first displayed. Such values are illustrative only and values for use in design calculations should be checked using appropriate source data. Notes. Input units are the same as the current model units unless otherwise stated on the dialog. When the prestress loads are calculated the prestress forces are converted into the current model units. The current model units can be found on the status bar of LUSAS Modeller. An approximate check is carried out that the specified jacking force is suitable for the tensile strength of commonly available strand, but the user should refer to EN1992-1-1 clause 5.10.3(2), manufacturer’s information for the strand strengths and the appropriate National Annex for values of k7 and k8 in order to ensure that the tendons are not overstressed. See also: Defining a Tendon Profile Defining a Tendon Profile Defining Tendon Loading Defining Tendon Loading Prestress Loading Prestress Loading

topics.text: Notes on post-installation losses calculated to EN1992-1-1 section 5.10 Elastic losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of clause 5.10.5.1, using the secant modulus of elasticity for concrete amended for age, cement and aggregate type as per clause 3.1.3. The simplified formula of expression 5.44 is not used; instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used. Time dependent losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of 5.10.6. The simplified method of exp 5.46 is not used directly; instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used. When the Eurocode 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be combined with the use of the EN1992-1-1 Concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material EN1992-1-1 Concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material in order to obtain the corresponding deformations at each time step in the analysis. The program will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , EN1992-1-1 "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter approach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. topics.text: Tendon details Tendon area [A p ]. The cross-sectional area of the tendon (or total area of a group of strands if a group is being represented by a single load assignment). In general, for internal prestressing, tendons of modest size are advisable to avoid difficulties in housing and anchoring larger tendons with the attendant increase in thickness of members and in the weight of reinforcement. 19 No 15mm strands (A p =2850mm²) or 27 No 13mm strands (A p =2700mm²) might be a practical upper limit per tendon. The prestress loading facility allows tendons of larger area to be defined. Modulus of elasticity for tendon [E p ]. Refer to the commentary to clause 5.3.5.2. The default value for the modulus of elasticity, E p is assumed to be 195GPa, representing strand. The value entered is used to determine change in tendon stress corresponding to change in strain - for instance, due to creep, shrinkage or elastic shortening in the concrete.

topics.text: Installation losses Unintentional angular displacement [k]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction, according to clause 5.4.5.3 eq 5.4-6, for the component sometimes referred to as “wobble” loss and also in determining anchorage losses. k describes the “unintentional angular displacement” for internal tendons in radians per unit length. The commentary to clause 5.4.5.3, part (a), gives the range 0.005 < k <0.01 rad/m for the case of bonded internal tendons made from prestressing steel. Duct friction coefficient [μ]. This value is used in the calculation of losses due to friction according to clause 5.4.5.3 eq 5.4-6, and also in determining anchorage losses. Suitable values may be found in the commentary to clause 5.4.5.3; the default value μ = 0.19 is for internal tendons made up of strand filling roughly half of the duct.

topics.text: Post-installation losses Include When set to 'Yes', prestress calculations include losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses, i.e. elastic shortening, creep, shrinkage and relaxation. When set to 'No', only installation losses are calculated, i.e. friction and anchorage. Tensile strength of prestressing steel [f ptk ] This value is not used for loss calculations but is used to provide an improbable data check on prestressing forces specified in any tendon loading attribute in which this tendon property is utilised. See clause 5.4.4.2. Relaxation loss at 100 hours [ρ 100 ]. This is used, along with [ρ1000] to calculate relaxation losses to clause 5.4.6.1.2, using the commentary eqn 5.4-10. The default value is 1.6%, corresponding to a low relaxation strand, when used together with [ρ 1000 ] = 2.5% as described below (the two values together will result in k=0.19 in eqn 5.4-10, corresponding to Class 2 in CEB-FIP Model Code 1990 commentary to clause 2.3.4.5). Relaxation loss at 1000 hours [ρ 1000 ]. This is used along with [ρ 100 ] to calculate relaxation losses using the equation referenced above. The default value is 2.5%, corresponding to the maximum specified isothermal relaxation for very low relaxation strand stressed to 70% Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS) according to clause 5.3.6.1, Table 5.3-2.

topics.text: Notes on post-installation losses calculated to fib Model Code 2010 Elastic losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of clause 5.4.5.3, using the reduced modulus of elasticity for concrete (accounting for initial plastic strain) from expression eq.s 5.1-23 and 24, based on strength class (clause 5.1.7.2), aggregate type (commentary table 5.1-6), amended for age (clause 5.1.9.3) and cement type (clause 5.1.9.1). A comprehensive summation using concrete stresses derived from an initial solution of the model is used. Creep and shrinkage losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of 5.1.9.4.3 (a), (b) and 5.1.9.4.4. The effects of temperature during curing may be taken into account by utilising a modified age at loading in the age age attribute. A comprehensive summation using concrete stresses derived from an initial solution of the model and allowing calculation of creep and shrinkage losses at any stage in the analysis is adopted. When the fib Model Code 2010 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be combined with the use of the fib Model Code 2010 concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material fib Model Code 2010 concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material in order to obtain the corresponding deformations at each time step in the analysis. LUSAS will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , fib Model Code 2010 "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter approach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. See also: Defining a Tendon Profile Defining a Tendon Profile Defining Tendon Loading Defining Tendon Loading Prestress Loading Prestress Loading

Relaxation class options are 'Low Relaxation' (to IS 14268), 'Normal' (to IS 1785 part 1, IS 6003 or IS 6006) and 'Other'. Relaxation loss at 100 hours [ρ 100 ]. Only available if Relaxation Class 'Other' is selected. This is used in Eq. A2-38, along with [ρ 1000 ] and the Relaxation Class, to calculate relaxation losses (to IS 14268). The default value of 1.8% is based on low relaxation. Relaxation loss at 1000 hours [ρ 1000 ]. This is used, along with the Relaxation Class, and optionally with [ρ 100 ] to calculate relaxation losses using Eq A2-38. The default value of 2.5% is based on low relaxation.

topics.text: Notes on post-installation losses calculated to IRC:112-2011 section 7.9.3 Elastic losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of 7.9.3.2(1), using the secant modulus of elasticity for concrete amended for age, cement and aggregate type. A comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used. Time dependent losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of Eq 6.8 , clauses 6.4.2.5 to 6.4.2.7 and Annexure A-2 and first principles, with a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution. When the 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be used with the IRC:112-2011 Concrete (Nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material IRC:112-2011 Concrete (Nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material .The program will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , IRC:112-2011 "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter pproach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. topics.text: Tendon details Tendon area [A p ]. The cross-sectional area of the tendon (or total area of a group of strands if a group is being represented by a single load assignment). In general, for internal prestressing, tendons of modest size are advisable to avoid difficulties in housing and anchoring larger tendons with the attendant increase in thickness of members and in the weight of reinforcement. 19 No 15mm strands (A p =2850mm²) or 27 No 13mm strands (A p =2700mm²) might be a practical upper limit per tendon. The prestress loading facility allows tendons of larger area to be defined. Modulus of elasticity for tendon [E p ]. Refer to Table 3.2.4. The default value for the modulus of elasticity, E p is assumed to be 195GPa, representing strand.

topics.text: Notes on post-installation losses calculated to JTG 3362-2018 Elastic losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of clause clause 6.2.5, using the elastic modulus for concrete from Table 3.1.5. A comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used as per eqn 6.2.5-1 Time dependent losses are evaluated in accordance with the principles of clauses 6.2.6, 6.2.7 and Appendix C. The simplified method of exp 6.2.7 is not used directly; instead a comprehensive summation using concrete stresses from an initial solution is used. When the JTG 3362-2018 'Losses based on time inputs and calculated stresses' option is used, it can be combined with the use of the JTG 3362-2018 Concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material JTG 3362-2018 Concrete (nonlinear) creep and shrinkage material in order to obtain the corresponding deformations at each time step in the analysis. The program will obtain input data from the material attributes assigned to each relevant concrete segment for use in the loss calculation. Alternatively, from the Material library Material library , JTG 3362-2018 "Advanced Define" material may be used. This latter approach will lead to suitable loss calculations but no creep or shrinkage deformations will be available from the analysis results. topics.title: Time integration scheme for structure response
toc_path: Time integration scheme for structure response
headings: Time integration scheme for structure response
topics.text: Time integration scheme for structure response The implicit time integration scheme used by IMDPlus to calculate the dynamic response of the structure. Hilber Hughes Taylor (HHT) This is the default time integration scheme and is the same as the method used for an implicit transient dynamic analysis in LUSAS. HHT Factor a The integration constant a used in the HHT integration scheme. For an unconditionally stable, second order accurate scheme a must lie between the limits -1/3 ≤ a ≤ 0.0. Values of a outside this range cannot be specified. The default value of a is 0.0, which reduces the method to the Newmark method. Duhamel’s Integral This is the time integration method used by IMDPlus in LUSAS 14.7 (and earlier versions of LUSAS) and is available as an alternative to the HHT integration scheme.

topics.title: Default Damping and Overdamped Mode Control
toc_path: Default Damping and Overdamped Mode Control
headings: Default Damping and Overdamped Mode Control
topics.text: Default Damping and Overdamped Mode Control This dialog provides control over the amount of default damping used in the IMDPlus analysis as follows: If the Default damping option is selected in the main analysis control dialog, all of the modes of vibration included in the analysis are forced to have the Default damping value set in this dialog. The Default damping value is initialised to 5% of critical when the main analysis control dialog is launched for the first time. If an alternative damping value is required then this can be set to any value less than critical (100%), including having no damping in the solution (0%). The Default damping option can only be turned off in the main analysis control dialog when viscous damping has been included in the eigenvalue analysis. If the Default damping option is deselected the viscous damping present in the eigenvalue analysis is used in the IMDPlus analysis and the Default damping value set in this dialog is ignored. The dialog also controls the inclusion of overdamped modes in the IMDPlus solution when viscous damping is included in the eigenvalue solution. In this case additional options for the inclusion of overdamped modes of vibration in the IMDPlus analysis may also become available in this dialog as follows: Ignore overdamped modes Modes of vibration with a damping ratio of 100% or more are omitted from the IMDPlus solution. This option is available when viscous damping is included in the eigenvalue solution irrespective of whether Default damping is selected in the main analysis control dialog. Limit overdamped modes to critically damped Modes of vibration with a damping ratio of 100% or more are limited to 99.9999% to allow them to be included in the analysis. This option is only available when viscous damping is included in the eigenvalue solution and the Default damping option is not selected in the main analysis control dialog. See also: IMDPlus Analysis IMDPlus Analysis

topics.title: Modal Combination History Options
topics.text: Modal Combination History Options The modal combination options allow control of the minimum mass participation factors to be included in the modal combinations generated by IMDPlus. By default the minimum mass participations included in the modal combinations is zero to include all modes of vibration. If this value is changed, the size of the combinations can be reduced for analyses where there are a large number of modes of vibration. Limits are between zero and 100% but if the value is close to 100%, all modal combinations are likely to include no modes of vibration for the calculation. Setting a value other than zero should only occur if you are sure that the value chosen still allows adequate representation of the response of the structure over the whole duration of the dynamic analysis. In addition, for structures where equal and opposite mass is moving in the modes of vibration, these can have low mass participation factors and therefore values other than zero should be avoided.

topics.title: IMDPlus Modal Force Calculator
topics.text: IMDPlus Modal Force Calculator The modal force calculator computes the equivalent modal forces associated with all of the load configuration positions set up by the moving load generator. These modal forces are output in the format required for IMDPlus.

topics.title: Procedure
topics.text: Procedure Select the first results file containing the eigenvalue results. If multiple eigenvalue results files are being used then this will be indicated in the total number of eigenvalue files reported. The first static / datacheck results file containing the moving load solutions is reported along with the number of load cases in each static file. The direction of the path can be set using the Forward or Backward radio buttons. Click the OK button to perform the calculations. Notes In a moving mass analysis a discrete unit load must always be used in the moving load generator to ensure that equivalent unit modal forces are computed by the modal force calculator. This enables the correct loading to be applied to the structure during an IMDPlus moving mass analysis, where unit modal forces are used in conjunction with the dynamic vertical loading from the spring-mass systems of the vehicle to obtain the total modal forces applied to the structure. Once the moving load generation and modal force calculation have been carried out in a moving load or moving mass analysis, these two steps may be omitted from subsequent analyses, even if the analysis type is switched from moving load to moving mass, or vice versa, but only if the moving load path, discrete load configuration and direction of the moving load do not change between analyses. If any of these are modified the moving load path generation and the calculation of the equivalent modal forces must be carried out again. See also: IMDPlus Analysis IMDPlus Analysis

topics.title: Included Modes Control
topics.text: Included Modes Control This dialog provides control over the modes of vibration to include in the IMDPlus analysis. If All modes is selected, all the modes of vibration of the structure will be included in the analysis. If All modes is not selected, a selection should be defined from the list and only those modes included in the selection will be included in the analysis. The total directional mass participation factors for the modes of vibration being included in the analysis is dynamically updated. The dialog also calculates the total participating mass for the included modes. For most analyses, up to 90% total participating mass should be used in the IMDPlus solution unless the mass can be guaranteed to exist in a mode of vibration which cannot be excited by the input excitation. You must ensure that this is the case otherwise the dynamic solutions may suffer from degraded solution accuracy. See also: IMDPlus Analysis IMDPlus Analysis

topics.title: Options for Loads Outside Search Area
toc_path: Options for Loads Outside Search Area
headings: Options for Loads Outside Search Area
topics.text: Options for Loads Outside Search Area For patch loads the load outside the search area can be moved into the search area along the paths defined by the local x and y axes of the loading patch. The patch load is transferred into the path along the projected directions and added to the first loading positions found inside the patch in the projected direction. Options are: Exclude All Load (default) Include Local X Projected Load Include Local Y Projected Load Include Local X and Y Projected Loads Include Non - Projected Load Include Full Local X Load Include Full Local Y Load Include Full Load The load cannot be moved if the entire patch load lies outside the search area. Loads inside the search area are not moved. See Processing Loads Outside the Search Area Processing Loads Outside the Search Area for explanations of each option. For point loads the load outside the search area can be moved into the nearest valid projection on any edge in the search area. If no such valid projection exists then the load is moved to the nearest node in the search area. Options are: Exclude All Load (default) Include Full Load The load can be moved even if all the point loads lie outside the search area. Loads inside the search area are not moved.

topics.title: Load Factor
topics.text: Load Factor Load factor specifies the factor by which the discrete loading is multiplied before the equivalent nodal loads are calculated. Notes In a moving mass analysis the load factor should always be set to 1.0 as the moving load generator needs to define the passage of a discrete unit load across the structure. Any factor other than 1.0 can cause the incorrect static and dynamic loads to be calculated during a moving mass analysis. See also: IMDPlus Analysis IMDPlus Analysis

topics.title: IMDPlus Moving Load Analysis +
topics.text: IMDPlus Moving Load Analysis + The IMDPlus moving load analysis option allows you to analyse the time domain response of a 2D or 3D structure to the passage of a moving vehicle or train, where the magnitude and configuration of the loading remains constant throughout the analysis. An IMDPlus moving load analysis can only be performed if the following steps have already been undertaken: The equivalent modal forces have been successfully calculated using the moving load generator and the modal force calculator If a composite axle definition is being used at least one moving load vehicle configuration has been defined in the model. The input consists of the loading information, solution control and output control.

The input consists of the loading information, solution control and output control.

topics.title: Moving Load Input
topics.text: Moving Load Input If a composite axle definition is being used in the analysis a vehicle configuration can be included by selecting the checkbox marked Vehicle configuration (Composite axle). This will enable the drop-down list that will contain all of the moving load vehicle configurations in the model. The required vehicle configuration can be selected for use in the IMDPlus analysis. Notes In an IMDPlus moving load analysis either a complete definition or a composite axle definition can be used to define the loading configuration. In cases where the lateral configuration of the discrete load components remain constant in terms of both their offsets and relative magnitudes, the composite axle definition method can be used to define the complete loading from a single unit axle. This method is generally only applicable to certain vehicles such as trains. To use this method, the moving load utilised in the definition of the path should have an overall load equal to unity. If this is the case, the load configuration can be defined using a vehicle configuration that contains the positions of the axles (relative to the initial position of the origin / front of the vehicle) and the total weights of the axles. Using vehicle configurations (composite axle method) enables multiple load configurations to be analysed without the need to recalculate the modal forces via the moving load generator and modal force calculator, thereby speeding up the analysis process significantly. This method is particularly useful for the solution of bridges where multiple train / vehicle configurations need to be analysed.

topics.title: Mode / Damping Control
topics.text: Mode / Damping Control Allows control over the modes of vibration included in the analysis and the damping of the structure. The Included modes Modify button allows you to use all of the modes of vibration or a selection of modes in the analysis. Ideally, total mass participation up to 90% should be used unless it is guaranteed that the modes of vibration associated with any missing mass are at frequencies that cannot be excited. Omission of modes of vibration with significant mass contributions that can be excited during the analysis will lead to unreliable solutions. You will be warned if a significant proportion of participating mass is missing based on the selected modes of vibration. The Default damping option allows you to control the amount of damping used in the IMDPlus analysis. If Default damping is selected, all of the modes of vibration included in the analysis are forced to have the current default value. The default damping value is set via the Modify button. The Default damping option can only be turned off when viscous damping has been included in the eigenvalue analysis. If Default damping is deselected the viscous damping present in the eigenvalue analysis is used in the IMDPlus analysis. When viscous damping is included in the eigenvalue solution additional options for the inclusion of overdamped modes of vibration in the IMDPlus analysis also become available.

topics.title: Solution Control
topics.text: Solution Control Advanced moving load solution options can be set via the Modify button. Define the range of speeds to analyse for the passage of the moving load along with quiet time and time step controls. Enter the minimum speed Enter the maximum speed. If the maximum speed is identical to the minimum speed then a single speed will be analysed. Enter the speed increment. If the speed increment is zero then a single speed equivalent to the minimum speed will be analysed. Enter the quiet time after the passage of the load in time units. If zero is entered, the IMDPlus analysis will finish immediately after the load has reached the end of the path. If a quiet time greater than zero is entered, this time will be added to the solution to allow the decay of the structural response to be analysed and visualised. Select whether IMDPlus should calculate the time step for the analysis based on the Nyquist time step (Maximum time step required to capture the response of the highest frequency of vibration included in the analysis) or choose to specify the time step yourself. When manually defining the time step, care should be taken to ensure that it is sufficient to capture the response of the structure. See also: IMDPlus Analysis IMDPlus Analysis

topics.title: IMDPlus Moving Load Generation
topics.text: IMDPlus Moving Load Generation The IMDPlus moving load generator is used to mimic the path of a load across a structure by automatically setting up a number of static loadcases at prescribed locations along a single line/arc/spline, or a collection of lines/arcs/splines, which define a single continuous path. These loadcases are subsequently used to calculate the modal forces equivalent to the applied loading for import into IMDPlus. Before entering the moving load generator, ensure that a discrete load group representing the load configuration to be moved across the structure has been defined in the Attributes Treeview and at least one line/arc/spline representing the vehicle path across the structure has been defined and selected. The line representing the vehicle path should not be one of the lines forming the model. In an IMDPlus moving mass analysis IMDPlus moving mass analysis a discrete unit load must always be used in the moving load generator to ensure that the correct loads are applied to the structure during the IMDPlus analysis. The discrete unit load is used to calculate the unit modal forces that are applied to the structure as the discrete unit load moves along the moving load path. These unit modal forces are used in IMDPlus in conjunction with the vertical loading from the spring-mass systems of the vehicle configuration to calculate the total modal forces applied to the structure. The following entries should be made in the moving load generation dialog: Moving load dataset Specify the moving load dataset ID for the configuration to be moved across the structure. Search area ID If the structure has multiple depths, ensure that a search area has been defined and assigned to ensure that the loading is applied to the required location. If no search area has been defined, all surfaces in the model will be used for projection of the load configuration onto the model. Projection of loading Loading can be projected onto a line (for 2D line and frame models) or projected over an area (for grillages, slabs and 3D space frames). If required, select the Advanced button to adjust the load factor and/or the treatment of load outside the search area. In a moving mass analysis the load factor should always be set to 1.0 as the moving load generator needs to define the passage of a discrete unit load across the structure. Any factor other than 1.0 can cause the incorrect static and dynamic loads to be calculated during a moving mass analysis. Incremental distance Define the incremental distance for the movement of the load across the structure. Direction Select whether the load moves in the forward or backward sense. For a single line, the forward direction is defined by the local direction of the line. For a selection of lines, the forward direction is defined by the selection order. The coordinates of the interpreted start and finish locations for the path are displayed on the form. Number of loadcases per analysis Select the number of loadcases per analysis for the subdivision of the Solver solution for the path. Typically this should be between 100 and 1000. Datacheck This option should be set active to speed up the solution process, if only the dynamic effects of the load configuration are required. This is the default. topics.search_text: IMDPlus Moving Load Generation IMDPlus Moving Load Generation IMDPlus Moving Load Generation dlgimdplus IDH IMDPLUS MOVING LOAD GENERATION.htm IMDPlus Moving Load Generation The IMDPlus moving load generator is used to mimic the path of a load across a structure by automatically setting up a number of static loadcases at prescribed locations along a single line/arc/spline, or a collection of lines/arcs/splines, which define a single continuous path. These loadcases are subsequently used to calculate the modal forces equivalent to the applied loading for import into IMDPlus. Before entering the moving load generator, ensure that a discrete load group representing the load configuration to be moved across the structure has been defined in the Attributes Treeview and at least one line/arc/spline representing the vehicle path across the structure has been defined and selected. The line representing the vehicle path should not be one of the lines forming the model. In an IMDPlus moving mass analysis IMDPlus moving mass analysis a discrete unit load must always be used in the moving load generator to ensure that the correct loads are applied to the structure during the IMDPlus analysis. The discrete unit load is used to calculate the unit modal forces that are applied to the structure as the discrete unit load moves along the moving load path. These unit modal forces are used in IMDPlus in conjunction with the vertical loading from the spring-mass systems of the vehicle configuration to calculate the total modal forces applied to the structure. The following entries should be made in the moving load generation dialog: Moving load dataset Specify the moving load dataset ID for the configuration to be moved across the structure. Search area ID If the structure has multiple depths, ensure that a search area has been defined and assigned to ensure that the loading is applied to the required location. If no search area has been defined, all surfaces in the model will be used for projection of the load configuration onto the model. Projection of loading Loading can be projected onto a line (for 2D line and frame models) or projected over an area (for grillages, slabs and 3D space frames). If required, select the Advanced button to adjust the load factor and/or the treatment of load outside the search area. In a moving mass analysis the load factor should always be set to 1.0 as the moving load generator needs to define the passage of a discrete unit load across the structure. Any factor other than 1.0 can cause the incorrect static and dynamic loads to be calculated during a moving mass analysis. Incremental distance Define the incremental distance for the movement of the load across the structure. Direction Select whether the load moves in the forward or backward sense. For a single line, the forward direction is defined by the local direction of the line. For a selection of lines, the forward direction is defined by the selection order. The coordinates of the interpreted start and finish locations for the path are displayed on the form. Number of loadcases per analysis Select the number of loadcases per analysis for the subdivision of the Solver solution for the path. Typically this should be between 100 and 1000. Datacheck This option should be set active to speed up the solution process, if only the dynamic effects of the load configuration are required. This is the default. Run analyses This option should also be set active if IMDPlus is being run interactively via Modeller. This is the default. topics.text: Time integration scheme for structure response The implicit time integration scheme used by IMDPlus to calculate the dynamic response of the structure. topics.title: IMDPlus Moving Load Vehicle Configuration
topics.text: IMDPlus Moving Load Vehicle Configuration Moving load vehicle configuration is used to create or modify vehicle configuration attributes for use in an IMDPlus moving load IMDPlus moving load analysis. A moving load vehicle configuration defines the position (relative to the origin / front of the vehicle) of the axles that form the vehicle along with the value of the moving load factor to be applied at each position. In a moving load analysis, a vehicle configuration is required if the composite axle definition method is being used in IMDPlus. In the composite axle definition method a discrete unit load should be used in the Moving Load Generation dialog to represent a subset of the overall load configuration. The equivalent modal forces obtained from the Modal Force Calculator dialog are factored by the loads in the vehicle configuration to build up the total load configuration in IMDPlus. Vehicle configurations enable multiple load configurations to be analysed without the need to recalculate the modal forces via the moving load generator and modal force calculator, thereby speeding up the analysis process significantly. This method is particularly useful for the solution of bridges where multiple train / vehicle configurations need to be analysed. A meaningful name should be entered into the Name field. Notes Care should be taken with the definition of the axle positions. The path length should be sufficiently longer than the structure to ensure that the load configuration correctly arrives onto and departs from the structure. The front of the moving load vehicle is always the position with the maximum co-ordinate. The rear of the vehicle is always the position with the minimum co-ordinate. The positions and loads that define the vehicle configuration can be copied and pasted from a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. This method is demonstrated in a worked example. See the worked example 'Train Induced Vibration of a Bridge'. Once created vehicle configurations will appear in the Utilities Treeview, from where they can be modified or deleted from the model. To modify a vehicle configuration either double-click or right-click on the Attribute name in the Utilities Treeview and select the Edit Attribute... menu item. Vehicle configurations can be easily transferred from one model to another using an attribute library file, accessed from the menu File> Import/Export model data... See also: IMDPlus Moving Load Analysis IMDPlus Moving Load Analysis IMDPlus Analysis IMDPlus Analysis
