LUSAS Solver - a powerful finite element analysis engine that carries out the analysis of the problem defined in LUSAS Modeller.

topics.title: LUSAS Application Products
topics.text: LUSAS Application Products LUSAS is made available as different application products with the user interface tailored specially to the needs of a particular application. `For example bridge engineers will see facilities provided specifically for the analysis of bridge structures. Such facilities are normally conveniently grouped together inside a product application menu, such as Bridge, Civil, LNG etc, that is loaded between the Utilities and Window menu items in the main menu. The application products include: LUSAS Bridge - for bridge engineering analysis, design and assessment. LUSAS Civil & Structural - for civil, structural, nuclear, seismic, geotechnical and offshore engineering. LUSAS LNG - for Liquid Natural Gas tank modelling, analysis and design. LUSAS Analyst - for automotive, aerospace, defence, manufacturing, and general engineering analysis. LUSAS Composite - for engineers designing composite products or components. LUSAS Academic - available to academic establishments for teaching and research use and allows use of all of the above products together with most of the options available for those products.
topics.search_text: LUSAS Application Products introduction Getting Started Guide Getting Started Guide LUSAS Application Products Getting Started introduction.htm LUSAS Application Products LUSAS is made available as different application products with the user interface tailored specially to the needs of a particular application. `For example bridge engineers will see facilities provided specifically for the analysis of bridge structures. Such facilities are normally conveniently grouped together inside a product application menu, such as Bridge, Civil, LNG etc, that is loaded between the Utilities and Window menu items in the main menu. The application products include: LUSAS Bridge - for bridge engineering analysis, design and assessment. LUSAS Civil & Structural - for civil, structural, nuclear, seismic, geotechnical and offshore engineering. LUSAS LNG - for Liquid Natural Gas tank modelling, analysis and design. LUSAS Analyst - for automotive, aerospace, defence, manufacturing, and general engineering analysis. LUSAS Composite - for engineers designing composite products or components. LUSAS Academic - available to academic establishments for teaching and research use and allows use of all of the above products together with most of the options available for those products.

topics.title: Analysis options
topics.text: Analysis options The following analysis related software options are available for all products: Fast Solvers - This option includes additional solvers. The Fast Multifrontal Direct Solver can provide solutions several times faster than the standard Frontal Direct Solver for certain analysis problems. The Fast Multifrontal Block Lanczos Eigensolver can, similarly, return results several times faster than the standard Frontal Eigensolvers for certain problems. The complex eigensolver provides efficient solutions for large-scale damped natural frequency problems. Nonlinear - The Nonlinear option provides the very latest powerful techniques for solving problems having either material, geometric or boundary nonlinearity. Dynamics - Straightforward modal dynamics problems can be solved using Interactive Modal dynamics (IMD) techniques provided in all LUSAS products. The Dynamics Option contains the facilities required to solve a wider range of dynamic problems in both the time and frequency domains. By combining the Dynamics and Nonlinear options both high and low velocity nonlinear impact problems can be solved using either implicit or explicit solution techniques. Thermal/Field - The Thermal / Field option contains extensive facilities for both simple and advanced steady state, and transient thermal / field analyses. By combining the Thermal / Field option with other appropriate options, heat transfer due to conduction, convection and radiation can be analysed. In addition, the effects due to phase change of material may also be included. Heat of Hydration - Allows modelling the heat of hydration of concrete and hygro-thermal analysis.. The heat of concrete hydration can be computed during a thermo-mechanical coupled analysis and the temperatures and degree of hydration can be read into a structural analysis. Hygro-thermal analyses allow the determination of heat of hydration across a body of concrete, taking into account the availability of water for the exothermic reaction with time, based on the concrete mix, shape, exposed faces, insulated surfaces, environmental conditions etc. IMDPlus - The IMDPlus option extends the Interactive Modal Dynamics (IMD) techniques provided in all LUSAS products. Whilst IMD models a single loading event in a single direction, IMDPlus allows multiple loading events with more advanced loading conditions to be solved. IMDPlus is used for three primary uses: Seismic response analysis of structures subjected to acceleration time histories of support motion; moving load analysis of structures, such as bridges, subjected to moving vehicle or train loads, where the magnitude and configuration of the loading remains constant throughout the analysis; and moving mass analysis of structures, such as bridges, subjected to moving vehicle or train loads, where spring-mass systems are used at the axle/bogie positions of a vehicle.

topics.title: Design options
topics.text: Design options The following design code related options are available for LUSAS Bridge only: Traffic Load Optimisation - The Traffic Load Optimisation facility complements and extends the vehicle loading capabilities of LUSAS Bridge and helps to simplify the evaluation of worst load position for various road and rail load configurations. Vehicle load optimisation is used to identify critical vehicle loading patterns on bridges and apply these loading patterns to analysis models. Rail load optimisation provides the means to define parameters for a particular design code, and generate the most critical rail track loading pattern for a selected track layout, for each influence shape under consideration. Both facilities reduce the amount of time spent generating models and leads to more efficient and economic design, assessment or load rating of bridge structures. Steel Composite Bridge Design - Design code checking of grillage, beam, mixed beam and shell or shell models to AASHTO LRFD 8th Edition. Results for each design check are tabulated and maximum utilisation factors obtained. Detailed calculations can be output and added to reports. Steel and Composite Deck Designer - Carries out comprehensive calculations for multiple sections on steel or steel/composite bridge decks to the Eurocodes. Rail Track Analysis - The Rail Track Analysis option permits track/bridge interaction analysis to the International Union of Railways Code UIC 774-3. It allows you to automatically build models from data defined in MS Excel spreadsheets, run an analysis, and quickly produce results in spreadsheet or results file formats. The following design code related options are available for LUSAS Bridge and LUSAS Civil & Structural only: RC Frame Design - Design checks due to bending with or without axial force can be carried out for regular or arbitrary shaped reinforced concrete sections at the Ultimate Limit State (ULS) and Serviceability limit states (SLS) for a specified RC design code. Detailed results can be output and added to reports. Steel Frame Design - Design code checking of steel members for a specified steel design code. Design check results are visualised as Utilisation ratios on a contour or values layer for a selected design code, and active load combination or design envelope. Results components for individual design checks can be chosen for viewing, and maximum utilisation factors can also be obtained. Detailed calculations can be output and added to reports.

topics.title: Avoiding and Identifying Problems
topics.text: Avoiding and Identifying Problems A team of engineers in LUSAS Technical Support is available to all clients who have a current support and maintenance contract, to provide modelling advice and assistance with any problems that may be encountered. However, to identify the cause of a problem may take time, especially if the analysis is large. Therefore preventative measures should always be taken in an effort to avoid problems in the first place. Your analysis model should be thoroughly checked against intended data input to verify that all geometry, attributes and assignments have actually been input correctly. Read and follow the advice in the Pre-Analysis Checks and Post-Analysis Checks sections of the Running an Analysis Chapter of the Modeller Reference Manual. It is always good practice to systematically carry out these checks as a matter of course whether or not problems are encountered. Contact your local LUSAS office or LUSAS distributor, preferably by email including the relevant information suggested above. Details for local offices and distributors can be found at http://www.lusas.com/distributors http://www.lusas.com/distributors

topics.title: Contacting the Help Desk
topics.text: Contacting the Help Desk With the aim of producing a more efficient service, some general guidance is given as to what information should be prepared before calling the Help Desk. Please note that if LUSAS was supplied to you by a LUSAS distributor then they should be your first point of contact for support. Your local distributor will have access to the main LUSAS Technical Support Centre for assistance if required. This information will help the LUSAS support engineers understand your problem more quickly: The exact text of any warning or error message(s). Preferably copied and pasted or in the form of a screen dump. Machine specification - operating system, physical memory, virtual memory and available disk space. A copy of the model or data file causing problems. A list of the last commands used in LUSAS Modeller or a copy of the session file. The contents of the last LUSAS Modeller error log, LUSASM_x.ERR Full details of the LUSAS Modeller/LUSAS Solver version numbers in use, the LUSAS Solver version number is written to the header section of the output file and the LUSAS Modeller version number is obtained from the Help> About LUSAS Modeller menu item. For complex or difficult to describe problems, email or fax a simple diagrammatic representation before calling to aid any discussion. If telephoning the Help Desk try to be logged onto the computer when calling or be close enough to the computer to try any suggestions provided by the support engineer. A support tool is available to help ensure that if a support query is raised all relevant model files can be submitted to LUSAS Technical Support to aid with the resolution of the query. It is accessed using the Help > Support Tool menu item.

topics.title: The LUSAS Modeller User Interface
topics.text: The LUSAS Modeller User Interface The image below shows the principal user interface components of LUSAS Modeller.
topics.search_text: The LUSAS Modeller User Interface User Interface Getting Started Guide The LUSAS Modeller User Interface Getting Started User Interface.htm The LUSAS Modeller User Interface The image below shows the principal user interface components of LUSAS Modeller.

topics.title: View window
topics.text: View window A View Window shows the model according to user-defined settings made elsewhere on the user interface. Each view window is completely independent and may show the model from a different angle, using different visualization options, with or without results. The image in a view window is built up from several drawing layers as listed in the Layers Treeview (see Main Panels below). Each draws over the top of the one before it. A Datatip provides model-related information about whatever is under the cursor. A Tool tip reports on uses of toolbar buttons or expected input for grid cells in dialogs etc.

A Datatip provides model-related information about whatever is under the cursor. A Tool tip reports on uses of toolbar buttons or expected input for grid cells in dialogs etc.

topics.title: Main panels
topics.text: Main panels Each of the main panels has its own Treeview showing a list of objects of a particular type. There are panels of Layers, Groups, Attributes, Analyses, Utilities and Reports. Each object in a Treeview has its own functionality. This can be invoked using a context menu, the main menu or the toolbar buttons. In summary: The Layers Treeview controls the display of model data and results data to a view window. Each drawing layer is responsible for drawing one particluar aspect of this data such as geometry, mesh, and attributes layers for instance. The Groups Treeview is used to store selected user-defined collections of objects (geometry, nodes or elements) under a collective name. The Attributes Treeview is used to store named collections of data that may be attached (assigned) to the model geometry, such as the element type and discretisation on the geometry; section properties and thicknesses; the materials used; how the model is supported or restrained; and how the model is loaded. The Analyses Treeview shows all analyses that have been defined including loadcases, eigenvalues, results, and control chapters. Also in this treeview are post-procressing concepts such as combinations and envelopes. The Utilities Treeview contains utility items used in the definition of model geometry or attributes, or to control an analysis, or to provide a particular functionality, such as to define a load combination or produce a report for example. The Reports Treeview contains named reports, each of which is made up of multiple chapters. Chapters may be defined to view modelling information, results, screenshots and similar.

topics.title: Other main panels
topics.text: Other main panels Two other main panels provide details of properties and associativity for selected objects. The panels are hidden until accessed by a selecting a feature/object and choosing the relevant context menu item for that feature/object. They can also be made visible by selecting the View > Main Panels menu item. The panels can be docked, and separate tabs are provided for each panel when done. Double-clicking a docked window will isolate it again. The panels are: Properties - displays the current properties of selected geometry features (points, lines, surface, volumes) and selected mesh objects (nodes, edges, elements, faces). Hierarchy - shows the merge status, and lists the higher and lower order features/objects of a single selected geometry feature or mesh object. The type and feature number of the selected feature is shown.

topics.title: Context menus
topics.text: Context menus A Context menu (displayed by pressing the right - hand mouse button with an object selected) provides access to additional functionality such as editing of data, control of visibility, visualisation of assignments, and selective control of results plotting on selected attributes. Context menus are provided for objects selected in the View Window, and most items in the various Treeview panels.

topics.title: Selection Panels
topics.text: Selection Panels Selected Items This panel can be viewed using the View> Selection Panels > Selection menu item. Once visible it will contain a list of all currently selected items which may then be individually deselected. Selection Memory This panel can be viewed using the View> Selection Panels > Memory menu item. Once visible it will contain a list of all items currently in Selection Memory which may then be individually deselected. Cyclable Items This panel can be viewed using the View> Selection Panels > Cyclable Items menu item. Once visible it will contain a list of all cyclable items. Where multiple items could possibly be selected by the same mouse click, cycling is the process of stepping through those items one at a time. An item can then be individually selected or deselected. Visible items This panel can be viewed using the View> Selection Panels > Visible Items menu item. Once opened it contains details of all visible items selected in the view window.

topics.title: Text Output Window
topics.text: Text Output Window The Text Output Window provides continuous feedback during a modelling or analysis process, and includes errors, warnings and progress messages. When an error message or warning relating to a particular object is written to the text output window, extra information is sometimes available by double-clicking on that line of text.

topics.title: Status bar
topics.text: Status bar The Status Bar displays progress messages and help text during a modelling session, the model units, the current cursor position in model units (if the model is displayed in an orthogonal plane) and the item or number of items in the current selection. A view of the model can be obtained by pressing one of the primary axes shown in the status bar.

topics.title: General notes
topics.text: General notes Within each View window, and within each Treeview, there is a current selection and all commands are assumed to apply to it. In both the View window and for particular entries within the Treeview several objects can be selected at the same time. Main menu and toolbar commands apply to whichever window was most recently clicked, either a View window or a Treeview panel. Some items within a Treeview support drag and drop functionality. Typically this will move them, copy them or connect them together. For example, dragging an attribute from the Treeview onto a View window assigns the selected attribute to the selected object in that window. All the menus, toolbars, tree frame, text window, status bar and other similar windows can be resized, moved, made visible or invisible, and docked or separated from the main program window. LUSAS Modeller will remember their new location for the next time the program is run. Additional customization is possible - see the Modeller Reference Manual for details. topics.title: Using LUSAS - An overview
topics.text: Using LUSAS - An overview Carrying out an analysis with LUSAS will involve three main stages: Modelling Running the analysis Viewing the results Modelling is sometimes referred to as ‘pre-processing’ and viewing and manipulating the the results is sometimes referred to as ‘post-processing’. Further details of these stages are provided below.

Further details of these stages are provided below.

topics.title: Model Types
topics.text: Model Types Two types of model can be created in LUSAS: Feature-based geometry models these are based on features (such as points, lines, surfaces and volumes) that are defined inside LUSAS, or are created from imported geometry and require the definition of mesh objects such as elements with their associated nodes. Mesh-only models - these comprise only mesh objects (elements and their associated nodes, edges and faces) and are created by importing only those types of LUSAS model data, or third party data that are supported. With very few exceptions the majority of LUSAS models are featured-based.

Mesh-only models - these comprise only mesh objects (elements and their associated nodes, edges and faces) and are created by importing only those types of LUSAS model data, or third party data that are supported. With very few exceptions the majority of LUSAS models are featured-based.

topics.title: Creating models
topics.text: Creating models When creating a new model number of settings will have to be initially made. These include a model filename, model units and an analysis type and category.
topics.search_text: Creating models Using LUSAS - An overview Getting Started Guide Using LUSAS - An overview Creating models Getting Started Using LUSAS.htm Creating models When creating a new model number of settings will have to be initially made. These include a model filename, model units and an analysis type and category.

topics.title: Choosing an Analysis Type
topics.text: Choosing an Analysis Type Choosing an Analysis type tailors the interface for the type of analysis to be carried out and also defines the class of model. When creating a new model it can be defined as being for a Structural, Thermal, Hygro-Thermal, Coupled Thermal/ Structural, or Coupled Hygro-thermal/Structural analysis dependent upon the licence key in use.

When creating a new model it can be defined as being for a Structural, Thermal, Hygro-Thermal, Coupled Thermal/ Structural, or Coupled Hygro-thermal/Structural analysis dependent upon the licence key in use.

topics.title: Choosing an Analysis Category
topics.text: Choosing an Analysis Category Choosing an Analysis category modifies the user interface to generally only show those options that are appropriate to the type of model being defined. Analysis category choices are: 2D Grillage/Plate, 2D Inplane, 2D Axisymmetric, and 3D. Selecting an analysis category as part of creating a new model defines which startup templates are available for selection. It also determines the initial vertical axis for a new model, and the orientation of element types and library items as displayed on the Geometric Line dialog prior to them being added to a model.

topics.title: Modelling
topics.text: Modelling Modelling involves creating a geometric representation of a structure and defining its characteristic behaviour in terms of its physical properties such as material, loading, and support.
topics.search_text: Modelling Using LUSAS - An overview Getting Started Guide Modelling Getting Started Using LUSAS.htm Modelling Modelling involves creating a geometric representation of a structure and defining its characteristic behaviour in terms of its physical properties such as material, loading, and support.

topics.title: Geometry
topics.text: Geometry Within LUSAS Modeller the geometry of the model is defined using points, lines, surfaces and volumes. A volume needs surfaces to enclose it and to define its boundary. Similarly a surface needs lines to form its perimeter and lines need points to define their ends. The shape of a surface between its boundary lines, and the shape of a line between its end points can be simple (straight lines, flat surfaces) or complex, depending on the manner in which it was created. Many different tools exist within LUSAS Modeller to aid the creation of geometry. In particular the geometry can be entered numerically, in terms of coordinates, by cursor (using the mouse) or by copying, splitting, intersecting and transforming previously existing parts of the model. Geometry can also be imported from third-party interface files.

A volume needs surfaces to enclose it and to define its boundary. Similarly a surface needs lines to form its perimeter and lines need points to define their ends. The shape of a surface between its boundary lines, and the shape of a line between its end points can be simple (straight lines, flat surfaces) or complex, depending on the manner in which it was created. Many different tools exist within LUSAS Modeller to aid the creation of geometry. In particular the geometry can be entered numerically, in terms of coordinates, by cursor (using the mouse) or by copying, splitting, intersecting and transforming previously existing parts of the model. Geometry can also be imported from third-party interface files.

topics.title: Meshing attributes
topics.text: Meshing attributes Whilst points, lines, surfaces and volumes allow the geometry of the problem to be represented or imported, to solve the problem, the geometric features must be broken down into discrete nodes and elements. This process is known as meshing and the collective term for all the elements and nodes, once created, is the mesh. Special attributes, called mesh attributes, are created and assigned to relevant geometry features to define the type and number of nodes and elements that will be used to represent each part of the geometry. A significant advantage of this approach is that the density of the mesh can easily be changed without rebuilding the geometry or reassigning any attributes. Simply modifying a mesh attribute automatically changes the mesh density in any part of the model where it is assigned. Similarly, the element type can be changed in exactly the same way. Different element types are suitable for different kinds of analysis, and the system provides an easy way to change from one to another. Generally LUSAS Modeller automatically and incrementally updates the mesh whenever a change is made to any part of the geometry or any mesh attributes. However these automatic updates are not allowed when results are being displayed, and they can also be switched off if at other times if required, for example to save time. This is known as locking the mesh. When the mesh is locked it will only be updated when specifically requested.

topics.title: Other attributes
topics.text: Other attributes Other attributes are used to define aspects of the behaviour of parts of the model, or the external factors which are imposed on it. Within LUSAS Modeller, there are several types of attribute such as materials, loading and supports. Within each attribute type there may be further sub-divisions, for example there are isotropic materials, anisotropic materials, and orthotropic materials, among others. In each case an attribute is first created, and then subsequently attached to all or selected parts of the model. This attachment process is known as assigning. Thus a material can be assigned to a line. Once assigned, the line takes on the properties of the material until further notice. Assignment often involves specification of additional information that does not define the attribute or the geometry, but rather defines how one is applied to the other. This includes directions, scale factors and similar. A special attribute, called a geometric attribute, is used when some or all of a model is comprised of lines or surfaces. In this situation, LUSAS Modeller needs to know the cross-sectional appearance and behaviour of lines, and also how thick the surfaces are. Geometric attribute assignments provide this information, and therefore form part of the model’s appearance. Models comprised entirely of volumes do not need geometric assignments. Many different tools exist within LUSAS Modeller to give interactive feedback on the nature of assigned attributes. This process is generally termed visualisation. Visualisation usually takes the form of coloured infills, arrows, textual labels or similar.

topics.title: Analyses
topics.text: Analyses Within a single model file any number of analyses may be defined. Each analysis will inherit most of the assignments, options and settings of what is called the base analysis for the model. Use of the multiple analyses facility does away with the need to create separate models, or maintain “clone” copies of a model, in order to switch between and create results from linear static analysis and other analysis types.

Use of the multiple analyses facility does away with the need to create separate models, or maintain “clone” copies of a model, in order to switch between and create results from linear static analysis and other analysis types.

topics.title: Loadcases
topics.text: Loadcases In a linear analysis, it is convenient to gather certain types of applied loading together, as for example gravity and wind loading which are applied at the same time. A loadcase is the term for such a collection of loading. Each loadcase is solved separately and the results are available separately. Results can be combined together during the results viewing stage if required. In a nonlinear analysis, LUSAS loadcases are equivalent to analysis stages. Within each loadcase, the loading, supports, or type of analysis can be changed. Control parameters can be set for each loadcase.

Results can be combined together during the results viewing stage if required. In a nonlinear analysis, LUSAS loadcases are equivalent to analysis stages. Within each loadcase, the loading, supports, or type of analysis can be changed. Control parameters can be set for each loadcase.

topics.title: Utilities
topics.text: Utilities Some kinds of analysis require or create extra data that is similar to attributes, but cannot be assigned to geometry. LUSAS Modeller refers to such data as utilities. Tendon profiles, reference paths and the settings made or entered to plot a graph or produce a report, for instance, are all examples of utilities.

topics.title: Controls
topics.text: Controls Finally, for analyses other than simple linear static, it is sometimes necessary to control the analysis process itself. LUSAS Modeller uses controls for this purpose. Controls are either nonlinear, transient, eigenvalue or fourier in nature.

LUSAS Modeller uses controls for this purpose. Controls are either nonlinear, transient, eigenvalue or fourier in nature.

topics.title: Running the Analysis
topics.text: Running the Analysis Once the modelling process is complete, the model is passed to LUSAS Solver for analysis. LUSAS Solver will then create results that are automatically loaded back into modeller for viewing and optional post-processing.
topics.search_text: Running the Analysis Using LUSAS - An overview Getting Started Guide Running the Analysis Getting Started Using LUSAS.htm Running the Analysis Once the modelling process is complete, the model is passed to LUSAS Solver for analysis. LUSAS Solver will then create results that are automatically loaded back into modeller for viewing and optional post-processing.

topics.title: Viewing the Results
topics.text: Viewing the Results Results are available to be viewed in many different ways, and the results can, if desired, be combined with attribute visualisation to make a plot, for example, that shows the applied loading and the resulting deformations. This is just a selection of some of the results facilities that are available: Deformed mesh Values of stress, displacement, reactions, etc. Inspection locations Averaged contours Unaveraged contours Wood-Armer reinforcement calculations Slicing a plane through a solid Slicing a line across a surface Yield markers Graphs Animations of the above, either through time or in response to excitation. Combinations and envelopes of results. Model reports

topics.title: Analysis Type
topics.text: Analysis Type Two analysis options are available: Coupled analysis allows for an accurate evaluation of temperature and stresses at every time step within the cure cycle. As a result it is more computationally and time demanding than the uniform cure option. Uniform cure analysis is conducted in three linear steps with the assumption that there are no temperature or cure gradients. It yields a quick solution with reasonable accuracy as long as component thickness does not exceed approximately 10 mm. See also: The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Assigning the RIHG loading attribute
topics.text: Assigning the RIHG loading attribute Following the selection of material properties in the Material Library Material Library dialog a Rate of Internal Heat Generation (RIHG) loading attribute is created in the Treeview. The internal heat attribute provides input data for the curing kinetics equation and hence controls the evolution of exothermic heat due to resin cure. This RIHG loading attribute must be assigned to all appropriate volumes or elements defining the part where the material selected forms part of the composite. The RIHG loading attribute must also be assigned to the Internal heat load curve in the thermal analysis.

headings: Assigning RIHG loading to the part
topics.text: Assigning RIHG loading to the part When defining Model Components Model Components using the HPM menu, a LUSAS group called " Part – Stage 1 " will be created in the Treeview and a group called " Part – Stage 2 " will also exist if a two stage process is to be simulated. To assign the RIHG loading select the members of a each group (by using a group's context menu) and drag and drop the RIHG loading attribute onto the selected features. It is possible that when using the Model Components Model Components dialog a part may have been further subdivided. For example, the groups “ Part – Outer skin - Stage 1 ” and “ Part – Honeycomb - Stage 1 ” may have been defined. Note that under these circumstances the RIHG loading attribute would only be assigned to the volumes in the first group, that is “ Part – Outer skin - Stage 1 ”.

topics.title: Checking the model
topics.text: Checking the model Before running an analysis it is prudent to check that the model has been defined correctly. Any features of the model not in the required group need to be added or removed as necessary. Parts of the model that have been defined as groups or subcomponents can be checked by accessing the Groups Treeview. From a group’s context menu the following commands will act on that group in the current window: Visible Makes all members of the group visible. Invisible Makes all members of the group invisible. Set as Only Visible Makes the whole model invisible and then sets all the members of the group to be visible. Advanced Visibility Enables the visibility of the higher and lower order features of the members of a group to be manipulated. Results Plots permits results to be selectively plotted for the chosen group. For details see plotting results for groups plotting results for groups in the results viewing section. Current Group Set the group to be the current group current group . Rename Enables a group to renamed. Delete Deletes the group. The group is deleted but the contents of the group are not. Select Members Adds the members of the group to the current selection. Deselect Members Removes the members of the group from the current selection. Add to Group Adds the currently selected items to the group. Remove from Group Removes the currently selected items from the group. Properties Displays a list of the member items of the group. See Manipulating Groups Manipulating Groups in the Modeller Reference Manual for more information. See also: Groups Groups The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.text: Creating a Model for use with the HPM menu Prior to using the HPM menu a suitable 'starting' model on which to apply the HPM specific modelling tasks must be created. Models for use with the HPM menu can be created in three ways: By importing a finite element mesh (created by LUSAS or by other software) By importing CAD geometry By defining a model directly in LUSAS Modeller For each method a new model file should be created in LUSAS Modeller ensuring that a Coupled Analysis type and appropriate units are selected. Import details, initial modelling and checking required for each modelling method before the HPM menu can be used are detailed here.

topics.title: Checking orientation of volume axes
toc_path: Creating a Model for use with the HPM menu
headings: Creating a Model for use with the HPM menu
topics.text: Checking orientation of volume axes For models built from imported CAD geometry the orientation of volume axes needs to be checked. The orientation of the volumes defining a part to be analysed should be such that all the z axes define a normal through the stack pointing away from the tool surface, or Part Contact Interface, ply number 1 will then reside adjacent to the tool. If the angles of ply orientations are to be defined with respect to element axes the x and y axes of the volumes should be cycled to consistent directions. Visualisation of volume axes can be done by accessing the Layers Treeview, double clicking on the Geometry layer name, and on the Properties dialog selecting Volume axes . To change the orientation of volume axes see Changing Geometry Orientation Changing Geometry Orientation in the Modeller Reference Manual for more details. Once suitable volumes have been created, a finite element mesh of quadratic hexahedral composite elements must be assigned assigned to them. Once assigned, the orientation of all element z axes will, by definition, be the same as the orientation of the volume z axes.

toc_path: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
headings: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
topics.text: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup After having defined the material properties on the Material Library Material Library dialog, and at any time before an analysis can be run, a composite layup must be defined. The composite lay-up can be created in one of three ways using the Attributes> Composites menu item: Solids and Shells Draped Solids FiberSIM Import

The composite lay-up can be created in one of three ways using the Attributes> Composites menu item: Solids and Shells Draped Solids FiberSIM Import

topics.title: Solids and Shells
toc_path: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
headings: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
topics.text: Solids and Shells This option allows a manual definition of the composite lay-up where orientations and thicknesses for the plies can be specified. The orientation angles can be applied with respect to the local element x-axis (in the x-y plane) or with respect to the x-axis of a predefined Cartesian set. The z-axis defines the direction of the lay-up with ply 1 located at the bottom of the stack. Once the composite is defined it is assigned to the volumes in the appropriate part groups as follows: Select the Treeview and right click on the group to which the material is to be assigned (e.g. “ Part - Stage 1 ”) and select the members. Click on the composite attribute just created and drag and drop the attribute into the View window. Make sure that the appropriate orientation option is selected.

topics.title: Draped Solids
toc_path: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
headings: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
topics.text: Draped Solids This option utilises the native draping functionality in LUSAS. A start point (which should lie on the drape surface) can be defined for each ply and the start direction is defined by the x-axis of a predefined Cartesian set. The orientations of fibres following the drape are computed by LUSAS and are tabulated with respect to the x-axis of the local element axes. As with the Solids and Shells option, it is essential that the z-axis of the volumes to which the composite is to be assigned are consistently oriented. Prior to assigning the composite to the appropriate part volumes, the draping surface must be specified. To achieve this: Right-click on the " Part Contact Interface " group in the Treeview and select members. Next, on the main menu, click on Edit> Selection memory> Set . The composite attribute is assigned to the appropriate volumes defining the part as described above for the Solids and Shells method. Note that this action causes a re-mesh of the model.

topics.title: FibreSIM import
toc_path: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
headings: Creating and Assigning the Composite Layup
topics.text: FibreSIM import This option reads in the composite stack details from an external xml file. The dialog prompts for the location of the file and a default fibre volume fraction can be specified. By default it is assumed that all plies are of the same thickness but this can be modified on the composite dialog. It is not necessary to select a draping surface or to define a start point when using this option. The composite attribute is assigned to the appropriate volumes defining the part in the usual manner; this action causes a re-mesh of the model. Items to note are: The coordinates of the ply data in the FiberSIM file must coincide with the coordinates of the drape surface of the part. If the tool is to be included then when the part and tool are brought into contact the tool should be moved to the part and not the part to the tool. Any xml file should only contain lay-up data relating to a single drape surface. For example, if a non-composite core is sandwiched between two composite skins then at least two xml files will be required. The volumes defining each skin must be selected in turn and the appropriate xml file assigned to it. Currently, only one element can be used in the thickness direction of the part if the lay-up is to be read from a FiberSIM file. The fibre directions can be examined as follows: Right-click on the Attributes entry in the Treeview and select Properties . On the Composite tab, click on Settings and select Visualise ply directions . The x and y axes define the warp and weft directions respectively; the item x&y displays both directions at the same time. The skew angles and fibre volume fractions can be visualised by right clicking on Contours and selecting properties in the Treeview. On the Contour results tab select the Composites (model) entity and select the composite attribute name in the right-hand panel. The fibre volume fraction and skew angle will then appear for selection in the Component combo box. See also: Composites Composites The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Cure Results
topics.text: Cure Results The Cure Results dialog can be accessed after an HPM analysis is complete to interrogate results in order to ensure that the cure kinetics and chemical shrinkage were as expected throughout the model and cure cycle. To use: Set the last structural loadcase to be the active loadcase Select a node of interest on the model Select the HPM> Cure Results menu item. Annotated graphs of the following can be created for the selected node: Degree of cure v Time Resin state v Time Glass transition temperature v Time Chemical shrinkage v Time Temperature rise v Time Resin state v Degree of cure Glass transition temperature v Degree of cure Chemical shrinkage v Degree of cure Example cure graph See also: The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Defining a Part Contact Interface
topics.text: Defining a Part Contact Interface Surfaces or element faces that define a Part Contact Interface need to be added to the Group of that name. This is done by selecting the required surface or element faces in the Graphics Area, then accessing the Groups Treeview and from the relevant group's context menu select Add to Group. Selecting surfaces or element faces can be done by: Selecting each surface or face that define the interface Using the Select Coplanar Neighbours facility Using a combination of the two above methods

topics.title: Selecting Coplanar Neighbours
topics.text: Selecting Coplanar Neighbours Selecting coplanar neighbours provides a quick way to select a number of surfaces or element faces according to their alignment in relation to a selected surface or element face. When a Part Contact Interface needs to be defined it is possible to select one element face that is known to lie on the interface between the part and the tool and then set an angular tolerance that will additionally select all surfaces or element faces where the angle between the normals of adjacent surfaces or elements lie within that tolerance. To use, select a surface or element face and use its context menu to select the Select Coplanar Neighbours menu item Specify an Angular tolerance to limit the number of faces selected. The option to Ignore internal faces helps to ensure that when an element has faces that both lie within the angular tolerance, only the external face is selected. See also: Model Components Model Components The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Export Tool Surface
topics.text: Export Tool Surface On a successful completion of an HPM analysis the deformed shape of the part should be inspected and accepted as reasonable prior to exporting the tool surface data. See Viewing Results Viewing Results for more details. If satisfied that the results obtained are reasonable, select the HPM> Export Tool Surface menu item to export an IGES file that will contain the surfaces required to define a compensated tool surface. The surfaces exported will be the element faces stored in the "Part Contact Interface" group. The position/orientation of the surfaces exported will define the theoretically predicted shape for a compensated tool surface in order to produce a part of nominal shape. Note. The surface exported in the IGES file will be faceted and it will ultimately be necessary to create a “best fit” surface through these facets. See also: The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Freestanding Surface
topics.text: Freestanding Surface The Freestanding Surface dialog allows the ambient conditions for the part surface to be defined upon its release from the tool. Choices of natural and forced convection are available but a convection coefficient can also be explicitly defined (using units of W/m2 C for SI units). It is possible to include radiation losses if required and for this the coefficient also has units of W/m2 C.

topics.title: HPM Group names explained
topics.text: HPM Group names explained HPM Model Components and Process Controls dialogs create named groups Part Contact Interface is a LUSAS group that must contain the part surfaces that are in contact with the tool. Part - Stage 1 (or Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 1 ) are LUSAS groups that must contain volumes (or elements if a mesh is being used) that define subcomponents of the part. Collectively all the subcomponents define the part component for stage 1. Part - Stage 2 (or Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 2) are LUSAS groups that must contain volumes (or elements if a mesh is being used) that define subcomponents of the part. Collectively all the subcomponents define the component of the part that is added for stage 2. Part Freestanding Surface is a LUSAS group that must contain the external surfaces of the part upon release from the tool and also for a freestanding post cure. Note that the external surface of the part is defined by the appropriate external surfaces of the volumes (or element faces) contained in the Part - Stage 1 (and Part - Stage 2, if present ) gr oups. Note that the external surfaces of the volumes, or the external faces of the elements described are used to populate this group automatically. Part-Bag Interface – Stage 1 is a LUSAS group that must contain part surfaces (or element faces) defining the interface between the part and vacuum bag for stage 1. Note that this group is populated automatically with the external surfaces (or element faces) of the Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 1 group(s) minus the surfaces (or element faces) contained in the Part Contact Interface group. Part-Bag Interface – Stage 2 is a LUSAS group that must contain part surfaces (or element faces) defining the interface between the part and vacuum bag for stage 2. Note that this group is populated automatically with the external surfaces (or element faces) of the Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 1 and Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 2 groups minus the surfaces (or element faces) contained in the Part Contact Interface group. topics.title: Overview of LUSAS HPM Software
topics.text: Overview of LUSAS HPM Software LUSAS High Precision Moulding (HPM) software can accurately predict the deformations that occur when thermoset composites are used in hot cure manufacturing processes. Knowledge of the distorted shape of the part can be used to compensate the tool so that a part of the desired shape is produced. The software offers the options to simulate autoclave and closed tool processes and a database of input data for commonly used resins and fibres is provided. For autoclave simulations, both one and two shot cures are available. The curing process is simulated in LUSAS via a thermo-mechanically coupled analysis that takes into account thermal expansion effects and shrinkage of the resin. Potential causes of post-cure deformations in composite production

topics.title: Modelling
topics.text: Modelling Data defining the geometry of the composite part and tool is first imported into LUSAS in either IGES or STEP format. Once in, the HPM user interface (which has been designed in collaboration with composite manufacturers), allows tooling engineers to define all aspects of composite layup and cure simulation modelling. High-performance linear and nonlinear elements are assigned to the model along with boundary conditions, material properties and layup orientation. Temperature profiles and analysis controls must also be specified.
topics.search_text: Modelling The HPM menu Overview of LUSAS HPM Software Modelling HPM HPM overview.htm Modelling Data defining the geometry of the composite part and tool is first imported into LUSAS in either IGES or STEP format. Once in, the HPM user interface (which has been designed in collaboration with composite manufacturers), allows tooling engineers to define all aspects of composite layup and cure simulation modelling. High-performance linear and nonlinear elements are assigned to the model along with boundary conditions, material properties and layup orientation. Temperature profiles and analysis controls must also be specified.

topics.title: Analysis
topics.text: Analysis Once a complete and correctly defined model has been created a coupled thermal-mechanical analysis is carried out in LUSAS to model the thermal curing and calculate residual stresses. The temperature and degree of cure throughout the manufacturing process caused by the internal heat generation during cure is calculated using a transient thermal analysis. This data is then passed to a transient nonlinear stress analysis to compute the deformations due to temperature change and chemical shrinkage.

This data is then passed to a transient nonlinear stress analysis to compute the deformations due to temperature change and chemical shrinkage.

topics.title: Results
topics.text: Results Results are viewed in LUSAS where displacements from the stress analysis can be factored to provide updated tool geometry. The revised tooling geometry calculated by the LUSAS HPM software can be exported in IGES format for use directly in the CNC tool cutting environment and will, in turn, produce a part that will cure into the correct shape for intended assembly purposes. topics.title: Benefits of use
topics.text: Benefits of use By using LUSAS HPM software in the design process competent design engineers can extract master model and tooling surfaces “right first time” ensuring that correctly sized post-cure components are obtained without iterative guesswork. As a result the product development cycle is significantly improved. See also: The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Material Library
topics.text: Material Library The HPM material library dialog permits fibre and resin types to be selected. Key properties for selected fibre and resin types are displayed to right of the dialog. Fabric properties must be specified and once defined the lamina properties for the composite can be predicted via the application of micro-mechanics formulae. For this it is essential that the fabric type , fibre volume fraction , the areal density , and the warp count and fill count are entered. Note that for the fabric type of 'UD tape' only the fibre volume fraction is required. The lamina properties for Glassy and Rubbery phases can be inspected by clicking on the Lamina properties... button. The material Name is automatically generated from the chosen fibre and resin types. This name can be manually changed if desired.

topics.title: Model Components
topics.text: Model Components For an HPM analysis, model geometry (or a model mesh) must be grouped together and named according to its purpose. For instance, all the volumes (or elements) of the model that define the part must be present in a group named Part Stage 1, and all the surfaces (or element faces) that define the interface between the part and the tool must be present in a group named Part Contact Interface. If a part consists of more than one material type then a group named Part Stage 2 would be created. Based upon selections previously made on the Process type Process type dialog, the Model Components dialog allows optional user-defined subcomponent names to be specfied for the part and creates groups of pre-defined names in the Groups Treeview. If no user-defined subcomponent names are entered then default group names are used when the OK button is selected. Note that Groups created by the Model Components dialog must not be renamed because the HPM analysis is based upon the expected pre-defined names. Subcomponent names are only really necessary if the part consists of more than one material type. If different materials need to be assigned to different sections of the part then creating groups of volumes that subdivide the part helps to organise the assignment process.

topics.title: Model Summary
topics.text: Model Summary The Model Summary dialog allows reference data, key properties and model history to be entered and stored with the model. The Reference tab permits data to be manually entered and stored with the model. The Key Properties fields, displayed on the second tab, are not accessible and this data is extracted directly from the model. The Model History tab contains two fields, the first displays the history to date and is inaccessible, and the second field allows details of any new changes made to the model to be logged so that they can be appended to the model history. Options are provided to write the summary to a Word file and/or to annotate the summary on the screen. If the summary is written to a Word file an isometric view of the mesh will also be included in the document. See also: The HPM menu The HPM menu

topics.title: Process Controls
topics.text: Process Controls Prior to using this dialog the features of the model that define the Part Contact Interface and the Part must have been added to the appropriate groups in the Treeview The Process Controls dialog sets up the time/temperature profiles for the cure and any post-cure along with the analysis control chapters required to simulate the cure process. A single stage process ("one shot") that includes a post-cure is essentially split into three phases: the cure phase, the tool release phase and the post-cure phase. The dialog allows the time - temperature profile to be entered for both a cure and post cure, where the time for each profile should start from zero, and the temperature is specified in degrees Celsius. A selection of predefined cure profiles is available and additional profiles can be entered, named and stored for future use by clicking on the New button. The profile entered or selected can be viewed in graphical form by clicking on the Visualise combined profile Visualise combined profile button. The radio buttons offering the choice of when to remove the part from the tool are only enabled if a post-cure is selected. If a two stage cure ("two shot") has been specified on the Process Type Process Type dialog, two tabs will appear on this dialog, one for each stage. The time step to be used in the analysis is also specified on this dialog. A reasonable value to enter for a time step is 10 minutes. Note that this would be entered as 600 seconds. After making selections, clicking OK will add groups, attributes and loadcase controls to the respective Treeviews and make a number of assignments as described below.

A single stage process ("one shot") that includes a post-cure is essentially split into three phases: the cure phase, the tool release phase and the post-cure phase. The dialog allows the time - temperature profile to be entered for both a cure and post cure, where the time for each profile should start from zero, and the temperature is specified in degrees Celsius. A selection of predefined cure profiles is available and additional profiles can be entered, named and stored for future use by clicking on the New button. The profile entered or selected can be viewed in graphical form by clicking on the Visualise combined profile Visualise combined profile button. The radio buttons offering the choice of when to remove the part from the tool are only enabled if a post-cure is selected. If a two stage cure ("two shot") has been specified on the Process Type Process Type dialog, two tabs will appear on this dialog, one for each stage. The time step to be used in the analysis is also specified on this dialog. A reasonable value to enter for a time step is 10 minutes. Note that this would be entered as 600 seconds. After making selections, clicking OK will add groups, attributes and loadcase controls to the respective Treeviews and make a number of assignments as described below.

headings: Group names created by the Process Controls dialog
topics.text: Group names created by the Process Controls dialog Groups created by the Process Controls dialog are populated automatically with appropriate features from the Part Contact Interface and Part - Stage 1 groups. Part Freestanding Surface is a LUSAS group that must contain the external surfaces of the part upon release from the tool and also for a freestanding post cure. Note that the external surface of the part is defined by the appropriate external surfaces of the volumes (or element faces) contained in the Part - Stage 1 (and Part - Stage 2, if present) groups. Note that the external surfaces of the volumes (or the external faces of the elements) described are used to populate this group automatically. Part-Bag Interface – Stage 1 is a LUSAS group that must contain part surfaces (or element faces) defining the interface between the part and vacuum bag for stage 1. Note that this group is populated automatically with the external surfaces (or element faces) of the Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 1 group(s) minus the surfaces (or element faces) contained in the Part Contact Interface group. Part-Bag Interface – Stage 2 is a LUSAS group that must contain part surfaces (or element faces) defining the interface between the part and vacuum bag for stage 2. Note that this group is populated automatically with the external surfaces (or element faces) of the Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 1 and Part - <Subcomponent name> - Stage 2 groups minus the surfaces (or element faces) contained in the Part Contact Interface group. If subcomponent names are optionally entered on the Model Components dialog to describe particular subcomponents of the part or tool the Part group names become: Part-Bag <Subcomponent name> Interface - Stage 1 Part-Bag <Subcomponent name> Interface - Stage 2

topics.title: Changes made to the Attributes Treeview (Coupled Analysis)
toc_path: Changes made to the Attributes Treeview (Coupled Analysis)
headings: Changes made to the Attributes Treeview (Coupled Analysis)
topics.text: Changes made to the Attributes Treeview (Coupled Analysis) As a result of data being entered on the Process Controls dialog, various attributes are also automatically added to the Treeview. For a coupled analysis, an environmental temperature load attribute named “ Tool surface temperature ” is added. This defines the heat transfer coefficient to be applied between the part and tool. This attribute is automatically assigned to the surfaces in the group named “ Part Contact Interface ” and to the load curve “ Cure phase temperature ” that can be seen in the Analyses Treeview. This attribute could also be assigned to other load curves depending on: when the part is to be removed from the tool, if a post-cure is required if a one or two stage cure process is being simulated. A support attribute named “ Normal restraint ” is added to the Treeview and is automatically assigned to the surfaces in the group “ Part Contact Interface ”. This provides a rigid normal support on the face of the part that comes into contact with the tool. To simulate removal of the part from the tool these restraints are subsequently removed after cure or post-cure depending on the selection made on the Process Controls dialog. To this end, an attribute “ Remove normal restraint ” is also added to the Treeview and this is automatically assigned to the “ Release part from tool ” loadcase control chapter in the Analyses Treeview. Note that to prevent unrestrained rigid body movement soft springs in each global direction are automatically assigned to three nodes on the mesh of the part in the structural analysis.

topics.title: HPM menu order
topics.text: HPM menu order On the HPM menu, it is important to remember that the menu items are listed in the order in which they should be used to correctly define a model, view results and ultimately export a tool surface. For example, the Analysis type menu item should be selected before Process type and so on. Some menu items are initially greyed-out because the specification of properties on some dialogs dictates the set-up and options available on subsequent dialogs. Definition of data required by a preceding menu item will make the greyed-out menu items become available. A suitable model must be created before the HPM menu can be used. See Creating a model for use with the HPM menu Creating a model for use with the HPM menu for details Note also that following the selection of the Material Library menu item and the subsequent defining of material properties, two additional tasks need to be carried out before an analysis can be run. These are: Assigning a Rate of Internal Heat Generation loading attribute Assigning a Rate of Internal Heat Generation loading attribute Creating and assigning the composite layup Creating and assigning the composite layup These tasks can be carried out at any time after the material properties have been defined. Once a suitable model has been created it can then be analysed and the results viewed. See also: Overview of LUSAS HPM Software Overview of LUSAS HPM Software

topics.title: Vacuum Bag
topics.text: Vacuum Bag If an autoclave process is to be simulated this dialog permits the properties of the vacuum bag to be included in the thermal analysis. For closed tool simulations this dialog is inaccessible. Vacuum bag, peel ply and breather cloth thickness can be entered and the type of ambient conditions defined as either forced or natural convection. Based on the input data a convective heat coefficient for the vacuum bag is computed and displayed in the lower text field of the dialog. The vacuum bag heat transfer coefficient should typically be between 10 and 60 (in W/m2 C for SI units). This value can be overwritten by clicking the Specify option allowing the coefficient to be explicitly defined.

By selecting Show values of selection on the Values Display tab only those values for nodes subsequently selected by cursor will be displayed.

topics.title: LNG Tank Analysis and Design System
toc_path: LNG Tank Analysis and Design System
headings: LNG Tank Analysis and Design System
topics.text: LNG Tank Analysis and Design System The LUSAS LNG Tank Analysis and Design System is a licensed software product that allows engineers to automatically create a range of 2D and 3D finite element models of full containment circular tanks from user-defined parameters. Using these models, a range of analyses can be performed and design checks can be optionally carried out for specified load combinations and supported design codes. The use of the LNG Tank Wizards require the MicroSoft Excel spreadsheet application to be installed in advance for full functionality as certain applications of the wizards may use it during the design or reporting process. For example, the Wizard for a Seismic Analysis produces a computation summary and the forces calculated can be exported to a spreadsheet.

topics.search_text: LNG Tank Analysis and Design System LNG Tank Analysis and Design System LNG Tank Analysis and Design System LNG tank index.htm LNG Tank Analysis and Design System The LUSAS LNG Tank Analysis and Design System is a licensed software product that allows engineers to automatically create a range of 2D and 3D finite element models of full containment circular tanks from user-defined parameters. Using these models, a range of analyses can be performed and design checks can be optionally carried out for specified load combinations and supported design codes. The use of the LNG Tank Wizards require the MicroSoft Excel spreadsheet application to be installed in advance for full functionality as certain applications of the wizards may use it during the design or reporting process. For example, the Wizard for a Seismic Analysis produces a computation summary and the forces calculated can be exported to a spreadsheet.

topics.title: New Facilities and Improvements in Version 17.0
toc_path: New Facilities and Improvements in Version 17.0
headings: New Facilities and Improvements in Version 17.0
topics.text: New Facilities and Improvements in Version 17.0 Version 17.0 of LUSAS sees steel frame design checking and vehicle load optimisation capabilities extended, prestress enhancements, additional creep and shrinkage models, and new facilities for soil-structure interaction modelling. New attribute viewing and editing features simplify the management and editing of assignments, improving general usability and enabling faster editing. The Steel Frame Design option now supports EN1993-2: 2006 Eurocode 3: Design of steel structures - Part 2: Steel Bridges. Steel frame design to EN1993-1-1: 2005+A1:2014 has been enhanced to include Class 4 sections and to support shear buckling of I-sections. The implementation for AASHTO LRFD 7th Edition has been updated to allow user-defined input of buckling properties. Vehicle load optimisation has been extended to include Finland's LO 24/2014 design code, Norway's NS-EN 1991-2.2003 NA 2010 + NA-rundskriv 07-2015, and the UK's BD21/01 Annexes D and E. Prestress modelling has been re-structured and sees the single tendon and multiple tendon prestress wizards, which were used to generate prestress loading, retired. Instead, a tendon loading attribute, which references tendon profile and tendon property data, can be directly assigned to selected line, surface or volume features in a model, consistent with all other attribute assignments made within LUSAS. New tendon loading assignment options state how the tendon loading is to be applied and, for assignment to lines, mapping and offset options can be used, as well as specifying in which loadcase(s) the tendon loading should apply. Prestress loading is now calculated as a function of solving a model. Prestress data can now be included in a model report by adding a prestress chapter. Graphs showing prestress losses in tendons are now produced using the graph wizard. Editing of tendon loading, property and profile data has been improved and can be done by individual selection of one or more attributes, or by selection of the parent folder containing a set of attributes. New material models include Creep and shrinkage for AASHTO LRFD 7th edition, IRC:112-2011, a Duncan-Chang soil material model, and a joint material model that allows definition of symmetrical matrix properties - useful for specifying a joint representing a pilecap sitting on a group of piles in a global (3D) model. Initial stresses in soil can now be calculated by providing Ko data for the supported material models that are used in soil analyses. Modelling of the variation of material properties at any location in a model can now be achieved by defining a profile variation. Typical uses include modelling of varying soil properties with depth, as obtained by borehole data Section property calculation of a range of riveted or welded section types is now provided in Bridge and Civil & Structural software products. Sections can be defined with reference to sections held in the main section library or from user-defined values. Indian and New Zealand steel sections have been added to the steel section library. Target values for stress and strain can now be stated such that a specified value for a selected results component for a feature will be obtained exactly when a solve has taken place. This facility is primarily for use when a specified jacking force is required to be applied to one end of a line representing a cable. Editing of attribute assignments is simplified by the new Assignments editor, which allows simultaneous viewing, editing and management of any number of attribute assignments, and is of particular use in editing tendon profile and property assignments. A new Attributes editor similarly enables easier viewing and editing of loading data for a range of structural load types, and is of particular use when editing tendon loading values when carrying out prestress modelling. For selections made in the View window, the Properties dialog has been replaced with a new Properties panel, which allows for changing the properties of any number of concurrently selected features/objects, and permits assigning or deassigning attributes to and from those items. A new Hierarchy panel lists the higher and lower order features/objects of the currently selected geometry feature or mesh object.

headings: Prestress modelling restructured and easier to use
topics.text: Prestress modelling restructured and easier to use The single tendon and multiple tendon prestress wizards that in previous versions were used to generate prestress loading have been retired. Instead, a tendon loading tendon loading attribute, which references tendon profile tendon profile and tendon property tendon property data, is defined having a specified prestress force and associated jacking and loss details. Once defined, this tendon loading attribute is added to the Attributes Treeview, where it can be directly assigned to selected line, surface or volume features in a model consistently with all other attribute assignments made within LUSAS. Tendon loading assignment Tendon loading assignment options state how the tendon loading is to be applied and, for assignment to lines, mapping and offset options can be used, as well as specifying in which loadcase(s) the tendon loading should apply. Tendon loading attribute dialog Tendon loading attribute assignment dialog

topics.title: Other improvements
toc_path: Prestress modelling restructured and easier to use
headings: Prestress modelling restructured and easier to use
topics.text: Other improvements Prestress loading is now calculated as a part of solving a model. When solved, LUSAS still calculates equivalent nodal loading from the assigned prestress tendon loads and assigns these forces automatically to selected features (and hence nodes and elements) of the model for a specified loadcase. The discrete loads and the applied forces / moments calculated are not created as attributes in the treeview but can be reproduced / viewed for checking purposes. See viewing prestress loading data. viewing prestress loading data. The properties, profile, loading, losses and setting-out data for all tendons defined and assigned in a model can now be reported upon by adding a prestress chapter prestress chapter to a model report. Graphs showing prestress losses in tendons are now produced using the graph wizard graph wizard . Editing of tendon loading, property and profile data has been improved and can be done by individual selection of one or more attributes, or by selection of the parent folder containing a set of attributes. See Viewing and Editing of Multiple Attribute Assignments Viewing and Editing of Multiple Attribute Assignments and Viewing and Editing of Multiple Load Attributes Viewing and Editing of Multiple Load Attributes .

toc_path: Prestress loading now supported by plain stress, plane strain, shell and solid elements
headings: Prestress loading now supported by plain stress, plane strain, shell and solid elements
topics.text: Prestress loading now supported by plain stress, plane strain, shell and solid elements The prestress loading capability has been extended to allow assignment to surfaces modelled with plane stress, plane strain and shell elements, and volumes modelled with solid elements. Assignment of tendon loads to a surface or volume modelled with these elements requires a tendon profile to be defined using 'Global coordinates' on the Tendon Profile dialog. The defined tendon length is used and the tendon is positioned in the model at the start coordinate specified within the tendon profile dataset. For more information see Defining a Tendon Profile Defining a Tendon Profile and Tendon Loading Assignment (Multi-tendon) Tendon Loading Assignment (Multi-tendon)

topics.title: AASHTO LRFD 7th edition creep and shrinkage material model added
toc_path: AASHTO LRFD 7th edition creep and shrinkage material model added
headings: AASHTO LRFD 7th edition creep and shrinkage material model added
topics.text: AASHTO LRFD 7th edition creep and shrinkage material model added The AASHTO LRFD 7th edition creep and shrinkage model can be used with beam elements, 2D/3D continuum elements, semi-loof and thick shells, and composite solid elements. AASHTO creep and shrinkage is only strictly applicable to beams, however, in LUSAS the creep equations have been extended to 2D and 3D stress states. The assumptions made in the derivation of this extension can be found in the LUSAS Theory Manual. Creep loss can be calculated with reference to either article 5.4.2.3.2 or the commentary clause C5.4.2.3.2-2. Shrinkage loss can be calculated with reference to equation 5.4.2.3.2-2 or the commentary clause C5.4.2.3.2-2 For more information see Concrete Creep and Shrinkage to AASHTO LRFD 7th Edition Concrete Creep and Shrinkage to AASHTO LRFD 7th Edition

topics.text: IRC112-2011 creep and shrinkage material model added The IRC:112-2011 creep and shrinkage model can be used with beam elements, 2/3D continuum elements, semi-loof and thick shells, and composite solid elements. IRC:112-2011 creep and shrinkage is only strictly applicable to beams, however, in LUSAS the creep equations have been extended to 2D and 3D stress states. Creep calculations are carried out to IRC:112-2011 clause 6.4.2.7 and Annexure A2, but elevated or reduced temperatures during curing are not considered. topics.title: Duncan-Chang soil material model added
topics.text: Duncan-Chang soil material model added The Duncan-Chang soil material model is a simple model whose parameters are calculated by curve fitting triaxial test data over a range of cell pressures. It takes an incremental elastic approach in which Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio are evaluated from current stresses. A predictor step is used to determine whether the soil is loading or unloading, following which, corresponding values of Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio are calculated for use in the incremental elastic modulus matrix. The model can be used with standard continuum elements as well as the two-phase elements. The modelling parameters required can be evaluated in standard laboratory tests. For more information see Duncan-Chang Model Duncan-Chang Model

topics.title: Initialisation of ground conditions (K 0 )
topics.text: Initialisation of ground conditions (K 0 ) K 0 data can now be defined for material models used in soil analyses, principally, elastic models, Modified Mohr-Coulomb Modified Mohr-Coulomb , Duncan-Chang Duncan-Chang and Modified Cam-clay Modified Cam-clay . Both the Duncan-Chang and Modified Cam-clay models need the definition of an initial stress state to calculate an initial stiffness. The initial stresses in the soil can be calculated by providing K 0 data. On element activation, the effective vertical stresses in the soil are calculated from the soil weight and any additional loads such as overburden. Horizontal stresses are then calculated using the K 0 value. For more information see K 0 Initialisation K 0 Initialisation

topics.title: Profile variations
topics.text: Profile variations Modelling of the variation of material properties at any location in a model can now be achieved by defining a profile variation. These are defined by selecting the Utilities > Variation menu item. A typical use is modelling the variation of soil properties with depth, as obtained by borehole data. A single profile variation is defined by sets of values against distance, but any number of profile lines in-plane or out-of-plane may be grouped to form a profile set variation. When used to define particular material properties in a supported material model, material properties for elements in any region of a model can be calculated by LUSAS by interpolating between the distance and values defined for each element between each profile variation location. When used to define particular material properties in a supported material model, material properties for elements in any region of a model are calculated by LUSAS Modeller by interpolating between the distance and values defined for each element between each profile variation location. The following images show how properties are calculated with respect to the profile variation types shown. Single profile variation (Variation with depth only) In-plane set of two (or more) profile variations (Variation with depth interpolated in-plane only) In-plane set of profile variations in a 3D model (Variation with depth is only interpolated in the plane of the profile set) Out-of-plane set of profile variations in a 3D model (Variation with depth is interpolated in 3 dimensions) For more information see Profile Variation Profile Variation

topics.text: Stress and strain target values (for cables) Stress and Strain loading has been enhanced to include a Target option. This is used to define a value for a selected results component for a feature that will be obtained exactly when a solve has taken place. This facility is primarily for use when a specified jacking force is required to be applied to one end of a line representing a cable. Note that target values are only appropriate for linear materials. For more information see Structural Loads Structural Loads

topics.title: New Properties panel

It allows for changing the properties of selected features/objects and for assigning or deassigning attributes to and from those items. Unlike the Properties dialog that it replaces, the new facility allows modification of any number of features at the same time. For more information see Properties panel Properties panel
